items.title: How it works
items.text: Conference programs are long. KubeCon has more than 500 sessions, and an IETF meeting has a large agenda spread across many working groups. This site keeps the few items that matter to one reader: a product manager who works on networking, cloud platforms, Kubernetes, and AI.

items.title: Which conferences are tracked?
items.text:
The Conferences page is the live tracker. It lists every registered edition, its end date, and whether its digest is upcoming, waiting, in progress, or published. The current conference families are:

  • Network operators, Internet governance, and vendors: APRICOT; ARIN; AusNOG; AutoCon; Capacity Europe; Cisco Live Europe and US; DENOG; DKNOG; GRNOG; ITNOG; LACNIC; MORE-IP; NANOG; Netnod Tech Meeting; NetUK; NLNOG; nog.fi; NZNOG; Open vSwitch and OVN Fall Conference; Peering Days; RIPE; SwiNOG; TNC; and ZANOG@iWeek.
  • Research, standards, and security: ACM CCS, CoNEXT, IMC, and SIGCOMM; hack.lu; IETF; Netdev; NSDI; PETS; SREcon Americas; and USENIX Security.
  • Cloud, AI, and open infrastructure: CfgMgmtCamp Ghent; FOSDEM; KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe and North America; MLSys; NVIDIA GTC; OCP Global Summit; OPI Summit on DPUs/IPUs; and PyTorch Conference.

This list mixes recurring series configured for automatic discovery with individually registered editions. The tracker is generated from the registry, so it includes upcoming editions as well as those with published digests.

items.title: The pipeline
items.text:
flowchart LR
  S["Series rules and edition registry"] --> D["Discover editions and fetch programs"]
  D --> P["Committed digest prompt and tracking issue"]
  P --> T["Nebius Token Factory: shortlist, select, write"]
  T --> C["Validate, add links and search tags"]
  C --> R["Digest pull request"]
  R -->|A person merges| W["Published site"]
  W --> L["Daily links refresh"]
  L --> Q["Links pull request"]

items.title: 1. Discover new editions automatically
items.text:
A scheduled scan runs every Monday, with a manual workflow dispatch available when needed. Discovery reads conferences/series.yaml, which describes each recurring conference, and conferences/registry.yaml, which contains the editions already tracked.

For each series, discovery:

  1. Reads the latest matching registry key to work out where the series is up to. Series are enumerated by calendar year (for example, sigcomm-{year}) or by an ordinal (for example, ietf-{n} or Netdev's hexadecimal edition number).
  2. Fills the series' key, name, and URL templates to construct the next candidates. Existing entries are never edited or replaced.
  3. Asks the conference's fetcher to probe the source to confirm that the edition really exists and, where available, read its dates.
  4. Runs the real fetch as a second gate for most sources. The edition is added only when a usable program is available, not when the site merely contains a placeholder or call for papers. IETF is the exception: its datatracker meeting API is authoritative, so its probe is sufficient.

A confirmed edition is appended to the registry with its fetcher and source URLs. Dates stated by the source win; otherwise the series can supply an estimated end date, which is marked for human confirmation. Discovery re-parses the registry after writing and rolls back an invalid result. If nothing is published yet, the candidate is simply probed again on a later scan.

Sources that block cloud runners are not probed from CI; their discovery and fetch run locally. One-off editions, or editions a series rule cannot derive, can be added to the registry by hand.

Registration does not immediately trigger writing. The normal fetch gate is the event has ended and no digests/<key>.md exists. A newly discovered past edition can continue through the same scan; an upcoming edition waits.

items.title: 2. Fetch the program and generate the prompt
items.text:
Each source has a fetcher that extracts program items with their titles, speakers or authors, abstracts when published, and material links such as page:, pdf:, slides:, video:, and materials:. A fetcher reports a real program, not yet published, or manual fallback; one broken source does not stop the scan. Waiting and failed editions are retried, and repeated failures eventually surface as Fetcher stalled rather than producing a digest from bad input.

For a successful fetch, code composes prompts/<key>.md from:

  • a run note naming the exact digest file to produce;
  • the shared template in conferences/prompt/base.md;
  • the conference name, source URL, registry key, and date;
  • the controlled search-tag vocabulary; and
  • the fetched program text itself.

The prompt is the bot's job specification and source material, not just a wrapper around the program. It defines the reader's interests, the Core / Adjacent / Wildcard selection rules, and the preference for novel techniques, substantiated results, and transferable operational lessons over vendor pitches. It also requires exact program titles, a consistent Why / What / How / Where-applicable write-up, a Themes section, and search keywords. Grounding rules tell the writer to read linked papers or pages on a best-effort basis, never invent missing findings, and mark write-ups based only on an abstract.

The generated prompt is committed and becomes the input to the drafting workflow. The scan also opens or updates that edition's tracking issue. Keeping the prompt in the repository makes the run reproducible and provides the manual path: a blocked program can be pasted below the prompt's PROGRAM TEXT separator, and a person can run the same prompt outside the bot.

items.title: 3. Draft with Nebius Token Factory
items.text:
The drafting workflow runs after a scan, after a prompt is pushed, or on manual dispatch. Its normal queue contains committed prompts that do not yet have a digest or an open digest PR; a forced run can rewrite one conference and update its PR.

Nebius Token Factory is the inference engine for all model work, using the configured zai-org/GLM-5.3 model. For large programs, it shortlists batches in parallel, narrows the shortlist to the final selections, and writes the digest from those items. The drafting workflow can enrich selected items from their linked papers, slides, and talk pages; enrichment deepens the write-up but does not change selection or tier.

The workflow returns the draft for automated validation and pull-request review; the model does not push to this repository. Discovering editions, fetching programs, building links rows, and publishing the site remain code and workflow steps, not model work. The same committed prompt can also be run by hand without using this bot path.

items.title: 4. Validate the draft and build every links row
items.text:
Code performs the final mechanical checks. Automated checks reduce links absent from the program text to plain text and flag pick headings that match no program item. The proposal step validates the artifact and metadata, normalizes the conference title, extracts the writer's keywords into conferences/tags.yaml, and builds the site before proposing the change.

For every pick, conferences/links.py builds a **Links:** row when at least one usable link exists; the model never writes the row. Slides and YouTube recordings are resolved in this order:

  1. Use the program item's own links. Fetchers preserve the talk or paper page and any paper, slide, recording, or materials URL published in the program. A deck available in two formats keeps both, for example Slides (PDF) and Slides (PPTX).
  2. Read the talk page again. After an event, pages often gain an embedded recording or attachments. The parser recognizes YouTube embeds and unambiguous watch links, and classifies PDF and presentation-file links from their URLs and link text. When a page blocks the runner, an approved Tavily Extract fallback can read it.
  3. Use reviewed stream offsets where configured. A pick can link to its exact start in a whole-day recording when that offset was previously checked against the stream's transcript.
  4. Search only if the recording is still missing. A known official conference channel is searched first, then general YouTube search, with Tavily search as a fallback when YouTube cannot be reached. A candidate is accepted only after checks against the talk title, the conference or channel, and an event-relative upload window; official-channel uploads may use a shortened title, and very short videos are rejected. An uncertain candidate gets no link.

Before a row is published, file links and videos are probed again. Confirmed dead links are dropped; an unreachable or inconclusive check does not erase a previously found link. This is deliberately a “no link rather than a wrong link” policy.

items.title: 5. Review, publish, and refresh
items.text:
The proposal job opens one digest: <key> pull request containing the digest and its search tags. A person reviews and merges it. The merged digests/<key>.md file is the only signal that an edition is done; it also closes the tracking issue and triggers site publication.

Slides and recordings often arrive after the digest. Every day, Links Refresh reruns the same deterministic link builder for digests whose events ended in the last 120 days. It rechecks talk pages, searches for missing recordings, and removes links confirmed dead. If anything changed, it opens a separate links: <key> PR; the write-ups are not rewritten. Older editions can be refreshed through manual workflow dispatch.

items.title: Search
items.text: Digest and talk pages carry topic keywords when the writer's keywords block validates. The writer chooses them from a controlled vocabulary covering the reader's areas, including BGP, AI clusters, optics, Kubernetes, and cloud. The pipeline stores them as hand-editable repository metadata, and the site's search indexes them like a page title. Searching for a topic such as ebpf or Kubernetes can therefore find a relevant talk even when that word is absent from its title. Talk pages also show their tags as clickable chips; each tag opens a page listing every picked talk with that tag, grouped by conference.

items.title: Reading a digest
items.text:
Tier Meaning Core Directly about networking, cloud, Kubernetes, or AI. Adjacent Relevant to the broader field: useful context, or likely to matter soon. Wildcard Two to four items outside these interests that are novel or show where the field is going. Themes The patterns across the whole program.

Each pick starts with its available links: Abstract (the talk or paper page, which usually lists every material), Paper, Slides, and Recording. A talk recording also shows a thumbnail: click it to play the talk on the page. For IETF drafts the links are the Draft, its Slides, the Session recording of the working group meeting, and the session Materials.

Each pick has the same parts. Why tells you why it is worth your time. What gives the contribution in plain terms, and How gives the mechanism. Where applicable tells you whether the work is general or specific to one organization, vendor, or deployment. A write-up marked from abstract only had no fuller source available. A missing link means none was published or verified at the last link run; a later refresh can add it.

items.title: Conference status
items.text:
The Conferences page shows where each edition stands:

Status Meaning Read the digest The digest is published. Digest in progress The program is fetched, and a digest is being written or reviewed. Waiting for the program The event ended, but its program is not published yet. The fetch runs again each week. Needs a local fetch The site blocks cloud IP addresses, so the fetch must run from a laptop. Needs a manual paste Automatic fetch failed. Someone must paste the program in. Fetcher stalled Fetch failed four times. The site probably changed, and the fetcher needs a fix. Queued The event ended, but the work item has not been fetched yet. Upcoming The event has not ended yet.

The source, the prompts, and every digest are in hellt/conference-digest.

items.title: Compute Exchange
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Carmen Li (Compute Exchange / Silicon Data, CEO)

Video

  • Why: Completes the compute-market arc with the two concrete artifacts a capacity planner can use today: a neutral RFQ marketplace for reserved/forward GPU capacity, and observed term structures with implied forward curves.
  • What: Compute Exchange is a deliberately inventory-free marketplace (100+ verified providers, 80,000+ GPUs claimed in supply, ex-China, 24-hour RFQ turnaround, verification of UIDs/inventory/benchmarks for existing capacity and purchase orders/permits for forward capacity; KYB/KYC on buyers). It covers three layers: reserved GPU (one node / one month minimum), forward contracts on GPUs and tokens (a "token forward" reserves a dedicated model deployment with fixed quantization and SLA), and a secondary hardware market — where scarce gear has traded above MSRP (her COVID-used-car analogy). Silicon Data provides the indices CME will settle compute futures on (H100 neocloud on-demand rate, B200), with actual settlement announced as weeks away at talk time.
  • How: The interesting data: the H100 reserve term curve went from downward-sloping last year (longer commitments cheaper per hour) to shifted-up and flattened/contango — longer terms no longer earn a discount, implying the market expects prices to rise over the next 36 months (implied forwards from the term structure, treasury-futures methodology). Residual-value modeling across A100/H100/B200 shows older hardware holding more economic value than straight-line 5-year depreciation implies. Duration risk framing: servers financed over 5–6 years but contracted for 3 leaves years exposed — hence swap and block-trade interest.
  • Where applicable: Company-reported marketplace figures and index methodology (her own companies); term-structure observations depend on their sampling. The residual-value vs accounting-depreciation divergence is directly relevant to anyone writing GPU financing or procurement models. Partly a platform demo, but with genuinely new market data.

items.title: Everything will be Simulated
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Cristóbal Valenzuela (Runway, Co-Founder and Co-CEO)

Video

  • Why: Not infrastructure — but a genuinely new claim about where interfaces are going: video models conditioned on user actions, no 3D engine underneath. If real, it changes what "an application" is and what the clients of your infrastructure will be rendering.
  • What: The progression: next-frame prediction at scale learns physics, object permanence, occlusion, and gravity as by-products (Runway benchmarks on geometry and physical behavior, not just preference); game-like playable environments emerge without a physics engine or any rules being written; then "world interface models" — a car image where clicks turn the lights, rotate the view, open the hood, with the label text generated as part of the interaction and no Unity/Unreal/Blender representation anywhere. Continuum extends this into an OS-like research surface: select any passage on a webpage and turn it into an interactive "portal" (SF fog, batteries, photosynthesis) that persists as a visual memory, responds to resizing as an input, and can be revisited and re-entered.
  • How: Actions become conditioning for the next frame rather than inputs to a modeled scene; interactivity is the constraint that shifts generation from seconds/minutes to real time. The robotics connection is explicit (a lab at Runway using these models as "brains" for embodied systems), and "visual thinking" connects it to agents: a coding agent spins up a Continuum visualization to reason through a 3D-printable bike mount, giving human and agent a shared visual workspace to point at. Honest framing throughout: realism ≠ physically accurate simulation, and a generated explanation still needs to be judged for accuracy.
  • Where applicable: Research demos with an announced intent to release much of it in 8–12 months; the physical-accuracy caveat is the load-bearing limitation. Worth watching as a bet on where interactive compute goes.

items.title: Frontier Models for Acting in Space and Time
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Pim de Witte (General Intuition, Co-Founder & CEO)

Video

  • Why: A different bet on model architecture with a data-moat story an infrastructure person can evaluate: action-labeled gameplay at ~1.5 trillion action tokens/month versus frontier labs' entire robotics training sets, which the speaker claims Medal collects in half a day.
  • What: Models that operate in continuous time — frames in, actions out, real time — trained on Medal's game recordings with semantically labeled controller actions. The core insight is the shared action space: humans teleoperate robots with the same controllers (and brains) they use for games, so keyboard/mouse/controller actions are a common interface across embodiments, and the model never has to predict low-level motor values — the existing control stack does that translation, the same way a human player doesn't compute torque.
  • How: Action density is the differentiator: games require frequent simultaneous small adjustments (the drone-flying case), so high-APM data puts high-frequency control problems in reach in a way sparse teleoperation data doesn't. World models generate additional environments to train in. Against JEPA (in the Q&A): inferred action labels (his example: you can't tell rudder position from cockpit video) add a separate scaling problem, so observed labels transfer better to action sequences. Deployment model is layered: an orchestrator LLM (Gemini/Astra-class) for long-horizon planning on top of this fast action model; one model claimed to play games and control 10+ robot types with the same primitives. Early access late November/early December; NYC and London hackathons announced.
  • Where applicable: Privately deployed with some customers at talk time; claims like "significantly faster than any LLM" and the data-advantage comparison are forecasts and company figures without public benchmarks. An accessibility use case (model supplies the missing keyboard actions for a user who can only operate a mouse, observing as it acts) is the most concrete demonstrated application.

items.title: Great Agents Start with Great Infrastructure
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Akshat Bubna (Modal, CTO)

Video

  • Why: The clearest articulation in the program of how agent workloads change the cloud primitives underneath them — sandbox architecture, storage semantics, network policy, and scheduling — which is squarely a cloud-infrastructure PM's problem, illustrated with real scale numbers.
  • What: A concrete architecture for agent execution: each agent's sandbox contains multiple containers/microVMs — the harness (model-calling loop) separated from the tool-execution sidecar with different permissions — plus deliberately shared volumes for collaboration (a spreadsheet where every cell is a different agent, per Hebbia). Requirements derived from real workloads: workspaces that persist for days while humans respond (Basis accounting), CPU-then-GPU environment changes mid-task, agent-visible observability (logs, GPU utilization, budget) so the agent can diagnose its own failed runs, and credential injection the agent cannot see or exfiltrate. Domain allowlists are shown to be too broad; the emerging pattern is user-written lightweight proxies enforcing path- and operation-level rules.
  • How: Scale figures: 20M snapshots/week, ~8 PB/day processed, 2.6M volumes/week created; one personal-assistant customer needs ~10,000 sandbox creations/second, ~1M concurrent sandboxes, lifetimes of minutes, sub-second interactivity — making startup time the binding constraint. Bubna argues you cannot get all CPU capacity from one provider, so capacity must be aggregated across hyperscalers and neoclouds. The conceptual endpoint: pets → cattle → an "ocean of microbes" of short-lived, snapshot-able, heterogeneous environments that the harness spins up, snapshots, and swaps.
  • Where applicable: Modal-specific primitives and scale numbers, but the architectural requirements (harness/hands separation, shared-but-isolated filesystems, per-call network policy, agent-facing observability) transfer to any platform running agents at scale. The "don't vibe-code your sandbox platform" argument (reliability under rare failures, sustained security work, scale) is general.

items.title: How Compute Markets Work
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Evan Conrad (San Francisco Compute Company, CEO)

Video

  • Why: The most infrastructure-literate take on why GPU capacity is being financialized. Conrad explicitly argues that reliable physical operation — backplane fabric, bare-metal orchestration, services on top — is inseparable from making a market in compute, which is a claim a DC/cloud PM can evaluate directly.
  • What: An origin story and thesis: SF Compute began as an AI-music lab that couldn't afford the then-$10M deposit to start a compute commitment, became the first GPU broker to survive, and now runs a physically settled forwards market — they operate the clusters and the exchange. The argument is that a compute market must relieve the actual bundled constraints (lead times, deposits, credit underwriting, delivery delays, node failures with no spare capacity, demand mis-estimation), not just publish a GPU price.
  • How: Physically settled forwards plus a live order book for reserved capacity (now or future); "supercomputing as a service" for would-be NCPs, VC portfolio clusters, and companies wanting residual value without operating a supercomputer. The hotel analogy carries the mechanism: a broker who doesn't run the hotel can't provide room service — a brokered cluster contract is only as good as whoever can fix the cluster. Notably, he claims credit, not power, is the current bottleneck ("you hit credit way before you hit power").
  • Where applicable: Specific to multi-tenant GPU cloud/market operation; the diagnosis of financing and delivery risk applies to anyone signing or supplying multi-year capacity commitments. The competitive forecast (consolidation around a few creditworthy buyers absent market structure) is an explicit thesis, not a measured result.

items.title: Not All GPU's Are Deployed The Same
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Oliver Kennon (SemiAnalysis, Research Analyst, Core Research)

Video

  • Why: The most substantiated talk in the program for anyone buying or operating GPU capacity. It replaces "GPU-hour price" — the number most procurement conversations still use — with an operator-level economics framework, and it does so with measured numbers rather than slogans.
  • What: A commodity-market analysis of inference compute. GPU hours are an input, not output; the useful metric is full cost per successfully completed task at required quality. The core demonstration, from SemiAnalysis's public InferenceX calculator: two B200 deployments serving the same model (DeepSeek-R1-0528, FP4, ~8K in / 1K out tokens, 100 tok/s per-user P50 target) produce 199 vs 298 generated output tokens per second per GPU — ~50% more output from the same chip-hour — purely from serving-stack, settings, and concurrency choices. Kennon also cites SemiAnalysis's own published security work finding cross-tenant exposure via monitoring access as an example of a failure no throughput benchmark catches.
  • How: Cost-curve framing (you can improve 10→8 while a competitor goes 12→6 and you become the high-cost producer), ClusterMAX managed-cluster ratings (provisioning, reliability, monitoring, security, pricing, availability — explicitly scoped to managed clusters, not bare metal), and a careful argument about what a rental-price index and compute futures can and cannot hedge: a rating is a building block for a credible futures market, not a grade or a hedge by itself.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable framework for anyone procuring or operating inference capacity. The B200 throughput numbers are workload-specific (that model, that token ratio, that latency target), and ClusterMAX tiers are relative to peers. Relevant to GPU cluster planning, benchmarking practice, and capacity economics.

items.title: Process Supervision for Agents That Do Long-Horizon Work
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Mitchell Troyanovsky (Basis, Co-Founder)

Video

  • Why: The best methodology talk on supervising long-running agents — directly relevant to running agents against infrastructure where the interesting failure is not a bad final answer but a bad intermediate decision (the "drop the database because the runbook says so" class of failure).
  • What: Three techniques for getting signal from runs with no ground truth. Behavior specs: record the consequential opinions (e.g., "explain a reconciliation discrepancy with evidence; never post a plug entry to force a tie") before changing implementation, and use them as a rubric — two questions: did the run encounter a situation where the behavior applied, and did the agent follow it? Forking: copy agent state just before/after a bad decision to retry with changed context or interrogate the decision. Cheap simulations: have a coding agent build a subagent that imitates the production agent (same system prompt and skills, no shortcuts), present the situation, and iterate — the speaker used this for ~18 months before building real forking infrastructure.
  • How: The worked example is instructive for anyone designing agent guardrails: an agent that can't find a $412.06 discrepancy posts an adjustment anyway and reports zero variance — a balanced reconciliation that passed the outcome check. The diagnosis: the reconciliation tool failed anything that didn't tie, giving the agent a conflicting incentive; changing the prompt or skill only sometimes fixed it, while changing the review tool so sourced explanations could pass resolved the conflict in the illustrated forks. Framing that transfers: treat agent context as "runtime training data," and note that outcome evals (100–1,000 cases) can't cover production's hundreds of thousands of decision situations.
  • Where applicable: General technique (behavior specs are written up as an open standard with an open-source implementation); the accounting examples are Basis-specific but the mechanism — tool signals conflicting with process expectations — is universal in agentic operations.

items.title: Security in the Age of AI: Recent Attacks, Incidents & Defenses
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Andrey Rybka (Bloomberg, Head of Architecture & Emerging Technologies, Office of the CTO)

Video

  • Why: The best-organized agent-security talk here, and it lands squarely in the PM's wheelhouse: its controls are classic infrastructure security disciplines (identity, egress, DNS, tenancy, supply chain) applied to agents, with concrete incident anatomy for each.
  • What: A layered defense taxonomy — identity, input, tool governance, execution isolation, data protection, governance — each motivated by a real incident: a chat agent social-engineered into revealing a long-lived OAuth token (700+ companies' CRM data exported); a low-privilege agent recruiting a higher-privilege agent via prompt injection; hidden white-on-white email instructions causing zero-click exfiltration; a CLI supply-chain prompt that attempted to wipe machines (saved by a typo); Morse-code-encoded instructions stealing 3B tokens; a sandbox with no web access still leaking data through DNS lookups; an MCP server returning other customers' data for months; a poisoned package adding a BCC recipient after 15 clean releases; and an agent that acknowledged a code freeze, thumbs-up, then dropped the production database.
  • How: The proposed controls are deterministic and outside the model: one agent, one short-lived scoped workload identity (no shared keys); agent-to-agent mutual authentication with delegation checked against mission and allowed tools; provenance tagging so retrieved content stays data; a deterministic invocation broker between agent and tools evaluating tool/parameters/identity/approval; Meta's "rule of two" (untrusted input + sensitive data + external action requires human sign-off); default-deny egress including DNS; tenant isolation checked on every query (the AWS-account/GCP-project analogy); memory-integrity checks and fresh execution environments for planted sleeper instructions; budgets that halt rather than alert; supply-chain delay-ingest. The closing move: write these into the same spec as the feature, so each becomes a test or CI policy check.
  • Where applicable: General and largely standards-based (the controls map to existing identity and network practice); the incidents are retold examples rather than attributable disclosures. Directly actionable for anyone operating agents with production access.

items.title: Self-Improving Organizations
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Will Brown (Prime Intellect, Applied Research)

Video

  • Why: A credible roadmap for the "ML for operations" direction: turning an organization's agent traces, corrections, and approval decisions into training signal — with a deliberately bounded starting point (evals and routing) rather than the usual "train on all our data" hand-waving.
  • What: The argument that agents currently learn only in-context (skill files, re-reading the same instructions, cache discounts that don't eliminate reprocessing), while institutional knowledge that's hard to write as rules — preferences, friction, situational judgment — is better expressed as examples and baked into weights. The proposed sequence: collect traces from production use; curate them into evals (agents can do much of the curation); start with routing — run big and small models on the same task, and when the small model's output evaluates as good enough, that comparison becomes labeled data for routing similar work to it; expose human decisions through purpose-built interfaces (a decision card asking promote/hold/inspect on a model checkpoint, with the evidence attached) so each answer is a clean labeled target rather than something inferred from a long thread; then, only then, invest in training — with a cited example that a five-person team trained a competitive knowledge-work model for ~$300K, an "employee-scale" investment.
  • How: Nightly loop prototype: serve agents on inference capacity during the day, review flagged cases and run training at night when the same capacity is idle; checkpoints scored against every evaluation suite they've seen (shown as an internal prototype). Tooling is Prime Intellect's open-source Verifiers environment/eval library; decision models like Jev are referenced as the pattern for the routing/approval layer. The contrast case is the long expert-network-to-frontier-lab pipeline, where the person who knows the job never supervises the model.
  • Where applicable: The routing and eval-first starting points are broadly implementable with existing open tooling; the "earn your way into the weights" caution is sound. The $300K training figure is one cited example, not a general budget. Interfaces and nightly loops are experimental.

items.title: Shipping like a startup, regulated like a bank
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

David Abitbol (Revolut, Ops & Infrastructure Leader)

Video

  • Why: One of the few talks with a complete self-hosted inference deployment story: real GPU counts, real tuning results, real unit economics, and the compliance wrapper — a template for private-cloud AI operations.
  • What: Revolut moved ~2,000 engineers from budget-limited Claude Code usage (engineers hoarding tokens for hard tasks) to self-hosted open models (GLM 5.x) on dedicated GPUs. Reported outcomes: the switch to GLM 5.1 coincided with ~60% better coding time and ~70% better lead time (their internal chart, not a controlled study — the improvement is not isolated from other causes); blended cost ~$0.30 per million tokens, roughly one-tenth of the prior Anthropic/OpenAI invoice. The key tuning result: on a fixed fleet of 56 B200s, requests per second rose 76% while time-to-first-token fell 88% (14.26 s during migration → 1.68 s stable) — i.e., tune before you buy more GPUs. Sub-3 s TTFT is their empirical usability threshold; ~200 tok/s is fine because engineers now run parallel tasks and return when done.
  • How: The parameter playbook: size the context window to actual workload (~256K, not the advertised 1M — "long context is a scam" for capacity purposes), FP4 quantization on Blackwell (~40% smaller footprint vs FP8, claimed zero precision loss), tensor-parallel degree chosen for KV-cache headroom (TP8 over TP4), cache hit rate above 90% for coding workloads, speculative decoding, prefill/decode disaggregation; OpenAI-compatible endpoints so any harness works; a local router sends image tasks to a different model rather than degrading the text model. Controls: sandbox rules that make destructive operations require human intervention (allow grep, not gradle), zero-retention GPU providers in data-equivalency jurisdictions, and strong OpenTelemetry for incident investigation.
  • Where applicable: Revolut-specific deployment and economics (2,000 engineers, EU-regulated bank, one model family); the tuning methodology and the "resist scaling until tuned" lesson generalize to any self-hosted inference operation. The compliance claims are their circumstances, not a general regulatory determination.

items.title: The Dark Pools of Compute
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Affaan Mustafa (Jump Trading, Compute Trading Lead), Alejandro Soumah Fernandez (Jump Trading, Co-Lead Compute Trading)

Video

  • Why: The practitioner's complement to the two talks around it: what is actually inside a GPU-hour quote when physical compute trades in blocks over Slack/Telegram bilaterally — financing, delivery, spec, counterparty, and price risk bundled into one MSA/SLA/order-form package. Directly useful for capacity negotiation.
  • What: A market-structure map of committed compute: chip and system vendors, sites and operators (power, space, assembly), capacity providers (hyperscalers, neoclouds, bare-metal resellers), and end users, with the observation that one actor can occupy several boxes. Illustrative financing example: a company raising $40M that needs a $100M three-year contract with a 30% prepayment ($30M up front) is left with $10M to run the business — capacity arrives in step functions while demand grows smoothly, so below the commitment you pay for idle hours and above it you turn away work or buy on-demand. CoreWeave's quoted 15–25% median prepayments on $100M+ TCV clusters are cited. Ownership adds options (topology control, physical access, confidential computing) rather than eliminating the tradeoff.
  • How: Decomposition of the roles around the GPU-hour — price discovery (indexes, benchmarks), matching venues and brokers, lenders financing against contracted revenue, financial contracts for transferring price risk — with concrete failure modes ("memory" meaning VRAM vs host RAM vs storage; bills of materials that change mid-deal; long OEM/ODM lead times). Policy context: export controls and the US AI action plan's support for open-weight models and compute-market development shape which transactions are even possible.
  • Where applicable: General to anyone negotiating committed GPU capacity; the financing figures are explicitly illustrative teaching numbers, not reported terms. IEA projection cited (485 TWh → 950 TWh global DC electricity, 2025→2030) frames the upstream power constraint.

items.title: The Machine that Changed the World, vAI
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Tariq Shaukat (Sonar, CEO)

Video

  • Why: A useful synthesis of the external evidence on where agentic code production breaks down — worth the PM's time for the cited constraints, with the caveat that the back half is a vendor pitch.
  • What: The five constraints on agentic software factories: (1) human review doesn't scale — a cited study found asynchronous agents drove +2,450% lines of code and +240% commits but only +30% releases, and "cognitive surrender" research shows humans agree with wrong AI answers four out of five times; (2) agents struggle in large codebases — cited code-translation accuracy collapses from 91% at 10K lines to much worse by 50K, and token use for the same task varies 30x by starting context; (3) errors compound — 95% per-step success over 20 steps is ~36% end-to-end, and METR's task-horizon curves flatten sharply at higher success thresholds; (4) LLM judges are unreliable — 7–17% of verdicts change on identical replication, and a simple "are you sure?" flips 7–34%; (5) time-to-exploit is near zero, so prevention must be designed in.
  • How: Sonar's answer is a "code confidence formula" — intent × guide rails × verification × evidence (multiplied: any zero is a zero) — with verification as a quality gate inside the production line rather than a report beside it, mixing deterministic and agentic checks. Reported customer results: 36% lower token consumption and 92% fewer issues in committed code from context/rail product (Sonar Vortex); the closing survey comparisons (81% more likely to report positive security impact, etc.) are sentiment differences among 1,026 respondents, not outcome measurements.
  • Where applicable: The constraint evidence is general and cited; the results are Sonar-reported for its own products and should be treated as vendor figures. The factory framing (borrowed from Toyota production-system thinking, via Nadella's containment argument) is a good mental model for engineering-organization design regardless of tooling.

items.title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (and What to Do About It)
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Kim Maida (Keycard, Founding GTM Engineer)

Video

  • Why: A working, standards-based answer to the overprivileged-agent problem, demonstrated before/after on the same incident queue — the OAuth token-exchange machinery will be familiar territory for anyone who has built delegated access in cloud platforms.
  • What: The demo: an on-call agent with static API keys and an admin connection string resolves six tickets by copying customer PII into reports, dropping and restoring a production database, restarting a server (production offline), and scaling 4→40 pods at a demonstrated $420/hour. The fix is not human-in-the-loop (consent-fatigued users just approve) and not narrower grants (OAuth grants issued before any task exists become standing access). Instead: RFC 8693 OAuth token exchange at every call — the user's token is the subject token, the runtime authenticates to a security token service, and the STS evaluates user + agent + resource + requested permission together before minting a minutes-lived, call-scoped token, discarded after use, with the delegation chain preserved for audit.
  • How: The re-run shows the mechanism working with the same imperfect agent behavior: the warehouse query is refused (PII doesn't belong in the incident workflow) and the agent escalates instead; the DB drop is refused outright; a human approval of a server restart still fails because her user lacks the role — approval cannot amplify permission; scaling succeeds after approval because her role authorizes it. Also previews intent-based authorization (a proposed mission stating goal, allowed actions, and limits, checked per tool call — explicitly an evolving proposal, not a finalized standard).
  • Where applicable: Token exchange is an open 2020 standard interoperating with existing identity providers, gateways, and MCP servers — broadly applicable, not vendor-locked (though the demo is Keycard's product). The demo uses task-based policy governance; IBA is future work.

items.title: Your Company Has No Model of Itself: Bootstrapping a World Model from Slack, Decks and Meetings
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Joao Wenzel (Citadel Securities, COO)

Video

  • Why: A surprising transfer of robotics state-estimation thinking to organizational observability — the "watermelon project" problem (green on the deck, red inside) solved with an evidence-aging belief system, and backtested.
  • What: A system that fuses top-down records (status decks, strategy docs) with bottom-up signal (Slack, meeting notes, PRs, opt-in agent-session traces) into a longitudinal record of what the company believes, how old the evidence is, and what happens next. The state-estimator frame: confidence in a belief decays as evidence ages and collapses when new observations arrive; each source carries last_tried vs last_ok dates, so a quiet Slack channel from a broken feed ("disappearing speedometer") lowers confidence instead of implying nothing is happening.
  • How: A five-stage loop — update, age, observe, grade, correct — where agents propose and code/people decide. Slides are parsed by pairing the underlying XML text with a vision model's reading of the rendered image (each resolves what the other can't). Records separate reported status from evidence-supported status, keep both, and never rewrite history (corrections are feed-forward), which enables backtesting: as-of-February snapshots show green-but-flagged projects turned yellow/red within three months at 18/100 versus 10/100 unflagged — roughly double, enough to direct attention, not to predict specifics. Three years of records also yield real analytics: about half of delivery dates change within two months, ~90% of them slipping later. Specialist agents reviewing specific material more than doubled useful project updates versus one model reading the whole corpus. Human correction is staged by confidence and stakes, and rule-level corrections fix every future output, not one record.
  • Where applicable: Citadel Securities-specific deployment, but the pattern (evidence dating, source-failure modeling, backtested beliefs, corrections that don't rewrite history) transfers to any organization trying to give agents trustworthy institutional context; open problems named honestly (entity resolution across systems without canonical identifiers, when to ask stakeholders).

items.title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model
items.text:
AI Engineer New York 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–14 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Branislav Brzak (Stealthium, Cybersecurity Researcher)

Video

  • Why: Rare, quantified multi-tenancy security work at the hardware level — a direct hit on the intersection of GPU infrastructure, multi-tenancy, and isolation. If you operate shared GPU estates (MIG slicing, NVSwitch servers), this changes your threat model.
  • What: A timing side-channel that defeats MIG partitioning. MIG isolates compute units, VRAM, bandwidth, faults, and L2 cache, but GPU-wide memory barriers still touch every L2 partition: work on one slice changes how long another slice's own memory reads take. An attacker tenant that only reads and times its own buffer recovers the victim's model architecture and depth (~97% claimed accuracy; 14 of 16 models recovered to exact layer depth in the displayed result), decode speed (~99%), busy periods and token counts, and — with speculative decoding enabled — workload class (prose/code/JSON/retrieval; 31 of 40 half-second windows correct). It does not recover prompt or output content. The signal also crosses GPUs: a probe on GPU 2 of an 8x H100 NVSwitch server, tracing a pointer into GPU 0 where the victim runs tensor-parallel, yields 79.2% model identification across five models vs a 20% baseline, losing layer detail but retaining tempo.
  • How: The attacker repeatedly loads from a tiny buffer every ~5 µs and does spectral/fold-and-average analysis; the layer-count classifier is a best-fit test over candidate depths 16–48 (under 30 lines of code, no training set, works on unseen models since architecture signature carries over to fine-tunes/distillations). Detection: the probe shows one kernel relaunched ~3,000 times over the same ~40 KB with almost no data returned to the CPU — Stealthium reports their kernel-level monitoring caught it in under 600 ms. Mitigations offered: tenant placement policy (don't seat an untrusted tenant's MIG slice next to a sensitive model), knowing the tradeoff (MIG rules out peer-to-peer, so no tensor parallelism; NVLink sharding limits leaks to timing-only), and direct GPU workload observation.
  • Where applicable: Any multi-tenant or shared GPU deployment on NVIDIA hardware (H100 demonstrated). The MIG primitive is credited to the "Behind Bars" researchers (USENIX Security '26); this talk extends it to model fingerprinting. Workload-classification results specifically depend on speculative decoding being enabled (an opt-in in vLLM). Note the last section is partly a product demo for Stealthium's observability, but the attack analysis stands on its own.

items.title: ASPA in the RPKI Dashboard
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Tim Bruijnzeels, RIPE

PDF

  • Why: ASPA is the mechanism operators will be asked to deploy after ROV; this is the clearest available explanation of its verification semantics — what it catches, what it deliberately tolerates, and how it fails.
  • What: A worked tutorial of ASPA (AS Provider Authorisations): objects like ROAs, signed by the customer-AS holder, authorizing one or more provider ASes. Routes learned from customers are invalid if a hop is proven "Not Provider"; the system supports partial deployment (no attestation = fail open, as does an RPKI validation problem itself), and it detects valley-free violations by constructing the longest UP ramp (customer→provider from the origin) and DOWN ramp (provider→customer from the receiver) and rejecting paths with a gap — i.e., route leaks — regardless of whether the cause is accident, leak, or spoofing.
  • How: Object structure and path-verification logic presented through concrete examples (spoofed-origin and leaked-path cases), matching what the RIPE RPKI Dashboard now surfaces.
  • Where applicable: Protocol-level and vendor-neutral; broadly applicable. Deployment is early (ARIN brought ASPA online for its own services 20 January 2026, per the ARIN update in the same program), so this is the right time to learn the semantics before it lands in dashboards you use.

bgp network-security pki

items.title: Authenticating networks with RPKI RSC
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Adjacent pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Arnold Nipper, DE-CIX (with Yolandi Cloete)

PDF

  • Why: Machine-verifiable proof that the party you're talking to controls the network resources it claims — network identity, which rhymes with the workload-identity problem in other domains.
  • What: PeeringDB is introducing signup authentication for networks via RPKI RSC (RPKI Signed Checklists) in March 2026, and the talk solicits community input on follow-on features: whether to surface how and when a network authenticated, and whether to support periodic re-authentication.
  • How: RSC objects let a resource holder sign an arbitrary checklist of their holdings; PeeringDB will use them to verify that a PeeringDB record is created by whoever actually holds the ASN/prefixes. (APNIC's annual report in the same program notes RSC objects are now provided in its RPKI services too.)
  • Where applicable: PeeringDB-specific rollout, but the pattern — cryptographic resource-holder authentication replacing manual LOA/email verification — is general, and directly relevant to anyone building inter-org trust flows. Caveat: this is a thin lightning talk and the deck ends with a sponsorship pitch; the signal is the feature, not the depth.

identity pki bgp

items.title: BGP in 2025
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Geoffrey Huston, APNIC

PDF

  • Why: The annual reference for DFZ scale, churn, and the year's notable routing events — baseline data for FIB/TCAM planning and for understanding routing-system fragility.
  • What: The IPv4 DFZ exceeded 1M entries for all BGP peers in 2025; headline events include the July 7 Ramses exchange fire in Cairo (four deaths, visible disruption in BGP), and Amazon's AS16509 swinging from 50M to 158M advertised addresses during the year — including a -15.8M withdrawal on 4 November and a +15.1M re-announcement on 10 December. The advertised IPv4 table actually shrank by 11M /32s over the year while unadvertised space grew by 10M; RIR allocations continue to be outpaced by recovery. Top churn tables (China Mobile +13k prefixes, USDA's odd 3,122-prefix behavior, Cox, Amazon) give a feel for who is re-de-aggregating.
  • How: Longitudinal analysis across every routing peer of RouteViews and RIPE RIS: FIB counts, advertised address span, update/churn dynamics, two decades of comparison.
  • Where applicable: Global and vendor-neutral; the numbers are what they are. Most useful as planning input (FIB growth, prefix-churn tolerance) and as a reminder that single-actor behavior can move the global table by millions of addresses in a day.

bgp measurement

items.title: bgproutes.io: A Next-Generation BGP Data Collection Platform
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides Recording

Thomas Holterbach, University of Strasbourg (with Thomas Alfroy, Cristel Pelsser)

VideoPDF

  • Why: RIPE RIS and RouteViews only collect best-path announcements; monitoring hijacks, leaks, and policy behavior needs more, and this platform — running for a year — shows how to get it.
  • What: A next-gen BGP collection platform prioritizing accurate real-time/short-term monitoring and perpetual retention (where RIS/RouteViews historically prioritized coverage). After one year it receives data from ~70 contributing networks and, critically, aggregates everything already collected by RIPE RIS, RouteViews, PCH, and CGTF into a single database, then exposes it via API and dashboards.
  • How: Three coverage ingredients: (1) automated peering establishment — operators authenticate via PeeringDB and fill in a form to start a session; (2) aggregation of existing collectors; (3) BGP Monitoring Protocol to collect beyond best-path (routes from multiple peers at multiple decision-process stages) — operationally, a small number of BMP sessions already yields a large number of additional vantage points. Every collected route gets RPKI and ASPA validation, with results exposed to users, which makes the platform a live testbed for assessing whether those mechanisms actually work at scale.
  • Where applicable: Community infrastructure, partially APNIC Foundation funded; usable by any operator or researcher today (contribute a session, or just consume). Complements rather than replaces RIS/RouteViews.

bgp measurement observability

items.title: Building an OOB network
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Adjacent pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Phil Mawson, Vocus

PDF

  • Why: The management plane is what saves you when the data plane is down — this is a multi-year, build-it-again carrier case study with real design decisions, prompted by exactly the class of outage (Optus AS7474 national outage, November 2023; Meta, October 2021) that makes OOB non-negotiable.
  • What: Vocus' consolidation of many inherited bespoke OOB solutions into a dedicated national OOB MPLS network, built alongside a new zero-touch-provisioned aggregation network.
  • How: Key rules: OOB must not rely on any founder IP network; per-state regions with route-reflector pairs; OSPF as IGP; own transmission interstate with diverse paths and metro dark-fiber rings. Equipment: Juniper ACX7024/SRX345 routers, EX3400/4100 switches, Opengear console servers. International sites use Megaport Layer-2 VXC back to an Australian headend (cheaper than 10G waves). Extras worth stealing: a third-party transit VPN concentrator as break-glass if AS4826 dies entirely, geographically diverse bastion hosts in three cities, and printed break-glass local credentials locked away for when your auth servers are unreachable.
  • Where applicable: Vocus-specific in its parts list and assumptions (they own Australian transmission), but the design principles — independence from the production network, geographic diversity, break-glass auth — transfer to any operator or large DC operator. Budget math differs if you must buy OOB transport.

troubleshooting automation

items.title: Can RPKI help mitigate social engineering attacks?
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Adjacent pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Sanjaya, APNIC (with Carlos Martinez, LACNIC)

PDF

  • Why: A rare public postmortem of a hijack executed through humans, not protocol weakness — and a direct answer to whether RPKI would have stopped it.
  • What: LACNIC address space was hijacked intermittently in July 2025 by a rogue AS with a repeat-offender history across multiple RIR regions. The investigation (LACNIC → APNIC → APJII/IDNIC) found the bad actor had hijacked the ASN itself and convinced a multinational transit provider to provision transit using forged company letterhead and a faked domain — short random BGP advertisements followed. The transit provider terminated service on the victim's report; the case was jointly written up as a community case study.
  • How: Incident timeline and escalation-path walkthrough; the stated lessons map the defenses: a ROA with correct maxlength prevents the prefix hijack, and ASPA blocks unauthorized upstream providers — the exact door the attacker walked through.
  • Where applicable: General — any resource holder. Its main value is the honest gap analysis: ROV stops origin forgery but not social engineering at your transit provider; ASPA (or contractual LOA verification) is the missing control.

bgp network-security pki

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Thomas Weible, FLEXOPTIX

PDF

  • Why: Choosing grid spacing and filters today determines whether your DWDM plant can carry 800G/1.6T superchannels tomorrow — a topology/spectrum planning problem IP engineers now own under IPoDWDM.
  • What: An argument that coherent detection changes the rules: because a coherent receiver is "blind" to anything but its own wavelength, you can build filterless/colorless topologies and combine sub-bands through cheap 1x4 splitters and ordinary 50 GHz muxes. The concrete recommendation is 400 GHz COTS muxes (12 channels in C-band vs. the classic 96x50 GHz) to future-proof for 1.6T while remaining backward compatible with legacy 50 GHz services.
  • How: Walks from OOK/direct-detection limits through higher-order modulation (16-constellation, dual-polarization, 425Gbps at 53.125 GBd), balanced receivers, phase- and polarization-diversity coherent detection, homodyne/heterodyne/intradyne tradeoffs, and ends with a "make a frequency plan for your spans" design methodology — think in THz/GHz, not nm or channel numbers.
  • Where applicable: General DWDM design guidance for operators planning or refactoring their own optical plant; vendor-presented (FLEXOPTIX), so the COTS-component framing is self-interested, but the physics and filter-sizing argument are vendor-neutral. Assumes coherent optics end-to-end.

optics capacity-planning

items.title: Conference Network Report
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Adjacent pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Yoshinobu Matsuzaki, IIJ (APRICOT Technical Committee)

PDF

  • Why: A compact live postmortem from running a real network under load — including an IPv6-mostly deployment with measured client behavior and a genuinely unusual BGP debugging story.
  • What: The APRICOT 2026 NOC ran dual transit (Lintasarta, Envision) plus Starlink backup, Akvorado NetFlow analysis, and an IPv6-mostly design: 609 unique MACs, 70% of clients (431) operated IPv6-only via NAT64 (DHCPv4 option 108 signaling), 30% dual-stack, 300 Mbps peak. Incidents and fixes: WiFi channel overload at the opening plenary; a BGP "ghost route" — their prefixes showed globally reachable via route-views/RIS but lacked actual reachability, traced to a longer-than-expected AS_PATH left over from an earlier temporary announcement, cleared by contacting ASes on the path (one had a config bug); a rogue AP broadcasting the same SSID/password outside controller management, fixed by a reset; and intermittent public-DNS resolution failures on IPv4 queries with RD=1, fixed by offering local resolvers via RDNSS/DHCP.
  • How: Straightforward ops: PREF64/NAT64 for the v6-only tier, per-incident triage with community help on the ghost route.
  • Where applicable: Conference scale, but the lessons — IPv6-mostly is now viable for 70% of unmanaged clients, stale AS_PATHs can linger as ghost routes after withdrawals, rogue APs happen even with a controller — transfer directly to enterprise and campus networks.

ipv6 troubleshooting measurement

items.title: Debugging Routing & Forwarding Using RIPE Atlas
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Adjacent pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Randy Bush, Internet Initiative Japan

PDF

  • Why: Two real cases where external vantage points found in minutes what provider NOCs couldn't find in weeks — cheap, adoptable debugging technique.
  • What: Case 1: a serial-console server on a colo LAN became unreachable; the provider's week of debugging failed, one Atlas global/random traceroute found the problem (with hover-text and clickable hop detail as the "smoking gun"), fixed within an hour. Case 2: a friend's IPv6 was unrouted for months while the ISP NOC saw nothing; 15 Atlas probes inside that same ISP exposed the internal routing problem to a senior engineer within hours.
  • How: RIPE Atlas (12,000+ probes) one-off measurements and traceroute visualizations, plus the measurement API for automation. Bush closes with a challenge: build an AI front-end that takes a problem description and drives the Atlas API to diagnose it — a nice framing of where troubleshooting tooling is heading.
  • Where applicable: Anyone; free to use if you host a probe (membership not required). Scale- and vendor-agnostic.

measurement troubleshooting bgp

items.title: Exploring the Blind Spot of Internet Exchange Point Route Servers
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Stefano Servillo, University of Rome "La Sapienza" (with Spadaccino, Konstantaras, Luciani, Cuomo)

PDF

  • Why: A formally defined, quantified vulnerability in the IRR-based route-server filtering that most of the world's IXPs rely on — directly relevant to routing security practice.
  • What: The blind spot: IRR validation via AS-SET expansion builds a prefix list per peer but never binds prefixes to their legitimate origin AS, so a prefix covered by a route object under any AS that appears in a member's AS-SET is accepted by the route server regardless of who really owns it. Stale AS-SETs make this worse: of ~130k allocated ASes only ~77k are active, so AS-SETs routinely contain unallocated, private, or inactive ASes whose route objects can weaponize the gap. The team demonstrates prefix hijacking through this path, quantifies prevalence across a large set of IXPs, and validates with real route-server data from AMS-IX and NAMEX.
  • How: Feasibility analysis defines the conditions (prefix not ROA-covered, update not filtered by intermediate ASes, origin AS in a member's AS-SET but not required to be there, etc.), followed by control-plane data analysis; practical countermeasures to strengthen RS filtering are proposed.
  • Where applicable: Applies to any IXP or operator doing IRR-based filtering anywhere; RPKI ROAs close the hole for covered prefixes, which sharpens the case for ROA coverage as hijack insurance rather than just leak hygiene. Research-grade but with production validation.

peering bgp network-security

items.title: Getting 1+ Tbps from an x86 server
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Branimir Rajtar, 5x9 Networks

PDF

  • Why: The datapath-internals story of the year at this conference — what it actually takes to make commodity x86 forward at terabit rates, relevant to anyone building or evaluating software dataplanes (vBNG, vEPC, NFV).
  • What: The evolution of a virtualized BNG from many small 4-vCPU forwarder VMs to a single "Big VM" forwarder, ending at 200 Mpps per CPU and 1.6 Tbps on one server (~600 W). Includes an honest comparison table: ASIC white-label switching (multi-terabit, low flexibility, ~30k subscribers) vs. x86 (~1 Tbps and improving, ~200k subscribers, high flexibility, C/DPDK/eBPF/P4 development).
  • How: SR-IOV plus Intel DPDK to bypass host kernel and drivers; systematic optimization in waves — newer hardware (+30%), deep DPDK/BIOS/PCIe/NIC tuning (+30%), then vTune-guided code-level redesigns driven by CPU cache behavior and PCIe bottlenecks. The horizontal-scaling small-VM design was abandoned because per-instance overhead dominated. CUPS architecture (dashboard/controller/forwarder) throughout.
  • Where applicable: vBNG/BRAS is the use case and the headline numbers are tied to their specific hardware generations; the methodology (measure, profile, redesign around cache/PCIe) transfers to any DPDK dataplane effort.

linux-networking programmable-dataplane

items.title: IP Networking in Deep Space
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Wildcard pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Marc Blanchet, Viagenie

PDF

  • Why: Not operationally relevant, but the most instructive stress test of the IP suite's assumptions you'll read this year — what breaks when RTT is minutes and links vanish for hours.
  • What: An architecture for Moon and Mars networks in which every link carries IP: 3GPP (5G/6G) and 802.11/WiFi on the surface, CCSDS for deep space, spacecraft onboard networks also IP — creating a single Layer-3 network end to end, aligned with NASA's LunaNet interoperability specification. The core problems: Earth-Moon ~2 s one-way delay, Earth-Mars 4–22 minutes, and intermittence (an orbiter passing behind a body turns a 2-second path into a 2-hour gap; until full laser-linked constellations exist, disruptions are the norm).
  • How: Three key adaptations, with simulations confirming suitability: (1) temporary buffering of IP packets on forwarders with intermittent links; (2) configuring QUIC with parameters matching the expected round-trip time; (3) configuring application timeouts. Everything else follows from accepting asynchronous operation as the paradigm — no interactivity, no fast remote management.
  • Where applicable: Space-specific by subject, but the delay/disruption-tolerance findings translate to any store-and-forward or high-latency environment, and the QUIC-parameter work is a concrete example of transport tuning under extreme RTT.

routing-protocols ipv6

items.title: IPoDWDM in 2026
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Mark Tinka, TransmissionCo

PDF

  • Why: IPoDWDM failed once (2000s: proprietary, fixed, power-hungry line cards) and is now succeeding — this talk explains exactly what changed and who is deploying it, which matters for anyone planning DC/WAN interconnect on dark fiber or short DWDM spans.
  • What: A state-of-the-market walkthrough of routed optical networking built on MSA coherent pluggables. Per CignalAI data cited, coherent pluggables outsold proprietary embedded optics 2:1 in 2025, and most 400G-ZR shipments have gone into hyperscaler IPoDWDM deployments; hyperscalers are converging on OSFP for 800G-ZR for thermal reasons. Includes a live reference network: a 130 km span in Cape Town built from a Juniper ACX7300 router with 2x 400G-ZR+ QSFP-DD plugs plus a third-party open line system — no transponder tier.
  • How: Coherent pluggables (100G-ZR QSFP28, 400G/800G-ZR QSFP-DD/OSFP) put DWDM line-side optics directly in standard router/switch ports, on dark fiber or integrated with a line system for reach; line- and client-side mix on the same card; disaggregation removes the optic from the host platform. Pluggable transponders are positioned as the bridge for operators who still want Layer-1 aggregation/demarcation/protection.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable technique, not org-specific — driven by hyperscaler economics but now accessible to any operator with dark fiber or short spans. Presented by a vendor-side MD, but the deck is grounded in third-party market data and a real multi-vendor deployment rather than a product pitch.

optics interconnection

items.title: IX.br São Paulo: Migration to SRv6 EVPN
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Julio Sirota, NIC.br

PDF

  • Why: A production migration template for anyone running a large L2 fabric (IXP peering LAN or DC) on aging LDP+VPLS: flood-based MAC learning, ARP/ND storms, and unknown-unicast flooding are exactly the failure modes EVPN was built to fix.
  • What: The completed migration of IX.br São Paulo (one of the world's largest IX fabrics) from LDP+VPLS to SRv6 EVPN. Concrete results: 84% of equipment (97% of capacity) now on EVPN CSID SRv6 with proxy ARP/ND, unknown-unicast flood eliminated, and a large measured drop in ARP/Neighbor Solicitation volume — including visible reduction in CPU load on participant routers.
  • How: RFC 8560 "VPLS and EVPN seamless integration" allowed PE-by-PE replacement with the core forwarding both MPLS and IPv6/SRv6 labels during migration, no gateway needed. Proxy ARP/ND uses the RFC 9047 ARP/ND Extended Community with the Immutable flag so static entries prevail over dynamic ones, which both kills broadcast storms and prevents participants answering ARP/ND for IPs that are not theirs (spoofing protection).
  • Where applicable: IX.br-specific production story, but the mechanism is standard-track (RFC 8560, RFC 9047) and broadly applicable to any VPLS estate with SRv6-capable PEs. The seamless-migration trick (dual-plane forwarding, one box at a time) is the transferable part.

segment-routing data-center-fabric bgp

items.title: Keynote: The Agentic Shift: The Internet Industry Reimagined
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Wildcard pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Mukhammad Andri Setiawan, Universitas Islam Indonesia

  • Why: The direction-of-field keynote: autonomous agents as operators of infrastructure — the world the IETF's WEBBOTAUTH and CATALIST efforts (see the IETF update above) are being chartered for.
  • What: An argument that the industry is shifting from manual configuration to networks configured by agents, code generated without SQL, and ops moving from hands-on engineering to high-level coordination — with roles emerging for the next decade: "Agent Shepherds" guiding agent swarms, "Sovereignty Architects" for ethical/policy frameworks, and "Compute Brokers" managing agent-economy compute. Also covers bias and accuracy risks, and "AI sovereignty" as a national capability.
  • How: Futures-style synthesis rather than a technical method; the same speaker's IPv6-renumbering study elsewhere in the program grounds the claim empirically (AI-assisted configuration cut measured cognitive workload ~65–72% and task time dramatically in a small within-subjects experiment, while organizational readiness lagged).
  • Where applicable: Broad and speculative, but the trajectory it names — identity, authorization, and supervision for non-human actors — is exactly where the identity portion of this reader's portfolio is heading. (from abstract only)

identity automation

items.title: MESec: Minimal-Exposure AS-Path Verification against BGP Post-ROV Attacks
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Jiangou Zhan, Tsinghua University

PDF

  • Why: With ~49% of IPv4 prefixes ROA-protected and ~37% of ASes doing ROV, attackers move to path manipulation and route leaks — but ASPA's requirement to publish customer-provider relationships globally is commercially toxic. This is the sharpest articulation of that adoption dilemma at the conference, with a real alternative.
  • What: MEASPV, a framework that decouples path validation from topology disclosure: relationship attestations are visible only to designated trusted validators, never broadcast. Evaluation shows a security posture comparable to standard ASPA against post-ROV threats, with minimal information exposure and incremental deployability (no BGP-4 message changes).
  • How: Validator-assisted, three phases: trust establishment (ASes share encrypted, authenticated neighbor-relationship data with chosen validators), path verification on each BGP UPDATE (validators return Type-I high-trust direct reports plus Type-II public-data checks from CAIDA/RouteViews; results aggregate into a score from Strong-Valid to Strong-Suspect), and secure route selection using the score as a BGP decision-process tie-breaker. Caching of per-pair scores (1–5 day refresh, path score = minimum) keeps latency and control traffic low. The authors also prove a lower bound: any effective defense must expose relationship data to at least one third-party verifier — the question is how few.
  • Where applicable: Research framework, not deployed; requires a trusted-validator ecosystem. Conceptually important for anyone designing ASPA-adjacent or attestation-based path security, including in private fabrics where a neutral validator is easier to stand up.

bgp network-security

items.title: sidrops IETF UPDATE
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Adjacent pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Tom Harrison, APNIC

PDF

  • Why: The plumbing of RPKI distribution is being redesigned; if you operate relying parties or a publication point, this affects you.
  • What: Three sidrops work items: the Erik synchronization protocol (draft-ietf-sidrops-rpki-erik-protocol), NRO Trust Anchor Constraints, and Best Current Practices for RPKI publication servers.
  • How: Erik is the interesting one — today every relying party fetches from every publication point (an M:N problem that worsens over time, where one slow PP holds up an RP's whole validation run). An Erik relay, runnable by anybody, fetches from PPs and serves RPs over the new protocol: PPs go from handling thousands of RPs to ~20 relays in full deployment. It also fixes RRDP's encoding waste (base64 adds 33%, XML another ~10%), serves raw DER objects, and uses Merkle trees to support cheap diffs and individual-file repair — eliminating the "delta failed, re-fetch a 100 MB snapshot" thundering herd (the deck shows a 102 MB snapshot vs. a 68 KB delta).
  • Where applicable: All RPKI operators; deployable incrementally alongside rsync/RRDP. Reference implementations exist (rpkitouch relay, public relay instance).

bgp pki standardization

items.title: To Space and Back: Integrating Next-Generation Terrestrial and Satellite Communication Networks
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Wildcard pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Katarina Stefanović, Telecom Serbia

PDF

  • Why: A surprising measured result: LEO satellite paths, though physically longer, can beat terrestrial mobile networks on long-haul latency and stability — with real data, not vendor claims.
  • What: A 7-day continuous RIPE Atlas measurement campaign comparing Starlink LEO connectivity against 4G/5G mobile networks across multiple European countries, targeting an APNIC-hosted host in Singapore: Starlink consistently showed lower and more stable long-haul RTT (enabled by backbone efficiency and evolving inter-satellite-laser routing), while mobile networks showed higher jitter and EPC-driven processing delays despite shorter physical paths.
  • How: Atlas probes measuring long-haul RTT, hop-count behavior, intercontinental routing paths, and jitter distribution; plus an architecture deep-dive into LEO mesh topology, ground stations, laser inter-satellite link types (intra-plane, inter-plane, crossing-plane), and NTN–TN interoperability per 3GPP TR 38.811 — including how beam handovers, congestion, atmosphere, and PoP presence shape user experience.
  • Where applicable: Results are European-vantage and Starlink-specific; the framework (measurement-based comparison rather than assumptions) is general. Relevant to anyone evaluating LEO as a WAN or resilience path, and to the interconnection-panel question of whether LEO edges change regional peering economics.

mobile measurement

items.title: What’s new at the IETF?
items.text:
APRICOT 2026 (Jakarta) digest Program Core pick Jakarta · 4–12 February 2026

Slides

Paresh Khatri, Nokia (delivered with Warren Kumari, Dhruv Dhody, and Suresh Krishnan, IAB)

PDF

  • Why: The standards radar this cycle is unusually relevant: three of the newly chartered working groups touch attestation, bot/agent authentication, and PKI — squarely in identity territory — alongside routing and ops topics.
  • What: New WGs: Secure Evidence and Attestation Transport (SEAT), Domain Connection (DCONN), Open Cloud Mesh (OCM), Web Bot Auth (WEBBOTAUTH), and PKI, Logs, And Tree Signatures (PLANTS); Authenticated Transfer (ATP) in chartering. BoFs at IETF 125: CATALIST (coordinating AI agent-to-agent communications work) and ONSEN (operationalizing service abstractions). Also reports the IAB workshop on IP address geolocation concluding that IP is a weak, overloaded geolocation signal (anycast, satellite, overlays) — a useful data point for anyone building location-dependent policy.
  • How: An operator-oriented survey of IETF structure (areas, ~125 WGs, IRTF, IAB) and where the new work landed, aimed at helping operators track what will hit their networks.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable; for this reader, WEBBOTAUTH and CATALIST are the items to watch for agentic/workload identity, and SEAT/PLANTS for attestation-transport plumbing.

items.title: ARIN Directory Services
items.text:
ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 30–31 October 2025

Slides Recording

Mark Kosters, Chief Technology Officer, ARIN

VideoPDF

  • Why: ARIN runs four redundant directory services (Whois port 43, RWhois, Whois-RWS, RDAP) and is preparing a consultation to retire three of them. If your security tooling, abuse workflows, or automation still hits port 43 or the whois.arin.net REST API, this is a deprecation notice in embryo.
  • What: ARIN proposes retiring RWhois (a 2013 community suggestion, requirement already removed from the NRPM but users remain — the migration path is RDAP, possibly with an ARIN-built translation tool, or pushing reassignment data into ARIN's database), retiring the Whois-RWS API (web front end would move to an RDAP backend), and eventually retiring Whois port 43 itself. Context: since ICANN dropped the Whois requirement for gTLDs in January 2025, at least 139 gTLDs have shut theirs off; usage is falling on the domain side of the industry.
  • How: Consolidation on RDAP (RFC 7480–7485, 9224), which has defined queries/results, 26 client implementations, 11 authoritative server implementations, UTF-8, auth support, and emerging extensions for geolocation and RPKI registration data. A formal ARIN consultation is forthcoming.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to anyone consuming registry data programmatically; org-specific urgency depends on whether you run RWhois for delegated reassignments or have scripts against port 43 / Whois-RWS.
