items.title: ASO AC Update/ICP-2 Consultation
items.text:
ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Wildcard pick 30–31 October 2025

Slides Recording

Amy Potter, ASO Address Council (ARIN region)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not a networking topic, but a rare look at hard governance machinery being redesigned in public — derecognition of failing RIRs, emergency continuity, audit triggers — which will shape who holds the keys to Internet number resources for the next decade.
  • What: The revised "RIR Governance Document" (ICP-2's replacement, consultation closed 7 November 2025) introduces: recognition of a new RIR without unanimous existing-RIR support if an ICANN-appointed third party finds a dissenting RIR made a material error; derecognition proposals initiable by 2,000 members or 25% of an RIR's membership (whichever is lower) or by ICANN (though derecognition still needs RIR approval); ad hoc audits requestable by RIR majority (previously unanimous), member threshold, or ICANN; mandatory periodic audits at least every three years; a new Emergency Continuity procedure to temporarily transfer an RIR's responsibilities to an "Emergency Operator" (90-day cap, unanimous RIR+ICANN agreement, mandatory published postmortem); a required member dispute-resolution mechanism; and an explicit good-faith clause.
  • How: Legal-structural mechanisms — thresholds, third-party review, time-boxed emergency authority with sunset and public review — rather than technology.
  • Where applicable: Governance watchers and multi-RIR organizations; clearly shaped by the AFRINIC experience, and the feedback loop was still open at meeting time.

internet-governance
path: ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting

items.title: ICANN/IANA Update
items.text:
ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 30–31 October 2025

Slides Recording

James Mitchell, IANA/ICANN

VideoPDF

  • Why: Two operationally significant DNSSEC events are on the calendar, and every operator running a validating resolver needs them on a roadmap, not a surprise.
  • What: The second-ever Root Zone KSK rollover is scheduled for 11 October 2026, establishing a recurring 3-year rollover cycle (delayed by COVID and a key-hardware vendor change). Separately, a proposal to change the KSK algorithm from RSA/SHA-256 to ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 goes to public comment in February 2026. The trust anchor has been published in the DNS itself since 11 January 2025; operators should verify their systems have adopted it via software updates.
  • How: Rollover propagates through vendor updates and the XML trust-anchor file rather than manual operator action for most deployments; the algorithm change is a slower, more disruptive migration being run through open IETF/community process. Also noted: .arpa domains are being published in the RDAP bootstrap (reverse-DNS queries will redirect to the relevant RIR) as ICANN sunsets WHOIS, and IANA is investigating participating in RPKI for reserved or special-use space — an early watch item.
  • Where applicable: General — anyone operating validating resolvers or DNSSEC-signing infrastructure. The RPKI-for-special-use-space item is exploratory but relevant to routing-security watchers.

items.title: Internet Evolution and IPv6
items.text:
ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 30–31 October 2025

Slides Recording

Geoff Huston AM, Chief Scientist, APNIC

VideoPDF

  • Why: The best strategic talk on the program. Huston connects trends the PM cares about — edge delivery, the end of per-core performance scaling, and why the DNS has quietly become the Internet's identity layer.
  • What: The argument: abundant fiber capacity, compute, and storage shifted provisioning from on-demand to just-in-case, shrinking "packet miles" and pushing service to the edge. The warning: processor clock speeds topped out a decade ago, so the IPv4-workaround stack (NAT, dynamic naming, content steerage) embeds ever more per-packet processing into infrastructure that no longer scales exponentially — IPv6 is the complexity-reduction escape valve, which is what India's and China's adoption curves show. The reframe: identity and authenticity credentials now attach to service names, not IP addresses; IP addresses are mere topology tokens dynamically bound by DNS — and that binding is masking dual-stack, removing traditional pressure from the IPv6 transition.
  • How: A synthesis of capacity, compute, and adoption trend data rather than a mechanism; the "application is the service" framing ties CDN/edge architecture to naming and identity.
  • Where applicable: General and vendor/region-agnostic; most useful as input to multi-year network strategy and IPv6 business cases rather than immediate operations.

ipv6 dns

ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 30–31 October 2025

items.title: Policy Block 1: ARIN-2024-5: Rewrite of NRPM Section 4.4 Micro-Allocation
items.text:
ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 30–31 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Chris Woodfield, ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

  • Why: This is the one policy text change with direct fabric-adjacent consequences: it rewrites the rules for the dedicated pool IXPs and core DNS operators draw IPv4 from, and it resolves the long-standing ambiguity about whether IXP space may be routed.
  • What: A Recommended Draft (closest to adoption of anything on the docket) renaming Section 4.4 from "Micro-Allocation" to "Critical Internet Infrastructure (CII)" allocations. Key terms: a /15-equivalent reserved for CII; allocations no smaller than /24, sparse where practical; IXPs must justify with at least three initial participants not under common control on a shared physical switching fabric (with ASNs and contacts named; the IXP's own ASNs don't count); IXP space may be publicly announced at the operator's discretion but must be used only for IXP operations; gTLD operators capped at a /23-equivalent per gTLD from the free pool or transfers, not the reservation; 24-month supply requests; renumber-and-return within 12 months when expanding; ARIN publishes a record of all 4.4 allocations.
  • How: Policy text with an implementable-as-written staff review, ~3-month implementation, and a full community-feedback trail (including pushback that "CII" is an arbitrary definition and on gTLD treatment).
  • Where applicable: IXP operators and root/ccTLD/gTLD operators in the ARIN region; indirectly relevant to anyone engineering IX fabrics or peering policy, since it shapes what appears (and routes) on exchange fabrics.

items.title: Policy Implementation and Experience Report
items.text:
ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 30–31 October 2025

Slides Recording

John Sweeting, Chief Experience Officer, ARIN

VideoPDF

  • Why: The one session with hard numbers on the IPv4 transfer market and an honest account of where policy text fails operational reality — useful for anyone acquiring address space or watching IPv4 market mechanics.
  • What: Three findings. (1) Section 4.10 (IPv4 for IPv6 deployment): ARIN cannot detect when IPv6 reallocations/reassignments are removed downstream, so it keeps landing in resource-intensive Section 12 audits — staff asked whether the policy needs rewriting. (2) The initial /24 policies (4.2.2/4.3.2) never stated in-region-only use, and have been broadly interpreted; staff suggests codifying it. (3) Inter-RIR transfers: 2020–2025 ARIN sent 126,326 /24-equivalents to RIPE NCC vs 38,176 received; in 2024 alone, 30,747 out vs 16,293 in. A single large broker moved 1,792 /24s for "network operational needs" into RIPE NCC, mostly now leased — driven by RIPE's permissive temporary-transfer/leasing policy vs ARIN's and LACNIC's stricter stances.
  • How: Policy-experience reporting with transfer tables and a cross-RIR comparison of needs-based tests and leasing rules as the explanatory mechanism.
  • Where applicable: Directly relevant to orgs buying/selling/leasing IPv4 or operating multi-region; the policy divergence analysis explains why transfer flows are so lopsided.

items.title: Routing Security Update
items.text:
ARIN 56 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 30–31 October 2025

Slides Recording

Brad Gorman, Director of Customer Technical Services, ARIN

VideoPDF

  • Why: RPKI is now table stakes for anyone announcing space, and this is the one session with concrete adoption data plus ARIN's roadmap for ROA tooling. Directly relevant to BGP/routing security work.
  • What: A data-driven state-of-RPKI report plus new features. Global RPKI-valid share of announced space rose from ~54% (Dec 2024) to ~57% IPv4 / ~59% IPv6 (Sep 2025, per NIST's monitor), with ARIN openly asking whether a plateau is coming. 7,612 organizations now use ARIN's RPKI services (39% YoY growth); 97.8% choose hosted RPKI, only 161 run delegated (88 of those on ARIN's Repository Publication Service). 47.1% of ARIN-allocated IPv4 is RPKI-valid. New shipped: ROA Modify, a year of ROA change history with CSV export, automatic ROA re-rolling during resource transfers, and ASPA object support in OT&E.
  • How: The interesting roadmap items are "RPKI Routing Intelligence" (show users live BGP announcements against their certificate, explain RPKI-invalid states, and offer a fix-the-ROA flow) and RPKI for reallocated/reassigned resources — letting direct holders delegate RPKI decision rights to downstream recipients, revocable at any time.
  • Where applicable: Any org announcing ARIN-region space; the hosted-vs-delegated guidance is broadly applicable. ASPA support in OT&E is an early signal for anyone planning ASPA adoption. Entity-type data (gov at 18.4% org adoption but 6.7% prefix coverage) is ARIN-region-specific.

items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 20–22 April 2026

Douglas Camin, Alison Wood, and Matthew Wilder, ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

items.title: Engineering Update
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Mark Kosters, ARIN (CTO)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Densely useful for three of the PM's interests at once: identity (ARIN's own MFA mix), physical DC work (ARIN's data center migration), and routing security infrastructure (RPKI trust anchor constraints, ASPA, and the planned retirement of legacy directory services).
  • What: The operational report on ARIN's public services. Highlights: MFA adoption across 53,065 users is 61% TOTP, 36% SMS, and only 3% FIDO2 — a sobering data point for anyone betting on passkey adoption in registry-adjacent systems; all authorizations have moved into ARIN Online (email-based approvals retired); ASPA support released; RPKI Trust Anchor Constraints work is underway, leveraging extended stats and extended transfer logs to attest registry contents per the IETF constraining-trust-anchors draft (already implemented in rpki-client); a consultation is planned on retiring RWhois and Whois-RWS, collapsing four directory-service interfaces (Whois, RWhois, Whois-RWS, RDAP) down toward RDAP.
  • How: On infrastructure, ARIN moved its computer room from HQ to a new Northern Virginia data center, replaced end-of-life hardware, and now runs public-facing services on Red Hat OpenShift with services under OpenShift KubeVirt virtual machines, with Prometheus monitoring displacing Sensu. RRDP is now the largest public-facing traffic class at 46.6% — a signal of how RPKI repo synchronization has become the dominant directory workload.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-specific as an implementation, but the pattern — registry services re-platformed onto hosted Kubernetes with VMs for legacy services, and protocol-surface reduction (retiring RWhois/Whois-RWS in favor of RDAP) — is a template any infrastructure registry operator (including internal IPAM/identity services) can study. The FIDO2-at-3% figure is a broadly citable adoption reality check.

items.title: Grant Reports
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Harlen Stenn (Network Time Foundation), James Harr (Internet2), Matt Griswold (20C)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Three community-grant reports, and the middle one is a genuinely reusable operator tool: a cheap, pre-configured device that stands up IPv6-only/IPv6-mostly test environments — the exact environments that are otherwise a multi-week lab project.
  • What: (1) Internet2's IPv6 Test Pod: a sub-$150 device, funded by a $16,000 grant (follow-on to $7,000 in 2023), that creates dual-stack, NAT64/DNS64, IPv6-mostly (DHCPv4 Option 108), and IPv6-only wired/wifi networks over an IPv6 tunnel, pre-configured and distributed free to participants (45 units delivered, 20 more in April). Testing to date includes the Windows 11 CLAT private preview, NetworkManager 1.58 CLAT support, and HPN-SSH Happy Eyeballs behavior. (2) NTF's grant adds native Markdown output to GNU AutoGen to unify NTP documentation formats. (3) 20C's "From Raw to Ready" delivers a web UI (reg.fullctl.io) over regCtl, which normalizes RDAP responses across RIRs into consistent object views.
  • How: The pod encapsulates the hard-to-assemble mix — NAT64 (poorly supported on low-end platforms), DNS64, PREF64, and Option 108 signaling — so a developer, IT support team, or network engineer can test client behavior in a v6-only environment without building the bed themselves. The rationale laid out is worth internalizing: dual-stack hides problems (Happy Eyeballs), doubles address pools and firewall policies, and makes troubleshooting ambiguous.
  • Where applicable: The pod is available by application (ipv6-pod.info) to anyone in the ARIN community — this is the transferable piece. The AutoGen and regCtl work is niche but the RDAP normalizer is handy for anyone scripting against registry data across RIRs.

items.title: KEYNOTE: Demystifying RPKI: Exploring Tools to Simplify ROA Planning and Visualize Validation
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Steve Wallace, Internet2 (NSF-supported, OAC-2530871)

VideoPDF

  • Why: ROA creation is the single biggest friction point in RPKI adoption — operators fear creating a ROA that accidentally invalidates their own (or a customer's) more-specific announcements. This is a set of free, working tools that directly address that fear, plus an early look at ASPA object planning.
  • What: Three web tools hosted at rootbeer.internet2.edu: an RPKI-ROA Planner that computes candidate ROAs for a prefix and the safest order to create them; an RPKI-ROA Visualizer that walks through Route Origin Validation bit by bit (useful for training staff who don't intuit maxLength semantics); and an experimental RPKI-ASPA Planner that suggests a draft ASPA object for an ASN.
  • How: The ROA Planner correlates three data sources — IRR route objects, currently observed Internet routes, and historical routing data — to derive the set of plausible origins for a prefix, then lets the user pick which apply and sequences ROA creation to avoid transient Invalid states. The ASPA Planner builds its suggestion from CAIDA AS-relationship data ("and some magic," per the speaker).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any operator with ARIN-region resources; the tools are public and free. The ASPA Planner is explicitly experimental and should be treated as a starting draft, not a turnkey ASPA — ASPA semantics are still moving through the IETF.

items.title: KEYNOTE: The Nine Lives of an Early Adopter: Leading Cats to Water in the IPv6 Era
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Nick Burlagio (Planning and Architecture) and Inder Monga (Executive Director), ESnet

VideoPDF

  • Why: ESnet is one of the few production networks that has actually gone IPv6-only on its management plane (with the ESnet6 buildout, completed 2022), and this keynote frames the "why now" argument in terms directly relevant to cloud-native and agentic workloads. It is a rare operator talk where the transition strategy, not the nostalgia, is the payload.
  • What: A history-to-present narrative of ESnet's IPv6 journey — 6Bone participant, 6REN founder, recipient of the first production IPv6 allocation from ARIN in 1999 — culminating in ESnet6, which runs an IPv6-only management plane with comprehensive automation and visibility. The forward-looking argument: AI agents on the network need simplicity (elimination of middleboxes), one consistent addressing scheme for end-to-end automation, and any-to-any hyper-connectivity — none of which survive NAT and dual-stack sprawl.
  • How: Primarily a strategy and lessons talk rather than a mechanism talk (the deck walks the 1995–2026 timeline of IPv6 touchpoints). The concrete operational takeaway is the IPv6-only management plane as proof that a large WAN can run single-stack for infrastructure traffic even while carrying dual-stack customer traffic.
  • Where applicable: ESnet-scale (DOE national labs, 100G/400G backbone) is specific, but the management-plane-first pattern is broadly transferable — it's the least risky place to go v6-only and it forces the tooling/automation to become v6-native. The agentic-workload argument is relevant to anyone planning for machine-dense networks.

items.title: Number Resource Organization Number Council and RIR Governance Document Status Update
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Wildcard pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Amy Potter, ASO AC Vice Chair / NRO NC

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not technical, but this is the rewrite of the constitutional document of the RIR system — including, for the first time, how an RIR gets derecognized and what happens to its registry in an emergency. After the AFRINIC governance crisis, this is where the field is heading institutionally, and it will shape who holds and administers number resources globally.
  • What: A status report on Version 2 of the "RIR Governance Document" (the ICP-2 replacement), targeting finalization by Q4 2026. Key mechanics agreed or in drafting: recognition of a new RIR at "unanimity minus one" (with conflict-of-interest handling); targeted compliance reviews initiable by any group of RIRs, by 25% of an RIR's membership (or 2,000 members, whichever is lower), or by ICANN; regular audits at least every 5 years; and an Emergency Continuity procedure allowing an affected RIR to trigger continuity for itself (or others/ICANN at sub-unanimity), with an "Emergency Operator" taking over the affected RIR's services, staged transfer, and no cap on renewals.
  • How: Multi-round global consultation (298 RIR questionnaire responses, two public comment rounds), with substantive issues tracked in published status reports.
  • Where applicable: Global RIR system governance — affects every resource holder indirectly, and directly if you operate in a region whose RIR ever enters distress. The Emergency Operator concept is the piece to watch: it is effectively a pre-agreed continuity plan for the Internet's number registry.

items.title: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2025-3: Change Section 9 Out Of Region Use Minimum Criteria
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 20–22 April 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Gerry George (with Matthew Wilder), ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

  • Why: A live example of how a seemingly small threshold change (/22 → /24) can materially shift address-market behavior — the staff review itself says so.
  • What: Reduces the in-region IPv4 utilization required to justify out-of-region use from a /22 to a /24. Staff and Legal review flags the consequence explicitly: nothing in Section 9 caps out-of-region use, so a single in-region /24 could in practice unlock substantially larger blocks for deployment entirely outside the ARIN region; staff anticipate a significant increase in IPv4 waitlist volume and ticket workload.
  • How: A one-line NRPM text change, with the "real and substantial connection" requirement as the only remaining guard.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region policy, but relevant to any multi-region operator's IPv4 planning: if adopted, it lowers the entry cost for using ARIN as the source of globally-deployed space, and community feedback notes it could push organizations with heavy out-of-region growth toward other RIRs.

items.title: Policy Block: Draft Policy ARIN-2026-1: Taking IP To Other Planets (TIPTOP)
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Wildcard pick 20–22 April 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alison Wood (with Brian Jones), ARIN Advisory Council

VideoPDF

  • Why: The first formal attempt to recognize off-Earth use cases in any RIR's policy manual, and a genuinely novel addressing problem: how do you allocate IP space for a topology whose "regions" are gravity wells? For anyone who thinks about aggregation and hierarchical addressing, this is a fun and occasionally rigorous stress test of the concepts.
  • What: A draft policy, proposed jointly with the IETF TIPTOP working group (see draft-li-tiptop-address-space and draft-many-tiptop-ip-architecture), to let ARIN allocate address space to Extra-Terrestrial Networks (defined as beyond the GEO arc — LEO and GEO excluded). It proposes hierarchically organizing allocations by "Celestial Region" (Moon, Earth-Moon Lagrange points, asteroid belt, planetary systems), prefers IPv6 with a /48 minimum, employs sparse allocation within the ETN block for growth, and relaxes utilization verification where "active host" checks are impractical for high-latency nodes.
  • How: Topology-aligned aggregation: agencies currently select space ad hoc from multiple RIRs, forcing disaggregated announcements when deep-space networks interconnect; contiguous per-region blocks would let each gravity well aggregate to a single route advertised back to terrestrial ground stations.
  • Where applicable: Not implementable as written — staff and legal review is explicit that it presumes unsatisfied prerequisites: an IETF determination, an IANA allocation, an ARIN Board finding that serving as (even interim) deep-space registry fits ARIN's mission, and concurrence of the other RIRs. Near-term demand is small and specialized. The precedent (first off-Earth recognition in RIR policy) and the routing-scalability framing are the real content.

items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

John Sweeting, ARIN (Chief Experience Officer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Where policy text meets operational reality — the most interesting part is ARIN staff's frank account of IPv4 leasing and inter-RIR transfer arbitrage, which affects the market everyone buys address space in.

(1) AFRINIC's inter-RIR transfer policy was ratified 4 February 2026; ARIN staff have reviewed it as reciprocal and will allow IPv4/ASN transfers to and from AFRINIC once AFRINIC implements. (2) On LACNIC's new third-party sub-assignment (leasing) policy: ARIN does not consider leasing to be efficient needs-based utilization for transfers (NRPM 8.⅜.4) or waitlist qualification — and staff have observed ARIN-originated space appearing on leasing platforms in other regions after inter-RIR transfer. (3) Options floated for encouraging IPv6 adoption: requiring demonstrated IPv6 deployment for IPv4 waitlist access.
  • How: A staff-practice report rather than a new mechanism; the leverage points are transfer approval criteria and waitlist eligibility rules.
  • Where applicable: Relevant to anyone acquiring or transferring IPv4 in the ARIN region, and to anyone modeling IPv4 market behavior across RIRs. The AFRINIC change materially alters the global transfer map.

items.title: Registry Integrity and Oversight
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Reese Radcliffe, ARIN (Senior Manager, Registry Integrity and Oversight)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The operational security underside of the registry: how number-resource fraud actually manifests, with numbers. Directly relevant to anyone whose address space could be hijacked or whose counterparties might not be who they claim.
  • What: A threat-landscape and casework report. Notable findings: of out-of-region organizations creating ARIN Org IDs "to expand into the region," roughly 30% are found announcing ARIN resources out-of-region within 60 days; ~240 Org Creates per month, of which ~35 are escalated to RIO, with 42% of those being out-of-region expansion attempts; NRPM 4.10 (IPv4-to-facilitate-IPv6) space is abused via out-of-region announcement, reassignment to customers, leasing, or announcing with no associated IPv6; 223 policy non-compliance reports were received in 2025, of which 28 were actionable.
  • How: RIO runs escalated review of suspicious Org Creates, Section 12 audits with video identity verification, fraud investigation, and law-enforcement collaboration, plus inter-RIR knowledge sharing.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-specific process, but the threat taxonomy (entity fraud, unauthorized reassignment, out-of-region leakage, IRR misinformation) is the same one any resource holder or IX should assume exists. The 30%-within-60-days figure is a good calibration for how quickly out-of-region misuse follows a new Org ID.

items.title: Routing Security Update
items.text:
ARIN 57 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 20–22 April 2026

Slides Recording

Brad Gorman, ARIN (Director, Customer Technical Services)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The best single data source on where RPKI actually stands in the ARIN region — which is directly actionable when prioritizing your own ROA coverage and when deciding how much to lean on ROV in filtering. Also the first production deployment of ASPA objects worth watching.
  • What: A quarter-over-quarter adoption report plus new features. Key numbers (NIST RPKI monitor, 1 April): global RPKI validity has climbed steadily through Q1 2026, with IPv4 and IPv6 both in the roughly 60–66% range. In-region: 8,403 organizations registered for ARIN RPKI services (25% growth since Q1 2025), 98% of them on Hosted RPKI — but ~15% of registered orgs have never created a single ROA, only 50% of RPKI-eligible IPv4 blocks are covered by ROAs, and 54% of ARIN-registered IPv4 blocks seen in announcements are RPKI Valid. ASPAs are live in production (198+ created and trending up), enabling IETF draft testing with real data. An upcoming "RPKI Routing Intelligence" feature will show orgs their prefixes as seen in the global BGP table, explain why announcements are Invalid or Not Found, and simulate the effect of proposed ROA changes.
  • How: The update combines NRO/NIST monitoring data with ARIN's own registry cross-referencing (allocations under agreement vs. ROA coverage vs. announcements). The Routing Intelligence feature is essentially a BGP-table diff against your resource certificate with counterfactual analysis.
  • Where applicable: The stats are ARIN-region-specific, but the gap they expose (signup ≠ protection; the bottleneck is ROA coverage, not registration) generalizes. The Routing Intelligence preview matters to any ARIN resource holder; worth benchmarking your own coverage against the 50%-of-eligible-blocks regional figure.

items.title: Address Supporting Organization Address Council (ASO AC) Update
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Wildcard pick 22–23 October 2026

Slides Recording

Kevin Blumberg (ASO AC / NRO NC)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not a technical talk, but it covers a genuine structural shift in Internet governance: the multi-year ICP-2 rewrite that will define how an RIR can be audited, placed under emergency operation, or derecognized. That's the failure-domain design of the registry system itself — worth one read even for a purely technical PM.
  • What: Status of the RIR Governance Document: a recommended draft published 1 September 2026 after two consultation rounds, now with ICANN for consideration after productive discussions at ICANN 87. Key changes: a five-year regular audit cycle, a distinct Compliance Review process with misuse safeguards, Rehabilitation Plans as the preferred path, a Temporary Emergency Continuity Arrangement an affected RIR can initiate for its own services (90-day limit, two-thirds RIR threshold), a derecognition process requiring two-thirds RIR support excluding the subject RIR, and amendment freezes during emergency arrangements or pending derecognition.
  • How: Multi-stakeholder consultation timeline running since October 2024; open mailing lists and ASO AC teleconferences; Oscar Robles selected to fill the vacant ICANN Board Seat 9.
  • Where applicable: Governance-level; affects all five RIRs. No operator action, but it is the framework that would govern any future RIR failure — the "datacenter redundancy plan" equivalent for the registry layer.

items.title: ARIN Directory Services Roadmap
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 22–23 October 2026

Slides Recording

Hollis Kara (ARIN, Director of Communications)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Directory-data consolidation onto RDAP touches the PM's directory/identity instincts, and the Port 43 WHOIS debate is a live case study in legacy-protocol retirement politics — relevant to anyone whose tooling still scripts whois.
  • What: Outcome of a community consultation on retiring three legacy services in favor of RDAP as ARIN's single directory protocol. RWhois: uncontested, retiring on a 365-day countdown after a migration tool ships. Whois-RWS: uncontested in principle, API sunset set for July 2026/2027 path (July 2027 per deck), gated on RDAP closing one parity gap (CIDR more-specifics / hierarchy walking); web UI to run in parallel with a beta Advanced RDAP Search for ~6 months. Port 43 WHOIS: real opposition — of 43 substantive comments, 24 opposed or wanted a much longer transition (56% against), 11 supported, 8 neutral — so ARIN paused and will reconsult once RDAP clients ship by default in OS distributions.
  • How: Analysis grounded in actual query traffic (79% IP lookups, 9% ASN, 10% org) and a candid visibility caveat: the top queriers all resolve to cloud provider addresses, so ARIN can't see the real end users. Engineering judged a WHOIS-compatible proxy in front of RDAP to cost more operational risk than keeping native WHOIS running longer — the reason the proxy compromise was rejected.
  • Where applicable: Anyone with scripts or products querying ARIN directory data. The security argument (unauthenticated, unencrypted, MITM-tamperable) vs. the ecosystem-readiness argument (RDAP clients not yet default in OS distros) is the transferable lesson for any forced protocol migration.

items.title: Data Accuracy Update
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 22–23 October 2026

Slides Recording

John Sweeting (ARIN, Chief Experience Officer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Registry accuracy is network security infrastructure — the stated objectives are preventing resource hijacking and supporting law enforcement. For anyone building systems that consume WHOIS/RDAP data or dealing with hijacked/legacy space, the mechanics of how ARIN is cleaning up non-agreement holdings are directly relevant.
  • What: Progress report on driving the remaining "not under agreement" space to zero: 372,877 /24-equivalents remain outside agreements (Q3 2026), down 26,313 quarter-over-quarter and down 81% since Q1 2024; 16,212 legacy CIDR blocks; 2,195 /24-equivalents already returned to the IPv4 waitlist. A Q4 2025 step change brought 1.28M /24-equivalents under RSAs in one quarter. The remaining center of gravity: 715 /16-sized blocks hold 49.1% of the outstanding space, and just 23 blocks of /15 or larger hold 38% of it.
  • How: A cohort model. Cohort 1 (2,660 orgs with zero usable contact info) gets services stopped, a 12-month quarantine hold, then release via the waitlist with rights extinguished. Cohort 2 (10,218 orgs with contacts pending verification) gets targeted outreach and DAP contact validation; organizations whose contacts prove inaccurate fall back to Cohort 1. The /16 population is managed as a named list with account-level engagement.
  • Where applicable: ARIN-registry-specific, but the quarantine-then-rights-extinguishment pattern for unreachable holders is a notable operational model for any registry-like system. The 49%-in-/16s concentration means most remaining work is a small number of very large legacy accounts.

items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 22–23 October 2026

Lee Howard (ARIN Board of Trustees)

VideoPDF

That's exactly the territory a networking PM lives in, and ARIN is soliciting input on how to structure the program.

Task force members are Lee Howard, Rob Seastrom, and Tina Morris, and they are explicitly asking for input on program structure and how to record and prioritize issues.

items.title: Policy Block 2: Draft Policy ARIN 2026-1
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Wildcard pick 22–23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alison Wood (Advisory Council; co-drafted with Brian Jones)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The most novel thing in the program: a first-of-its-kind proposal to allocate IP address space for networks beyond Earth orbit, with topological aggregation by celestial region. Even in draft form, it signals where hierarchical addressing thought is heading and is tightly coupled to a live IETF working group.
  • What: "Taking IP To Other Planets" (TIPTOP) would let ARIN allocate IPv4/IPv6 for extra-terrestrial networks (beyond GEO — the Moon, Mars, Lagrange points), organized hierarchically by celestial region so lunar/planetary prefixes can aggregate into single advertisements back to terrestrial ground stations. Staff's verdict: not implementable as written — it presumes IETF determination that dedicated space is needed, IANA allocation, RIR concurrence on who runs the registry, and a Board mission-scope decision. Meanwhile the IETF TIPTOP WG advanced its use-case and IP-architecture documents, and a joint IPv6 address-space draft (draft-limarsjenwar-tiptop-address-space-00, by Li, Eubanks, Atkinson, Kumari, and Linkova) was published 15 September, asking IANA for dedicated space with suballocation per celestial body and the NRO to determine allocation within celestial bodies.
  • How: Policy defines an Extra-Terrestrial Network, a dedicated allocation pool, sparse allocation within the ETN block to allow growth without fragmentation, and utilization exceptions where "active host" verification is impractical (high-latency cold-storage nodes, orbital relays).
  • Where applicable: Aspirational and multi-year; contingent on IETF/IANA/NRO process. Watch it as an addressing-architecture thought experiment — aggregation-by-gravity-well is the interesting design idea, and the deep-space transport assumptions (intermittent links, buffering, long delay) are in the WG documents.

items.title: Policy Block 2: Draft Policy ARIN 2026-2
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 22–23 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Matthew Wilder (Advisory Council; co-drafted with Alicia Trotman)

VideoPDF

  • Why: This is a proposal to rewrite the entire IPv6 allocation framework from formula-based sizing to documented network plans. If the PM's organization (or its customers) ever requests IPv6 space from ARIN, this changes what "justification" means — it effectively makes IPAM discipline the allocation criterion.
  • What: A full revision of NRPM Section 6.5 that replaces rigid sizing calculations, utilization thresholds, and IPv4-dependent qualification with a planning-based evaluation model. Requests must include a network plan identifying typical assignment sizes (/48, /56, /64), the addressing hierarchy, and projected utilization at 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons. Subsequent allocations require 75% assignment of the prefix units in the 2-year plan plus evidence deployment matched the submitted hierarchy, with ARIN issuing additional space contiguously to protect aggregation. Deployment must begin within 12 months of issuance. Community survey at the meeting: 40% support, 40% oppose, 20% neutral — genuinely contested.
  • How: The mechanism shifts review from arithmetic (e.g., the 75%-of-/48s nibble-boundary rules elsewhere in Section 6.5) to evaluating a documented plan: hierarchy, aggregation strategy, and growth projections over defined time horizons, applied consistently to LIR and end-user/PI allocations.
  • Where applicable: Applies to ARIN-region IPv6 allocations only, but the shift from formula-based to plan-based justification is a direction other RIRs watch. Broadly applicable to any org requesting space; the open community question — should ARIN require network plans, and does ARIN need to define what a plan is — is where the practical friction will land.

items.title: Policy Block 2: Draft Policy ARIN 2026-5

items.title: Policy Implementation and Experience Report
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Adjacent pick 22–23 October 2026

Slides Recording

John Sweeting (ARIN, Chief Experience Officer)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The rare policy session with quantified operational results, and the waitlist/transfer mechanics matter to any org acquiring or moving IPv4 space.
  • What: Three implementation reviews. (1) The waitlist multi-block question: policy forces single contiguous blocks, so an org qualifying for a /22 that accepts down to a /24 gets one /24 even when four noncontiguous /24s are free — staff asked the community whether that restriction, aggregation-driven, is still necessary. (2) The NRPM 8.⅜.4 12-month recipient-to-source wait is invisible in the recipient-facing policy text, causing surprises. (3) ARIN-2025-2 (implemented 3 March 2026) removed the "within the last two versions" RSA constraint: of 490 transfer-participating orgs in the first six months, 72 were spared a new RSA — faster transfers, less legal overhead (vs. 11.7% forced re-signing in the prior six months).
  • How: Staff-experience reporting with before/after ticket-level numbers, feeding directly into new policy proposals (several ARIN-2025/2026 items originated here).
  • Where applicable: ARIN-region transfer and waitlist operations; broadly relevant as a model of policy-implementation feedback loops.

items.title: Routing Security Update
items.text:
ARIN 58 Public Policy and Members Meeting digest Program Core pick 22–23 October 2026

Slides Recording

Brad Gorman, ARIN (Director of Customer Technical Services)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Routing security is squarely in the PM's network-security remit, and this is the one session with hard adoption data and a preview of ASPAs — the next RPKI object after ROAs. It also matters for anyone building products that depend on customers having their RPKI in order.
  • What: A data-driven status report on RPKI adoption in the ARIN region plus ARIN's RPKI roadmap. Headline numbers: 9,673 organizations registered for RPKI (up 27% year over year), but roughly 1 in 7 hosted-RPKI organizations has never created a single ROA — "registered is not the same as protected." 59.4% of ARIN-registered IPv4 blocks seen in announcements are RPKI Valid. Globally, 3,389 ASPAs (Autonomous System Provider Authorizations) now exist across the five RIR repositories (2,081 at RIPE NCC, 685 at ARIN), and all five RIRs will support ASPA creation by end of 2026 as the RFC finishes ratification.
  • How: The adoption analysis slices coverage by entity type (government vs. education vs. commercial) and by geography within the ARIN region, isolating where ROA coverage lags. On the tooling side, ARIN is building "BGP Insight": correlating prefixes on a resource certificate with what's actually seen in the global BGP table, explaining Invalid/Not Found states, showing the impact of proposed ROA changes before they're made, and presenting paths to a Valid state. Also in flight: ASPA info in the RPKI changelog, new Reg-RWS RESTful API capabilities, and inter-RIR work toward RPKI feature parity.
  • Where applicable: RPKI validity and ASPA trends are global; the hosted/delegated/repository service tiers and the adoption figures are ARIN-region-specific. ASPA momentum is the transferable takeaway for any operator doing BGP security planning in 2027 — the object class is about to become generally creatable across all RIRs.

items.title: Agent Memory at Meta Scale: One Query Language for Graph, Vector, and Memory
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Abdullah Ozturk, Yiting Li, Vishal Gandhi, Ming Chen, Junjie Qi (Meta)

  • Why: Agent memory is becoming a real infrastructure layer, and today's stacks stitch vector indexes, graph services, and RAG frameworks together on the critical path of every agent turn. This proposes treating memory as a query-surface problem — a genuinely architectural move.
  • What: The Cypher Query Layer (CQL): a declarative query surface over agent memory built on the openCypher/GQL ISO standard, collapsing hybrid retrieval (vector + text + graph + scope + freshness + provenance) into one optimizable query, with identity-aware ACLs as first-class primitives (from abstract only).
  • How: A pluggable backend routes each query to a right-fit substrate — in-process Velox for sub-50 ms agent-loop reads, reusing Meta's existing graph/vector/hybrid stores — with bi-temporal memory on the roadmap to enable agent-debugging replay, and procedure packs for distillation/consolidation/governance.
  • Where applicable: The standard-based query surface is broadly interesting; the substrate choices are Meta's. The in-process vs. distributed boundary discussion is exactly the kind of design decision that transfers. Early-stage — production patterns come from one early internal consumer.

items.title: Agentic Data Flywheel: A Multi-Agent System for Scalable Multimodal Training Data Production
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Wendy Jiang, Selahattin Akkas, Alan Li, Antoine Simoulin (Meta)

  • Why: Off the PM's beaten path (data annotation), but a well-instrumented multi-agent design with a surprising result: multilingual bootstrapping turned a per-language staffing bottleneck into a prompt configuration change across 100+ languages.
  • What: A multi-agent annotation pipeline — specialist VLM labeler, parallel quality reviewers with summarizer, self-correcting adjuster, and a thinking-model judge — delivering a 3x efficiency gain with 60%+ of annotations needing no human involvement; remaining cases go to humans prefilled with agent corrections (from abstract only).
  • How: Probabilistic VLM reasoning wrapped in deterministic scaffolding: agent isolation to prevent confirmation bias, deterministic routing around probabilistic judgment, and structured closed-choice output constraints with every failure mode defaulting to human escalation.
  • Where applicable: Demonstrated on image-text labeling with claimed generalization to scene understanding, chart/document VQA, and grounding. The escalation-defaults-to-human principle is the transferable design lesson for any probabilistic-agent pipeline.

items.title: Agentic Inference Optimization for RecSys ML models
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Core pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Shuyao Bi (Meta)

  • Why: GPU inference optimization is core AI infrastructure work, and this replaces a documented, quantified expert bottleneck (~40 hours of manual fusion work per model) with an automated agent — a pattern likely to spread to every ML platform team.
  • What: An automated optimization agent that detects kernel-fusion opportunities in PyTorch recommendation models, generates and validates Torch FX graph transformations, and converges iteratively — removing the manual per-model fusion effort that went stale as architectures changed (from abstract only).
  • How: Fusion opportunities are detected from GPU traces plus FX graph structure; the agent then authors graph transformations (replacing operation sequences with fused kernels to cut launch overhead and host-device transfers) and validates them in a self-converging loop.
  • Where applicable: PyTorch/Torch FX specific, aimed at production inference latency targets for recommender-class models. No headline numbers are given in the abstract, so treat impact as directional until the full write-up; the technique itself is broadly usable wherever FX graphs apply.

@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Core pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Bikash Sharma, Aashik Gowda, Angineh Keshishian, Mia Gu, Michael Fulthorp, Jinfu Leng (Meta)

  • Why: "ML for infrastructure operations" is a core interest, and this is the most complete production example in the program: an agentic platform running the full optimization lifecycle over a serving fleet drawing hundreds of megawatts, with validated dollar savings.
  • What: ASEA turns a multi-day, expert-only optimization workflow (stitching telemetry, profiling, and capacity data) into an autonomous fleet-wide loop, claiming tens of millions of dollars in validated efficiency savings; the motivating observation is that service overhead often reaches 50% of total serving footprint (from abstract only).

The architecture — single-skill agents over a shared telemetry/profiling data plane with canary-gated rollout — is a transferable pattern for any large serving or infrastructure estate.

items.title: Cache the Session, Not the Data: 40x Faster ML Iteration with a Shared Sidecar at Meta
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Rohil Bansal, Eric Fu (Meta)

  • Why: A small, sharply executed piece of systems engineering with a measured ~40x improvement (391s → 9s) on the developer inner loop — the kind of operational win that transfers to any ML platform with a preprocessing cold-start tax.
  • What: The Shared Sidecar (SSC), an out-of-process daemon caching warmed data-preprocessing sessions across local runs, rolled out to all Meta developer workstations by default with no correctness regressions (from abstract only).
  • How: Sessions are keyed on a hash of input dataframe + preprocessing plan; matching reuses a pre-warmed session and skips session setup, query optimization, metadata lookup, and reader warm-up. Lifecycle is bounded (8h idle eviction, 1h process timeout, capped session count) with graceful degradation if the daemon dies.
  • Where applicable: General technique, not Meta-specific — any environment where preprocessing startup dominates iteration. The 5-minute cold start is environment-dependent, so measure your own baseline first. Single-benchmark evidence (a CTR model); the "no correctness regressions" claim is the authors'.

items.title: Citrine: Catching Million-Dollar ML Anti-Patterns Before They Ship
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Core pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Prakash KL, Chenguang Zhu, Shyam Sundar Chandrasekaran, Jon Dyer (Meta)

  • Why: GPU/accelerator efficiency is now measured in fleet-wide megawatts and billions of dollars, and AI coding agents are reproducing inefficiencies at machine speed. This is one of the few systems that attacks waste at code-authoring time with measured fleet-scale results, and it has a real open-source footprint.
  • What: An always-on, zero-overhead lint-layer system detecting 45+ PyTorch and Triton anti-patterns, with 4,700+ accepted fixes in 90 days across 10+ product groups, up to 43% improvement on affected Triton kernels, and claimed millions of dollars in annual GPU savings (from abstract only; numbers are the authors' own).
  • How: Static analysis and AST transformation via LibCST integrated into Meta's arc lint pipeline; every detector ships a deterministic AST rewriter giving one-click suggested edits. It also shifts left by injecting the same rules into LLM code-authoring agents at generation time, plus an attribution methodology tying individual fixes to fleet-scale efficiency wins.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable well beyond Meta — 13 TorchFix rules and 12+ Triton-lint rules are upstreamed into open-source projects, so the pattern (and much of the rule set) is directly consumable. The Meta-specific parts are the arc lint integration and the internal attribution pipeline.

items.title: Data Governance in the World of Agents
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Core pick 17 June 2026

Abstract Session recording Materials

Komal Mangtani (Meta)

  • Why: Agents in production is a core interest, and this names precisely why human-era IAM breaks under machine-speed, parallel, persistent agents — identity confusion, entitlement creep, recursive leakage across agent chains — then gives a full defense-in-depth reference architecture.
  • What: Meta's governance stack for production agents: Isolation Domains (domain-scoped encryption and output closure), Agent Identity (end-to-end attribution distinct from the user), Agent-Aware Access Control (classification-aware ABAC evaluated at query time), AccessMate (zero-standing-permissions triage), CodeGuard (secure codegen/execution guardrails), and DataVM (a unified trusted environment bounding inputs, tools, and outputs) (from abstract only).
  • How: Rather than bolting IAM onto agent harnesses, controls are evaluated in the data path at query time with classification awareness, permissions default to least-privilege with no standing grants, and each agent action carries its own identity for audit — turning governance into the harness for autonomy.
  • Where applicable: The named components are Meta's, but this is presented explicitly as a reference architecture, and the failure modes it catalogs (trajectory/embedding/log/tool-output persistence as new data surfaces) are universal to agentic systems. Directly reusable as a requirements checklist for any agent platform.

items.title: Designing for Human Agency in AI-Augmented Software: A Quality Attribute Approach
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Rohan Vardhan

  • Why: Not infrastructure at all — but a genuinely novel framing: treating human-centeredness as a measurable software quality attribute (like performance or security) rather than a design philosophy, which changes how AI features would be specified and tested.
  • What: An argument that ISO/IEC 25010:2023 and similar quality models don't capture what makes AI-augmented software supportive rather than corrosive to human judgment, proposing the ACCL framework — Agency Preservation, Calibrated Trust, Contestability, Learnability of Limits — plus three previously undocumented failure modes: reflexive bypass, trust debt, and the right-sized explanation problem (from abstract only).
  • How: For each attribute, architectural implications and organizational patterns grounded in field observation across multiple organizations; the failure modes come from practitioner experience rather than formal study.
  • Where applicable: Conceptual/framework work rather than a deployed system — no empirical validation claimed. Useful as a vocabulary for anyone writing requirements for AI-assisted internal tools (including agent platforms of the kind the rest of this program deploys).

items.title: Evaluating Opsmate: Grading AI Incident Investigations at Scale
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Chinmay Gandhi, Narayanan Sankaran, Khushbu Thakur, Ankit Agarwal, Vaidyanathan PK, KC Balsu, Akash Jothi (Meta)

  • Why: Everyone is deploying incident-investigation agents; almost nobody can answer "did it do a good job?" This tackles the evaluation gap for an agent handling ~1.5K incidents/day — the hard prerequisite for trusting autonomous ops.
  • What: Opsmate Evals: an orchestrator- and model-agnostic framework for scoring autonomous incident investigations, combining automated ground-truth synthesis from post-incident artifacts with LLM-as-judge graders scoring 0–100 on root-cause accuracy, investigation path logic, and mitigation actionability (from abstract only).

  • Where applicable: General pattern for any org running incident agents — the ground-truth-synthesis idea works wherever post-incident artifacts exist. Calibration and judge reliability are the unvalidated parts; treat scores as a starting point, not ground truth.

items.title: How Meta Scaled AI Training Storage via Data Normalization
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Core pick 17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Sarang Masti, Weiran Liu (Meta)

Video

  • Why: Training-data storage is becoming a first-order cost driver as sequence-based and multimodal models inflate feature sizes 10–100x. For anyone planning storage and data-path capacity for training clusters, this is a concrete, quantified answer to the duplication problem.
  • What: A co-designed data and infrastructure change that cut storage cost 10x for Meta's largest recommendation training feature (long user sequences) by eliminating feature duplication in training samples (from abstract only).
  • How: Features are moved out of the per-request training rows (where a popular content feature could be duplicated a million times) into a high-performance indexing store, with model access-pattern-aware pushdown so the trainer fetches features at read time instead of materializing them per sample.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific production setup today, but the normalization-vs-duplication tradeoff and access-pattern pushdown idea transfer to any large-scale ML training data pipeline. The gains depend on read patterns being predictable enough to push down; highly random access would erode the win.

items.title: LP Planner: Synchronization-Aware Sharding Optimization for Large-Scale DLRM Model Training
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Core pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Mine Su Erturk, Greg Macnamara, Caner Gocmen, Isuru Janith Ranawaka, Felicity Liao, Ahmed Shuaibi, Alireza Tehrani, Hammad Ather, Shafeeq Ibraheem, Kaustubh Vartak, Nipun Gupta (Meta)

  • Why: Sharding embedded-table models across devices is one of the hardest practical problems in large-scale distributed training, and this is a deployed optimizer with production numbers on some of Meta's highest-spend models — exactly the kind of firmly substantiated result worth a PM's attention.
  • What: A tool that automatically generates DLRM sharding plans, deployed on multiple production models including some of the largest by training spend, delivering up to 8% QPS improvement and 14% peak memory reduction per model launch (from abstract only).
  • How: The sharding problem is formulated as a linear program that jointly optimizes table placement and partitioning strategy across devices and device memory hierarchies, minimizing peak memory while maximizing training throughput; the "synchronization-aware" part accounts for cross-device sync costs in the objective. It is also integrated into agentic auto-tuning pipelines.
  • Where applicable: DLRM/embedding-table specific — directly relevant if you run recommendation-model training; less so for dense LLM training. Ongoing work (critical-path modeling, shard-type selection, heterogeneous hardware awareness) indicates current limitations. Production numbers are Meta's.

items.title: SparkSentry: Autonomous Error Detection, Triage, and Repair for Spark at Scale
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Core pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Varun Srinivas (Meta)

  • Why: This is the cleanest production example on the program of the full agentic-ops loop — detect → classify → triage → fix → review — running continuously on real fleet failures with concrete throughput and noise-reduction numbers. Anyone thinking about AIOps→autonomous-ops will want this pattern.
  • What: An autonomous pipeline over Meta's millions of daily Spark jobs: twice-daily runs ingest ~10K errors, produce ~20–50 root-cause clusters, file Phabricator tasks with full investigation context, and delegate fixes to AI agents that locate the bug, write a fix with tests, and submit a diff for human review — eliminating the 7–10 duplicate tasks per error class that manual monitoring produced (from abstract only).
  • How: A three-stage clustering stack — deterministic regex (36+ patterns), TF-IDF + DBSCAN for unknown errors, then LLM semantic merging (Llama 3.1-70B) — with rate-based severity detection scaled to fleet size, and a multi-layer dedup system (exact cluster ID, flexible title, normalized title with diff migration) to prevent duplicate tasks across runs.
  • Where applicable: The pipeline is Meta-internal (Scuba, Phabricator), but every stage maps to standard equivalents elsewhere; the layered "deterministic first, ML for the residue, LLM for the remainder" classification and the human-review gate are directly transferable design decisions. Error-fix autonomy is bounded to the Spark codebase context.

items.title: The Agent Feed: A Communication Layer for Multi-Agent Collaboration
items.text:
@Scale: AI & Data 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 17 June 2026

Abstract

Chinmay Gandhi, Vlad Tsvang, Patrick Walsh (Meta)

  • Why: Signals where multi-agent systems are heading: when many agents work the same problem, the missing primitive is a shared, trust-ranked communication layer — an early stab at what agent-to-agent interoperability might look like.
  • What: A standardized API where agents publish findings, read each other's outputs, and collaborate: specialist agents contribute evidence, a coordinating agent ranks competing hypotheses against independent sources, and human thumbs-up/down feedback shapes which findings and agents get promoted (from abstract only).
  • How: A tiered channel system ranks agent output by trust level (Core > Validated > Experimental) with self-serve onboarding and quality-gated graduation, so responders always see highest-confidence findings first; consensus strengthens as independent signals corroborate.
  • Where applicable: Built for incident-response context at Meta but explicitly generalized: wherever multiple agents operate on a shared artifact, you need a structured communication layer, a consensus mechanism, and a trust framework. Early-stage pattern, no scale numbers given.

Velox's appearance here and in the agent-memory poster is a notable shared-substrate trend.

items.title: Building scalable AI cloud interconnects with SRv6 + 3 min Q&A
items.text:
@Scale: Networking 2026 digest Program Core pick 25 August 2026

Abstract

Alexey Gorovoy (Nebius)

  • Why: AI-cloud tenants need predictable bandwidth into their virtual networks and services that behave identically from the virtual edge out to the WAN. Nebius' answer — SRv6 as the single architectural building block across both domains — removes the protocol-translation seam that plagues multi-domain interconnects. Directly relevant to the PM's cloud, interconnect, and segment-routing interests.
  • What: Nebius' evolving architecture for customer cloud interconnects: SRv6 bridges the virtual cloud environment with the physical network edge, enabling end-to-end VPN and traffic-engineering services without protocol translation between datacenter and WAN domains, with latest implementation experience shared. (from abstract only)
  • How: SRv6 network programming — segment-encoded service instructions — applied uniformly from the cloud edge across datacenter and WAN, so one forwarding architecture carries customer VPNs and traffic engineering end to end instead of stitching per-domain protocols.
  • Where applicable: Nebius' AI cloud — a single-operator, SRv6-capable fabric is required end to end, so it is operator-specific. The unifying pattern (one overlay architecture across domains instead of DC/WAN protocol stitching) applies to any provider or large enterprise building multi-domain interconnects.

segment-routing cloud interconnection

items.title: Co-Designing Communication for AI Accelerators
items.text:
@Scale: Networking 2026 digest Program Core pick 25 August 2026

Abstract

Rajeev Nair (Meta), Wes Bland (Meta)

  • Why: MTIA 300 treats communication as a first-class architectural citizen — dedicated message engines — and introduces "network fungibility," where the same NIC hardware flexes between scale-up and scale-out roles. That flexibility is a genuinely different point in the accelerator interconnect design space, relevant both to AI networking and to how non-GPU accelerators change fabric requirements.
  • What: The communications architecture of MTIA 300, Meta's custom AI training and inference accelerator: dedicated message engines offload communication workloads, decoupling communication from the primary compute grid, minimizing resource contention and raising both compute and network efficiency. "Network fungibility" lets the same NICs adapt to scale-up or scale-out configurations depending on production needs, within a tight co-design loop across hardware, software, and models. (from abstract only)
  • How: Communication offload into dedicated engines rather than shared-resource handling on the compute grid; NIC role flexibility instead of parts hard-partitioned into scale-up-only or scale-out-only.
  • Where applicable: Meta's MTIA custom silicon — the specific implementation is Meta-specific, but the principles (offload communication from the compute grid; don't hard-partition NICs by role) transfer to any accelerator program, and the scale-up/scale-out fungibility question is live for GPU fleets too.

items.title: Lightning Talk - 10x Network Design Engineer
items.text:
@Scale: Networking 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 25 August 2026

Abstract

Maaz Mohiuddin (Meta)

  • Why: Pairs with Loom (Core): where Loom automates physical design as a constraint system, this talk is about agents owning design judgment end-to-end, and it is candid about what still fails — validation above all. items.title: Lightning Talk - The Plan That Learns
items.text:
@Scale: Networking 2026 digest Program Core pick 25 August 2026

Abstract

Core to the PM's ML-for-infrastructure-operations interest.
  • What: Agents applied to the judgment-heavy decisions that stayed manual: acting inside narrow buy windows (continuous signal triage surfacing the handful of truly novel sites, weeks down to minutes); trusting data across systems that disagree on basic definitions (a measure-enrich-regrade loop); and choosing among coupled, timing-sensitive levers (a ranked, costed menu of moves with the reasoning attached). The stated frontier: agents that remember every decision and its outcome, so judgment compounds instead of resetting with each planner. (from abstract only)
  • How: Agentic triage over continuous signal streams, a cross-system data-trust reconciliation loop, and decision memory — explicitly framed as buying optionality under wrong forecasts, not improving the forecast.
  • Where applicable: Meta's capacity planning (years-ahead commitments, correlated demand shocks) — org-specific context and lightning-talk-stage maturity, but the optionality framing and decision-memory idea transfer to any large operator. The companion talk AI-Native Network Capacity Management covers the same lifecycle pipeline stage-by-stage with agents as first-class participants.

items.title: MetaRoCE: Meta's RDMA Transport
items.text:
@Scale: Networking 2026 digest Program Core pick 25 August 2026

Abstract

Arvind Srinivasan (Meta), Kingshuk Mandal (Keysight Technologies)

  • Why: Meta redesigned RDMA from scratch for clusters growing past a million accelerators, and its core bet — accept lossy Ethernet, push all transport intelligence into the NIC, decouple from topology — is the same architectural direction other frontier operators are taking. This is the overview talk: mechanisms, the topology it enables, and the standards push.
  • What: MetaRoCE is a clean-sheet, multipath, out-of-order, receiver-driven RDMA transport that treats Ethernet as inherently lossy and pushes all intelligence into the NIC. Decoupling transport from topology is what makes TCO-optimized multiplane FPF topologies viable on commodity Ethernet with frictionless application adoption. A conformance suite developed with Keysight validates implementations from software reference through hardware emulation to production silicon, and Meta is opening MetaRoCE to the industry as a candidate ubiquitous RDMA transport for AI-scale networks. (from abstract only)
  • How: NIC-resident intelligence with receiver-driven operation and out-of-order delivery, so the transport survives loss and reordering without requiring a lossless fabric underneath; multipath operation replaces fabric-wide coordination. The conformance suite is the mechanism for multi-vendor interoperability.
  • Where applicable: Meta's accelerator clusters (million-scale, multi-region) and its multiplane FPF fabric plans — org-specific scale, but explicitly positioned for industry-wide adoption; the Keysight conformance chain signals serious intent for portability across NIC and silicon vendors.

Together they cut design time from months to hours and produce more complex, more efficient designs with fewer resources. (from abstract only)

items.title: Resilient AI Supercomputer Networking using MRC and SRv6
items.text:
@Scale: Networking 2026 digest Program Core pick 25 August 2026

Abstract

Jitendra Padhye (OpenAI)

  • Why: Tail latency — not average throughput — is what stalls synchronous pretraining at frontier scale, and one colliding flow or one failed link can throttle a job of tens of thousands of accelerators. This is OpenAI's production answer, and it is a transport-plus-routing co-design rather than a tweak to either.
  • What: MRC, a new RDMA-based transport that sprays across many paths and actively load-balances between them, eliminating flow collisions; paired with static SRv6 source routing that lets the transport bypass failures on its own. Run in production at OpenAI to train frontier models, where MRC lets training jobs ride out network failures that previously would have interrupted the run. (The abstract calls this a three-pronged approach but enumerates only two prongs; the third is not specified in the program text.) (from abstract only)
  • How: Path spraying removes the ECMP flow-collision problem by not pinning flows to single paths; active load balancing keeps utilization even as paths churn. SRv6 segment lists encode the path, so on failure the endpoints — not the routing protocol — select alternates: failover without reconvergence.
  • Where applicable: OpenAI's production training clusters, org-specific at extreme scale. The pattern (spray plus endpoint-controlled, source-routed failover over richly connected Ethernet) is broadly transferable, but it presumes a multipath topology and an SRv6-capable fabric.

rdma ai-networks segment-routing load-balancing

Design principles: resilience, observability, deployability, and multi-building scale. (from abstract only)

  • Why: A well-described systems problem (video seek/scrub under continuous interrupting requests and mobile device limits) with a 10x measured improvement, plus a forward-looking "AI-native" refactor — a useful case study in engineering systems so coding and observability agents can extend them.
  • What: An engine for serving frames during video scrubbing in Edits: handling a continuous stream of seek requests, abandoning stale work mid-flight, GOP-aware seeking off a keyframe list, finger tracking on backward scrubs while decode runs forward, and precision-for-speed trades where users can't perceive the difference. Delivered 10x improvement in seek latency and frames shown per second. The team is now refactoring toward portability and "agentic just-in-time observability," agent skills for extending the engine, and a vision of agents profiling production data and generating/experimenting with algorithmic variations. (from abstract only)
  • How: Request-shaped adaptive behavior rather than any fixed seek policy — each scrub's speed, direction, and composition shape resolves keyframe distance, frame selection, and work-abandonment decisions differently.
