items.title: The Secret to Network Config & Security Compliance at Scale
items.text:
AutoCon 4 (Austin) digest Program Core pick Austin · 19–21 November 2025

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Vincent Phelan — Head of Network Architecture & Automation (financial sector)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The PM's network-security interest gets its strongest entry here: a working, scaled config-compliance system at a bank, with real numbers, built on open components (OPA, TextFSM, GitOps) rather than a compliance product.
  • What: A config/security compliance pipeline that runs compliance for 7,000 devices against 70 policies in about one minute, treating architecture (constraints, standardization, cutting the product count) and automation as one discipline rather than two teams. Includes five anti-patterns from 20 years of war stories — premature optimization, snowflake-tolerant design, manual data massaging, imaginary scaling fears, and forcing formats (YAML/Jinja2) on engineers who don't natively speak them.
  • How: Collect generic data from any source via device command output, parse with TextFSM ("yet to find something more generic and not AI"), filter junk before processing, and keep everything with a "not yet" adage. Compliance rules are expressed as Open Policy Agent (Rego) policies — and, in the "write programs that write programs" spirit, the OPA policies themselves are auto-generated with expected/actual/allow fields and control-mapping metadata (control ID, description) baked into each evaluation, producing per-device, per-control, per-evaluation overviews. The GitOps repo scales to 3.5M objects / ~20GB. Drift detection and remediation close the loop.
  • Where applicable: Technique is org-agnostic and built on open source; the control-mapping metadata pattern is especially transferable to any regulated environment (financial, healthcare) where compliance evidence must tie to specific controls. The architecture-first stance (reduce product count before automating) is a prerequisite, not an option — the speaker is explicit that automation bolted onto a patchwork fails.

network-security automation gitops

items.title: Toward Autonomy
items.text:
AutoCon 4 (Austin) digest Program Adjacent pick Austin · 19–21 November 2025

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Scott Robohn — NAF | Solutional

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The best framing talk of the cycle for where closed-loop network operations is heading — useful context for any PM whose roadmap touches autonomous remediation.
  • What: "Control Plane 3.0": autonomy as a continuum (scripted automation → goal-driven adaptive behavior), not a feature you turn on. Argues we already run autonomous systems — BGP being the exemplary model (distributed, convergent, bounded impact) — and enumerates the necessary ingredients: control loops fed by telemetry, fail-safe error handling for states you didn't anticipate, incremental workflow-by-workflow development, and people and trust built through measurable experiments and gated rollouts.
  • How: Phased rollout per use case (experiment → PoC → limited prod → scale), with a difficulty tiering that rings true (easy: device OS upgrade, branch CPE turn-up; medium: SP edge turn-up, multi-tenant segmentation; hard: global failover orchestration, brownout mitigation, intent-drift remediation). AI is positioned as a "how, not a what" — one tool among several, with hybrids of AI and traditional mechanisms called the most likely effective path. Reference scaffolds: TM Forum autonomy models, ETSI ENI, IBN — "models as scaffolding, not doctrine."
  • Where applicable: Conceptual rather than a case study, but the difficulty tiers and cross-domain orchestration framing (LAN + DC + WAN + cloud + security, and IP/optical alignment as an opportunity) are directly relevant to DC/WAN planning. No org-specific dependencies.

orchestration ml-for-networking

items.title: "A Computer Must Never Make a Management Decision." Can We Let AI Run Our Infrastructure?
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Wildcard pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX)

Marc Stadtherr · Kumorai Inc.

PPTXPDF

  • Why: The governance counterpart to the AI enthusiasm: the binding constraint on safe AI adoption is systemic legibility — can your organization even explain what its infrastructure is, who owns it, and what intent governs it? This framing has obvious resonance with identity and ownership models.
  • What: The claim is we have an "execution surplus and an understanding deficit": more tools, less coherence. Four recurring symptoms — operational drag, fragmented automation, broken governance, and an AI readiness gap — all traced to the same root: no unified model reconciling Source of Truth (what infrastructure should look like) with System of Record (what it looks like now). The proposed fix is an "Infrastructure Intent Control Plane" that renders, encodes, and reconciles both.
  • How: An advise-versus-act boundary: AI may act only when intent, ownership, and reconciliation are explicit and continuous; it must explain itself whenever any of the three is missing. Three grounding scenarios show the failure modes: a 300-site SD-WAN migration stalled on unknown owners and dependencies; an MSP outage with fragmented accountability; a 15k-rule firewall cleanup impossible without explicit intent ("maintain until Q2 decommissioning" vs "delete this rule").
  • Where applicable: Conceptual, with vendor framing (Kumorai) rather than a deployed system. Still, the 30-second test it implies — can you explain what happens when the AI is wrong? — is a useful gate for any agentic-ops roadmap, and it converges with the supervision tiers in the Lerena talk.

ml-for-networking automation

items.title: Architecting Network Automation with Software Engineering Principles
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Wildcard pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Leandro Lerena · zebbra AG (per slides)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The most genuinely novel technical idea in the program: applying database-transaction semantics and typed safety profiles to network operations — and deriving a principled safety model for agentic AI from it.
  • What: A response to scripts reaching their structural limits (no versioning, unknown safety profiles, undetectable race conditions, weak auditability). The replacement: "function blocks" with declared properties (pure / idempotent / reversible), pessimistic locking, and a workflow state machine distinguishing FAILED_SAFE (pure steps only, or rollback succeeded) from FAILED_UNSAFE (side effects may have occurred; resources stay locked to prevent more workflows from touching unknown state).
  • How: Race conditions are treated as the read-modify-write problem relational databases already solved — a central orchestrator locks context, executes blocks transactionally, rolls back reversible ones, and escalates unsafe ones. Vendor plugins (Cisco IOS via Scrapli, SR Linux via Netmiko, etc.) implement capability interfaces so business logic stays vendor-agnostic; every block is tested against netlab virtual labs via pytest fixtures (remote-lab developer preview on GitHub). The agentic tiers fall out naturally: autonomous read-only agents (pure blocks only), autonomous allow-list (pre-approved idempotent/reversible blocks), and supervised everything else — agents never touch device credentials.
  • Where applicable: Greenfield framework thinking from a consultancy, not a hyperscaler postmortem — but the safety-tier model is directly reusable by anyone designing the agent-to-network boundary, which this PM will likely have to opine on soon.

automation orchestration

items.title: Automating firewall rule deployment in a highly regulated environment
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

João Soares · Ørsted (per talk content)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The strongest network-security item in the program: policy-as-code firewall automation with hard production numbers, in a highly regulated energy company.
  • What: DRAGØN, Ørsted's self-service firewall platform: internal customers define, validate and deploy their own rules via a request form or full GitOps workflow, with no firewall team involvement. Results as of 2026: 40+ teams, 150+ users, 3,500+ successful deployments, 3,000+ rejected-by-validation attempts, automated requests 0% → 80%, human-handled lead time down 88% — and total request volume up ~250%, exposing the hidden cost of the old slow process.
  • How: Security principles were moved out of SharePoint/Word/gut-feeling into policy-as-code: custom Nautobot models abstracting business/security concepts, related to real network constructs, connected by policy, exposed to humans via GUI and machines via API. Validation runs automatically against those policies; security is pulled in automatically when a rule requires it; Terraform deploys to the firewall management platform and Ansible commits to the firewalls. Compliant-by-design, fully versioned and revertable.
  • Where applicable: Regulated-enterprise specific (Danish critical energy infrastructure), but the pattern — security policy as queryable models rather than documents, plus treating the automation as a real product with versioning/changelog/support — transfers to any security-governed org.

firewall automation network-security

items.title: Automation at Scale Across Domains: DC, Campus, and WAN
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Christian Breunig · Network Architect — Rohde & Schwarz

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: A full EVPN-VXLAN fabric program — dual DCs, campus, WAN — with a quantitative answer to "how much Day-2 work will there really be?" (much more than you think).
  • What: 500+ devices under unified Git/Ansible/GitLab CI. Change volume grew from 109 (2021) to 1,060 (2025) as the network became a service-provider-like internal backbone — the "few VLANs a year" assumption died quickly. They maintain a 100% EVE-NG replica of the network at all times and spend ~80% of their time in the QA environment.
  • How: Declarative, data-driven model: NetBox as SoT, data determines what gets rendered (VLANs on port-channels, VLAN database, VNIs). One inventory per domain (DC/LAN/WAN) with domain-specific inheritance (DC.yml/LAN.yml/WAN.yml); ANTA for post-change validation (e.g., detecting decommissioned endpoint ports); ansible-lint/yamllint enforced. Scaling tips include 2-byte vs 4-byte ASN pitfalls (the RD is only 32-bit) and careful MLAG peer-link addressing to avoid customer-VRF conflicts.
  • Where applicable: Single-vendor (Arista + AVD + CloudVision) — that's the constraint. The QA-digital-twin discipline, the change-rate data, and the MLAG/ASN gotchas transfer to any EVPN fabric program.

items.title: From Data to Decisions: Real-Time Network Context
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Adjacent pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Víctor Fernández · Senior Network & Systems Architect — Colt Technology Services

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The data-layer talk that underpins both safer automation and the agentic-AI direction: unifying configs, telemetry, BGP data, service relationships, and change history into one live model.
  • What: A real-time context platform (ingest → normalize → relate → expose) that answers, when an interface goes down: which services are affected, which customers, whether redundancy exists, and whether there was a recent change. Exposed via API, MCP, and web UI to three consumer types — engineers, automation, and agents.
  • How: The core scenario: a change in New York and a degradation in Paris — independent events or a hidden dependency? Lessons from applying it at scale: data quality over everything, "same thing, same id" identifiers, relationships expose hidden risks, semantics over links. Framing: "automation scales actions, context speeds up decision-making."
  • Where applicable: Colt-scale carrier environment; requires serious data-quality discipline first. The MCP exposure makes it a concrete early example of the agent-context plumbing several other talks gesture at.

items.title: GitOps the Hard Way: Rebuilding a Source of Truth (Three Times)
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Radim Roška · ALTEPRO solutions (per slides)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The hardest problem in EVPN fabric automation is the data model, not the tooling — demonstrated by rebuilding the schema three times before it survived production. Directly relevant DC-fabric territory.
  • What: A dual-DC EVPN/VXLAN fabric, ~40 Arista switches, automated from day one with AVD, Git and GitLab CI. The real work: extracting a coherent service model from a network that had no source of truth, discovering vendor-provided data models (AVD's) didn't fit their operational requirements, and building operator tooling (a CLI editor, validator, and search) so junior engineers could actually use the SOT. One year on, the ops team uses it daily; the biggest shift was in how they think about configuration, not speed.
  • How: Two layers: a CRA service SOT capturing service intent, and a translator to the AVD data model — service identity is global while VLAN/VNI mapping is POD-local, which forced the separate abstraction. Day-2 pipeline: edit → commit → MR → validate → translate → build → deploy, with avd-editor/avd-validator/avd-finder as operator-facing tools.
  • Where applicable: Arista/AVD-specific implementation at small-mid scale (40 switches, 2 DCs). The core lesson — service intent needs its own abstraction above the vendor model — generalizes to any fabric program.

gitops automation data-center-fabric

items.title: How NetOps Can Embrace AI to Lead Enterprise Innovation
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Wildcard pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Chris Wade · CTO — Itential

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The closing keynote and the clearest articulation of where the field believes it's heading: agents, skills, and MCP as complementary layers of an operating model. Vendor vantage point (Itential CTO), so read it as direction-setting rather than deployed practice.
  • What: Agents decide WHEN (orchestrators with observe→think→act loops), Skills encode HOW (procedural knowledge in ~100-token SKILL.md files — "runbooks turned into agent-consumable procedures"), MCP provides WHAT (a "USB-C for AI" connector to databases, APIs, tools). An honest capability map for 2026: LLMs are strong on protocols, RFCs and general reasoning; weak on vendor specifics behind paywalls, unpublished APIs, and TAC-ticket knowledge.
  • How: A build/execute/operate arc: build agents doing spec-driven development of deterministic automations (LLMs have vastly more training data for native code than Ansible YAML); centrally-run "execute" agent fleets with tools fixed and limited at build time (a read-only device-health agent literally lacks the tool to change config); and "operate" agents managed by engineers like team members, picking tools at runtime. A worked NOC connectivity-troubleshooting agent shows restricted tools, skills, and policies in action. Notably, customer conversations put AI governance and guardrails above the question of whether agents functionally work.
  • Where applicable: Vision-stage. The NAF-block framing appears throughout (down to musing "Network Agentic Forum? — can we consider agents as users?"), which is a strong signal the framework intends to absorb the agentic wave.

ml-for-networking automation

items.title: How Workflow-Driven Automation Becomes Operable Under Air Gap & Compliance Constraints
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Adjacent pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Henry Ölsner · NTT Germany & Christian Miene · 50Hertz

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: Automation under German critical-infrastructure rules where always-on connectivity is not a given — and the use-case list includes an 802.1X migration (the only identity-adjacent item in the whole program) and MPLS VRF WAN segmentation.
  • What: A transmission-system operator's journey from unmanaged Python scripts, regex parsing and undocumented cron jobs on a backup server to a platform (DINA) run by a 5-person team: 106,654 workflow executions and 719 sub-process executions, covering CMDB sync, 802.1X migration, MPLS VRF rollout, a DC self-service portal, and VM network provisioning across ~4,000 devices in 6 network zones.
  • How: The Workflow Definition Document (WDD) is the centerpiece: one formal, auditable contract per use case containing goal/KPI, BPMN workflow, UI design, data models, constraints, and external dependencies — reviewed by stakeholders on a fixed cadence. Platform principles: air-gapped by design, build once/deploy unchanged, develop without live-system access, workload distributed via Django + Celery.
  • Where applicable: Specific to air-gapped, compliance-heavy critical infrastructure (dependency wheels chains, no GitLab connectivity), but the WDD-as-contract pattern is a strong fit for any change-managed environment, regulated or not.

automation network-security

items.title: Lessons Learned Testing Network Automation Solutions
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Adjacent pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Ivan Pepelnjak · ipSpace.net

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The most transferable engineering talk of the conference — the testing methodology behind netlab, plus a multi-vendor NOS bug catalog that anyone testing across platforms will hit.
  • What: ~100 transformation tests plus ~100 error tests comparing against YAML-stored expected results (diffs reviewed in PRs); 25+ integration suites, 250+ individual tests across ~30 device types, requiring 3,700+ lab instances and days of runtime. Hard lessons: testing distributed systems takes longer than planned and vendor implementations will surprise you.
  • How: Multi-platform testing is solved by not parsing show output on ~20 platforms — instead, FRRouting probe containers attached to the device under test run JSON show commands and validate protocol behavior indirectly. Tiered CI: pre-commit (linting, some tests) → push → PR (all transformations) → dedicated server (full integration before release).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to anyone building or testing multi-vendor automation. The quirks list is directly useful: Junos advertising wide IS-IS metrics as 63, Aruba CX invalid VXLAN IP checksums, mostly-broken OSPF NSSA implementations, divergent EVPN/ARP defaults, unresolved VRRPv3 checksum and MPLS entropy-label disagreements.

testing automation

items.title: Migrating the GÉANT Network to a new vendor
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Simone Spinelli · GÉANT (per talk content)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: A two-year, zero-major-disruption Juniper → Nokia migration of a pan-European IP/MPLS WAN at 800G — physical backbone and interconnection work at continental scale, exactly this PM's core.
  • What: GÉANT (31 PoPs, 44 nodes, >1,000 services: BGP-based L3, L2 circuits, directly attached servers) migrated to Nokia 7750-SR (SR-OS, not SR-Linux) between June 2024 and February 2026, while simultaneously building the in-house GÉANT Automation Platform (GAP) on open-source Workflow Orchestrator and Ansible.
  • How: Top-down modeling: every config line exists because it belongs to the node or to a service; one network construct = one Ansible role, with lifecycle management embedded. Peering is modeled org-centrically with lifecycle states (provisioned/active/disabled), covering IX peering, private peering, and upstreams. Concrete migration example: moving an IX port where GAP finds all peers, Moodi starts monitoring, Ansible generates config, operator confirms — AMS-IX with ~120 peers took 30 minutes.
  • Where applicable: GÉANT/NREN scale, but WFO is a genuinely open, joinable community (SURF, ESnet as partners; public money, public code). The "design as the primary source of truth" and per-construct role patterns transfer to any multi-vendor WAN.

mpls interconnection automation

items.title: Modernizing Workflows as Old as the Railways: Operationalizing Network Automation
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Adjacent pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Leo Fleskes · Network Automation Architect — DB Systel GmbH (with Gerasimos Tzakis, Network to Code)

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The best data-quality war story in the program — two years of IPAM/inventory cleanup before any automation was possible at a 2,500+-router railway WAN. IPAM data hygiene is directly in this PM's wheelhouse.
  • What: Building a Single Source of Truth uncovered the brownfield mess: empty locations, "Düsseldorf" vs "Dusseldorf", VRF mismatches, DNS misconfigurations, missing or mis-attributed prefixes. A dedicated cleanup team plus daily issue reports produced +25% documented IP addresses and, crucially, organizational momentum. A VPN rollout that took 70 minutes across four teams now takes 25 across one.
  • How: Stage-by-stage: SoR interaction through small Nautobot jobs (allocation 25 → 5 min), configuration through an NSO service fed by the Nautobot job (30 → 1 min), documentation still manual. Platform scaling follows Conway: weekly integration meetings, shared responsibility split between platform team and device-owner teams, PRs reviewed from both sides.
  • Where applicable: Deutsche Bahn-scale brownfield WAN; the sequencing (data first, MVP workflows, blameless cleanup culture) and the "give us a 'let's fix it' mentality" tactic transfer to any brownfield IPAM/SoT effort.

ipam automation

items.title: NAF Framework — Deep Dive (Parts 1 & 2)
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Adjacent pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Christian Adell & Damien Garros · CoreWeave / NAF

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The shared vocabulary the rest of the conference keeps mapping to (LINX explicitly, CoreWeave's monitoring talk, the anti-patterns talk). For a PM, it's a vendor-neutral yardstick to assess automation claims against.
  • What: A tool-agnostic decomposition of any automation system into functional blocks — Intent, Orchestration, Executor, Collector, Observability, Presentation, Infrastructure — each with MUST/SHOULD/MAY capabilities, boundaries, and responsibilities. Explicitly not a protocol or reference architecture; any tool can map to one or more blocks, and you implement only what your use case needs.
  • How: Worked example: deploy a subnet across 50 mixed-vendor NETCONF branch sites — Infrahub (intent) → AAP (orchestration) → Ansible (executor via NETCONF) → gNMIc/SuzieQ/Kentik (collection) → Prometheus/SuzieQ/Kentik (drift detection) → orchestrated re-run on the failing site → Grafana compliance dashboard, closing a 5→6→3→4→5 remediation loop.
  • Where applicable: Generally applicable as a vocabulary and scoping tool; no ordering imposed and no requirement for completeness. Useful as the mental model that ties together the LINX, DE-CIX and Colt architectures in this digest.

orchestration automation

items.title: Network Operations Automation at DE-CIX
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Lucas Immanuel Nickel · Network Operations Engineer — DE-CIX

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: One of the few talks treating network automation itself as production infrastructure with SRE discipline — reliable delivery, observability, safe failure — at an interconnection platform whose fabric is the product.
  • What: DE-CIX (3,700+ connected networks, 100+ routers, hundreds of circuits) runs 15+ production web services, 20+ cron jobs and 500+ executions/day from one shared library. Two shipped patterns: a gNMIc config-generation job driven from Zabbix + NetBox, and a geospatial network view service; both deploy via GitOps in under 10 minutes.
  • How: All workloads (cron jobs and web services) run in Kubernetes behind a single standardized CI/CD path (Kaniko → Harbor → Helm → K8s, Renovate for deps). The gNMIc generator turns Zabbix host/proxy and NetBox device data into proxy configs exposing device telemetry as Prometheus metrics. "Geo" correlates NetBox + Zabbix into a live geographic view, inferring relationships from imperfect data and preferring "incomplete but honest output" over silent success. 1 in 3 deploys is rejected before production — failure moved deliberately left.
  • Where applicable: The GitOps delivery and defensive-automation patterns are broadly applicable; the scale and IXP workflows (route servers, FPU fiber switching) are DE-CIX-specific. The Kubernetes investment assumes you already run a container platform for network tooling.

automation sre

items.title: Practical Network Reliability Engineering
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Adjacent pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

John Howard · Head of Network Infrastructure — Proton AG

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: Four years of applying NRE (SLI/SLO discipline) to a real network, with outcomes: 10x capacity since 2021, -40% per-port cost, zero extra headcount, zero out-of-hours change windows.
  • What: A reframing from device health to capabilities and services: a 100G wavelength is a service; "packets DC1→DC2 within 8–10ms with N+1 redundancy" is a capability — and capabilities map cleanly to SLIs. Notably, "we missed targets early on. That was a feature not a bug — it surfaced which layer needed attention."
  • How: Design contracts between layers (Edge ↔ Core ↔ Fabric ↔ OOBM) and between network and applications — e.g., apps never exceed 50% of assigned capacity (p99), the network never reduces capacity >50%, anycast instead of VRRP, default-deny VRF egress. SLIs composed in Prometheus recording rules (port state + MACsec CA + IS-IS adjacency + BGP session = DCI health); a gNMIc/NATS/Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager stack with Sloth for SLO burn-downs; canary rollouts and auto-isolation for residual risk.
  • Where applicable: Proton-specific design (EVPN fabrics, MACsec-protected DCI wavelengths), but the capability→SLI method and the bilateral contract framing are generally applicable. Includes a hot take worth arguing with: you cannot be a network engineer and a software engineer concurrently — pick one.

sre observability

items.title: Reaching Fully Automated Backbone Networks: A Network Developer's Journey
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Eugen Serban & Bartek Bacal · Swisscom

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: A production SRv6 backbone at carrier scale, with the honest four-year delta between architecture PowerPoints and reality — squarely in this PM's WAN/protocol territory.
  • What: Today: >3,000 devices (~10k target) running SRv6 orchestrated by NSO with zero manual CLI, >25k public-facing service instances (>150k target), and zero escalated major incidents. The candid part: standardization struggles, early engineering choices that hurt, toolkit woes, organizational and cultural hurdles (Dev vs Ops, Network Engineer vs Developer), and northbound processes that didn't adapt.
  • How: A virtual dev stage with repeatable testing superseded earlier tooling; automatic documentation; a deliberately small standardized service catalog (L2VPN/EVPN, L3VPN, SRv6) so each component is replaceable. Open challenges named explicitly: true CI/CD, scale testing (YANG leafrefs and "for loops" causing exponential runtime growth), and closed-loop self-healing split into awareness → analysis → decision → execution.
  • Where applicable: Swisscom-specific SP environment, NSO-centric. The org lessons (the hardest problems were not the network) and the scale-testing pitfalls transfer to any backbone automation program.

segment-routing automation

items.title: Rethinking Network Monitoring
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Christian Adell & David Flores · CoreWeave

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: The clearest architectural statement at the conference that monitoring is the feedback signal for automation, not a dashboard problem — from a GPU-cloud operator running hyperscale DC fabrics.
  • What: The argument is that the gap isn't tooling but architecture: observability is a pipeline (collector → processor → distribution → persistence → visualization) that must be diverse (metrics, logs, flows, state, config), integrable (tied to the SoT and the orchestrator so the loop closes), and scalable (federated, cardinality-aware). The stated goal: a device added to the SoT starts being monitored automatically; a 3am interface degradation is verified and remediated by a workflow, no human.
  • How: Normalize multi-vendor telemetry (gNMI vs SNMP schemas) into a common shape; enrich with SoT context (role, location, owner, maintenance status) — but only with labels that drive decisions, since every label multiplies time series. SoT decides what gets monitored (push/webhook over periodic sync); "an alert is a contract, not a notification" — alerts must be machine-consumable by the orchestrator.
  • Where applicable: The pipeline pattern is vendor-agnostic and transfers to any fleet. The "hundreds of thousands of devices" framing is CoreWeave-scale; smaller operators can adopt the architecture without the federation complexity.

observability ai-networks

items.title: Ten Years of Network Automation at LINX
items.text:
AutoCon 5 (Munich) digest Program Core pick Munich · 10–12 June 2026

Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Riccardo Verzeni · Director of Software Engineering — LINX

VideoPPTXPDF

  • Why: A decade-long incremental journey at a large IXP — customer port provisioning, MAC ACL port security, rate limiting, quarantine testing, thousands of route-server BGP sessions — the physical interconnect + BGP combination this PM lives in.
  • What: Three phases: NCA (config-as-code from structured data, Jinja2/Ansible/NAPALM, reviewable diffs, git audit trails), NCA 2.0 (unsupervised, asynchronous member self-service via API → message queue → worker), and OMS-based service orchestration plus route-server automation. A bespoke SoT (TSI) was built because nothing on the market fit an IXP with a telco's workflows but not its scale — today they'd probably use NetBox.
  • How: The standout pattern is the pause–resume hybrid model: the OMS workflow pauses when external action is required (member validates config in quarantine VLAN, invited member accepts a private VLAN, NOC patches a physical port) and resumes automatically once satisfied. Explicit guardrails: locking, serialized deploys, hash-verification of pushed files, defaulting to humans for corner cases.
  • Where applicable: IXP workflows are LINX-specific, but the pause-resume pattern, the phase-by-phase trust building, and the DO/DON'T list (don't build bespoke by default; don't over-engineer error handling) are broadly transferable.

automation peering

items.title: Panel 2: Fibre, Routes & the Fragility of Global Connectivity
items.text:
Capacity Europe 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract

Marc Halbfinger (Red HMH), Steve Roberts (EXA Infrastructure), Andy Palmer-Felgate (Submarine Cable Engineer, Meta), Paul Gabla (Alcatel Submarine Networks)

  • Why: Route diversity has become a first-class design constraint in WAN/DC interconnect, and this panel includes both a hyperscaler's cable engineer (Meta) and a subsea vendor — the closest this program gets to people who actually design cable systems.

items.title: Automating Config Deployment with NetBox
items.text:
CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract

Christopher Rössler, network engineer at the Berlin Commercial Internet Exchange (BCIX)

  • Why: A real, production network-automation story from an Internet Exchange — exactly the physical-networking source-of-truth problem (scattered data across IXP Manager, NetBox, and running configs) that anyone running switch fabrics faces. No vendor pitch; this is an operator describing how they closed the loop from intended-state database to deployed switch config.
  • What: BCIX's journey from hand-written switch configurations to a mostly automated pipeline centered on NetBox as the single source of truth, plus how that foundation now also drives maintenance prep and peering-platform announcements (from abstract only).
  • How: A four-step pipeline: collect/normalize data into NetBox with Ansible; generate configs from Jinja2 templates; diff and validate actual vs. intended configuration; deploy to switches. The interesting part is reconciling IXP Manager (INEX's IXP operations platform) with NetBox so both agree with what's actually on the boxes.
  • Where applicable: IX/peering-specific in its tooling (IXP Manager), but the pattern — consolidate sources of truth, generate, diff, deploy — is broadly applicable to any multi-tool network environment. Worth watching for how they handle intended-vs-actual drift detection in a fabric where consistency errors cause real outages.

automation configuration-management

items.title: Beyond SHA Pinning: Security for CI/CD Pipelines
items.text:
CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides

Andoni Alonso (Prowler) and Paco Sanchez

PDF

items.title: Inspecting your Kubernetes cluster with eBPF and Inspektor Gadget

CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract

Soham Chakraborty, SRE at Sematext

  • Why: eBPF-based in-cluster observability sits squarely in your cloud-native networking space: seeing TCP connections per pod, DNS requests, and syscall-level behavior in real time is the debugging layer under Cilium-style networking. Inspektor Gadget is the CNCF toolkit that makes eBPF debugging approachable without writing your own programs.
  • What: A practical walkthrough of using Inspektor Gadget's gadget suite for real-time, in-cluster debugging — TCP connections by pod, DNS requests, syscalls, and traceloop, a syscall flight recorder for post-incident root-cause analysis (from abstract only).
  • How: Inspektor Gadget dynamically instruments the Linux kernel with eBPF — no agent installation required — and the talk covers capturing gadget output in a parseable format for later analysis rather than staring at raw bpftrace-style output.
  • Where applicable: General technique for any Kubernetes environment on modern kernels; the speaker is a Sematext SRE, so expect an practitioner's framing rather than a project-maintainer internals talk, and the eBPF intro portion will be 101 if you already live in this space. The flight-recorder (traceloop) pattern for intermittent network issues is the transferable idea.

ebpf kubernetes observability

  • How: Lab-based on Containerlab with Python >3.10 and Docker locally (or a DigitalOcean playbook), moving from raw gNMI/streaming telemetry to modeled, correlated, and reactive telemetry integrated into CI/CD and automation workflows.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — vendor-neutral, open-source stack on containerized lab topology. The event-driven automation angle (telemetry → Kafka/NATS → automated action) is the piece most programs skip and is directly relevant to DC fabric operations. Budget the full morning; it's a workshop, not a talk.

observability telemetry

items.title: OpenTelemetry Tracing, not just for webapps

If you care about DNS operations or about making non-HTTP infrastructure observable, this is a rare detailed treatment.

This is one of the few talks here with genuine engineering detail promised.

dns observability

items.title: Overengineering my personal infrastructure with NixOS

CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract

Lander Van den Bulcke, Open Source consultant at Inuits

  • Why: Homelab-scale, but the networking content is real: WireGuard and GENEVE tunnels, Bird BGP peering into DN42, and fully declarative config for it all. DN42 is one of the few places to run experimental BGP outside production, and this is a worked example of the whole stack under Nix.
  • What: A tour of a personal NixOS infrastructure: remote hypervisor install (nixos-anywhere), SSH-based remote disk unlock in initrd, impermanence with ephemeral root, VM management via microvm.nix, tunnel and BGP setup, and automated nameserver/Prometheus configuration (from abstract only).
  • How: Everything as Nix declarations — microvm.nix for VMs, declarative WireGuard/GENEVE tunnels, Bird configured for DN42 peering, with monitoring automated end to end.
  • Where applicable: Personal/lab scale — the ideas (impermanence, declarative tunnel/BGP config, nixos-anywhere provisioning) transfer to production NixOS estates, and DN42 itself is a general-purpose BGP playground anyone can join. Not a production case study; treat as techniques, not results.

configuration-management bgp

items.title: Reactive Nix: Enabling Functional Reactive Configuration with mgmt
items.text:
CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides

Jannik Höfler, DevOps Engineer at Dev Specialists GmbH

PDF

  • Why: A genuinely novel configuration-management idea: Nix evaluates to a static snapshot of desired state, and this work asks what happens if configuration is a function over time instead. It's a new point in the declarative/reactive design space, from the mgmt (functional reactive configuration management) ecosystem.
  • What: The rx.nix (Reactive Nix) project — combining Nix's purely functional configuration model with mgmt's FRP runtime so systems stay declarative and reproducible yet react continuously to environmental change, instead of being frozen between builds (from abstract only).
  • How: Nix models system = f(configuration) — a fixed value per build. FRP generalizes to system(t) = f(configuration, environment(t)): the config stays pure but depends on signals that evolve continuously; mgmt's runtime observes, reacts, and converges to declared state without re-evaluation.
  • Where applicable: Research/frontier territory rather than production tooling — an exploration of what continuous convergence would mean for NixOS-style systems. Most interesting as a conceptual reframing of drift: instead of re-running to correct drift, the configuration itself is time-aware.

configuration-management orchestration

items.title: Reliable Network Backups & Restore with Ansible: Idempotent, Vendor-Neutral, — with AI/ML Diff Severity
items.text:
CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Rohit Thakur, Principal Engineer, Ansible Networking (Red Hat)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Network backup/restore is unglamorous but critical network-automation plumbing, and this goes deep into the operational pitfalls (device-native paths, transfer methods, idempotency across IOS/IOS-XR/NX-OS) that matter if you run Cisco gear. Caveat: the speaker is the Red Hat Ansible Networking content lead, so this is contributor-led but also adjacent to product marketing for Ansible Validated Content — evaluate the patterns, not the pitch.
  • What: A battle-tested backup/restore workflow for Cisco IOS/IOS-XR/NX-OS with Ansible, plus a lightweight rules/ML approach to score the severity of config diffs (VLAN, ACL, BGP, interface changes) so review and rollback can be prioritized by risk (from abstract only).
  • How: Concrete mechanics: absolute on-device paths (bootflash:/, disk0:, /misc/config) because network OSes don't expand ~; SFTP/SCP via internal file servers; canonicalizing configs and SHA-256 hashing so backups only write on change; a single role interface across the three Cisco OSes; restore as stage → replace/merge → post-verify by hash. Diff severity uses feature extraction plus rules, with optional scikit-learn, running offline — no cloud dependency.
  • Where applicable: Cisco-heavy estates specifically (the path and OS details are vendor-specific by design), but the idempotent-backup, hash-verified-restore, and diff-risk-ranking patterns are broadly applicable. The ML severity scoring is the speculative part — expect rules to do most of the work — but the idea of ranking network config diffs by blast radius is worth stealing.

automation configuration-management

items.title: Static vs. Dynamic Secrets: What Are We Really Talking About?

CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract

Leon Krass, Technical Leader for HashiCorp Vault at SVA System Vertrieb Alexander GmbH

items.title: The Day Two Problem: Examining Decades of Infrastructure Automation Evolution

CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Yair Etziony, Engineering Manager at AMBOSS

Video

items.title: Watch paint dry - Monitoring what doesn't change
items.text:
CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract

Ole Herman Schumacher Elgesem, Northern.tech (the company behind CFEngine and Mender)

  • Why: A clever inversion of monitoring: alert on changes to things that should never change — DNS records, released-software checksums, tag commit SHAs, admin counts, unsigned commits — as a lightweight compromise-detection tripwire. It's a new open-source tool launch with a genuinely simple, transferable idea.
  • What: The concept and open-source implementation (PostgreSQL-backed, modular) of monitoring invariants: anything whose change is itself the signal, tracked with full history so any change to a monitored variable raises an alert (from abstract only).
  • How: Modular architecture with a PostgreSQL database tracking history and changes per monitored variable; new check modules are easy to add. Example invariants: number of script tags on your site, checksum of a release, number of org admins, your website's DNS/IP.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable and lightweight — this pattern (change-of-invariant alerts) is orthogonal to, and composable with, existing monitoring, and is directly useful for supply-chain and account-takeover detection. Early-stage project from a talk launch, so expect rough edges.

observability troubleshooting

items.title: We Built for Predictability; the Workloads Didn't Care
items.text:
CfgMgmtCamp Ghent 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Recording

Michael Stahnke, VP of Engineering at Flox (previously CircleCI and Puppet leadership)

Video

  • Why: Not networking, but it names a fault line that will run through DC and network operations: AI/agentic workloads are probabilistic, and config-management-era guarantees (determinism, no drift, reproducible environments) don't transfer to the application layer. For anyone whose products promise predictable infrastructure, this reframes what you're actually selling.
  • What: An argument that infrastructure's predictability model doesn't fail but is simply insufficient for probabilistic workloads — a perfectly reproducible environment can still behave differently run to run — and a framework for deciding what must stay deterministic versus where randomness is safe (from abstract only).
  • How: Conceptual/operational reasoning rather than a mechanism: partitioning systems into deterministic foundations and probabilistic workloads, and adapting troubleshooting and reliability practices for "it depends" outcomes.
  • Where applicable: General and early — this is a mental-model talk, not a tool or result. Relevant as strategic input to product thinking about AI-era infrastructure requirements.

automation ml-for-networking

items.title: Advanced Innovations in SRv6 uSID and IP Measurements - BRKSPG-3198

Speakers: Alexey Gorovoy (NEBIUS), Pablo Camarillo (Cisco Systems, Inc.)

  • Why: One of the few sessions with a real end-user architecture story (Nebius) plus hard performance numbers for a next-generation dataplane that collapses VPN, TE, and NFV into a single stateless IPv6 dataplane — directly relevant to DC/WAN interconnect and dataplane-internals interests.
  • What: A status report on SRv6 uSID at claimed scale (85,000+ routers deployed across operators), a Nebius case study of a Frontend DC design that integrates VPN, TE, and NFV from front-end to peering on a single SRv6 uSID dataplane, and new IP Measurements (IPM) results: 14 million probes per second on Silicon One hardware for one-way loss, latency, and liveness. Also covers Path Tracing for per-hop visibility. (from abstract only)
  • How: uSID encodes multiple micro-segments inside a single IPv6 address, letting one end-to-end header express VPN membership, traffic-engineering paths, fast reroute, and service steering without MPLS-style shim layers. IPM embeds measurement instructions in the data plane so probes follow the same path as production traffic, giving SLA measurements that correlate with actual routing.
  • Where applicable: uSID requires SRv6-capable silicon and IOS-XR/Silicon One platforms; the IPM figure is tied to Silicon One hardware specifically. The Nebius frontend-DC design is operator-specific but the pattern (stateless end-to-end dataplane across DC-to-peering domains) is broadly transferable. Treat vendor-scale claims (85k routers) with the usual skepticism until verified.

items.title: Advancements and Applications of Coherent Pluggable Technology in High Bandwidth Transport Networks - BRKOPT-2556
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Anuj Malik (Cisco)

  • Why: Coherent pluggables are the driving force behind the IP/optical convergence reshaping DC-WAN interconnect economics (400G/800G ZR/ZR+ directly in router ports) — central to physical DC networking interests.
  • What: A technical treatment of coherent pluggable transceivers: the key components (tunable lasers, high-speed ADC/DACs, DSP algorithms), performance metrics (data rates, reach, power consumption) compared with traditional line-side coherent solutions, real-world deployment scenarios, and the trend toward IP and optical layer convergence. (from abstract only)
  • How: Covers how coherent DSP, tunable lasers, and modern ADC/DAC integration let a pluggable form factor carry coherent modulation over metro-to-long-haul distances, displacing separate transponder shelves and moving coherent optics into router/switch ports.
  • Where applicable: Optical transport and DCI design generally; vendor-neutral in physics, though examples will skew to Cisco's pluggable portfolio. Useful for anyone deciding between pluggable-coherent and transponder-based DCI architectures.

items.title: AI-Ready Data Center - Sustainability vs. Infrastructure Requirements - How to get your Data Center Ready for the Coming AImagedon - BRKGRN-2419
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Adjacent pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Christopher Liljenstolpe (Cisco), Heiko Ebermann (Vertiv), John Bean (GR Cooling)

  • Why: The facility-side constraint on everything else in this program: the cited trajectory from 16–30 kW to 150–250 kW per rack over two years is an order-of-magnitude shift that reshapes what network (and compute) designs are even buildable.
  • What: An exploration of how choices in rack power and thermal density ripple through facility design, and how AI can be used to optimize cooling energy, workload placement, and operating conditions — plus guidance on modernizing toward energy-efficient hardware and cooling systems. (from abstract only)
  • How: A panel-style session (network vendor + cooling/infrastructure vendors) working through the power/thermal design space of AI-ready facilities and where energy-efficiency optimization (including AI-driven workload distribution and cooling control) can pay off.
  • Where applicable: Datacenter planning and facilities engineering; the power trajectory figures are the transferable datapoints. Adjacent for this PM (facility, not network, engineering), but it's the physical envelope the AI-fabric sessions above must live within.

items.title: Cisco 8000 and OVHcloud a Successful Adoption since 2020 - CSSSPG-2389
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Adjacent pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Antoine Petit (Cisco Systems, Inc.), Laurent Galais (Cisco), Simon Peccaud (OVHcloud)

  • Why: A multi-year end-user deployment at Europe's largest cloud provider is the kind of case study the triage rules favor — but the abstract reads as a partnership success story with no scale, performance, or cost numbers disclosed, so keep expectations measured.
  • What: The OVHcloud deployment of Cisco 8000 Series (Silicon One) routers since 2020: deployment process, collaboration with Cisco support, integration into the existing network, and lessons learned. (from abstract only)
  • How: A narrative walkthrough of a large European cloud provider adopting Silicon One-based routing across its infrastructure, emphasizing operational efficiency and the support relationship.
  • Where applicable: Large cloud/SP operators. The useful content depends entirely on whether the recorded session includes real deployment figures (scale, migration friction, power/TCO outcomes) — the abstract's absence of any numbers is a warning sign that this may be closer to a customer-appreciation slot than an engineering case study.

items.title: Connecting Your Data to LLMs: Identity, Functions and Agents are all you Need - BRKETI-2411
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Adjacent pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Marcelo Yannuzzi (Cisco)

  • Why: Agentic identity — who is allowed to touch which data when an LLM acts on a user's behalf — is squarely in the PM's identity wheelhouse, and this session describes an authorization architecture for LLM data access, albeit with heavy Cisco product framing.
  • What: Architectures and tools for connecting enterprise data to LLMs without migrating it: real-time prompt inspection that identifies what data a request needs, determines whether the user has rightful access to it, and serves only authorized data — plus Cisco's products in this space. (from abstract only)
  • How: Prompt-time analysis extracts data requirements from the user's natural-language request, then an authorization decision (presumably against existing identity/entitlement systems) gates which data the LLM is actually allowed to retrieve and serve, keeping data on-prem under enterprise control.
  • Where applicable: Enterprises bringing GenAI to their own data rather than moving data to public clouds. Cisco-specific tooling is the demo vehicle, but the access-control-on-top-of-LLM-retrieval pattern is the generalizable part. Skeptic's note: expect product positioning; the identity architecture questions are the substance worth extracting.

items.title: Deep Dive into Cisco's Use of QUIC, MASQUE and OS Native Capabilities to Deliver Frictionless Zero Trust Access - BRKSEC-3027
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Vinny Parla (Cisco)

  • Why: Sits exactly at the intersection of the PM's identity and network-security interests: standards-track access (MASQUE/QUIC) combined with passkeys/WebAuthn and OS-native clients — the credible near-term replacement for legacy VPN.
  • What: How Cisco is building "frictionless" Zero Trust access on industry standards: MASQUE (proxying over HTTP/3/QUIC) instead of legacy tunnel protocols, WebAuthn/passkeys for user authentication, and native OS clients from Apple and Samsung alongside Cisco's Zero Trust Access module in Secure Client. (from abstract only)
  • How: MASQUE provides an encrypted proxy over QUIC so per-app access control replaces full-tunnel VPN; authentication moves to passkeys (FIDO/WebAuthn) eliminating phishable credentials; OS-native integration makes connection as transparent as associating to Wi-Fi, with private 5G as another access path.
  • Where applicable: Enterprise remote/hybrid access replacing or augmenting VPN. Standards-based in principle (IETF MASQUE, W3C WebAuthn), but the seamless-experience pieces depend on specific vendor partnerships (Apple, Google, Samsung) and Cisco's client — evaluate the protocol design separately from the product packaging.

items.title: Deployment of Micro-Segmentation in Cisco NX-OS VXLAN EVPN Fabrics with VXLAN Group Policy Option (GPO) - BRKDCN-2933
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Max Ardica (Cisco)

  • Why: East-west micro-segmentation in DC fabrics is a core security-plus-fabric problem, and GPO is an IETF-draft-track mechanism for carrying policy through VXLAN itself — an alternative to firewall-per-everything that's worth understanding on its merits.
  • What: How to implement micro-segmentation in NX-OS VXLAN EVPN fabrics using security groups and security group ACLs carried via VXLAN Group Policy Option (IETF draft-smith-vxlan-group-policy-05), covering control-plane and data-plane components, common use cases, and service-chaining simplification. (from abstract only)
  • How: GPO piggybacks a group policy ID in the VXLAN header, so every packet carries its source's security group; enforcement happens on group-tagged ACLs at the destination leaf rather than mid-fabric firewalls, decoupling policy from IP/subnet and following workloads anywhere in the fabric.
  • Where applicable: NX-OS VXLAN EVPN fabrics specifically (Cisco implementation of a draft-stage IETF mechanism — note it's not yet a ratified standard). The policy-follows-workload pattern is general, but interop across vendors is limited while the draft is immature.

items.title: Designing Routed Optical Networks: IP/MPLS Considerations - BRKSPG-2029
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Emerson Moura (Cisco)

  • Why: Routed Optical Networking (RON) — collapsing IP and DWDM into one managed layer — is a genuine architectural shift in WAN/DCI economics, and this is the IP-routing-layer half of the story, which is where the interesting design questions live.
  • What: How the IP routing layer of a RON architecture works: how a simpler, IP-centric multi-service design reduces operator cost, improves asset utilization and resiliency, and enables network optimization for distributed applications, content, and peering. Includes a traditional IP/DWDM vs. RON comparison. (from abstract only)
  • How: Rather than managing a separate optical layer with its own control plane, RON exposes optical capacity to the IP layer (coherent pluggables in routers), so routing decisions account for optical reach and spectrum directly — simplifying the architecture and letting the IGP/BGP layer drive end-to-end path selection.
  • Where applicable: Service-provider and large DCI WANs primarily; requires coherent-pluggable-capable routers and a greenfield-ish willingness to restructure transport operations. Less applicable to enterprise campuses or small DC footprints.

items.title: Ethernet Based Fabric for AI Cluster - Powered by Silicon One & SONiC, an Ultra High Performance, Scalable & Non-Blocking Ethernet Fabric - BRKCOC-3005
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Lieven Colman (Cisco), John Banner (Cisco)

  • Why: AI-cluster fabric build-out is the hottest physical-DC topic right now, and this is a practitioner's account of actually standing up non-blocking Ethernet fabrics for 256- and 512-GPU training clusters — scale, config choices, and failure discussion, not just a roadmap.
  • What: A Cisco-on-Cisco internal deployment story covering the technology stack (Silicon One switching running SONiC, Nexus-based networks), the key configuration decisions, the challenges hit, and lessons learned while building production AI-cluster fabrics. (from abstract only)
  • How: Builds non-blocking (oversubscription-free) Ethernet fabrics for GPU compute using commodity-OS (SONiC) on Silicon One silicon, integrated with Nexus-based underlay/management networks; the abstract promises concrete design trade-offs rather than architecture diagrams alone.
  • Where applicable: Cisco-specific silicon and NOS stack, but the design questions (buffering, congestion management, non-blocking topology at 256–512 GPU scale) apply to any Ethernet-for-AI effort. Watch for whether they discuss RoCEv2/PFC vs. alternative lossless approaches — the abstract doesn't say which they chose.

items.title: Everything You Ever Wanted to Know about Power in Routers and Switches (and Quite a Bit More) - BRKGRN-2161
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: LJ Wobker (Cisco), Lane Wigley (Cisco)

  • Why: Power is becoming a first-order design constraint in physical DC networking (AI racks at 150kW+ make it unavoidable), and this is a systematic, test-data-backed treatment rather than a sustainability marketing talk. Wobker is a long-time hyperscale operator voice.
  • What: A comprehensive grounding in power behavior of routers and switches: provisioning vs. typical vs. peak power; per-component breakdowns; how traffic, temperature, and other factors change draw; PSU efficiency and conversion loss; optics power; redundancy models; thermal limits in high-power systems; power modeling; and what actually saves power off-peak — with system-testing examples. (from abstract only)
  • How: Walks from nameplate to real-world: how to model consumption from component-level data, where losses occur (PSU conversion, optics), how load and ambient temperature shift the curve, and quantifies which operational levers (e.g., idling ports, lower speeds) do and don't move the needle.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any DC operator doing capacity planning, power budgeting, or sustainability reporting — the physics and methodology are vendor-neutral even if examples come from Cisco gear. Especially relevant alongside the AI-rack-power trends discussed elsewhere in this program.

items.title: IP/Ethernet Storage Networking for AI Infrastructure - BRKDCN-2945
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Paresh Gupta (Cisco)

  • Why: Lossless Ethernet for RDMA is squarely in the PM's core, and this is one of the few sessions that grounds PFC/ECN in a concrete workload: storage I/O for AI training and inference, where a single loss can stall an entire job.
  • What: A design-and-operations guide for storage networking under AI workloads: lossless Ethernet foundations (Priority-based Flow Control) for RoCEv2, the interaction of PFC and ECN for RoCE congestion management (RCM), QoS effects on storage traffic, and fabric designs using 100G/400G/800G Nexus switches for RDMA, iSCSI, and NVMe-over-TCP, with NVMe-oF best practices. (from abstract only)
  • How: Explains how to engineer a lossless Ethernet class of service for RoCEv2 (PFC headroom tuning, ECN thresholds, RCM), and how to decide between dedicated and shared storage networks depending on QoS contention, plus operational tooling via Nexus Dashboard.
  • Where applicable: Cisco Nexus switch families and UCS server connectivity; the PFC/ECN/RCM mechanics are general to any RoCEv2-over-Ethernet deployment. Org-specific parts are the Cisco product recommendations; the lossless-fabric engineering is broadly applicable.

items.title: Kubernetes (K8s) Infrastructure Connectivity for ACI Network Designs for the Modern Data Center - BRKDCN-2663
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Camillo Rossi (Cisco)

  • Why: The session explicitly covers Cilium with eBGP and no overlay — the cloud-native dataplane combination the PM tracks — compared head-to-head with Cisco's ACI CNI, which is a useful lens on where vendor CNIs sit relative to generic eBPF/eBGP ones.
  • What: An integration guide for running Kubernetes on ACI fabrics, comparing two CNI architectures: Cisco's free ACI CNI plugin versus Cilium with eBGP peering and no network overlay, ending with a demo of both. (from abstract only)
  • How: ACI CNI bridges K8s networking into the ACI policy model (endpoint groups, contracts); the Cilium path runs eBPF dataplane in the pods with eBGP advertisements into the fabric, avoiding overlay encapsulation and keeping routing native end-to-end.
  • Where applicable: ACI-based fabrics specifically for the first path; the Cilium/eBGP pattern generalizes to any BGP-capable underlay (including EVPN fabrics with a BGP peering policy). The comparison framing is valuable even outside ACI environments.

items.title: Multi-Tier Fabrics: Network Designs for the Modern Data Center - BRKDCN-2999
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Marina Ferreira (Cisco)

  • Why: Topology and cost-engineering of DC fabrics (fat-tree/Clos, super-spine, 400G/800G economics, fixed vs. modular) is core physical-DC design knowledge, and this session covers the modern tier-expansion beyond classic leaf/spine.
  • What: A tour of DC fabric topologies — fat-tree, Clos, leaf/spine — extended to super-spine layers and hyperscale-plane designs, plus practical guidance on cost-effective 400G/800G adoption and where fixed versus modular switches make sense. (from abstract only)
  • How: Builds up from fat-tree/Clos math to multi-tier (super-spine / planar) architectures that scale past single-fabric limits, and frames the fixed-vs-modular and 40G→400G/800G speed decisions as cost-per-port and cabling/practicality trade-offs.
  • Where applicable: General DC topology design, vendor-neutral in principle; expect Cisco port-count/pricing examples. The opening is introductory (definitions of Clos), but the super-spine and 400G/800G economics material is substantive for anyone planning a fabric refresh.

items.title: Observing GenAI-Infrastructure: You Can't Protect What You Can't See - DEVNET-3310
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Shannon McFarland (Cisco)

  • Why: Directly combines the PM's cloud-native networking stack (Cilium/eBPF, Tetragon) with the emerging operational problem of GenAI workloads and agents — where runtime security and observability for LLM infrastructure is largely unsettled.
  • What: A hands-on technical session on using OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Cilium with eBPF, and Tetragon to observe and secure GenAI infrastructure including AI agents, with practical demos rather than slideware alone. (from abstract only)
  • How: eBPF-based agents (Cilium/Hubble for flow-level visibility, Tetragon for policy enforcement and syscall-level runtime security) are wired to OpenTelemetry traces and Jaeger, correlating what agents are actually doing — network flows, process events, data movement — into one observability picture.
  • Where applicable: Kubernetes-hosted GenAI/agent workloads primarily; the eBPF toolchain is open source and vendor-neutral, so this transfers outside Cisco shops. The specific value is the application to agentic/AI serving stacks, which few production runbooks cover yet.

items.title: Packet Buddy - Chatting with your PCAPs, via the Cloud or Locally on Your Own Machine! - AIHUB-2000
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Wildcard pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Dave Zacks (Cisco), Prapanch Ramamoorthy (Cisco)

  • Why: Not a core interest, but a genuinely novel application of LLMs to a networking-native workflow — querying packet captures conversationally — and it's open source, so it can be inspected and run locally rather than just watched.
  • What: An open-source tool ("Packet Buddy") that lets an LLM analyze your own Wireshark captures: answering what traffic is present, what errors it detects, and explaining packet flows — deployable either in the cloud or locally. (from abstract only)
  • How: Feeds pcap data to a choice of LLMs and lets the analyst interrogate it in natural language; the local-deployment option keeps sensitive captures on-prem.
  • Where applicable: Any network operator doing packet-level troubleshooting; most valuable as a signal of where LLM-assisted network diagnostics is heading. Note the privacy/trust question of sharing captures with cloud models — the local mode exists precisely because of it.

items.title: QKD Impact on Optical System and PQC Solution - BRKOPT-3086
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Adjacent pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Maurizio Gazzola (Cisco)

  • Why: Sits at the junction of optics and security: what hosting quantum key distribution channels would actually mean for optical transport design, and how that trade-off plays against post-quantum cryptography.
  • What: The system-level implications for an optical transport network of hosting quantum channels (QKD), and an overview of Cisco's strategy favoring PQC. (from abstract only)
  • How: Examines what co-hosting QKD requires of the optical layer (wavelength planning, attenuation budgets, coexistence with high-speed data channels), implicitly comparing that cost/complexity against a software-based PQC migration path.
  • Where applicable: Optical transport operators and DCI planners weighing long-term cryptographic risk; the abstract is thin, so treat this as a strategy overview rather than a deep design session. Relevant background for the PMI's network-security + optics intersection, but not a working guide.

items.title: Secure Operations for an IPv6 Network - BRKSEC-2044
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Adjacent pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Eric Vyncke (Cisco)

  • Why: Authored by an author of RFC 9099 (IPv6 Security Operations), this is the authoritative treatment of the IPv6-specific security deltas — practical and standards-grounded rather than vendor-feature-driven.
  • What: What changes between IPv4 and IPv6 security operations: attack surfaces specific to IPv6 (extension headers, NDP/RA issues, L2 threats), prevention techniques, and how to run audit and event correlation in dual-stack environments from DC to wireless. (from abstract only)
  • How: A structured walk through the IPv6 security differences — extension header filtering dilemmas, link-layer attack mitigation (RA guard, SEND considerations), address-scan resistance that changes attacker recon, and dual-stack logging/correlation practice — grounded in RFC 9099.
  • Where applicable: Any dual-stack network; vendor-neutral in content since it follows the RFC. Adjacent rather than core for this PM only because IPv6 ops hardening is steady-state practice rather than a new frontier — but high quality within that lane.

items.title: Securing the Olympics: The Cybersecurity Architecture for Paris 2024 - BRKSEC-2019
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Wildcard pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Piotr Jarzynka (Cisco)

  • Why: A one-of-a-kind adversarial environment — a globally targeted, time-boxed, sprawling venue network — with real lessons on architecture for ephemeral, high-threat deployments that no vendor lab can simulate.
  • What: The cybersecurity architecture actually implemented for the Paris 2024 Olympics and Paralympics: the governance, prevention, detection, and response design, lessons learned, and best practices extracted. (from abstract only)
  • How: A holistic architecture spanning governance to response, built to protect competitions against a wide range of threat actors for the duration of the event; the value is in the incident-informed design decisions rather than any single product.
  • Where applicable: Large temporary events and any environment requiring a complete, from-scratch security posture on a hard deadline; generalized best practices rather than a repeatable blueprint. Worth a skim for the operational design constraints alone.

items.title: The New, Encrypted Protocol Stack Taking over the Internet and How to Deal with It - BRKSPM-2024
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Adjacent pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Andreas Enotiadis (Cisco), Bart Van de Velde (Cisco)

  • Why: The QUIC/HTTP-3/DoH/ECH transition obsoletes core assumptions about network visibility and congestion management — a structural shift any network-security-literate PM should understand even if the session's remediation focus is service-provider oriented.
  • What: How the new encrypted stack (QUIC + HTTP/3 + DoH + ECH/eSNI) is constructed and evolving, its measured share of traffic (claimed ~50% and doubling every 18 months), how it changes flow behavior and visibility, and what techniques SPs can use to keep pace on visibility, QoE, and spectrum efficiency. (from abstract only)
  • How: Walks the protocol stack mechanics (QUIC's UDP-based encrypted transport, DNS encryption, encrypted client hello) and their consequences: application disintermediation of the network, loss of flow-level visibility, and congestion control moving to endpoints — then surveys SP countermeasures.
  • Where applicable: Service-provider networks primarily (5G spectrum, QoE management), but the visibility-loss analysis applies to enterprise security monitoring too. Traffic-share figures are the speakers' claims; worth sanity-checking against independent measurements.

items.title: Using Agentic IaC for Managing Infrastructure: the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly - BRKETI-2286
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Wildcard pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Peter Bosch (Cisco)

  • Why: Agentic AI operating infrastructure-as-code is arriving fast in exactly the network/security ops domain this PM owns — and the promising "good, bad, ugly" framing plus an explicit open call for contributors suggests honest failure discussion rather than triumphalism.
  • What: An approach where agentic AI teams create, validate, replicate, review, and approve infrastructure changes autonomously — capturing cloud-native and network state in GitHub as source of truth, managing it through GitHub, reducing PR-review overhead (claimed up to 30% of team time) while maintaining governance, and auto-writing Terraform/IaC/network config from natural language. Includes worked use cases and demos of what works and what doesn't. (from abstract only)
  • How: Infrastructure and network state is mirrored in GitHub; agents propose changes against it, learn from review outcomes, and validate updates automatically — aiming to shift humans from reviewing routine PRs to supervising agent teams.
  • Where applicable: Teams already running Terraform/IaC with GitHub-centric workflows. Explicitly experimental (the speaker asks the audience to help test and contribute). Caution: autonomous PR approval for network changes is a governance and safety frontier — the "ugly" section is likely the most valuable part.

items.title: Using Ethernet for AI Networking - CISCOU-2038
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Peter Jones (Cisco)

  • Why: The Ethernet-vs-InfiniBand question for AI clusters is the defining physical-DC debate of this cycle, and Peter Jones is a long-time standards hand at Cisco; this frames what Ethernet still needs to solve to win the AI fabric.
  • What: A short strategic session on the unprecedented GenAI-driven build-out of AI-focused datacenters, InfiniBand's incumbency, and what it will take for standards-based Ethernet to displace it — a requirements list for Ethernet-based AI networking. (from abstract only)
  • How: Expected to cover the well-known gaps (lossless behavior without fabric-wide PFC pathology, congestion control, multi-job performance isolation, scale-out topology) and how standards efforts (e.g., the Ultra Ethernet direction) aim to close them; the abstract itself is short, so depth must be verified from the recording.
  • Where applicable: Strategic rather than a how-to; relevant to anyone planning AI-cluster fabrics or evaluating vendor AI-Ethernet offerings. Cisco-employee speaker means expect a pro-Ethernet (and pro-Cisco) framing.

items.title: VXLAN BGP EVPN Multi-Site - BRKDCN-2913
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Lukas Krattiger (Cisco)

  • Why: DC-to-DC interconnect is core to the PM's remit; this is the canonical session on how Cisco thinks separate EVPN fabrics should be stitched together, and where the approach is heading.
  • What: The evolution of Cisco's approaches for interconnecting separate VXLAN BGP EVPN fabrics — from multi-pod to multi-fabric to the current VXLAN multi-site design, positioned as the recommended interconnect for discrete EVPN islands. (from abstract only)
  • How: Uses the VXLAN data plane with EVPN as control plane across sites — typically via a DCI overlay where EVPN routes leak between sites with scoped route targets and designated-forwarder election extended across sites, aiming for L2 extension plus integrated L3 without full-mesh state.
  • Where applicable: Explicitly NX-OS standalone VXLAN EVPN only — it excludes ACI's multi-pod/multi-site solutions, so multi-vendor or ACI shops get design philosophy rather than recipes. The general multi-site EVPN patterns are broadly applicable.

items.title: VXLAN EVPN: A Deep Dive into Packet Forwarding - BRKDCN-3966
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2025 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–14 February 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Lukas Krattiger (Cisco)

  • Why: Pure dataplane-internals material — exactly the kind of "what actually happens in the silicon" session the PM values. Krattiger's deep dives are typically among the most technically dense Cisco Live breakouts.
  • What: A packet-by-packet walkthrough of VXLAN EVPN forwarding: how bridging and routing work, how multi-destination (BUM) traffic is handled, and what happens from ingress VTEP through the underlay to egress VTEP and beyond. (from abstract only)
  • How: Follows a single packet's life through VTEP encapsulation, ARP/suppression behavior, routing between VNIs, and multicast/ingress-replication handling of broadcast traffic — the mechanics that determine real-world behavior such as asymmetric vs. symmetric IRB and head-end replication scaling.
  • Where applicable: NX-OS standalone VXLAN EVPN (the session is a companion to the multi-site talk below). The forwarding concepts are generic to any VXLAN EVPN fabric, though implementation details (e.g., specific replication modes) are Cisco-specific.

items.title: 400G, 800G, and Terabit Pluggable Optics: What You Need to Know - BRKOPT-2699
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2026 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–13 February 2026

Abstract

Mark Nowell (Cisco), Errol Roberts (Cisco)

  • Why: The optics roadmap determines what DC and WAN fabrics can look like 2-3 years out — form factor, reach, power, and breakout capability constrain every topology decision. Nowell has long been one of the more credible voices on high-speed interconnect.
  • What: A forward-looking technical survey of pluggable optics: current 400G technologies and applications, next-gen form factors for 800G and 1.6T (including breakout use cases), the 800Gb/s and 1.6Tb/s Ethernet standardization efforts, and the state of co-packaged optics for integrating optical interfaces into ASICs (from abstract only).
  • How: Covers both coherent and noncoherent optics and frames developments around what is driving them and what must be prioritized for success — aimed at attendees who already deploy optical modules.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to anyone specifying DC/WAN interconnect; the co-packaged portion is necessarily forward-looking and standards-dependent rather than deployable today.

optics ethernet

items.title: Advancements and Applications of Coherent Pluggable Technology in High Bandwidth Transport Networks - BRKOPT-2556
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2026 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–13 February 2026

Abstract

Anuj Malik (Cisco)

  • Why: Coherent pluggables in routed ports are the mechanism behind the IP/optical convergence several operators at this conference claim as their headline win. Understanding the DSP/laser internals separates real capability from datasheet numbers.
  • What: A technical breakdown of coherent pluggable technology: tunable lasers, high-speed ADC/DACs, and DSP algorithms, plus performance comparisons (data rate, reach, power) against traditional coherent solutions, with deployment scenarios and case studies (from abstract only).
  • How: Component-level walkthrough of the coherent DSP chain, then comparison of metrics and discussion of the trend toward IP/optical layer convergence.
  • Where applicable: High-bandwidth transport / WAN and DCI contexts. The "convergence" framing is vendor-aligned (Cisco Routed Optical Networking); the component physics is general.

optics interconnection

items.title: Agile Services Networking: Scaling Across Data Centers and Workloads - PSOMSI-1186
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2026 (Amsterdam) digest Program Adjacent pick Amsterdam · 9–13 February 2026

Abstract

Krithika Moorthy (Cisco), Tim Hu (Cisco)

  • Why: The newsworthy part is not the router — it's SONiC running on Cisco Silicon One hardware for DCI. A major incumbent shipping its own silicon with a disaggregated NOS is a real shift in the DC/WAN interconnect market.
  • What: The Cisco 8223 router and Silicon One P200 processor positioned for Data Center Interconnect: deep-buffer architecture to minimize congestion and packet loss for latency-sensitive and bandwidth-heavy workloads, plus SONiC OS on the 8223 for AI networking and disaggregated architectures (from abstract only).
  • How: Deep-buffer P200-based system design, SONiC as the OS layer, framed under Cisco's Agile Services Networking architecture.
  • Where applicable: Largely a product launch session — throughput and efficiency claims will be vendor numbers. Worth attending for the SONiC-on-Silicon-One angle and buffer-architecture rationale, not for neutral evaluation data.

open-source interconnection data-center-fabric

items.title: Are You Prepared for the Next Typhoon? - BRKGEN-2499
items.text:
Cisco Live Europe 2026 (Amsterdam) digest Program Core pick Amsterdam · 9–13 February 2026

Abstract

Paul Giralt (Cisco)

  • Why: Salt Typhoon is the reference event for nation-state compromise of network infrastructure, and this session goes beyond incident retelling: it previews concrete secure-by-design changes across Cisco's OSes and controllers — operational implications the PM will have to absorb regardless of vendor.
