Video

  • Why: Routing security is moving from origin validation to partial path validation, and ASPA deployment decisions are landing on BGP operators now — directly within the PM's network-security scope.
  • What: An introduction to Autonomous System Provider Authorization, the next RPKI feature being deployed after Route Origin Authorization: each AS can cryptographically declare which ASes are expected to provide it transit, and operators performing ASPA validation can drop routes arriving via unauthorized providers. (from abstract only)
  • How: RPKI-signed provider-authorization objects let validators check a received route's propagation path against the declared transit graph, catching route leaks and hijacks propagated through unauthorized providers — complementing, not replacing, ROV.
  • Where applicable: Any BGP operator — transit, enterprise, or DC — building on existing RPKI/ROV deployments. Deployment is early, so the practical constraints (who signs objects, which platforms validate) are the things to listen for. RIPE NCC is a registry, not a vendor, so no product-pitch risk.

bgp network-security

items.title: Auto-bandwidth for SR-TE
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Dmytro Shypovalov (Vegvisir Systems)

Video

  • Why: Bandwidth-aware SR-TE has been vendor-locked to date; this is an open-standard, multi-vendor prototype with an open-source component — the kind of adoptable tooling that matters for anyone running SR policies across a WAN or DC interconnect.
  • What: A prototype auto-bandwidth solution for Segment Routing Traffic Engineering that is open-standard and multi-vendor (in contrast to existing vendor-specific mechanisms), plus an open-source "SR-TE bandwidth sampler" that collects SR policy counters via gNMI, calculates traffic rates, and converts them into BGP-LS format per RFC 9857. (from abstract only)
  • How: Streaming telemetry of SR policy counters (gNMI) → traffic-rate computation → BGP-LS encoding per RFC 9857, so the SR-TE control plane or controller can resize policies from measured load without any vendor-proprietary signaling.
  • Where applicable: Networks running SR policies — SP WANs and large DC-interconnect fabrics; requires gNMI-capable devices and BGP-LS support for the relevant encodings. It is explicitly a prototype, so expect a demo and roadmap rather than production tooling. Vegvisir Systems is a vendor in this space, but the open-source sampler lowers the pitch risk; evaluate the open components on their own merits.

segment-routing automation

items.title: Automate what makes sense: Data, principles and practice
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Brian Jeggesen (no affiliation listed)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Diagnoses the commonest automation failure mode — tools are fine, the organization stalls — and gives a concrete starting step rather than a framework pitch.
  • What: An explanation of why "automate what makes sense" becomes a permanent excuse to automate nothing: unclear definitions of "safe" and "correct," fragile inputs, and changes that can't be proven before shipping. Offers a pragmatic path to make automation a normal way of working, with guardrails and evidence instead of optimism, and a first step implementable immediately. (from abstract only)
  • How: Principles-and-practice approach — pre-ship proof of correctness, guardrails, and incremental confidence-building rather than heroic one-off projects.
  • Where applicable: Any network organization; general technique with no scale or topology dependency.

automation

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Thomas Weible (no affiliation listed; material made with FLEXOPTIX Research)

Video

  • Why: Grid and spectrum planning for 800G/1.6T superchannels is a near-term, irreversible decision for anyone owning DWDM for DC/WAN interconnect; filter choices made today can lock a network out of 1.6T tomorrow.
  • What: A case for moving DWDM channel plans to larger grids (up to 400GHz, with COTS filters) to accommodate 400G/800G/1.6T coherent superchannels, while retaining backward compatibility with legacy 50GHz services — and an argument that IP engineers must now understand coherent optics in the IPoDWDM era. (from abstract only)
  • How: High-baud coherent superchannels need far more spectrum than legacy 50/100GHz slots; coherent detection being "blind" to anything but its own wavelength enables filterless topologies, but at the cost of flexibility. Wider COTS filters both open the growth path to 1.6T and coexist with legacy narrow-grid services.
  • Where applicable: Operators of their own DWDM/IPoDWDM infrastructure — DC interconnect, metro, and regional transport. Networks locked into 50GHz-gridded plants face the harder migration. The content is standard transport engineering despite the FLEXOPTIX Research affiliation; discount for any product positioning around their filter/solution portfolio.

optics capacity-planning

items.title: Command-Line to Codebase: Learning Software to Expand Your Engineering Toolkit
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Thomas Kjær (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: A replicable method for network engineers building small software tools, anchored on ECMP troubleshooting — a problem anyone running DC fabrics knows is painful and manual.
  • What: The story of building a small ECMP-aware probing tool while learning a new programming language, starting from familiar tools (traceroute, Wireshark, RFCs). The contribution is the method, not the tool: start in a domain you trust, measure everything, build in small slices, test one change at a time, explain results to yourself as you go. (from abstract only)
  • How: Incrementally translating a manual troubleshooting workflow into code, with validation steps at each slice.
  • Where applicable: Any network engineer; ECMP troubleshooting is universal. Light on novel technical results — the value is the low-risk method for starting and sustaining small tool projects.

troubleshooting automation

items.title: Geopolitics and Digital Sovereignty in Greenland
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Wildcard pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Signe Ravn-Højgaard (Tænketanken Digital Infrastruktur)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: An extreme-case stress test of resilience design: an entire national ecosystem hanging off two submarine cables with routing terminating abroad. It exposes failure modes (single-corridor dependence, no traffic localization) that softer versions exist in most networks.
  • What: An examination of Greenland's structural dependence on U.S.-controlled infrastructure across multiple layers: two submarine cables plus limited satellite links, routing and traffic flows largely terminating outside Greenland, and minimal local traffic localization — and how that constrained path diversity intersects with heightened geopolitical attention. (from abstract only)
  • How: Case analysis of connectivity topology and traffic flows (15-minute short talk).
  • Where applicable: Greenland-specific, but the failure patterns — path diversity below the redundancy threshold, external hosting, no local traffic retention — generalize directly to any WAN resilience review. A good forcing function for asking "what is our two-cable equivalent?"

internet-governance interconnection

items.title: How far can you get with IX Route Servers?
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ben Cartwright-Cox (bgp.tools)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Peers rarely question whether route server routes are actually imported; this replaces that folklore with measurement across many exchanges. Evidence-based peering strategy at a large scale.
  • What: A quantification of route server effectiveness — how relevant they are, how many participants actually import from them, and who those importers are — using the bgp.tools route collector network's deployment footprint across many internet exchanges. (from abstract only)
  • How: Collector-based observation at many IX fabrics, comparing routes offered by route servers against what participant networks actually accept.
  • Where applicable: IXP participants of all sizes; findings depend on bgp.tools's collector footprint (large but not exhaustive). Useful input for deciding how much to invest in bilateral peering vs. relying on the RS.

peering bgp measurement

items.title: Introduction to Design-Driven Network Automation
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Mark Coleman (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: The design/intent layer above config generation is where network automation platforms are converging; this gives the conceptual grounding and — usefully — covers where the approach still fails.
  • What: Design-driven automation treats the high-level design as a first-class artifact: an explicit model of topology, roles, relationships, and constraints, independent of any device configuration. Traces the idea from early topology-aware NMS and fabric controllers to modern intent-based systems, and covers how state, drift, refactoring, and unplanned change are reasoned about from a design model. (from abstract only)
  • How: Modeling and reasoning mechanics rather than a specific tool — how networks are represented as designs and how change over time is interpreted against them.
  • Where applicable: Networks at the scale or complexity where per-device config models break down; relevant to DC fabrics and multi-site estates alike. Conceptual survey; judge it by the "where it still struggles" section.

automation orchestration

items.title: IXP+ based observations on peering and routing changes after Middle East cable outages
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Kaj Kjellgren and Bernd Speiss (DE-CIX)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: A physical-layer failure with measurable routing consequences — exactly the kind of concrete postmortem that transfers across environments. Relevant to anyone whose traffic depends on intercontinental cable paths.
  • What: Observations from DE-CIX data of trends and changes in routing and traffic after the cable cuts near the shore of Yemen in September, explicitly framed as do's and don'ts for routing setup, with the authors arguing the findings hold globally. (from abstract only)
  • How: IXP-side analysis of traffic volumes, route announcements, and peering behavior before and after the cuts — who rerouted successfully, who lacked alternate paths, and what the shifts revealed about regional routing setups.
  • Where applicable: The specific observations are tied to the Middle East corridor and DE-CIX's vantage points (single-IX perspective), but the resilience lessons — path diversity, alternate peering, routing hygiene under failure — apply to any operator with intercontinental dependencies.

peering interconnection measurement

items.title: Merging Service Provider Networks
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Bastian Hoss and Markus Jungbluth (Xantaro Deutschland GmbH)

Video

  • Why: SP consolidation makes IP/MPLS integration a recurring real-world project, and this is practice-based technical content (architecture, routing, interop pitfalls) rather than a methodology pitch.
  • What: A technical walkthrough of merging distinct IP/MPLS network infrastructures: the general project approach, key architectural considerations, and challenges in routing-protocol integration and vendor interoperability, based on past project experience. (from abstract only)
  • How: Experience-driven — lessons from actual merge projects rather than a single mechanism.
  • Where applicable: Service-provider mergers and acquisitions; the routing-protocol and interop pitfalls also apply to enterprises consolidating DC fabrics after acquisitions. The underlying projects are unnamed, so treat specifics as consultancy experience; the pitfall list is the transferable part.

mpls routing-protocols

items.title: Network Automation in the Modern Age
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Adjacent pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Marcus Stoegbauer and Veit Heller (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: The "source of truth / data model" problem is the current wall in netops automation — most teams past the template stage hit it. This names the next stage rather than selling a tool.
  • What: A reflective talk tracing automation from template-pushing to variable storage in documentation systems/DCIMs, arguing the next stage demands modeling the world explicitly, unconstrained by DCIM limits — and that automation designers now need deeper data-modeling skills than the tools teach. Explicitly a conversation-opener, with a glimpse of an early draft solution. (from abstract only)
  • How: Conceptual — decoupling the network's world-model from the documentation system that stores it; no finished tool is presented.
  • Where applicable: Any netops team that has outgrown templates and found its DCIM's model shaping (and limiting) its automation. Conceptual rather than deployable; the value is the framing and the community discussion it opens.

automation configuration-management

items.title: Sovereignty for whom? Between digital (in)dependence and Big Tech expansionism
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Wildcard pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Signe Sophus Lai and Sofie Flensburg (University of Copenhagen)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Not technical, but it argues the sovereignty debate is missing the layer the PM works on — who owns the submarine cables and routing economics underneath "sovereign cloud" marketing. Strategic context for infrastructure decisions, from researchers who focus on the physical layer.
  • What: An academic analysis of how "digital sovereignty" is deployed politically — by governments (including Denmark's "liberation" of the public sector) and by hyperscalers selling sovereignty as a service — arguing that a persistent focus on applications and services over underlying infrastructure obscures the real power structures. Illustrates with research on global submarine data cable ownership changes and the conditions around global internet routing. (from abstract only)
  • How: Social-science research synthesis — stakeholder analysis of the sovereignty debate tied to concrete infrastructure examples.
  • Where applicable: EU/Danish policy and procurement context; strategic framing rather than operational technique. Worth the PM's time precisely because it connects cable ownership and routing to the policy language increasingly attached to infrastructure budgets.

internet-governance

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Core pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Gerhard Stein (Flexoptix GmbH)

Video

  • Why: Transceiver power draw is a growing slice of DC and WAN opex, and this is one of the few talks showing how to extract savings from data the optics already expose — no hardware swap required. Squarely in the PM's physical-optics territory.
  • What: An analysis of Versatile Diagnostics Monitoring (VDM) metrics in modern (>100G) optical transceivers, focused on Thermoelectric Cooler (TEC) current, correlated with temperature and cable length, to find operating conditions that minimize power while holding performance. Software prototypes were built to evaluate and visualize transceiver efficiency in Watts using real-world VDM data. (from abstract only)
  • How: TEC current acts as a proxy for how hard the module is working to hold its temperature setpoint; correlating it with temperature and cable length across real deployment data reveals which optics and link types operate inefficiently and quantifies the per-link watts.
  • Where applicable: Any fleet of >100G pluggables that expose VDM — the metrics come from the transceiver, not a specific switch, so the technique is broadly transferable to DC, metro, and WAN optics. Caveat: the speaker is from a transceiver vendor, so expect some product framing around a genuinely vendor-neutral technique.

optics power

items.title: Who put the "inter" in internet?
items.text:
DKNOG16 digest Program Wildcard pick Scandic Copenhagen · 5–6 March 2026

Abstract Recording

Poul-Henning Kamp (no affiliation listed)

Video

  • Why: The conference keynote (60 minutes) by Poul-Henning Kamp, a veteran of internet infrastructure and FreeBSD; his keynotes reliably challenge assumptions about how the internet's interconnection and economics actually work, and the title suggests exactly that target.
  • What: No description was published at the time of this digest ("More to come" in the program); the title points to a critical examination of what the "inter" in internet — interconnection and its ownership — actually consists of. Slides and a recording are attached to the event page, so the content can be reviewed after the fact. This item cannot be assessed beyond title and speaker.
  • How: Unknown — no abstract available; do not assume content from the title.
  • Where applicable: Unknown given the missing description; keynote length (1 hour, per the event page) and speaker track record alone justify attention.

internet-governance peering

items.title: A Toolset for the Internet of Threads (IoTh): Fine-Grained IPv6 Networking in User Space
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides

Renzo Davoli

PDF

  • Why: A genuinely novel networking model: instead of containers or VMs, assign full IPv6 identities — addresses, routing, protocol stacks — to individual processes or threads, using user-space TCP/IP stacks. Not on any roadmap you'd be reading, but it reframes what "identity" means at the network layer.
  • What: A complete toolchain: libioth (pluggable user-space stack framework with a Berkeley-sockets API where the stack is chosen at runtime — stacks include vdestack, which recycles the kernel TCP/IP stack via a dedicated netns thread + TUN/TAP, a picoTCP-ng-based stack, and a lwIP proof of concept), netlink configuration libraries (libnlq, and nlinline implemented entirely in a header file), one-string stack configuration (iothconf: "stack=vdestack,vnl=...,eth,dhcp"), plus DNS tooling.
  • How: The DNS layer is the interesting part: hash-based IPv6 addressing (names deterministically hash to addresses within a prefix, with reverse DNS), OTIP one-time IPv6 addresses for privacy, and namedhcp, a DHCPv6 server that assigns addresses by looking up the node's FQDN in DNS — so a node's identity is its name, and addressing follows.
  • Where applicable: Experimental/research; useful today for sandboxed per-service networking, testing, and VDE-based virtual labs. The FQDN-as-address-source idea and the netlink-configuration libraries are the transferable bits.

ipv6 linux-networking

items.title: BPF Tokens in Linux Distributions: A Path to Safe User-Space eBPF
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Recording

Daniel Mellado

Video

Watch the recording

  • Why: eBPF's privileged-by-default model has blocked unprivileged-but-legitimate uses (observability agents, service meshes) in containers and distros for years; BPF tokens are the kernel's new delegation mechanism, and this is about how distributions adopt them.
  • What: An explanation of BPF tokens as a kernel mechanism for delegating restricted eBPF privileges to unprivileged processes, plus how distros (Fedora is the example) can package token policies to give users tracing/observability/networking tools without root or CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
  • How: (From the abstract: walkthrough of real token policies, the delegation model, and the implications for developer workflows, container runtimes, and system services in Fedora and other distros.)
  • Where applicable: Distro and platform teams designing safe eBPF access for non-root users; relevant to anyone running eBPF-based networking in multi-tenant or least-privilege environments. (from abstract only — no slides available)

ebpf authorization linux-networking

items.title: Building Cloud Infrastructure for AI
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Dave Hughes, Lukas Stockner (Stelia)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Most "GPU clouds" are really HPC clusters with a portal. This is a full-stack recipe for an actual elastic multi-tenant GPU cloud from open-source parts — including the parts vendors never discuss (PCIe P2P through the IOMMU, RDMA partitioning, firmware).
  • What: An end-to-end architecture: standard OEM 8-way GPU servers, K8s used internally only (customer workloads run in containerized VMs for real isolation), ephemeral nodes imaged via mkosi + UEFI HTTP netboot, and a performance-focused storage split (local NVMe via SPDK at ~26 GB/s / 98% of raw throughput; Ceph for durable networked storage via virtio-fs/SPDK/Rook).
  • How: Networking is the highlight: SONiC underlay with routing-to-host, VXLAN/EVPN overlays isolated in their own namespaces (cluster / public / per-tenant), and a custom SDN where endpoints announce prefixes via K8s CRDs that a daemon translates to BGP for hardware edge routers — IPv6-first public overlay, with per-instance port slices of a shared IPv4 address. RDMA: one NIC per GPU (3.6 Tbit/s, no sharing), InfiniBand partitioned via PKeys + GUID/VF assignment, or RoCE isolated at the switches. Virtualization: plain QEMU wrapper (KubeVirt rejected as integration-first rather than isolation-first), NUMA-local GPU/CPU selection, and PCIe topology modeled through QEMU — with the pitfall that IOMMU forces GPU-NIC P2P through the CPU root complex unless you use ATS on the NIC and ACS Direct Translation on the PLX.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building or evaluating GPU cloud infrastructure. Explicitly not hyperscaler-specific — the entire point is reproducibility with open source — but it does assume you control the physical fleet and fabric.

ai-networks cloud-native

items.title: Credentials for Linux: Bringing Passkeys to the Linux desktop
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alfie Fresta, Martin Sirringhaus

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS all have platform FIDO2 APIs; Linux has none, leaving browsers and sandboxed apps with no standard way to do passkeys. This is the cross-desktop effort to fix it, with working code.
  • What: Two components: libwebauthn (a Rust FIDO2/U2F platform library with pluggable transports — USB HID, BLE, NFC, and hybrid/QR "caBLE" all supported today, TPM 2.0 platform authenticator planned) and credentialsd (a D-Bus service and proposed XDG portal for credential management, with a reference UI, a Firefox web extension, a patched Flatpak Firefox build, and Fedora/openSUSE packages).
  • How: The portal design separates frontend (protocols, devices, credential providers) from backend (trusted UX prompt owned by the desktop environment), request verification in portal style, and integration work is underway with xdg-desktop-portal (WIP PR) plus Chromium/Firefox/WebKit/Servo. The hard open problems are Linux-specific: origin scoping (how do you determine the requesting origin?) and app identity verification (Linux has no app signing keys, unlike Android/iOS), leading to a privileged-vs-unprivileged API split.
  • Where applicable: Desktop Linux identity broadly — distro engineers, browser maintainers, and anyone whose passkey strategy must include Linux clients. Third-party credential providers (Bitwarden is among the contributors) are an explicit design goal.

authentication identity open-source

items.title: Demystifying Post-Quantum Cryptography: The Hybrid Approach
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Rutvik Kshirsagar, Shreyas Mahangade, Clemens Lang (Red Hat)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: PQC migration is shifting from "someday" to procurement requirements, and hybrid classical+PQC is the only deployment path that doesn't break interoperability. This is the practical migration talk with a live TLS demo.
  • What: The hybrid transition using NIST's standardized algorithms — ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key exchange, ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for signatures — where hybrid applies only to the key exchange (X25519MLKEM768), keeping TLS 1.3's cipher-suite agility intact, plus PQC signatures for software supply chain (hybrid EdDSA/ML-DSA OpenPGP signing of RPMs via Sequoia).
  • How: Deployment math: time-to-transition (standards → vendor support → upgrades → decommissioning) must be shorter than the time data must remain secret — hence harvest-now-decrypt-later concern. Momentum numbers: ~60% of Cloudflare's human TLS traffic already negotiates hybrid ML-KEM, Chrome 116+ by default, OpenSSL 3.5+ native support, Fedora 43, IBM z16 firmware.
  • Where applicable: Any TLS-terminating service, PKI, or signing pipeline with long-lived artifacts (firmware, root certs, package signing). The guidance on ML-KEM/ML-DSA variant selection (fast handshakes vs. long-term margins) is directly usable.

quantum-safe encryption standardization

items.title: Extending AF_XDP for fast co-located packet transfer
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Debojeet Das (IIT Bombay, SynerG)

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: AF_XDP has no efficient way to forward packets between sockets — even localhost redirection today needs SR-IOV or an external switch. This closes the gap and keeps AF_XDP competitive with DPDK-style chaining. Also a published SoCC'25 paper.
  • What: FLASH, a ~700-LoC kernel extension enabling low-overhead, in-kernel packet transfer between AF_XDP sockets: zero-copy for sockets sharing a UMEM, single-copy otherwise. Measured 1.1–2.5x higher throughput than SR-IOV-based approaches, with the lowest latency among all compared options (baseline: OpenNetVM/DPDK chaining).
  • How: Backward-compatible MP/MC lockless rings (CAS serialization in-kernel, SP/SC preserved for userspace, no API changes); batched redirections with partial-TX + descriptor buffering to handle capacity changing mid-batch; smart polling with early backpressure (POLLOUT blocking, MSG_MORE wakeups) extending hybrid interrupt/busy-poll across the redirection path; a sysfs interface (/sys/kernel/flash) for chaining rules; and a Rust runtime + FLASH monitor for multi-tenant isolation.
  • Where applicable: Co-located network functions (firewall → LB → router chains) on one host. Driver support already exists for ixgbe, i40e, ice, and mlx5. Roadmap replaces sysfs with an XDP_EGRESS hook, making steering programmable via eBPF.

ebpf linux-networking

items.title: Going full IPv6 in Kubernetes: No limits, just 128 bits!
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ole Mathias Heggem (Redpill Linpro)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: IPv4 scarcity is now a cost line item (AWS public IPv4 charges, RIPE waiting list, CGNAT). IPv6-only Kubernetes with Cilium is newly practical, and this is a practitioner's account including the failure modes.
  • What: The current state of K8s IPv6 (IPv6-only since 1.9, dual-stack GA since 1.23), a production IPv6-only deployment on Cilium, and the honest challenges: organizational readiness, apps/libraries that assume IPv4, managed services (LBs, storage, monitoring) that are IPv4-only, and lagging tooling.
  • How: Concrete design choices — public prefix (requires ISP/cloud allocation and BGP to route to the cluster; per-node /64s from a pod /60; hardening via ACLs since pods are globally addressable) vs. ULA private prefixes (NAT66 or proxies for egress). Cilium 1.18 supports IPv6 underlay (example Helm/k3s config given: ipam: kubernetes, ipv6.enabled, underlayProtocol: ipv6, masquerade settings). IPv4-only services are reached via NAT64 + DNS64 or pull-through caches.
  • Where applicable: Greenfield clusters, internal/server-facing estates, and anyone paying real money for IPv4. Client-facing services still need dual-stack; cloud provider maturity is mixed (Azure AKS uses NAT66). The numbers are operational guidance rather than benchmarks.

ipv6 kubernetes cni

items.title: Harnessing Hardware for High-Performance Traffic Management in FD.io/VPP
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Venkata Ravichandra Mynidi, Alok Mishra

VideoPPTX

Watch the recording

  • Why: VPP does all traffic management (shaping, scheduling, policing) in software today, and CPU cost grows with traffic classes — a real SLA risk at 100G/200G+. This is the project's answer for QoS at 400G/800G, directly relevant to physical DC/telco datapaths.
  • What: A vendor-neutral, capability-based framework that offloads VPP's TM to hardware TM engines in NICs, SmartNICs, and DPUs. Software TM remains fully supported; upstream patches are planned (the slides also reference Marvell DPU/adapter solutions).
  • How: Hardware advertises TM capabilities; VPP adapts. Flows are classified in software (coupled with VPP's classifier, driven via binary APIs) and steered to hardware queues where hierarchical scheduling, dual-rate shaping (committed/peak, per the abstract RFC 2698-compliant), strict priority + weighted fairness, and line-rate policing are enforced. TM nodes support runtime add/update/suspend/resume/delete.
  • Where applicable: Any VPP deployment needing per-tenant SLAs at high bandwidth; the API is designed to be silicon-agnostic, but real support depends on NICs/DPUs exposing TM engines. Caveat: the slides are mostly architecture diagrams — no benchmark numbers were presented, so treat the performance claims as directionally right but unproven.

linux-networking congestion-control

items.title: Keeping applications secure by evolving OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alexander Schwartz (Keycloak maintainer)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: OAuth 2.0/OIDC are being actively hardened — FAPI 2.0 (2025), RFC 9700 Best Current Practice, and the OAuth 2.1 draft — and this maps exactly what changes for real applications, with Keycloak as the enforcement vehicle.
  • What: A standards-evolution walkthrough anchored in the FAPI 2.0 attacker models (what's assumed safe — TLS, JWKS, browsers, sessions — vs. what attackers can do), followed by the concrete practice set: PAR (pushed authorization requests) to keep flow parameters out of URLs, PKCE S256, private-key JWT (no public clients), no wildcard redirect URIs, and sender-constrained tokens.
  • How: Deep, current treatment of DPoP (demonstrating proof-of-possession): ephemeral client key pairs bind access and refresh tokens so stolen tokens are unusable — including the HTTP method/URI/proof/nonce alignment that makes or breaks a DPoP request — and mTLS-bound tokens with their operational constraints. Keycloak implements all of this via client profiles/policies validated on client update, login, and token issuance (FAPI 2.0 and OAuth 2.1 draft both supported). Migration tactics are practical: enforce one practice at a time, then "brownouts" (temporary enforcement windows) to force cleanup before permanent cutoffs.
  • Where applicable: Any IAM rollout — the migration playbook is vendor-neutral even where the demos are Keycloak. Especially relevant if you operate public clients or SPAs, where DPoP changes the threat model for token theft.

authorization authentication standardization

items.title: Lessons from scaling BPF to detect RDMA Device Drivers Bugs in real time
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Prankur Gupta, Maksim Samoilov (Meta)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: RDMA driver bugs are a top killer of AI training jobs — 10–20% of Meta's daily AI job crashes are RDMA-related (syscall errors), wasting 32K+ GPU-hours in six months, 5K+ attributable to the RDMA subsystem. This is the eBPF observability answer, with measured production overhead.
  • What: RDMATracer, an eBPF-based framework that detects RDMA driver bugs in real time by tracing the opaque control path between verbs ioctls and the NIC, then differring live traces against known-good ones. Diagnosis time dropped from 10+ minutes to seconds.
  • How: Since all RDMA interactions map to one syscall, they use static analysis to prune the traced call graph (skip reads, pure-kernel internals, refcount/cleanup functions; focus per-vendor driver calls). They chose fexit over kretprobes (~72% of the overhead), shared maps with a ~256KB ring buffer for error context, per-CPU counters for syscall/error/errno tracking, and a reactive "collect on error" design. Production impact: bpf_tax p50 down 88.7%, p99 down 98.9%, no measurable QPS change.
  • Where applicable: Any large RDMA fleet (Meta-scale, but the static-analysis pruning idea generalizes to other opaque syscall interfaces). Notably it triaged a bug in a black-box vendor driver that dmesg alone couldn't localize.

items.title: OpenPERouter: Turning Your Kubernetes Nodes into a Provide Edge Router
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Miguel Duarte, Federico Paolinelli (Red Hat)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Bridges the PM's two worlds directly: it moves VPN/EVPN termination from the ToR leaves onto Kubernetes nodes, resolving the classic "who configures the fabric" friction between networking and cloud teams.
  • What: A lightweight open-source Provider Edge router running on Linux hosts / K8s nodes in a separate network namespace, with FRR as the control plane. The host sees normal interfaces and BGP peers — anything that can talk to a router can talk to OpenPERouter. Configuration is CR-driven (Underlay, L3VNI, L2VNI CRDs).
  • How: EVPN-VXLAN tunnels are created dynamically per VNI; L3 routes (including MetalLB's, translated to EVPN Type 5) propagate over the corresponding veth session; L2 domains are exposed as veth legs bridgeable to any virtual switch. Underlay to the ToR is set up either by moving the interface into the namespace or via Multus. The result: leaves get "dumber" — no per-network tunnel config, no networking-team ticket for each new overlay.
  • Where applicable: Bare-metal K8s clusters that need L3VPN/L2VPN integration with an existing EVPN fabric. Integrations documented for MetalLB, Calico, and KubeVirt. Roadmap: SR-IOV interface handling, a Day-0 standalone systemd mode, SRv6 as just another VPN type, and a pluggable faster datapath (kernel today, DPDK-based Grout later).

items.title: Optimizing eBPF loading with reachability analysis
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Dylan Reemerink (Isovalent/Cisco; Cilium committer, ebpf-go maintainer)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Cilium still ships a compiler and builds eBPF on-target — the last major project not on CO-RE. The blocker is a genuine kernel bug class: with load-time config, dead code still creates maps and tail calls because the verifier increments map refcounts before dead-code elimination runs. This is the fix that unlocks Cilium's CO-RE migration.
  • What: A userspace reachability analysis (in ebpf-go) that predicts, given a set of global constants, which eBPF instructions are unreachable — so unused maps are never created and unused tail calls never loaded. The analysis has false negatives but no false positives.
  • How: Builds a basic-block graph over the program's instructions, evaluates branches on .rodata-backed config variables, and handles the hard cases: backtracking through stack spills, sign extensions (including the new ISAv3 32-bit forms), bitmask/shift patterns, 64-bit immediates beyond branch-imm width, and more. Cilium has 94 datapath settings, so the payoff is large: smaller images, faster loads, less attack surface.
  • Where applicable: Cilium first, but the technique applies to any CO-RE project with heavy feature toggles. The speaker also flags that the verifier's map-refcount handling could be improved in-kernel. Watch the Cilium roadmap: this is a direct signal of the project's pre-compiled future.

ebpf testing

items.title: Path Safety in the Trenches
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Aleksa Sarai (runc maintainer, cyphar)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The most bang-for-the-buck container runtime exploits for a decade have been filesystem confused-deputy attacks, including the November 2025 runc CVEs. This is the definitive taxonomy and the state of kernel-side fixes.
  • What: A walkthrough of "regular" path safety (TOCTOU on path components) versus "strict" path safety (exact-path requirements for procfs, magic links, and overmounts), cataloguing ~15 years of CVEs, and the migration of runc's codebase to a path-safe, file-descriptor-centric design.
  • How: The kernel primitives are openat2(2) with RESOLVE_IN_ROOT/RESOLVE_BENEATH/RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS, plus the new mount API (fsopen/fsmount/open_tree) to create a private, validated procfs. libpathrs (Rust with C/Go/Python bindings) packages it all. The November 2025 CVEs (CVE-2025-31133, CVE-2025-52565, CVE-2025-52881) are dissected concretely: racing a bind-mount source swap to turn /volume into a writable bind of /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern, and chained mounts faking /proc/.../attr/apparmor paths.
  • Where applicable: Container runtime and daemon authors, and honestly any privileged Unix program that operates on paths. Also a candid threat-model discussion: runc has no formal threat model, and most of these bugs live in the "misconfiguration" gray zone.

containers vulnerability-management

items.title: Rich Packet Metadata - The Saga Continues
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Jakub Sitnicki (Cloudflare)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The Linux network stack gives packets only 32 bits of sticky metadata (SO_MARK), and everyone is fighting over them. Cloudflare wants 128+ bytes for config consistency across layers, XDP classification, and drop attribution — and this is the unvarnished three-year engineering history, dead ends included.
  • What: A progress report on three successive designs: (1) SKB Traits, a per-packet key-value store — abandoned ("don't introduce a second metadata area"); (2) XDP/skb metadata via a new bpf_dynptr_from_skb_meta() kfunc (v6.18), with helpers preserving metadata (v6.15) and metadata tracking decoupled from MAC-header offsets (v6.19) — necessary because L2 tunnels and header pushes corrupt or strand metadata otherwise; (3) the current idea: an skb_ext extension backed by BPF local storage (BPF_MAP_SKB_STORAGE), which lives separately from packet headers.
  • How: Approach 3 reuses the existing bpf_local_storage machinery (flexible-array elements, map-backed) attached to sk_buff via the skb extension mechanism. The unsolved problem is memory allocation on the hot path — which is exactly why approaches 1 and 2 were tried first.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building multi-layer in-kernel pipelines (XDP → TC → netfilter → socket) that need per-packet context to survive. Watch this if you do XDP classification or drop accounting; the landing kernel version will determine what's expressible.

linux-networking ebpf

items.title: Scaling GoBGP: Lessons from Building a Dynamic, API‑Driven BGP Control Plane
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Maxime Peim (Cisco)

VideoPPTX

Watch the recording

  • Why: Real lessons from running GoBGP as a multi-tenant, API-driven control plane at fabric scale — including an honest comparison showing GoBGP scales worse than Bird/FRR, and what's being done about it upstream.
  • What: Architecture and operational patterns for a multi-tenant BGP daemon: per-tenant BGP servers, route policies, and address families sharing one control plane; tenant lifecycle (create/update/delete) handled via gRPC without disrupting existing sessions.
  • How: GoBGP was chosen for its API dynamism, path manipulation strength, and Go integration (goroutine-native, Go package + gRPC interfaces), against Bird 3.0 (now multi-threaded, fast, but static config) and FRR (multi-threaded, static). Scaling targets: tens of thousands of peers per region, hundreds of thousands of routes. The deck includes benchmark methodology and results (mostly graphs), and reports that v4.2.0 shipped some contention fixes; PR #3303 (global mutex relaxation) improves benchmarks significantly in the same configuration — an explicit call for contributors.
  • Where applicable: Service-provider-style fabrics, SD-WAN control planes, or any system needing programmatic BGP (service discovery, orchestration feedback). If you need raw route-processing throughput, Bird/FRR still win; the value here is the API surface.

items.title: Scaling Secure Network Functions: High-Performance IPsec with FD.io VPP for VNFs and CNFs
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Benoît Ganne (Cisco, VPP committer)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: One of the few IPsec talks with real production scale behind it: Cisco runs 50K tunnels, 7 PB/month, 10 trillion packets/month on VPP IPsec. The benchmarks are concrete and actionable.
  • What: A deep dive into VPP's IPsec implementation plus 2024–2025 improvements (unified crypto+HMAC single-op-per-packet, template-based ESP, full IPv6 NAT-T, async handoff tuning), with a decision framework for the three tunnel modes.
  • How: Key measured results (FD.io CSIT, 10K tunnels, AES-256-GCM, Intel ICX): policy-based IPsec is unusable without the flow cache (which is ~40x faster); with it, 1–4 cores deliver 20–49 Gbps; route-based P2P reaches 78 Gbps on 100G. Async crypto decouples crypto from packet processing, enabling 70 Gbps on a single tunnel (2.5x sync) and preventing noisy-neighbor starvation. For 1000+ VRFs, switching the IPv4 FIB mtrie from 16-8-8 to 8-8-8-8 cuts memory 41x (330 MB → 8 MB) at the cost of one extra lookup step.
  • Where applicable: SD-WAN, 5G UPF (N3/N9), edge, and large DC VPN gateways. Kernel-IPsec shops hitting per-tunnel interface or memory ceilings are the natural audience. No kernel modules, so it runs cleanly in containers.

items.title: So you want to do RDMA programming? RTRS: An easy to use, reliable high speed transport library over RDMA
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Haris, Jinpu Wang

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: RDMA programming is notoriously harder than sockets, yet it's now the default fabric for AI training and lossless DC workloads. RTRS is battle-tested infrastructure (5,000+ servers) that hides most of that complexity.
  • What: A reliable high-speed transport library over RDMA, already in the mainline kernel (drivers/infiniband/ulp/rtrs as of v6.17.7), presenting a socket-like abstraction with production-grade reliability features.
  • How: Establishes stateful sessions with heartbeats and multipath (selectable policies) with I/O failover and load balancing; sizes the connection count to CPU count with IRQ pinning for data transfers; accepts scatter-gather lists directly; and pre-allocates/pre-maps DMA buffers on the server side to shorten the data path.
  • Where applicable: Building blocks for any module that wants RDMA without verbs-level expertise — the speakers call out ML/AI training as a beneficiary of the pre-mapping work. Being an in-tree kernel ULP, it constrains you to its session model. (The event page adds nothing beyond the abstract, which this write-up is based on.)

items.title: SSH logins in practice: certificates vs. OPKSSH
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Erich Birngruber

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: SSH access at scale with unmanaged clients is an identity problem most enterprises have and few solve well — private keys on unmanaged endpoints, server-side key sprawl, awkward MFA. This is a hands-on comparison of the two leading answers from a real multi-user cluster evaluation.
  • What: OpenSSH certificates versus OpenPubKey/OPKSSH, evaluated for a compute cluster of dozens of machines and hundreds of unmanaged clients, with live demos of both from client and server perspectives (lab environment: Kanidm as IDM/OAuth provider, step-ca as CA).
  • How: Both deliver short-lived credentials via an OAuth flow. Certificates add host validation and stay within core SSH features (forwarding, agent control), but require CA setup and lifecycle. OPKSSH offers highly customizable policies (including claims-based) and works with multiple existing IdPs, but does not cover host verification — you need a third-party tool beyond the SSH client for that.
  • Where applicable: Any multi-user SSH estate, HPC clusters, and organizations wanting OAuth-bound short-lived SSH access. The comparison table is a useful decision matrix if you're weighing these two today.

authentication identity open-source

items.title: Standardization and Open-source Implementation of Attested TLS for Confidential Computing
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Muhammad Usama Sardar (TU Dresden), peg (Peg Jones, Flashbots)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Attested TLS is becoming the identity primitive of confidential computing, and it's being standardized right now in the new IETF SEAT WG. This talk comes from the people driving it, with formal proofs of why the obvious designs are broken.
  • What: A taxonomy of attested TLS — pre-handshake, intra-handshake, post-handshake attestation — plus formal-analysis results: replay attacks on pre-handshake attestation (including Intel's RA-TLS), diversion and relay attacks on intra-handshake designs (one shown to break Cocos AI), leading to a post-handshake candidate draft built on exported authenticators (RFC 9261) with a cmw_attestation extension carrying RATS evidence in the Certificate message.
  • How: The WiP implementation is Rustls-based, transport-agnostic (QUIC included, tested with Intel TDX), supports one-way and mutual attestation, and supports both the RATS "passport" and "background check" models. Notable engineering friction: Rustls deliberately doesn't expose handshake internals, and there's essentially one partial open-source reference for exported authenticators — so they implemented it from scratch.
  • Where applicable: Server-to-server attested channels where you control both ends (Flashbots uses a similar protocol for TEE-based Ethereum block building), and proxies that terminate attestation for naive clients. Explicitly not yet: browsers (APIs don't expose TLS keying material) or paths through TLS-terminating proxies — many deployments paper over this with nested encryption.

tls encryption standardization

items.title: Suricata 8 - shaping the future of network detection and prevention
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Eric Leblond, Peter Manev (OISF / Stamus Networks)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Suricata 8 is two years of work (160K lines inserted) and materially changes what the engine can do — including two new deployment modes that signal where open-source network security is heading.
  • What: Contributor-led overview of the release: 107 new rule keywords (a 38% increase, under the motto "if you log it, you can use it in a rule") for LDAP, MIME/email, DNS, SMTP, FTP, TLS, WebSocket, and DoH; transactional rules that match both stream directions in one signature (fixing a long-standing false-negative class); and datasets with JSON context so IoC matches carry attribution instead of bare values.
  • How: New protocol decoders (WebSocket, LDAP, ARP, DoH/DoH2, SIP over TCP, SDP, POP3, mDNS); 27% of the codebase is now Rust (libhtp built-in and no longer a dependency, plus FTP, ENIP, MIME); Lua 5.4 vendored and sandboxed. Two structural additions: a firewall runmode (suricata --firewall, drop rules keyed on e.g. JA4 hashes — AWS reportedly runs it this way) and Suricata-as-a-library, where embedders bring their own packets/threads and register parsers, loggers, and keywords at runtime.
  • Where applicable: NDR/IPS vendors, appliance builders, and any SOC running high-volume monitoring (100G is described as common, 400G on a single server as achievable). The library mode is the one to watch for product people — it changes the build-vs-embed calculus for detection engines.

network-security open-source

items.title: The Russian Censorship Circumvention, Tom's Traps, and Jerry's VPN: A 5-Year Journey
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Vitaly Repin

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A rare first-hand, five-year longitudinal account of state-level DPI censorship versus a commercial VPN provider (150+ servers, millions of users) — and the speaker expects these techniques to spread to other states. Directly relevant to anyone thinking about protocol fingerprinting and traffic obfuscation defensively.
  • What: The evolution of the "Great Russian Firewall": pre-2022 no VPN blocks → 2022–23 DNS/IP blocks → 2023 DPI blocking of standard VPN protocols (PPTP, L2TP, OpenVPN) → 2025 DPI detection of OpenVPN-with-XOR obfuscation within hours → 2025 white lists (only pre-approved IP/port traffic allowed). Non-technical pressure runs in parallel: app-store deplatforming, hosting bans, ad/payment cutoffs, and a 2024 law criminalizing VPN promotion.
  • How: Detection mechanisms detailed: SNI-based blocking (with ECH declared illegal in Russia in Nov 2024), DNS/reputation-driven detection of VPN infrastructure (services like spur.us flagging IPs), and partial blocks (all ports except 443) that reveal the censor's confidence level. The speaker frames evasion as statistical hypothesis testing — the provider's goal is maximizing the censor's false-negative rate — and notes that user reports from "unimportant" regions are early-warning telemetry for new blocking capabilities being beta-tested.
  • Where applicable: Censorship circumvention design, and more broadly any protocol that must resist adversarial traffic classification. The provider withheld current evasion methods, so this is a threat-model history, not a how-to.

censorship privacy

items.title: Weaving the Fabric: EVPN overlays for multi-cluster KubeVirt deployments
items.text:
FOSDEM 2026 digest Program Core pick 31 January – 1 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Miguel Duarte, Federico Paolinelli (Red Hat)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The companion session to OpenPERouter, focused on the fabric problem: stretched L2 for cross-cluster VM live migration, DR, and hybrid cloud — done with open components rather than a proprietary DCI.
  • What: Multi-cluster KubeVirt L2/L3 overlays built from OpenPERouter + KubeVirt + any bridge-based CNI (OVS-CNI, bridge-cni, macvlan, ipvlan). L2VNI stretches a Layer 2 domain across clusters with a distributed anycast gateway and live-migration support; L3VNI (EVPN Type 5) gives VMs direct routed ingress from provider networks — no Kubernetes Services, no NAT.
  • How: Declarative CRDs configure VTEPs (Underlay CRD with vtepcidr), MAC VRFs (L2VNI), and routing domains (L3VNI); FRR advertises Type 2 (MAC/IP) and Type 5 (prefix) routes. VMs attach via a bridge on the host defined with a standard NetworkAttachmentDefinition. A public demo repo and asciinema recording accompany the talk.
  • Where applicable: Multi-cluster or multi-site KubeVirt estates needing VM mobility, legacy broadcast/multicast workloads, or direct fabric ingress into VMs. Requires an EVPN-capable underlay and OpenPERouter on each participating cluster — this is a design-patterns talk on top of the architecture session above.

items.title: ASPA and Roles: What's up with that?
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Program Core pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Antonis Chariton (AS4601 | Cisco)

  • Why: Routing security is a core interest, and ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization) is the current frontier of RPKI-based BGP security — the mechanism that extends protection beyond ROAs/origin validation to AS-path verification. "Roles" refers to the ASPA registration taxonomy (e.g., provider vs. peer relationships) that has been actively debated in the RPKI working group. A talk titled "What's up with that?" from an operator/standardista (Chariton runs AS4601/Packet Clearing House infrastructure and works on RPKI tooling) is likely a candid status-and-interop report, exactly the kind of transferable operational content this program should surface.
  • What: An update on ASPA adoption, the roles model in RPKI, and the practical questions operators face when registering ASPA records and enabling AS-path verification (program text and speaker metadata only).
  • How: Presumably: RPKI-signed ASPA objects binding a customer AS to its authorized providers, plus BGP AS-path verification at receiving ASes, with discussion of the role registration semantics that caused deployment confusion.
  • Where applicable: Any operator running BGP with RPKI ROV today. Broadly applicable and standards-based (not org-specific), though real-world enforcement value depends on upstream adoption rates — which is likely the crux of the talk.

bgp network-security

items.title: EVPN – One Control Plane to Rule Them All
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Program Core pick 30 June 2026

Abstract

Patrick Prangl (Arista Networks)

  • Why: EVPN is the de facto control plane for modern physical DC fabrics (VXLAN overlays, multi-dimensional ECMP, integrated bridging/routing) — directly in the PM's physical DC networking core. The "one control plane" framing speaks to a live operational debate: collapsing L2/L3/overlay/underlay services onto a single BGP-based control plane instead of stitching VLANs + IGP + separate overlay signaling.
  • What: A position/tutorial-style talk arguing for EVPN as the unified control plane across datacenter (and possibly WAN) services, per the title and the speaker's vendor affiliation (program text only).

items.title: MPTE update
items.text:
GRNOG 20 digest Program Core pick 30 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Dr Kireeti Kompella (HPE Networking)

PPTX

  • Why: Kompella is one of the principal authors of the MPLS and segment-routing protocol family, and "MPTE" refers to the emerging multi-path traffic engineering work (the successor direction to per-flow SR-TE and PRECISION-style path steering) being pursued in the IETF SPRING/RTGWG space. DC/WAN interconnect and TE internals are core to this PM. An "update" from the author himself is a first-hand read on where large-scale path steering is heading — worth the slot even with no abstract.
  • What: A progress report on the MPTE architecture — steering traffic across multiple paths with fine granularity, aimed at fixing what per-destination ECMP and heavy per-flow TE can't do well (program text and speaker metadata only; the MPTE.pptx deck exists but was not readable here).
  • How: Presumably the MPTE label/segment approach: encoding per-path/per-flow steering state compactly so a single tunnel can carry many flows with independent placement, without per-flow session state in the core.
  • Where applicable: Operators with SR-MPLS or SRv6 underlays, or building DC-to-WAN fabrics that need granular steering (elephant/mice separation, non-minimal path routing, loss-aware placement). Vendor-neutral in intent (it is IETF-track work presented by a long-time individual contributor), but expect it to reflect HPE's implementation timeline.

segment-routing standardization

items.title: Break Communication Barriers: Scale AI and HPC with NCCL, NIXL, and NVSHMEM
items.text:
GTC 2026 digest Program Core pick San Jose · 16–19 March 2026

Abstract

Matthew Nicely (NVIDIA) — Talk, Thursday, March 19

  • Why: The internals of the GPU communication stack — symmetric memory, copy-engine collectives, zero-SM communication, and NIXL's tier-spanning async transfers — are datapath and RDMA-adjacent content central to the PM's interests.
  • What: A year of evolution across the three libraries: NCCL added Symmetric Memory and Copy Engine collectives enabling zero-SM communication; NVSHMEM enhanced GPU-initiated operations in the Python ecosystem; NIXL emerged for inference, providing async noncontiguous transfers across memory tiers (HBM, DRAM, local/networked storage) with GDS, UCX, and S3 backends. Plus developer-level material: custom NCCL collectives, KV-cache and storage innovations in NIXL, expert-parallelism patterns, and Spectrum-X plugins for multi-site scale-across. (from abstract only)
  • How: Library-level mechanisms per above; the zero-SM collectives and NIXL's cross-tier transfers are the pieces that matter for disaggregated inference architectures.
  • Where applicable: NVIDIA GPU clusters — vendor stack, but the de facto standard for GPU collective communication; the NIXL/disaggregated-inference material applies wherever KV cache and weights move between memory tiers over a fabric.

gpu-clusters rdma

  • Why: The main non-NVIDIA silicon and optics perspective on AI fabrics at NVIDIA's own show — worth tracking for competitive triangulation even though the abstract reads as pure positioning.
  • What: Cisco + NVIDIA joint work on AI networking across silicon, systems, software, and optics, with scale-fabric architectures and validated designs aimed at bandwidth, latency, and security limits of AI workloads. (from abstract only)
  • How: No mechanism specifics in the abstract — expect validated-reference-design content rather than internals.
  • Where applicable: Cisco + NVIDIA joint stack; sponsor-flavored and number-free, so treat as directional. Kept in the digest because a second vendor's view of AI-fabric scaling (especially optics) is otherwise absent from this program.

ai-networks silicon

items.title: 2038 is gonna be epoch!
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Pedro Umbelino, Trey Darley

Video

  • Why: Y2K38 is a slow-motion systemic event with a hard deadline (19 Jan 2038) and orders of magnitude more fielded systems than Y2K — and attackers don't have to wait for it.
  • What: Controlled experiments documenting how IoT, ICS/OT, and embedded systems actually behave as they approach and cross the 2038 epoch threshold — failure modes where naively implemented state machines logically reverse time — with a classification framework, and the observation that a resourceful attacker can make "2038" happen any day via clock manipulation. (from abstract only)
  • How: Exhaustive search and classification of failure modes across device classes in controlled lab environments, presented in plain language for both technical and policy audiences.
  • Where applicable: Any system relying on 32-bit signed Unix time — especially long-lived embedded and OT equipment that must be pulled from the field, tested, and remediated over the next ~13 years; general, not org-specific.

vulnerability-management time-sync

items.title: Attacking The Developer Environment Through Drive-by Localhost Attacks
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Joseph Beeton

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Punctures the "bound to loopback = invisible" assumption that underpins how developers run services — relevant to anyone whose engineers run K8s dashboards, dev servers, and tooling locally.
  • What: JavaScript from any visited website can reach services bound to localhost via non-preflighted HTTP requests; abusing common Spring/Quarkus misconfigurations or newly found vulnerabilities yields RCE on developer machines (Quarkus, older Spring) and exfiltration of AI training models from MLflow. (from abstract only)
  • How: Compromise a site developers use (or inject JS via ads / phishing to open a page), then cross-origin-request the localhost service; the talk details the browser mechanics, limitations, and what browser vendors are changing to close the class.
  • Where applicable: Any machine running less-securely-configured local services, especially Java frameworks and MLflow; time-limited — browser vendors are closing this class, but it is live today.

vulnerability-management offensive-security

items.title: BoD: Bytes Over DNS
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Didier Stevens

Video

  • Why: DNS remains the most reliable egress channel, and knowing which public resolvers forward arbitrary bytes changes the calculus for DNS egress policy.
  • What: Some DNS servers (1.1.1.1 named) accept and forward any byte values inside DNS packets, enabling a C2 channel with higher throughput than hexadecimal encoding, despite label formats being nominally limited to letters/digits/hyphen. Scripts are shared for attendees to test resolvers of their own choosing. (from abstract only)
  • How: Abusing permissive label handling in DNS implementations that accept more than the LDH character set.
  • Where applicable: Any environment where clients can reach open recursive resolvers; a short overview-format talk — quick but practical.

dns network-security

items.title: Building an unmarshelling chain from hydrators
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Speakers not listed in the program text (companion outline: "Exploitation by using laravel-crypto-killer")

  • Why: A reproducible unserialize-to-RCE chain in one of the most-deployed PHP stacks, with a shipping product vulnerable by default, is a concrete at-scale risk worth understanding even outside web-appsec focus.
  • What: A three-step Livewire (Laravel) chain to remote command execution given the APP_KEY: first a phpinfo leak via FnStream / ShardedPrefixPublicUrlGenerator, then RCE via SerializableClosure / Queueable / BroadcastEvent gadgets, and finally a rebuilt chain reaching a Terminal-initiated exit so the request completes normally (no error 500) for stealth. The whole process is automated in a new exploit mode of synacktiv's laravel-crypto-killer; invoiceninja ships a default APP_KEY and is vulnerable by default. (from abstract only)
  • How: Gadget-chain analysis across GuzzleHttp, League Flysystem, and Laravel framework classes, with payload construction on Livewire's hydration mechanism.
  • Where applicable: Laravel/Livewire applications where APP_KEY is known, leaked, or default; org-agnostic but framework-specific.

vulnerability-management offensive-security

items.title: CLI ambush
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

William Robinet

VideoPDF

  • Why: The TLS/SSL toolkits administrators run by hand are themselves an attack surface — crafted ASN.1 input trapping the operator is a novel trust-boundary problem at the CLI/PKI layer the PM cares about.
  • What: A vulnerability class common to various TLS/SSL cryptographic toolkits, triggered by crafted ASN.1 messages, demonstrated in the OpenSSL CLI and extended to other toolkits, with attack vectors that can trap unsuspecting administrators. (from abstract only)
  • How: Crafting ASN.1 messages that expose handling issues in CLI applications, then walking through the discovered attack vectors.
  • Where applicable: Any workflow where admins process untrusted cryptographic input (certificates, keys) via OpenSSL-like CLIs; general technique, toolkit-dependent.

tls vulnerability-management

items.title: From YAML to Root: CI/CD Pipeline Attacks and Countermeasures
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Hugo

Video

  • Why: IaC-driven self-service pipelines have widened pipeline access from a few admins to contributors and even external clients — this maps the resulting attack surface for exactly the cloud-native infrastructure the PM's world runs on.
  • What: A demonstration that a standard contributor account can be escalated to full CI/CD and infrastructure compromise — RCE via pipeline-file manipulation and Terraform constructs (external data sources, custom providers/modules, provisioners), bypasses of provider/module blacklists and step filters, then cloud-credential theft and pipeline persistence — followed by a defensive playbook (secret handling, runner hardening, integrity checks, pipeline log analysis and IoCs). (from abstract only)
  • How: Chaining misconfigurations and legitimate features in Azure DevOps / GitHub Actions with Terraform and Ansible, under realistic enabled protections.
  • Where applicable: Organizations running self-service or multi-tenant CI/CD with IaC; broadly applicable to modern pipeline stacks.

vulnerability-management automation

items.title: Instrumenting software builds to detect stealth backdoors and other curiosities
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Hilko Bengen

Video

  • Why: Post-xz (CVE-2024-3094), detecting build-time tampering is an open supply-chain problem; this is a concrete attempt at build observability rather than signing/provenance paperwork.
  • What: A Linux-based prototype toolset that instruments build processes (./configure && make, cargo build, pip install, CI) to generate and analyze lower-level build logs, inferring whether a binary was actually built from the presented sources and detecting abnormal compiler/linker use — with curious findings and limitations discussed. (from abstract only)
  • How: Instrumentation of what actually happens during builds, then log analysis for source-to-binary correspondence and anomalous toolchain usage.
  • Where applicable: Linux software builds generally; prototype maturity — a research direction and detection idea, not a deployable control.

vulnerability-management attestation

items.title: Integrating Zeek With Third-Party Applications
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Christian Kreibich

Video

  • Why: Zeek is the other pillar of open NDR; this covers the runtime integration surface that turns it from a log producer into an active component of detection infrastructure.
  • What: A tour of Zeek's live integration mechanisms — asynchronous intel ingestion, event exchange with custom services, web-API calls from JavaScript, runtime state load/save, and operational telemetry — with real-world applications including ML models, threat-intel platforms like MISP, and round-tripping network inventory data. (from abstract only)
  • How: Walkthrough of each mechanism with relative pros and cons and example integrations.
  • Where applicable: Organizations already running (or considering) Zeek; broadly applicable, though the tooling itself is Zeek-specific.

anomaly-detection open-source api

items.title: Lethal Language Models: From Bit Flip to RCE in Ollama
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Paul Gerste

VideoPDF

  • Why: First-cycle signal: AI inference infrastructure became a Pwn2Own target category in 2025. Every security org will soon own an LLM-runtime attack surface; this is early, systematic evidence of what it looks like.
  • What: Research on Ollama (widely used for running Llama/DeepSeek-R1 locally) in the Pwn2Own Berlin 2025 context: the architecture, the GGUF model-file format, memory-corruption bugs in its handling, and a deep dive turning a bit-flipping primitive into arbitrary code execution on a vulnerable Ollama instance — ending with a live exploit demo and disclosure notes. (from abstract only)
  • How: Analysis of how models are serialized to GGUF files and how their parsing yields memory corruption, then exploitation of one bug from bit-flip to full RCE.
  • Where applicable: Anyone running Ollama with untrusted model files — the notable framing is that model files are a new "untrusted input" channel for memory corruption.

ml-for-networking vulnerability-management offensive-security

items.title: LOLBlue : Living Off the Land with Blue Team tools
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Maxence Fossat, Antoine C (Synacktiv)

VideoPDF

  • Why: DFIR tools are pre-deployed, privileged readers of memory and protected files — inverting them into offensive LOLBins creates a detection blind spot squarely in the PM's network-security remit.
  • What: A systematic review of forensic/collection tools (Velociraptor, KAPE, DFIR-ORC and lesser-explored others) repurposed for credential access and covert exfiltration, expanding the known LOLDFIR toolkit, plus detection opportunities and the events to monitor. (from abstract only)
  • How: Analysis of how each tool accesses low-level filesystem/memory data, including abuse of Velociraptor's client/server architecture, with real-world scenarios demonstrating security-tool bypass.
  • Where applicable: Any organization that deploys or pre-installs these tools; realistic in late-stage red team engagements after initial execution. General technique.

offensive-security anomaly-detection

items.title: Nightmare on NTLM street: Legacy’s Revenge
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Core pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Marina Bochenkova

Video

  • Why: Microsoft announced NTLM family deprecation in June 2024; every identity and infrastructure team will live through this migration. This is a field report of actually doing it, not a deprecation-recap.
  • What: A retrospective of disabling NTLM in a mid-sized enterprise — why it survives 24 years past its replacement (application development lag, flaws in the replacement paths, decision-making, underfunded IT), plus resources and lessons learned for completing the removal elsewhere. (from abstract only)
  • How: Deployment methodology rather than exploitation: dependency discovery, organizational blockers, and remediation strategy for phasing out NTLM (and similar legacy protocols).
  • Where applicable: Enterprise AD environments broadly; the case study is one mid-sized enterprise (org-specific experience), but the dependency classes it documents are general.

authentication identity

items.title: No way to enable SSH access to your new router? The vendor might have something to hide
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Core pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Stanislav Dashevskyi, Francesco La Spina (Forescout / Vedere Labs)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A rare documented case of a network-device vendor actively obstructing analysis — patched Lua compiler, hidden SSH backdoor — in OpenWrt-derived firmware, a class that spans much of the consumer and enterprise gear in real networks.
  • What: Reverse engineering of a major (redacted) vendor's OpenWrt-based device OS: the vendor patched the Lua compiler solely to hinder static analysis; a "patched" backdoor survives in the restricted SSH service; and an authenticated OS command injection sits deep in a custom Lua module — together enabling full remote takeover of the device line. (from abstract only)
  • How: Static and dynamic RE of OpenWrt-derived binaries, recovering the modified Lua compiler's behavior, and auditing the restricted SSH implementation and custom Lua modules.
  • Where applicable: One vendor's device line (vendor-specific; name redacted in the program). The command injection requires valid credentials; the findings signal a broader audit need for proprietary firmware built on OpenWrt.

vulnerability-management offensive-security

items.title: OverLAPS: Overriding LAPS Logic
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Core pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Antoine Goichot (PwC Luxembourg)

Video

  • Why: LAPS is the mechanism most enterprises rely on to eliminate shared local-admin credentials across AD/Entra fleets. All prior research attacked it from the directory side; this flips to the endpoint, where the password actually lives — directly relevant to identity and endpoint posture.
  • What: Client-side attacks against Windows LAPS ("LAPSv2") that let an attacker capture, manipulate, and rotate the local admin password on demand, using LAPS as a persistence mechanism on both on-prem and Entra-joined devices — a genuinely new angle, and by the same researcher who did the original 2017 LAPS abuse work. (from abstract only)
  • How: PDB symbols plus light static analysis to understand LAPS internals; Frida dynamic hooking to intercept and control the password lifecycle; PoCs reproduced with Microsoft Detours for in-process hooks.
  • Where applicable: Any Windows fleet running Windows LAPS or legacy LAPS; requires attacker code execution on the endpoint (a client-side precondition, not a directory compromise). General technique, not org-specific.

identity vulnerability-management offensive-security

items.title: Palo Alto GlobalProtect : Remote Full Compromise Exploit Chain
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Core pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Maxime Escourbiac (Michelin CERT)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: The VPN client is the trust anchor of enterprise remote access. A same-network attacker achieving RCE and SYSTEM on Windows via the client is a realistic rogue-AP/hotel scenario, and the chain runs through broken certificate verification and root CA management — core PKI trust problems.
  • What: Six CVEs in the Palo Alto GlobalProtect client (CVE-2024-5921, CVE-2025-0117, CVE-2025-0118, CVE-2025-0120, CVE-2025-0131, CVE-2025-2183) chained to full remote compromise: certificate-verification bypass to impersonate the VPN portal, arbitrary root CA insertion, HTA payload delivery through the embedded authentication browser for RCE, and privilege escalation to SYSTEM via the impersonation mechanism or weak system update. (from abstract only)
  • How: Systematic weaknesses in certificate verification, root CA management, embedded-browser authentication, and client-server communications; the talk walks each step toward a full chain.
  • Where applicable: Windows workstations running the GlobalProtect client; the attacker must be on the same network as the victim (not internet-remote). Vendor-specific to Palo Alto.

vulnerability-management offensive-security

items.title: Red Team Story: Offline SCCM backup secrets decryption
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Core pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Martino

Video

  • Why: SCCM/MECM is high-value, AD-integrated infrastructure, and its backups — often sitting readable on network shares — carry encrypted secrets. This is a common real-world exposure with no complete public walkthrough until now.
  • What: The first concrete, end-to-end offline decryption of SCCM backup secrets with no access to a live SCCM server: the exact artifacts required, the encryption scheme, and a released script to reproduce the workflow. (from abstract only)
  • How: Explanation of how SCCM backup-secret encryption works, which artifacts must be collected from a backup, and a step-by-step decryption workflow, demonstrated against the public GOAD SCCM lab.
  • Where applicable: On-prem SCCM deployments where backup files are readable (network shares or other exposed locations); requires only read access to the backup artifacts. Vendor-specific to Microsoft SCCM.

offensive-security vulnerability-management

items.title: Revisiting RAND’s Lost Monte Carlo Simulations: Sharla Perrine, Paul Baran, and the True Business Case for the Internet
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Trey Darley

Video

  • Why: The survivability math that justified building the Internet has never been re-run against today's centralized cloud topologies — a sharp question for anyone whose job is DC/WAN topology and resilience.
  • What: A reintroduction of Sharla Perrine and Paul Baran's early-1960s Monte Carlo simulations (punched cards, octal assembly) that proved a distributed packet-switched network could survive attack — work later used to argue for ARPANET funding — plus a proposal to re-run the simulations under modern assumptions (traffic models, failure modes, time-synchronization shear effects in packet networks) to test whether resilience has quietly rotted as architectures centralized. (from abstract only)
  • How: Historical reconstruction plus a proposed modern re-simulation using contemporary toolchains, comparing 1960s modeling assumptions with cloud-era reality.
  • Where applicable: Conceptual / research-stage — a lightning talk proposing a research effort rather than presenting completed results; closer to the PM's core topology interests than a typical wildcard.

measurement internet-governance

items.title: RomCom exploits Firefox and Windows zero days in the wild
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract

Damien Schaeffer

  • Why: A fully documented, in-the-wild zero-click chain attributed to a Russia-aligned group — a reference-quality case study of browser sandbox escape plus OS privilege escalation.
  • What: October 2024 discovery of a zero-click chain: a use-after-free in Firefox's animation timeline (code execution in the sandboxed content process, affecting then-current Firefox and Tor Browser) combined with an undocumented permissive Windows RPC endpoint executing code at medium integrity regardless of caller privilege — sandbox escape and EoP, ending in RomCom's backdoor. (from abstract only)
  • How: Fake website redirects to the exploit server; successful exploitation drops and executes the backdoor with no user interaction. Mozilla patched in ~25 hours, Microsoft in early November; the talk covers RomCom's TTPs, victimology, and both exploits in detail.
  • Where applicable: Victims were users of then-current Firefox/Tor Browser on Windows; both bugs are patched — the value is as an exploit-chain case study and a capability benchmark for a state-adjacent actor.

threat-intelligence offensive-security vulnerability-management

items.title: Silent Killers: Unmasking a Large-Scale Legacy Driver Exploitation Campaign
items.text:
hack.lu 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–24 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Jiří Vinopal (Check Point Research)

Video

  • Why: A measured, large-scale proof that hash-based and allowlist-based driver defenses (including Microsoft's Vulnerable Driver Blocklist) can be defeated at industrial scale — important context for any endpoint defense stack.
