items.title: VoLUT: Efficient Volumetric streaming enhanced by LUT-based super-resolution
items.text:
MLSys 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 12–15 May 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Chendong Wang, Anlan Zhang, Yifan Yang, Lili Qiu, Yuqing Yang, XINYANG JIANG, Feng Qian, Suman Banerjee (networking-community author roster)

  • Why: A bandwidth-vs-compute trade made explicit: ship downsampled volumetric (3D) video and reconstruct with lookup-table super-resolution at the receiver — 70% bandwidth reduction at line rate on commodity mobile devices. It's the classic edge/cdn rate-adaptation problem with a novel twist, from a networking research group.
  • What: The first system enabling high-quality 3D super-resolution of volumetric streams on commodity mobile devices at line rate: LUT-based upscaling of pre-downsampled content, plus an adaptive bitrate loop that picks the downsampling rate based on network conditions. 70% bandwidth reduction, 36.7% QoE improvement, 8.4× faster 3D super-resolution with no quality loss. (from abstract only)
  • How: Precomputed LUTs map low-resolution volumetric values to high-resolution reconstructions, replacing expensive on-device SR inference with fast table lookups; ABR logic sits on top, treating fidelity level like a video bitrate ladder.
  • Where applicable: Volumetric/immersive media delivery over constrained last-mile networks to mobile receivers; the LUT-for-neural-SR substitution pattern generalizes to any receiver-side computationally-bound reconstruction. Evaluation is on mobile devices, not datacenter delivery.

cdn mobile measurement

items.title: A Lightweight High-Throughput Collective-Capable NoC for Large-Scale ML Accelerators
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Luca Colagrande, Lorenzo Leone, Chen Wu, Tim Fischer, Raphael Roth, Luca Benini (affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: With thousands of compute elements per die, on-chip fabrics now face the same problems as DC fabrics — collective offload, multicast, in-network reduction, buffer/area budgets. This is fabric design and in-network compute at the silicon level, and the boundary between NoC and scale-up interconnect is exactly where the field is heading.
  • What: A lightweight NoC supporting barrier synchronization, scalable high-bandwidth multicast, and in-network reduction, co-designed for next-generation ML accelerators. Introduces Direct Compute Access (DCA), giving the interconnect direct access to the cores' computational resources for in-network reduction at a 16.5% router area overhead. Measured 2.9× and 2.5× geomean speedups on multicast and reduction (1–32 KiB), and up to 2.1× estimated end-to-end GEMM performance vs a unicast-only NoC baseline (from abstract only).
  • How: DCA lets the fabric itself perform reductions using core compute resources, keeping communication off the critical path in GEMM-heavy workloads.
  • Where applicable: Applies to accelerator ASIC design, not to retrofitting existing clusters — and the end-to-end GEMM gains are estimates from architectural simulation rather than silicon measurements. The in-network-reduction tradeoff (area vs throughput), however, is a broadly transferable design lesson.

silicon switching multicast

items.title: ADR: AN AGENTIC DETECTION SYSTEMFORENTERPRISE AGENTIC AI SECURITY
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Chenning Li, Pan Hu, Justin Xu, Baris Ozbas, Olivia Liu, Caroline Van, Manxue Li, Wei Zhou, Mohammad Alizadeh, Pengyu Zhang, KK Sriramadhesikan, Ming Zhang (deployed at Uber, per the paper; affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: AI agents speaking MCP are entering enterprises with almost no dedicated security tooling — EDR sees file writes, not prompts, reasoning, or the causal chain from intent to execution. This is one of the first production-proven detection-and-response systems for agentic AI, sitting squarely at the intersection of network security and the emerging agentic-identity problem.
  • What: A three-part system: an ADR Sensor for high-fidelity agentic telemetry (prompts, reasoning, causal chains), an Explorer for pre-deployment red teaming and hard-example generation, and a two-tier Detector that combines fast triage with context-aware reasoning to keep LLM inference costs down. Deployed at Uber for 10+ months across 7,200+ hosts and 10,000+ agent sessions daily; surfaced hundreds of credential exposures (97.2% precision). Includes ADR-Bench (302 tasks, 17 techniques, 133 MCP servers), where it detects 67% of attacks with zero false positives, beating three SOTA baselines by 2–4× F1 (from abstract only).
  • How: EDR-style instrumentation applied to agent sessions, plus a cost-aware two-tier detection pipeline and a systematic red-team loop for generating hard examples.
  • Where applicable: Enterprise MCP deployments. The production numbers are Uber-specific, but the architecture, the benchmark, and the credential-exposure findings generalize — and the telemetry gap it names (agents invisible to host-based tooling) is universal.

items.text:

Zhongshu Gu, Enriquillo Valdez, Salman Ahmed, Julian James stephen, Michael Le, Hani Jamjoom, Shixuan Zhao, Zhiqiang Lin (affiliations not listed in the program)

items.title: DreamDDP: Accelerating Low-Bandwidth Geo-Distributed LLM Training with Layer-wise Partial Synchronization
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Zhenheng Tang, Zichen TANG, Junlin Huang, Xinglin Pan, Rudan Yan, Yuxin Wang, Amelie Zhou, Shaohuai Shi, Xiaowen Chu, Bo Li (affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: Geo-distributed training is the workload that will stress (and justify) DC-to-DC WAN interconnects. This paper quantifies how much of that WAN bottleneck can be clawed back on the ML side — directly relevant to capacity planning for AI-over-WAN before you buy bandwidth.
  • What: A training framework that decouples model synchronization layer-wise: instead of synchronizing the whole model every N iterations (Local SGD) or every iteration (S-SGD), only a subset of layers is synchronized per iteration. Delivers 1.49×–3.91× speedups over leading baselines on 32 GPUs across ResNet-18/50, GPT-2, and Llama-2, with convergence rates theoretically comparable to S-SGD (from abstract only).
  • How: Layer-wise partial synchronization enables overlapping parameter sync with computation without extra GPU memory; fine-grained layer-wise profiling drives the communication/computation schedule.
  • Where applicable: Low-bandwidth geo-distributed data-parallel training. Evaluated at modest scale (32 GPUs) — frontier-scale behavior is unproven. It is an ML-side technique that complements, not replaces, WAN capacity planning; its value to a network PM is as a signal of what traffic geo-distributed training will and won't generate.

ai-networks interconnection

items.title: fabric-lib: RDMA Point-to-Point Communication for LLM Systems
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Nandor Licker, Kevin Hu, Vladimir Zaytsev, Lequn Chen (Perplexity AI, per the paper's open-source repository)

  • Why: Disaggregated inference, MoE expert routing, and async RL fine-tuning all need flexible point-to-point RDMA, not just collectives — but today's implementations are locked to specific NICs. This is the clearest statement of the problem at the point where RoCE fabrics and LLM serving actually meet, and it ships as open source.
  • What: A NIC-abstraction library that exposes uniform one-sided WriteImm operations across heterogeneous NICs, demonstrated at 400 Gbps on both NVIDIA ConnectX-7 and AWS EFA, and proven through three production use cases: KV-cache transfer for disaggregated inference, RL weight sync (1.3 s for trillion-parameter models), and MoE dispatch/combine that beats DeepEP decode latency on ConnectX-7 — with the first viable EFA latencies (from abstract only).
  • How: Bridges common NIC functionality behind one interface; an ImmCounter primitive provides completion notification without assuming transport ordering; multiple NICs per GPU are managed transparently. It complements collectives rather than replacing them.
  • Where applicable: Any RoCEv2 or EFA environment with point-to-point LLM traffic. The headline numbers are specific to ConnectX-7 and AWS EFA, and the MoE comparison is against DeepEP — but the portability argument and the code (pplx-garden on GitHub) are broadly usable.

rdma ai-networks interconnection

items.title: GUARD: SCALABLE STRAGGLER DETECTION AND NODE HEALTH MANAGEMENT FOR LARGE-SCALE TRAINING
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

guanliang liu, Abhinandan Patni, congzhu lin, et al. (affiliations not listed in the program; deployed on large-scale foundation-model pretraining)

  • Why: NCCL tests and GPU burn-ins catch fail-stop, not fail-slow — and on multi-month, tens-of-thousands-of-GPU runs, silent stragglers quietly eat efficiency. This is operational health management for training fleets, and the approach transfers to any large fleet.
  • What: A system combining lightweight online performance monitoring during training with an offline node-sweep mechanism that qualifies nodes before production admission. In production: up to 1.7× improvement in mean FLOPs utilization, run-to-run training-step variance reduced from 20% to 1%, higher MTTF, and reduced debugging overhead (from abstract only).
  • How: Continuous workload-level performance signals (not synthetic micro-tests) detect both acute failures and long-running degradation; systematic sweeps pre-qualify nodes.
  • Where applicable: The deployment is a large-scale pretraining cluster (org not fully specified in the program), so exact gains are fleet-specific. The core lesson — workload-level signal beats synthetic health checks for fail-slow detection — is broadly applicable.

anomaly-detection sre ai-networks

items.title: LearnedCache: An eBPF-Integrated Perceptron-Based Eviction Policy for the Linux Page Cache
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract

Zejia Qi (poster; affiliation not listed in the program)

  • Why: Two of your interests in one title: eBPF as a safe extension mechanism for kernel policy, and learned replacement decisions — here applied to the Linux page cache rather than a network cache, but the architecture question (can you wire a learned policy into kernel hot paths via eBPF without killing performance?) is the same one for LRU-vs-learned eviction in CDN caches, connection tracking, and flow caches.
  • What: Not assessable from the program — no abstract is provided, and the MLSys poster page lists only the title and author. By title: a perceptron-based (learned) eviction policy for the Linux page cache, integrated with eBPF.
  • How: Unknown from available material.
  • Where applicable: Unknown from available material; by construction it is Linux-kernel-specific, and the interesting question for you is the eBPF-integration pattern, not page caching per se.

ebpf linux-networking

items.title: MLCommons Chakra: Advancing Performance Benchmarking and Co-design using Standardized Execution Traces
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Srinivas, Andrey Balogh, Brad B, et al. (MLCommons-led effort with industry participation from NVIDIA, AMD, Meta, Keysight, HPE, and others, per the paper)

  • Why: There is no portable, vendor-neutral way to characterize distributed AI workloads' behavior on a fabric. Chakra's standardized execution-trace format is becoming the interchange layer for AI-cluster benchmarking and co-design — effectively the telemetry standard to watch.
  • What: An open ecosystem whose core is Chakra Execution Traces (ETs): graph-based representations of compute, memory, and communication operations with data/control dependencies, timing, and resource constraints, plus tools for collection, analysis, generation, and replay into simulators and emulators. Includes analysis of traces from production AI clusters and real-world case studies; adopted by MLCommons (from abstract only).
  • How: Workload traces are captured as interoperable graphs, then fed to simulators/emulators/replay tools for performance prediction and SW–HW co-design without needing the original cluster.
  • Where applicable: Cross-vendor by construction — the whole point is portability across NVIDIA, AMD, and other stacks. Adoption is still growing; value scales with ecosystem uptake.

benchmarking telemetry ai-networks

items.title: NEST: Network- and Memory-Aware Device Placement for Distributed Deep Learning
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Irene Wang, Vishnu Venkata, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Divya Mahajan (affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: Device placement is where ML frameworks and the physical fabric actually meet. Most placement tools treat the network as an afterthought and memory as a post-hoc fix; NEST makes topology, allreduce latency, and memory feasibility first-class joint constraints — the co-design point a fabric-owning PM cares about.
  • What: A placement framework that unifies model parallelism (tensor, expert, sequence, context — composed with pipeline, data, and ZeRO), explicit allreduce latencies over hierarchical or arbitrary network topologies, and per-device memory/compute profiles, solved via structured dynamic programming. Up to 2.43× higher throughput over SOTA baselines across diverse hardware and networks; open source (from abstract only).
  • How: DP over operator graphs annotated with per-op parallelism configurations and measured network latencies, jointly optimizing co-location, communication cost, and memory feasibility rather than patching feasibility after placement.
  • Where applicable: General technique, not tied to one operator's fabric — but its quality depends on accurate allreduce-latency and memory profiles for your specific network. Most useful as a foundation for co-designing parallelization strategies with datacenter interconnects; needs real fabric measurements as input.

ai-networks data-center-fabric orchestration

items.title: Optimizing Deployment Configurations for LLM Inference
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Sungmin Cho, Jaewon Lee, Chunqiang Tang, et al. (Meta, serving the Llama family to ~1B monthly active users, per the paper)

  • Why: Production experience from one of the largest inference fleets in existence, systematically mined for configuration lessons — the operational counterpart to NEST-style placement search, from the team living with the results.
  • What: A systematic approach analyzing millions of deployment configurations across hardware (H100, H200, MI300X), parallelism strategies (tensor, pipeline, expert, context, data), and runtime choices (continuous batching vs prefill–decode disaggregation) under SLO constraints. Shares lessons on runtime trade-offs, the phase-specific nature of parallelism strategies, hardware heterogeneity, scaling behaviors, and MoE system implications (from abstract only).
  • How: Large-scale design-space search with workload-specific SLO constraints on production traffic.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific fleet, workloads, and SLOs — the specific optima do not transfer. The structural lessons (phase-specific parallelism, heterogeneous hardware opportunity) do.

ai-networks capacity-planning benchmarking

items.title: ProfInfer: An eBPF-based Fine-Grained LLM Inference Profiler
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Bohua Zou, Debayan Roy, Dhimankumar Airao, Weihao Xu, Binqi Sun, Yutao Liu, Haibo Chen (affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: eBPF is in your core stack, and this paper shows its reach extending beyond networking into runtime-level observability of LLM inference — with under 4% overhead and zero source modification. The pattern (dynamic probes on runtime functions, rich derived views) transfers to other "black-box runtime, need operator-level visibility" problems.
  • What: A fine-grained, non-intrusive profiling framework for LLM inference engines, focused on resource-constrained edge devices and exemplified by llama.cpp, exposing operator-level time, memory-vs-compute boundedness, MoE routing behavior, and operator offloading, rendered as operator graphs, timelines, and hardware-counter trends (from abstract only).
  • How: eBPF probes dynamically attached to runtime functions across multiple layers without recompilation; collected traces are transformed into visualizations of operators, graphs, and counter trends.
  • Where applicable: llama.cpp-class CPU/edge inference runtimes on Linux — this is not a GPU-cluster profiler, and the fidelity claims are tied to that runtime architecture. The eBPF technique itself is broadly portable.

ebpf observability measurement

items.title: REPARO: LOSS-RESILIENT GENERATIVE CODEC FOR VIDEO CONFERENCING
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Tianhong Li, Vibhaalakshmi Sivaraman, Pantea Karimi, Lijie Fan, Mohammad Alizadeh, Dina Katabi (affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: A genuinely surprising inversion of loss recovery: instead of adding redundancy (FEC) or retransmitting (impractical for real-time), generate the lost visual content conditioned on what did arrive. Whatever you think of the ethics of hallucinated pixels, it is a new point in the design space for real-time loss resilience.
  • What: A video-conferencing framework where a generative model fills in missing frames or frame regions when packets are lost, conditioned on the data received so far and on learned priors of how people and objects appear and move. On public video-conferencing datasets it beats state-of-the-art FEC-based solutions on video quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) and freeze occurrence (from abstract only).
  • How: Conditional generation over partially-received frames, exploiting the model's visual-world priors instead of parity redundancy.
  • Where applicable: Real-time interactive video over lossy Internet paths. Research-stage, evaluated on public datasets rather than live conferencing at scale — but as a signal of where loss recovery could go beyond ARQ/FEC, it is worth ten minutes.

ml-for-networking measurement

items.title: Rethinking Open Source Contribution in the Age of AI Agents
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract

Roger Wang (vLLM core maintainer, per the talk description)

  • Why: Not a networking talk, but a maintainer's-eye view of what AI-generated contribution pressure is doing to the maintenance economics of critical infrastructure — and vLLM is production LLM-serving infrastructure that the rest of this program depends on. If you run an open-source project or consume one, this is the operational reality arriving at your doorstep.
  • What: A core maintainer's account of the surge of AI-generated PRs in vLLM: the cost of producing a plausible PR has collapsed while review cost has not; PRs that look correct but miss design intent; fixes that paper over deeper issues. Not anti-AI — agents are now part of how vLLM gets built — but the argument is that human leverage has shifted from producing code toward understanding systems, picking the right problems, and owning what ships (from abstract only).
  • How: Concrete examples from vLLM's day-to-day maintainer experience, plus practical guidance for new contributors and for maintainers of critical infrastructure.
  • Where applicable: Any OSS project, especially infrastructure projects with high PR volume and shallow review capacity.

open-source automation

items.title: SAKURAONE: An Open Ethernet–Based AI HPC System and Its Observed Workload Dynamics in a Single-Tenant LLM Development Environment
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Fumikazu Konishi, Yuuki Tsubouchi, Hirofumi Tsuruta (SAKURA Internet Research Center)

  • Why: A top-100 TOP500 system built on a fully open networking stack — 800 GbE, SONiC, RoCEv2 — is the strongest public existence proof yet that vendor-neutral Ethernet fabrics scale to frontier LLM training. For anyone evaluating SONiC/white-box options for AI clusters, this matters more than another InfiniBand case study.
  • What: A 100-node managed HPC cluster (8× H100 per node, 2 PB all-flash Lustre) on a rail-optimized 800 GbE leaf–spine fabric with RoCEv2 and SONiC, ranked 49th in ISC 2025 TOP500 (33.95 PFLOP/s HPL, 339.86 PFLOP/s FP8 HPL-MxP) — the only top-100 system using a fully open network stack. The paper also reports single-tenant workload dynamics: small jobs dominate by count, a few large jobs consume most GPU-hours, and usage shifted from large-scale training to mid-scale iterative refinement over the project's life (from abstract only).
  • How: Built on the SAKURA KOKARYOKU PHY bare-metal GPU platform; rail-optimized leaf–spine topology; open control and data plane end to end.
  • Where applicable: The fabric architecture and its measured scalability are broadly relevant to Ethernet-for-AI decisions. The workload observations are specific to one research project's exclusive use of the cluster — treat them as a single-tenant data point, not a general cloud workload distribution.

ethernet data-center-fabric rdma open-source

items.title: SHIP: SRAM-Based Huge Inference Pipelines for Fast LLM Serving
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Core pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Andrew Bitar, Aravind Vayalapra, Baorui Zhou, et al. (Groq, per the paper — the deployment studied is Groq's public cloud)

  • Why: A production counterpoint to HBM-based GPU serving: SRAM-resident weights eliminate the decode memory-bandwidth bottleneck, and the system runs at hundreds of billions of tokens daily. The interconnect story — a synchronous, low-diameter network scaling to thousands of chips — is a live example of topology choices driving serving latency.
  • What: A review of Groq's first-generation SRAM-based inference pipelines: (1) a synchronous low-diameter interconnect enabling low-latency scaling across thousands of chips, (2) serving optimizations under tight memory capacity, and (3) large-pipeline designs that sustain efficiency and latency across varying prefill-to-decode ratios and context lengths, delivering state-of-the-art latency (from abstract only).
  • How: Model weights and KV state live in SRAM spread across a chip fabric; deterministic, synchronous pipelining keeps communication off the critical path.
  • Where applicable: Groq-specific silicon and interconnect — this is one vendor's architecture, not a technique you can adopt. But as a data point on how scale-up fabric topology and memory placement shape the throughput–latency frontier, it is directly relevant to anyone comparing interconnect strategies for inference.

ai-networks silicon interconnection

items.title: SONAR: Benchmarking Topology and Collaboration in Decentralized Learning
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Joyce Yuan, Yichuan Shi, Abhishek Singh, et al. (affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: It treats topology as a first-class, controllable variable — and finds sparse structured graphs (rings, tori) can match or beat dense ones at far lower communication cost. That finding rhymes directly with datacenter fabric intuition, even though the domain is peer-to-peer federated learning, not DC networks.
  • What: A modular framework unifying communication, topology management, and fine-grained telemetry for topology-aware decentralized learning, enabling reproducible measurement of performance, communication, robustness, and privacy. Key findings: topology's impact amplifies with scale and data heterogeneity; sparse structured topologies sit on a better efficiency frontier than dense graphs; and it identifies "collaborator collapse," a systematic failure mode where similarity-based neighbor selection reduces diversity and degrades generalization (from abstract only).
  • How: Controlled, reproducible evaluation across topologies under a common measurement harness spanning performance, communication, robustness, and privacy dimensions.
  • Where applicable: Decentralized/P2P learning research settings, not datacenter fabrics — but the topology-efficiency results and the collaborator-collapse failure mode are conceptually portable to any system where participants choose communication partners adaptively.

benchmarking measurement ml-for-networking

items.title: Sparing Strategies to Minimize Reliability Impact On Large Training Jobs
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Kevin Quirk, Matthew Lennie, Ehsan K. Ardestani, et al. (Meta, per the paper's framing around Meta's AI clusters)

  • Why: Sparing — pre-allocated spare compute that replaces failed components — directly trades capex against goodput on multi-month training runs. Closed-form sizing guidance for that tradeoff is rare and welcome.
  • What: An analytical framework with closed-form expressions for choosing sparing strategy — compute block size, number of spare blocks, spare GPU trays — cross-validated by simulation, and applied in Meta's hyperscale infrastructure to inform fault-tolerance, downtime, and goodput decisions (from abstract only).
  • How: Analytical modeling of failure/replacement dynamics, plus a simulation component for validation; yields first-order production recommendations.
  • Where applicable: The framework is generally formulated, but the optimal sparing parameters are strongly fleet-specific (Meta's failure rates, tray topology, job sizes). Use the method and the first-order rules, not Meta's numbers.

sre capacity-planning ai-networks

items.title: TokenWeave: Efficient Compute-Communication Overlap for Distributed LLM Inference
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Raja Gond, Nipun Kwatra, Ramachandran Ramjee (Microsoft, per the paper's open-source repository)

  • Why: Tensor-parallel AllReduce costs ~20% even over NVLink, and — usefully documented here — none of the major serving engines enable overlap by default because it backfires at small token counts. This paper explains why and fixes it.
  • What: The first system enabling efficient compute–communication overlap for tensor-parallel inference at batch sizes as small as 1024 tokens: up to 1.28× lower latency and 1.19× higher throughput across models and workloads on an 8×H100 DGX, in several settings beating an equivalent model with all communication removed. Open source (from abstract only).
  • How: Identifies RMSNorm as the overlooked fusion partner and implements a fused AllReduce–RMSNorm kernel that exploits the NVSHARP/Multimem hardware feature, using only 2–8 SMs for communication on Hopper/Blackwell-class GPUs.
  • Where applicable: Requires modern NVIDIA GPU interconnects (NVLink + NVSHARP/Multimem on Hopper/Blackwell) — the mechanism is silicon-specific. The diagnosis of why overlap is off by default in vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM is broadly instructive.

gpu-clusters ai-networks

items.title: Unleashing Scalable Context Parallelism for Foundation Models Pre-Training via FCP
items.text:
MLSys 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Paper

Yilong Zhao, Xiaonan Nie, Kan Zhu, et al. (affiliations not listed in the program)

  • Why: Context parallelism over variable-length training data wastes fabric capacity — over-sharding short sequences, or imbalanced bin-packing of long and short ones. FCP relaxes the rigid-ring assumption, which is a scheduling/communication co-design relevant to anyone provisioning collective fabrics.
  • What: A flexible context-parallelism paradigm that shards and schedules sequences at block-level granularity, achieving near-linear scalability to 256 GPUs and 1.13×–2.21× improvement in attention MFU (from abstract only).
  • How: Block-level sharding enables arbitrary peer-to-peer communication topologies (not just rings) and bin-packing of blocks from short and long sequences for balanced, communication-efficient placement.
  • Where applicable: Foundation-model pretraining with heterogeneous sequence lengths. Evaluated at up to 256 GPUs — mid-scale by today's standards — so frontier-scale behavior is extrapolated.

ai-networks gpu-clusters

items.title: Defending Europe against DDoS in a multi-polar world

It is also a rare operator talk about collective defense — scrubbing and mitigation as shared infrastructure — rather than a box to buy.

(No abstract published — from title and speaker only.)

Broadly transferable to any multi-tenant mitigation effort; the geopolitical framing is Europe-specific. No abstract published; treat this write-up as title-level only.

items.title: IPv6-only IXPs Are Coming?
items.text:
MORE-IP 2025 digest Program Core pick 4–5 June 2025

Recording

Aleksi Suhonen - TREX Tampere Region Exchange Oy

Video

For a PM whose portfolio includes DC/WAN interconnect and IPAM, this is a preview of a real operational shift rather than a compliance checkbox.

items.title: Panel: The Power of Precision: Why Time as a Service Matters
items.text:
MORE-IP 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 4–5 June 2025

Recording

Jos van Eycken - Adtran, Michael van Schaik - VSL, Jan van Boeschoten - AMS-IX, Erwin uit de Bos - Digital Realty, Miguel Regalado Querol - AMS-IX

Video

  • Why: Not something this PM would search for, but the panel composition is the tell: a national metrology institute (VSL), an optical/timing vendor (Adtran), a datacenter operator (Digital Realty), and an IX. That mix means the talk is about distributing precision timing (think PTP-class accuracy) as a commercial/managed service into datacenters — a small field today that grows as 5G, sensing, HFT, and distributed measurement workloads demand better than NTP.
  • What: A panel arguing for "time as a service" — delivering precision timing as an offered service rather than something each operator builds. (No description published — from title and panel composition only.)

items.title: IPv4-with-IPv6 Next-Hop: Towards an IPv4-Free Internet Core
items.text:
MORE-IP 2026 digest Program Core pick 27–28 May 2026

Tobias Fiebig — Vienna University of Technology

  • Why: For anyone who cares about BGP/datapath internals and the long, slow IPv6 transition, this is one of the sharpest technical titles on the program. The question it names — can we carry IPv4 reachability with IPv6-only transport in the core, so the core stops speaking IPv4 entirely — is one of the few genuinely structural changes still available to the internet without a flag day.
  • What: The title indicates a proposal or evaluation of running the core network IPv6-only: advertising IPv4 prefixes while using IPv6 next-hop addresses (the mechanism standardised in RFC 8950), eliminating the need for IPv4 addresses on core-facing interfaces and shrinking the core's IPv4 configuration surface. No abstract was published, so the exact contribution — measurement of current adoption, an operator how-to, or a transition proposal — cannot be confirmed. (from abstract only; no description published)
  • How: Presumably by combining extended-nexthop BGP encoding (IPv4 NLRI, IPv6 next hop) with v6-only core links, so IPv4 survives only as payload/edge reachability. Fiebig's group is known for large-scale BGP measurement, so expect deployment data or adoption obstacles rather than a purely theoretical argument.
  • Where applicable: Transit providers, IXs, and large DC/WAN interconnect operators — exactly the environments this event's audience runs. The main constraints are real-world ones: hardware/daemon support for extended nexthops on all core routers, and the operational discipline to keep v4 out once it's out. items.title: SCION
items.text:
MORE-IP 2026 digest Program Core pick 27–28 May 2026

Adrian Perrig — ETH Zurich

  • Why: SCION is the most serious sustained attempt at a clean-slate, security-first internet architecture that has reached actual deployment discussions, and it speaks directly to the PM's network-security and interdomain-routing interests. Having its chief architect present at an operator event means the talk is aimed at people who run networks, not academics.
  • What: SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation on Next-Generation Networks) is a path-aware internetworking architecture: instead of letting BGP's path selection decide transit opaque to endpoints, receivers and senders hold visible, cryptographically authenticated path choices. The program publishes no description for this session, so the specific content (architecture overview vs. deployment status vs. operator onboarding) is unknown — but any of those would be valuable. (from abstract only; no description published)
  • How: SCION organizes the internet into Isolation Domains containing ASes, and lets endpoints select among authenticated AS-level path segments — enabling path failure isolation, protection against route hijacks, and control-plane attacks that today's BGP can't defend against. The Swiss financial sector has run SCION pilots over an exchange infrastructure, making this relevant to IX/peering operators like the host.
  • Where applicable: Interdomain/WAN transit and any environment with strict integrity or availability guarantees (finance, critical infrastructure). Not a DC-fabric or LAN technique — it's about the internet core and inter-AS paths. Deployment is still early; treat it as a signal of where interdomain security is heading rather than something to adopt next quarter.

items.title: AI Backend: Deploying SRv6 uSID and SONiC for Deterministic Load Balancing
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Pablo Camarillo — Cisco Systems; Rita Hui — Microsoft

VideoPDF

  • Why: The AI backend load-balancing problem is the defining fabric issue of this cycle: synchronized, bursty, low-entropy training flows destroy ECMP hash assumptions, and congestion/loss stalls GPU collectives. This is a production answer from one of the world's largest AI infrastructures, not a whitepaper.
  • What: Microsoft's deployment of SRv6 uSID strict source routing in the AI backend for deterministic, conflict-free traffic placement, implemented in SONiC. The deck grounds it in real cost data (Llama3 406B: 6k GPUs, 54 days, 419 unplanned interruptions; a single job crash loses 15-30 minutes of compute since the last checkpoint) and includes a taxonomy of every LB approach attempted — switch-based (flowlet, adaptive routing, packet spray) and NIC-based (oblivious spray, entropy recycling) — and why probabilistic entropy-value switching can't guarantee a new path.
  • How: GPU/NIC controls the full end-to-end path by encoding a uSID list in the packet header; on congestion or failure the NIC swaps SIDs and the path changes immediately with no state propagation through the fabric. The backend runs as a statically provisioned fabric with static SIDs and static routes — no dynamic routing, avoiding the ~120,000 packets lost when an ECMP group updates after a link flap on a fully utilized 400G link. Also covers tenancy/slicing via SRv6 policy without DPU cycles, and the SONiC SRv6 ecosystem (uN/uDT functions, FRR, contributors incl. Microsoft, Alibaba, Broadcom, Nvidia). The Alibaba eCore SRv6 DCI design is shown as the scale-across analog.
  • Where applicable: Microsoft-scale AI backends on SONiC whiteboxes; requires SRv6-capable NICs/DPUs and merchant silicon (Broadcom/G400-class). The "deterministic path placement" idea is also feeding UEC standardization, so the architecture is transferable even where the exact stack is not. Co-presented by Cisco's SRv6 lead — expect enthusiasm — but the operational data and failure math are the substance.

segment-routing ai-networks load-balancing

items.title: Automation for Operations -- T-Mobile Journey
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Issa Abu Eid, Udaya Tadikonda — T-Mobile USA

VideoPDF

  • Why: A Tier-1 operator's account of moving from manual workflows to automation-first operations, with the guardrail design spelled out — the "how do we make automated actions safe" question is where most automation programs actually fail, and this addresses it head-on.
  • What: Reactive and proactive automation categories: alert correlation/deduplication and auto-created tickets with SLA clocks starting at detection, multi-signal service-aware outage detection with impact identification before customers notice, guarded break/fix (explicitly not automating ambiguous failures or one-off fixes; every automated action gated by redundancy-aware checks, capacity validation, audit trail, and rollback), pre/post-change validation with policy-driven rollback evaluation, continuous compliance/drift/EOL-EOS monitoring, and capacity early-warning with trend analysis. A maturity model — Visibility → Intelligence → Enablement — with the honest sequencing rule that automation cannot succeed without reliable state and that early efforts must focus on visibility, not action. AI is framed as an assistive layer on top of strong automation foundations, not a replacement for operator judgment.
  • How: Automation treated as production software; one deliverable described is a centralized internal platform used by 1,300+ engineers with incident correlation across multi-vendor networks.
  • Where applicable: T-Mobile US Tier-1 scale (org-specific tooling and metrics), but the guardrail taxonomy, the "explicitly not automated" list, and the visibility-first phasing are directly transferable patterns for any operations organization, including much smaller ones.

items.title: BGP in 2025
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Geoff Huston — APNIC

VideoPDF

  • Why: The annual ground truth on DFZ health — directly relevant to FIB sizing, deaggregation trends, and (this year) a genuinely new datapoint: the IPv4 routing table and the advertised address span are now moving in opposite directions.
  • What: IPv4 FIB passed 1M entries for all peers, yet the advertised address span shrank by 11M /32s during 2025 (3.1B advertised vs 580M unadvertised, +10M) — IPv4 use declining in access networks (notably the US) while cloud use still grows. Biggest movers: China Mobile (+13,382 prefixes), Amazon (+14,004), AT&T (−2,605, echoing its consolidation described in the Ukraine talk), IPXO broker growth visible. Amazon's super-aggregate games through the year (+4.3M, −15.8M, +15.1M address swings). IPv6: ~20k entries/year (~10%) growth with 45% of prefixes being /48s; 2,096 new IPv6 advertisers vs 956 departing. Projections: best 5-year fit still polynomial for IPv4 but a 3-year linear fit is competing; IPv6 growth model highly uncertain.
  • How: Longitudinal analysis across Route-Views/RIPE RIS peers; churn (updates/withdrawals) notably stable — the IPv4 network is "surprisingly stable" with withdrawals flat for ~15 years.
  • Where applicable: Universal for capacity planning and RIB/FIB trend work. The headline nuance — prefix count growing while address span shrinks — matters for anyone modeling router table growth or arguing about IPv4 scarcity.

bgp measurement

items.title: Decentralizing Software Defined Networking: The Hidden Complexities of SDN & What We Can Do About Them
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alexander Krentsel — Google / UC Berkeley

VideoPDF

  • Why: A rare quantified indictment of centralized SDN: at Google, >50% of large outages are root-caused to the control plane itself — the dedicated controller infrastructure, control-plane network, instrumentation services, and fallback protocols that SDN drags in. For anyone building WAN control systems, this is the architecture conversation to have.
  • What: Decentralized SDN (dSDN): run the operator's SDN control program as a container on every router instead of on external servers. Each node floods its local state (topology, link capacities, demand), each node independently computes all paths with the operator's TE algorithm, and traffic follows strict source routes programmed at the ingress. This removes central/regional controller jobs, dedicated servers, the control-plane network, instrumentation services, and traditional fallback protocols from the critical path while keeping SDN's benefits (operator-defined code, global-view TE, consensus-free path selection) and restoring fate-sharing between control and data planes.
  • How: Enabled by three industry shifts: on-router third-party containers, standardized APIs (gRIBI, gNMI, OF/P4), and multi-core router CPUs. Source routing makes decentralization simple — historically infeasible in WANs due to path length in the header, now practical via hardware advances and a novel encoding (details in the paper). Evaluation: a production-grade implementation on real routers, fed live B4 topology and demand, replaying production failure events — convergence 120-150x faster than centralized SDN (faster propagation and programming outweigh slightly slower local computation) with markedly lower convergence impact on low-priority traffic.
  • Where applicable: Global WAN operators (Google B4-class). Requires vendor on-router container support and vendor-neutral programmatic APIs — realistic on modern platforms but a real dependency. Research-to-production direction from Berkeley NetSys + Google, not a deployable product; the simplification argument (fewer components on the critical path → fewer complex cascading outages) generalizes to any control-plane design review.

sdn troubleshooting

items.title: End-system controlled, dynamic multihoming and multipath transport
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Saleem Bhatti — University of St Andrews, Scotland, UK.

VideoPDF

  • Why: Multipath today means MPTCP or waiting on QUIC multipath. This demonstrates generic, end-system-controlled multipath for any transport — with working code, real transatlantic tests, and no changes to routers, applications, DNS infrastructure beyond what exists, or routing. It is a genuinely different architectural bet worth knowing about even if you never deploy it.
  • What: ILNP (Identifier-Locator Network Protocol, RFCs 6740-6748) reuses IPv6 address syntax but splits semantics: the routing prefix acts as a mutable Locator while the remaining bits become a stable end-system Identifier — only end systems examine the Identifier bits, so IPv6 routers forward unchanged. Transport state is keyed on the Identifier (not the address), so a connection survives locator changes; dynamic multihoming and multipath are signaled end-to-end via ICMPv6 Locator Updates, no NAT, tunnels, or proxies.
  • How: A FreeBSD 14 implementation tested between IETF 124 in Montreal and St Andrews: dynamic 4-way multipath with TCP CUBIC over iperf3, and DASH video streaming over nginx + Firefox with 3-way multipath — using standard, unmodified applications and libraries. Supporting ecosystem exists: DNS NID/L64 records (RFC 6742) in BIND, Unbound, Knot; a Wireshark dissector (v4.6+); FreeBSD binaries published.
  • Where applicable: Research testbed; IPv6-only; requires ILNP-aware end-system stacks (FreeBSD today). No network-side prerequisites, which is the interesting inversion — the network stays dumb and the edge controls path selection. Position this as a direction signal for edge-controlled multipath rather than a deployable capability.

load-balancing linux-networking

items.title: EVPN Interconnect Architecture for Resilient Multi-Domain Fabrics
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Patrice Brissette — Cisco Systems

VideoPDF

  • Why: Multi-site EVPN over heterogeneous underlays (IPv4 WAN meeting IPv6 DC fabrics) is exactly the DC/WAN interconnect problem the PM owns. This is a coherent answer to the two failure modes that plague DCI overlays: control-plane stability during fabric isolation, and L2 loops across sites.
  • What: A hierarchical multi-site design where each fabric stays an independent EVPN domain and Border Gateways provide DCI: dual physical-IP VTEPs per BGW (one for the DC domain, one for the WAN domain) so tunnels are terminated and re-originated at the BGW — creating a clean scaling and policy boundary. Key mechanics: Inter-site ESI for all-active BGW multi-homing, DF/NDF election with local-bias BUM forwarding rules and explicit per-bridge egress filtering to prevent loops, Normalized-VNI translation to resolve overlapping VNIs between independently administered sites, downstream-assigned VNI option, host mobility via /32 advertisement re-origination, and step-by-step packet walks for L2 unicast, BUM, and L3 flows.
  • How: Failure-isolation walkthroughs for both WAN loss and DC loss show the alternate BGW-to-BGW path preserving host reachability; decoupling DC from WAN VTEP space means either side can change without re-coordinating.
  • Where applicable: Any multi-site EVPN/VXLAN program; not tied to specific silicon, though presented by Cisco's lead EVPN architect (and SONiC routing workgroup chair), so feature availability on non-Cisco gear (I-ESI, normalized VNI) should be verified. Concepts (re-origination boundary, VNI normalization, DF local-bias) transfer across vendors.

items.title: Exodus of IPv4 from War-torn Ukraine
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Doug Madory — Kentik

VideoPDF

  • Why: A striking data story about IPv4 as a war-driven national commodity, with direct consequences for anyone reasoning about IP address markets, proxy abuse, and routing-table hygiene — it also explains several of the movers in this year's BGP table.
  • What: Four years of war produced a ~20% reduction in Ukraine's footprint in the global routing table. Ukrtelecom's AS6849 dropped from 4,728 to 1,377 /24s (−71%), with the space leased via brokers (IPXO) and re-originated by Amazon, Windstream, NTT, Lumen, Orange; sister ASN AS6877 vanished from the table entirely. Mariupol's Trinity (AS43554) space popped up under as many as 54 foreign ASes and was confirmed in use as residential-proxy infrastructure. The second act is AT&T's 2025 BGP housekeeping: AS7018 collapsed from 3,200+ IPv4 routes to 641 via super-aggregation and a new policy requiring customers to originate from their own ASN — which chased out the proxy services; the displaced prefixes scattered across ~150 new origins. Also covers AWS's Dec 2024 move to originating 1,000+ super-aggregates (IPv4 footprint 49M → 157M addresses, absorbing space from Volia and legacy ranges) and similar patterns in Iran (Hetzner as recipient).
  • How: Longitudinal BGP/WHOIS analysis; RIPE database version-diffing to document the "Russification" of registrations and subsequent purging of records; proxy-use confirmation via Krebs's investigation.
  • Where applicable: Global — this is analysis anyone can replicate with public data, and the lessons (origin-ASN policy as abuse defense, prefix-count consolidation, broker-mediated leasing risks) apply to any large origin AS.

address-policy measurement

items.title: From Datacenter to AI Center, building the networks that build AI
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Tyler Conrad — Arista Networks

VideoPDF

  • Why: The best single "orientation map" for engineers moving from general-compute DC design to AI backends. Vendor-presented, but dense with concrete numbers you can reuse in capacity planning, and refreshingly honest about failure rates.
  • What: A design guide across topology (single-box vs 2-tier vs 3-tier with GPU-count ceilings per form factor; rail-isolated vs rail-optimized vs fat-tree; multi-plane scaling by port-speed fan-out — 1x800G/2x400G/4x200G), subscription ratios (target 1:1 or better), optics economics, load balancing and congestion control (ECMP hashing vs RDMA-aware static hashing vs DLB vs packet spraying vs SRv6 steering), RoCEv2 mechanics (DCQCN, PFC victim flows, ECN/ECT tuning, a concrete QoS queue design with CNP in SP queues), and segmentation options from VLANs to VRFs to SRv6 uSID.
  • How: Prescriptive with arithmetic: for a hypothetical 100k-GPU back-end, 257,904 links and 515,808 optics; at 2.3M-hour MTBF that is one optic failure roughly every 4.45 hours — about five per day. LPO optics (no DSP, DSP moved into switch silicon) claimed at ~0.5x power, ~0.7x cost, ~0.01x latency. Includes a common-failure checklist (QoS mismatch, dirty fiber, FEC/autoneg mismatch, MMU tuning) that mirrors what real AI-cluster escalations look like.
  • Where applicable: Greenfield AI back-end builds; the talk's own takeaway is that back-end reuse of existing gear is unlikely and power/heat is usually the first constraint. Arista perspective throughout, so silicon-specific framing (radix/speed tables) should be re-derived for other vendors.

ai-networks data-center-fabric capacity-planning

items.title: Improving Routing Security for Global Research and Education
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

steven wallace — Internet2.edu (with CAIDA, per ROOTBEER/NSF CICI)

VideoPDF

  • Why: R&E networks deterministically prefer R&E routes over commodity, which makes their route leaks high-impact (US scientific traffic transiting unintended international paths). Beyond the R&E story, this is a template for measuring local-pref policies you cannot see in public BGP views.
  • What: A measurement system that announces the same prefix from two origins — one via an R&E path (Internet2), one via commodity transit — with varying AS-path prepends, then pings responsive hosts to infer which route each of ~2,600 R&E ASes actually chose. June 2025 results: 80.8% of prefixes/75.3% of ASes always used the R&E route regardless of prepending; 7% always commodity; ~9% switch by AS-path length (implying equal local-pref). Real 2024 incidents documented: a South American R&E network leaking commercial routes (traffic rerouted through South America) and a Middle East member leaking R&E routes to a commercial provider (cloud return traffic transiting the Middle East, some members withdrawing specifics defensively).
  • How: Building on this, the ROOTBEER project is constructing an operational routing-security observatory at Internet2 — leak detection between R&E and commodity, a stakeholder dashboard, and a move toward an actively maintained public route filter on all peers, shareable by other R&E transit networks.
  • Where applicable: R&E-specific topology (route-preference policy), and public BGP visibility is thin here (only 27 of 2,659 R&E ASes provide RouteViews/RIS views). The dual-origin measurement technique, though, transfers to any policy-visibility problem, and the public-filter approach is a model for any community network with trusted transit.

bgp network-security

items.title: IP Geofeeds: Trust, Accuracy, and Abuse
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Calvin Ardi — IPinfo (with Oliver Gasser, William Leung)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Self-published IP geolocation (RFC 8805) is now consumed by every major geolocation provider and feeds compliance decisions (gambling law, content geo-blocking) — and this is the first large-scale measurement of whether geofeeds are true, plus documentation of active adversarial abuse of the format. Not a typical PM search topic, but the findings are broadly useful.
  • What: Validation via two methods: RTT multilateration from a ~1,300-probe global network (27.7M RTTs covering 205k IPv4 / 74.5k IPv6 prefixes) and GPS ground truth from mobile devices. Results: country-level consistency 92% (96.6% IPv4, 79.6% IPv6), but city-level only 79.6% for infrastructure measurements (median error a startling 759 km) and just 29.9% on mobile networks — the gap between infrastructure location and actual user location. Top mismatch sources: CDNs, tier-1s, VPNs, cellular, IP leasing. Adversarial geofeeds are real and quantified: one maps ~101k IPv6 prefixes to 249 countries and ~80k cities (including Antarctica and North Korea); 17 of 20 popular VPN providers had exit traffic in a different country than claimed; public guides exist for crafting metadata to manipulate geolocation databases.
  • How: Proposals to fix the ecosystem: format updates (validity periods/TTL, standardized location identifiers such as H3), validation and feedback mechanisms (geofeed-validator, OpenGeoFeed), and public/private hosting options — with an IAB workshop and possible future IETF WG.
  • Where applicable: Anyone publishing geofeeds (the companion best-practices talk gives authoring guidance) or consuming geolocation for compliance/security. The mobile-network city-level number is the one to remember when someone proposes city-level geo-enforcement.

measurement internet-governance

items.title: Keynote: AI Data Center Networking: Lessons from Meta's Evolution
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Recording

Omar Baldonado — Meta

Video

  • Why: Meta operates some of the largest AI clusters in the world and, unusually for a hyperscaler, shares openly (FBOSS, TorchComms, OCP). A cross-generation retrospective on AI fabric design from the person who runs Meta's global DC networks is the highest-signal keynote on the program for physical DC networking.
  • What: A retrospective through successive AI network deployments — what each iteration taught and where false starts occurred — framed as a stack: PyTorch/framework behavior shapes xPU selection, accelerator traffic patterns drive topology choices, NIC capabilities enable or constrain operations. Also covers network automation at scale, density constraints (power, cooling, space), telemetry for AI workloads, and managing rapid technology transitions without destabilizing production, with gigawatt-scale clusters on the roadmap.
  • How: Lessons-learned format across production generations rather than a single architecture pitch; the value is in the cascade framing (framework → hardware → topology → operations) and the operational truths behind open-sourced artifacts like FBOSS and TorchComms.
  • Where applicable: Explicitly Meta-scale — multi-gigawatt buildouts, custom switch OS, OCP hardware. The layer-interaction reasoning transfers to anyone designing AI clusters, but the specific density and automation numbers are org-specific (from abstract only; the NANOG content page could not be retrieved and no slides were published in the source material).

ai-networks data-center-fabric

items.title: Keynote: Beyond the Chip: The Unprecedented Infrastructure Demands of AI and HPC
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Bill Conrades, Chris Stewart, Michael Balasko — AHEAD

VideoPDF

  • Why: The most concrete "facility-to-fabric" framing of AI datacenter buildouts at this meeting. For anyone whose remit includes physical DC design, this maps how power and cooling constraints now dictate network architecture choices — the limiting factors are no longer transistors but power delivery, cooling, and system-level architecture.
  • What: A structured survey of AI/HPC infrastructure: rack density evolution from air-cooled (<10-15kW) through hybrid/liquid (30-80kW+) to liquid-everything (100-150kW+); a cooling technology ladder (perimeter CRAC → containment → rear-door heat exchange → direct-to-chip → immersion) with capacity bands per technology; and the networking backbone — AI backend (East/West, 1:1 oversubscription) vs frontend (North/South) reference architecture, rail-optimized topology for AllReduce collectives, and a useful comparative table of Ethernet variants (standard ECMP → enhanced ECMP+advanced LB → scheduled packet-spraying/VOQ → Ultra Ethernet) with honest cluster-size and losslessness trade-offs.
  • How: Built around AHEAD's own 10MW specialized integration facility case study (permitting timelines, hybrid air + facility-water cooling, D2C and RDHx plans) plus a Gartner impact radar for timing investments (DLC and AI Ethernet fabrics rated "act now"; in-package microfluidics, HVDC, 800V distribution on longer horizons). Includes physical-layer detail: MPO/xPC/breakout planning, 800G still riding 100G SerDes with 200G SerDes emerging, DC bus bar and ORv3/MGX rack standards.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable planning guidance for AI-era facilities, though presented by a systems integrator (with Cisco-credited diagrams and NVIDIA NVL72 examples), so expect consultative framing rather than an operator postmortem. The cooling-capacity numbers and Ethernet-variant table transfer to any AI DC program.

ai-networks power

items.title: Lightning Talk: Seeing Through the RDMA Fog: Monitoring RoCEv2 with sFlow
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Peter Phaal — InMon Corp.

VideoPDF

  • Why: AI/RDMA clusters create a genuine blind spot: kernel bypass means tcpdump, wireshark, and even eBPF-based host agents see nothing. For a PM who tracks both lossless fabrics and host-based observability (eBPF), this is the counterpoint — some visibility has to come from the switch ASIC.
  • What: A demonstration, on SDSC's Expanse production cluster (93k cores, 208 GPUs, 100G hybrid fat-tree), of sFlow-based RoCEv2 monitoring: RDMA I/O operations decoded from sampled packet headers (opcode, queue pair, PSN, DMA length, virtual address), ECN/CNP congestion-message rates, RoCE ack-credit tracking, per-link queue depth and transit delay, and — critically — immediate notification of every dropped packet with where/why/who.
  • How: Standard sFlow agents in leaf/spine switches stream sampled headers and counters over the out-of-band management network (no interference with RoCE); three lines of SONiC config enable it (sflow collector, sflow drop-monitor-limit 50, sflow enable), similar on Arista/Cisco/Dell/NVIDIA. sflowtool + tshark decode the InfiniBand transport headers from samples; new extensions add per-sample transit delay/queue depth and per-discard reports (reason-coded, e.g. dst_net_unknown). Ultra Ethernet is just another header format for the pipeline — no agent change needed.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — this is a standard switch feature, not new silicon, and the technique covers exactly the visibility gap that host tooling cannot. Drop-notification support requires current releases (202511 SONiC for drop-monitor). The one honest caveat: sampling-based, so it complements rather than replaces per-flow precision.

rdma observability ai-networks

items.title: Lightning Talk: You Don't Need The DNS Root Server System
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Wes Hardaker — Google (with Geoff Huston, Warren Kumari, Jim Reed)

VideoPDF

  • Why: A DNS root server operator standing up at NANOG to ask you to stop sending him traffic is the most memorable pitch on the program, and it's technically sound: your resolver can hold the entire signed root zone locally (RFC 7706/8806). Root query load grew ~40% in two years to 130B queries/day — for data resolvers could already have.
  • What: The case for LocalRoot: fetch the ~1.5MB signed root zone 2-3x/day from IANA/CDN sources, serve it locally. Security improves (DNSSEC validation of unmodified data, ZONEMD integrity), robustness improves (multiple sources and protocols; survives a 24h+ DDoS of the root system), privacy improves (no queries to root at all), and performance improves (root RTT = 0, ~1.5-2.4MB/day of bandwidth).
  • How: Trivial deployment paths shown for the three major resolvers: Knot Resolver's prefill module, BIND type mirror, Unbound auth-zone with the IANA root-zone URL and prefetch. AXFR adoption to B-Root already visible and growing. Active IETF drafts (draft-wkumari-dnsop-localroot-bcp, publication-point and transfer-scheme drafts) aim to standardize and default this in 2026.
  • Where applicable: Any recursive-resolver operator, from enterprise to ISP; no client-side changes. The one cultural hurdle is accepting that the root system becomes an emergency backup rather than the bootstrap queried every time — exactly the inversion the talk argues for.

dns

items.title: Multipath Traffic Engineering for WAN & AIDC
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Zhaohui (Jeffrey) Zhang — HPE (with Kireeti Kompella)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Challenges a 25-year-old either/or — you could have ECMP load balancing or fine-grained TE with bandwidth control, not both. Kompella (co-author of the original MPLS TE RFCs) proposing a unified construct for both WAN and AI datacenters is a notable architectural signal, and the IETF drafts are live.
  • What: MPTE programs an optimally weighted load-balancing DAG (MPTED) across the network: a single construct with per-junction split ratios replaces the many parallel LSPs that conventional TE needs to fill fat pipes (their example: 1600 Gbps R1→R12 needs four LSP constructs conventionally, one MPTED with 25/25/50/50 splits under MPTE). Link failure adjusts junction ratios without reshaping the DAG; multiple ingresses and multiple egresses (multi-egress load spreading, not multicast) are supported with far less state than per-path tunnels.
  • How: Junction state = incoming bandwidth + previous-hops + next-hops with weighted load shares; signaling via RSVP-TE (prototype), with BGP/PCEP/programmable-API (gRPC, YANG-backed) prototypes underway. Contextualized against the existing toolkit (auto-bandwidth, container LSPs/TE++, cBPS AI/ML bandwidth prediction, tactical TE), and connected to the new IETF RTGWG conversation on ML network scheduling (draft-kompella-rtgwg-mlnwsched) — reserving and isolating network resources per inference/training task, since TE only makes sense in an ML cluster when it is split among multiple tenants/tasks.
  • Where applicable: WAN/MAN/DCI and multi-tenant AI clusters; assumes MPLS or IP-tunnel data planes and a controller/computer to originate MPTEDs. IETF draft-stage — conceptual architecture now, not shipping broadly. HPE/Juniper-heritage perspective.

load-balancing ai-networks

items.title: Redefining Netflix BGP architecture
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Fred Cuiller — Cisco; Elise Vennegues — Netflix

VideoPDF

  • Why: A large, real BGP architecture migration with the validation methodology, defect discovery, and phased cutover shown — the parts that usually get omitted. Netflix's edge is 400+ PoPs, 19,000+ OCAs, ~175 countries, 20,000+ eBGP sessions to 2,800+ ASNs; moving that off iBGP full-mesh is a serious operational story.
  • What: Replacement of iBGP full mesh between Edge Switches and Provider Edge routers with a route-reflector hierarchy built on Cisco IOS XRv9000 UCS M7 appliances (chosen over traditional routers and VNFs on integrated TPM, CoPP, operational simplicity). RRs placed in six global sites; production scale runs to 37M IPv4 paths / 300+ clients in North America, 20M paths / 250+ clients in EMEA. Interesting appliance-selection comparison table (router vs VNF vs appliance across scale, CoPP, security, cost).
  • How: Early Field Trial with the vendor caught real defects before deployment (early-release memory leak, BGP process rlimit misassignment, duplicated LLDP entries on Mellanox NICs); one miss escaped lab — telemetry YANG path performance at scale with sub-60s polling, discovered only in pre-production, reinforcing that production churn/scale is unique. Migration: phased per-device (staging RR peering with pilot prefixes → release prefixes to RR → per-device depref-then-pref-up → remove mesh), driven by internal tooling with a per-device migration tag; telemetry dashboards track CPU/memory, session counts, and received paths per address family. BMP activation is the stated next step.
  • Where applicable: The Cisco appliance choice is Netflix/Cisco-specific, but the RR placement reasoning, EFT-style validation discipline, phased-migration mechanics, and telemetry checklist transfer to any iBGP-mesh-to-RR program at hundreds-of-PoPs scale.

bgp troubleshooting

items.title: Removing Barriers to RPKI Adoption
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Cecilia Testart — Georgia Institute of Technology

VideoPDF

  • Why: ROA coverage passed 50% but adoption is uneven, and this is a rigorous answer to why: it identifies planning complexity — not awareness — as the choke point, with numbers on where the remaining headroom is.
  • What: Combines 13 semi-structured operator interviews with BGP/WHOIS/delegation/RIR data analysis, framed by a technology-adoption model (RPKI is in the late-majority phase). Four barrier areas: IP resource management (years of poor recordkeeping), awareness/training, RPKI software, and monitoring/incident tooling. The core contribution is a systematic ROA-planning framework — who can issue, which more-specifics are routed, which delegations/other orgs are involved — made concrete via ru-RPKI-ready, a platform characterizing unrouted space: 47% of IPv4 and 71% of IPv6 prefixes not in RPKI could be covered with minimal technical effort, and if just ten organizations acted, global coverage would rise 7% (IPv4) and 19% (IPv6).
  • How: Worked examples show a single /20 requiring 7 ROAs across 7 origin ASNs and two organizations — the realistic complexity that scares operators off. RIRs are identified as pivotal actors across all four barrier areas.
  • Where applicable: Most actionable for small/mid-size operators and RIR outreach programs; the planning framework and tool are directly usable for anyone with messy, inherited address space.

bgp pki

items.title: RoVista+: Mapping Real ROV Deployments, Dependencies, and Delays
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Tijay Chung — Virginia Tech

VideoPDF

  • Why: "Do you filter RPKI-invalids?" has always been hard to answer honestly — prior methods couldn't tell local enforcement from an upstream doing it for you. This work separates the two, and the findings about RP (relying-party) concentration are a systemic-risk result every operator should see.
  • What: A measurement framework that runs its own ASN and its own RPKI publication points, serving different test ROAs to specific relying parties, then probing the Internet to see who drops the route. Results across 21,827 measured ASes: 1,127 self-deploy ROV while 1,815 ASes rely entirely on upstream filtering — and 69.6% of those "protected" ASes remain vulnerable to local hijacks. 52% of ROV-deploying ASes depend on exactly one RP server (only 14% use multiple RPs in different ASNs, contra RFC 7115). Router enforcement lags ROA updates by ~37 minutes (60-120 minutes end-to-end). Simulation: ROV in the top 100 ASes protects 27.6% of networks; disabling it in Tier-1s exposes 23.8% to hijacks. ~74% of top-5,000 ASes self-deploy; smaller networks overwhelmingly depend on upstreams.
  • How: Dynamic publication points + controlled test-ROA-to-specific-RP delivery + Internet-wide ping/traceroute scanning. Timing-based inference distinguishes upstream filtering (downstreams drop in synchronized clusters when the upstream filters) from self-deployment (independent drop times due to unaligned RTR polling) — validated against Comcast (private RP, synchronized), Cloudflare (public RP, varied), and NTT (both patterns).
  • Where applicable: The tooling and datasets are open-sourced, and the operational lessons are immediate for everyone: diversify your RPs across ASNs, and understand your ROV posture may be inherited rather than enforced. The methodology (selectively invalidating to one RP at a time) also generalizes to AS-path exploration. Research-grade but production-relevant.

bgp measurement network-security

items.title: Shaping the Future of BGP Observability: BMP Evolution at IETF
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Core pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Narasimha Prasad S — Cisco (with Paolo Lucente, NTT DATA; Thomas Graf, Swisscom)

VideoPDF

  • Why: BMP is quietly becoming the vendor-neutral BGP telemetry substrate, and its IETF evolution this cycle is substantial. If the PM's world includes BGP monitoring pipelines (and the Netflix talk explicitly names BMP activation as next), this is the standards map.
  • What: A structured tour of the foundational RFCs (7854 Adj-RIB-In, 9069 Loc-RIB, 8671 Adj-RIB-Out — including the useful correction that pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out is not the Loc-RIB) and then the active drafts: BMPv4 TLV-ization making all message types extensible; Path Marking, which exports the best-path decision outcome per path with reason codes (finally answering "why wasn't this path installed" without memorizing the 13-step selection process); structured timestamps separating trigger time from export time; Generic Event Notification for non-route events; Route Event Logging for alerting on policy discards and validation failures; Snapshots for mid-stream collector sync and time-binned archives; ~20 new statistics types; and a YANG model for managing what gets exported.
  • How: Performance drafts attack BMP's high-scale cost — Route Monitoring Aggregation across peers, Common Updates across RIB-views (up to 4x), and Multi-Peer headers — claiming up to n-fold reduction in router/collector CPU and message volume. Security: TCP-AO as the RFC 7854 IPsec alternative, plus early BMP-over-QUIC (multi-streaming + TLS) and BMP-for-RPKI-monitoring proposals.
  • Where applicable: Standards-track and vendor-agnostic; directly relevant to anyone building or buying BGP observability. Implementation timing varies by draft status (some are WG documents, some proposed work) — the talk's own closing point is that operator use cases should drive which drafts advance.

bgp telemetry standardization

items.title: The BGP Clock and the BGP Observatory: Hunting Stuck Routes​
items.text:
NANOG 96 digest Program Wildcard pick 2–4 February 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Kemal Sanjta — Cisco ThousandEyes

VideoPDF

  • Why: BGP zombies — routes that persist in RIBs long after withdrawal because a router lost the UPDATE — happen hundreds of times a day on the public Internet and quietly direct traffic onto dead or congested links. Prior work showed withdrawn-and-RPKI-invalid prefixes persisting for months; this is the follow-up operational tool, and it's free.
  • What: The BGP Clock: a continuously running beacon that advertises a fresh prefix every 10 minutes and withdraws it, encoding time in the prefix itself (IPv6 2a0d:3dc1:NNNN::/48, N = 10-minute index since Jan 1, recycled yearly; IPv4 147.189.(216+N).0/24, N = hour mod 8, recycled every 8 hours — details retrievable via whois). Anyone can check their own RIBs for stale entries. On top of it, the Stuck Route Observatory: a free, no-login web tool where you search by AS and see whether stuck routes are present in your paths, plus a heuristic guess at whether the failure to propagate a withdrawal is yours or an upstream's. RFC 9687 is the new standards attempt at reducing impact — the presenters explicitly ask operators to request vendor support for it.
  • How: Beacon advertise/withdraw cycles correlated against RIPE RIS, RouteViews, and Cisco's near-real-time monitors. Honest limitations: direct visibility covers ~1,500 ASNs (~1% of all), extended to >50% via customer-cone inference; IXP route servers can misattribute blame; intra-AS inconsistency (only some routers in a large AS holding the stuck route — found cases with just 5% of a Tier-1's downstreams seeing it) makes root-causing genuinely hard, with BMP named as the partial future fix.
  • Where applicable: Universal — any operator can check their AS in the Observatory today and grep their RIBs for the clock prefixes tonight. The measurement-visibility limits mean absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, but it's the best available Internet-scale stuck-route diagnostic.

bgp measurement troubleshooting

items.title: 50 Years of Networking
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Program Wildcard pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Geoff Huston – APNIC

VideoPDF

  • Why: Not a technique talk — a direction-of-field argument from one of the Internet's longest-running observers, and the argument lands squarely on questions this PM cares about (openness, centralization, what the AI build-out means).
  • What: Why Ethernet won (open, cheap, simple, self-operating, and — crucially — an invariant frame format that preserved capital across 50 years of speed and medium changes); IP as "large-scale Ethernet" pushing complexity to the edge. Then the uncomfortable present: name-based service delivery has replaced hop-by-hop address networking, the Internet's "core" is now private CDN feeder systems, and transit is dead. The alternate tomorrow: if Moore's Law stalls, the AI build-out looks like a return to centralized, expensive, specialized compute — and Huston's real warning is the resurgence of closed, black-box platforms whose applications deliberately avoid standard open technologies, making open standards the endangered species.
  • How: Historical analysis and argument; no mechanism to evaluate.
  • Where applicable: Speculative and big-picture, but a useful stress test for any strategy that assumes the next 50 years look like the last 50.

internet-governance

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Program Core pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Thomas Weible – Flexoptix

VideoPDF

  • Why: With IPoDWDM, IP engineers inherit the spectrum-planning problem that used to belong to the transport team, and the shift from narrow-grid channel-count thinking to wide-grid superchannels changes topology and filter decisions that lock in for a hardware generation.
  • What: An argument that as per-channel bandwidth grows (400G/800G/1.6T coherent superchannels), 400GHz COTS muxes future-proof the C-band (12×400GHz vs 96×50GHz) while remaining backward-compatible with legacy 50GHz services. Includes a compact coherent-detection primer (DP-QAM16, 425Gbps at 53.125GBd, phase- and polarization-diversity balanced receivers), the grid math (1.6T DP-QAM16 needs ~300GHz channel bandwidth), DIY superchannels via low-cost PLC 1x4 splitters feeding regular 50GHz mux/demux, and a market snapshot (800G ZR+ in DD/OSFP, 12.8T liquid-cooled XPO approaching).
  • How: Think in THz/GHz rather than nm and channel numbers; make a frequency plan per span; exploit the fact that coherent receivers are "blind" to foreign wavelengths to build filterless/colorless topologies — at the acknowledged cost of flexibility, which wide-grid filters win back.
  • Where applicable: For anyone planning or refreshing DWDM plant, especially IP engineers newly owning transport decisions. Caveat: this is Flexoptix research content and the 400GHz-COTS recommendation aligns with their product line — the physics and tradeoffs are general, the shopping advice is vendor-flavored.

optics capacity-planning

items.title: Crafting Network Configurations at Meta
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Program Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Santiago Alfonso Munoz Rodriguez – Meta

VideoPDF

  • Why: How a hyperscaler generates config for thousands of multi-vendor backbone devices daily is a useful reference point for anyone designing (or buying) network automation — and the compiler framing is genuinely clarifying.
  • What: Meta's stack — FBNet object store, Skynet Thrift API, Jinja2 config generation — extended with Skypath, a minimal query DSL embedded directly in templates ({$ Router[name={dev}]/asn $}), which turns templates into self-contained specifications that engineers can reason about close to plain CLI. The multi-vendor layer is a "Confpiler": vendor-agnostic IR (OpenConfig-like), frontend authoring/analysis, backend IR→vendor-YANG schema translation separated from serialization — so delivery protocol (CLI for humans, NETCONF/gNMI for machines) can switch on the fly, and the multi-vendor network is operated as if single-vendor.
  • How: Lazy-evaluating interpreter preprocesses templates; compile-time static blueprint with runtime-rendered dynamic values (a Java bytecode analogy); versioned packages pin code commits so rollback knows which implementation to return to.
  • Where applicable: Meta-scale backbone with daily change volume. The stated lessons temper transfer: "our ability to be declarative can only be as good as our database models," there's a limited budget for tooling change, and "abstraction only makes sense when behavior is portable." Concepts transfer; the surrounding systems are the hard part.

automation configuration-management

items.title: Designing Cloud Workloads For LEO Satellite Internet Users
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Program Wildcard pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Sid Mathur – Fastah Inc.

VideoPDF

  • Why: LEO connectivity is quietly becoming a real user population, and it breaks assumptions (stable egress, stable IP geo, predictable RTT) that most cloud architecture takes for granted.
  • What: A mental model and design-pattern set for LEO-served users: traffic lands at ~200 (Starlink) / 300+ planned (Amazon LEO) ground gateways mapped to IX/PoPs; static users behave like fixed broadband, while in-motion users (aviation, maritime) change egress mid-session — the talk traces one flight's IP geolocation through Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan, Bulgaria, Hungary, Germany, and France, with all the GDPR/jurisdiction questions that implies. Amazon LEO B2B rides AWS Direct Connect, so once traffic lands it's ordinary VPC traffic; new multicloud interconnects (AWS Interconnect Multicloud, GCP Cross-cloud Interconnect) enable cross-cloud failover patterns.
  • How: Three patterns — pin static low-latency users to the nearest region with PNI for predictable RTT; build in-motion users as multi-region active-active with stateless services and HTTP/3 tolerance for TLS/TCP resets; use cross-cloud interconnects for "too expensive to fail" B2B workloads. Decision inputs: user-population geography, data sovereignty, egress cost, latency budget, failover topology.
  • Where applicable: Teams building applications for LEO user populations; the interconnect specifics are AWS/GCP-specific. Key takeaway: the routing path is the only truly different part.

mobile cloud-native

items.title: From Metrics to Investigation: How Agentic SRE Could Change Network Operations
items.text:
NANOG 97 digest Program Adjacent pick 1–3 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Mohibul Mahmud, Shamir Abdul Aziz, Karthik Srinivas Muthuramakrishnan – Microsoft

VideoPDF

  • Why: A working — not aspirational — agentic investigation system for network incidents, with an honest list of what still doesn't work; for anyone thinking about agentic identity and trust boundaries, this is the ground truth from an early deployment.
