  • What: A regulator's update on the EC's "complex voluntary conciliation" on fair share — the deck frames it as "From Fair Share to Ecosystem Cooperation: how the EC's DNA proposal plans to reshape IP interconnections" — with the outcome still undecided among the co-legislators.
  • How: Policy talk, not technical; explicitly tentative about where the discussions will end.
  • Where applicable: EU-operating networks, IXPs, and content delivery players. Finnish-regulator (Traficom) perspective on an EU-wide process still under debate.

internet-governance interconnection peering

items.title: Knowledge is the power - Network Automation beyond the vendor
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Amin Hamidi Younessi (Reonel Oy)

Video

  • Why: Demonstrates that vendor-portable automation is achievable with plain Python and native APIs — a counterpoint to framework lock-in, relevant to anyone running mixed estates or setting automation strategy.
  • What: One Python skillset — querying live state, provisioning BGP peers, pushing wide config changes — applied across MikroTik RouterOS and Cisco IOS-XE via their native APIs, demonstrated on a real ISP/IXP lab built on EVE-NG. No Ansible, no heavy frameworks: HTTP, JSON, and a few dozen readable lines of Python. (from abstract only)
  • How: Direct API calls against each vendor's native interface, with the protocol (BGP) as the stable abstraction — "when you understand the protocol underneath, the vendor becomes just a detail."
  • Where applicable: General technique, but the demo is lab-based (EVE-NG) and covers exactly two vendors, so expect small adapters per platform. Most practical for small/mid-size operators; not a scale-out automation architecture.

automation api

items.title: Managing Cryptographic Transitions: Crypto‑Agility as an Enabler and a Challenge
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Markus Rautell (VTT)

Video

  • Why: PQC migration will land squarely on identity and network-security infrastructure — passkey, token, and certificate stacks all need swappable primitives. This talk frames the architectural problem that precedes any migration plan.
  • What: A position talk: cryptographic primitives offer temporary rather than permanent protection, PQC transition timelines are external and time-critical, and system architectures are still widely designed so that cryptographic updates are risky, slow, and resource-intensive; crypto-agility is hard but the work must continue. (from abstract only)
  • How: Architectural/design discussion rather than a specific mechanism — the abstract offers no concrete technique.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any system with long-lived cryptographic dependencies (identity, DNSSEC, TLS, control-plane protocols). Conceptual rather than deployable — treat it as framing for migration planning, from a research organization's perspective.

quantum-safe encryption identity

items.title: NAF Framework
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Jaakko Rautanen

Video

  • Why: A shared vocabulary for network automation systems helps compare tools, architectures, and roadmaps — directly useful to a PM defining automation product strategy.
  • What: A 5-minute introduction to NAF, a community-driven effort that helps understand network automation systems by giving them shared vocabulary. (from abstract only)
  • How: Not detailed in the abstract — expect taxonomy and concepts rather than a runnable artifact.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building, buying, or comparing network automation. Early-stage community effort; judge maturity accordingly.

automation orchestration

items.title: RFC8950 for a V4LESS(-AS) World: Diving into the magic of IPv4-with-IPv6 Next-Hops
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Daniel Wagner (DE-CIX), Tobias Fiebig (TU Wien)

Video

  • Why: The most directly relevant fabric/interconnect talk on the program. Carrying IPv4 routes with IPv6 next-hops dissolves several standing design pains in both IXP peering LANs and large ECMP fabrics — exactly the DC/WAN interconnect territory this PM works in.
  • What: A working walkthrough of what IPv4-with-IPv6 next-hops (RFC 8950, which extends RFC 5549-style extended next-hop encoding to eBGP) enables: IXPs without IPv4 peering-LAN growth pain, seamless IPv4 routing at /32 granularity, IPv4-free transport links, a fully ARP-free infrastructure, and ECMP-enabled L3 underlays for 100G+ fabrics without LACP. Includes an open invitation to peer with V4LESS-AS (AS215250), their live RFC 8950 testbed at an internet exchange.
  • How: IPv4 NLRI is advertised over BGP sessions using IPv6 next-hops, so the entire L3 core — peering LANs, transport, fabric underlay — can be IPv6-only while still serving IPv4 destinations; with no IPv4 at L2/L3, ARP disappears and routed ECMP replaces LACP-bundled L2 links.
  • Where applicable: A standards-based technique, not vendor- or org-specific in principle. Constraints: every router on the path must support extended next-hop encoding, and the ARP-free/no-LACP benefits are easiest to realize in greenfield or single-administrator fabrics. The V4LESS-AS testbed (AS215250) is the concrete proof point.

bgp ipv6 peering

items.title: Root KSK Rollover 2026: An Operator's Readiness Checklist
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Roy Arends (ICANN)

Video

  • Why: October 2026 brings the first root KSK rollover since 2018; validating resolvers with badly managed trust anchors are the ones that break. This is a concrete, adoptable checklist — exactly the kind of ops content worth taking away.
  • What: A minutes-long readiness checklist for validating-resolver operators: verify resolvers use managed trust anchors, confirm the active root KSK, and inspect RFC 5011 state — with concrete commands and expected outputs for common resolver software, designed to slot into existing workflows. (from abstract only)
  • How: Relies on RFC 5011 automated trust-anchor updates (or RFC 9718 operation); the checklist catches hardcoded/static trust-anchor configurations before they break.
  • Where applicable: Any operator of validating recursive resolvers, regardless of scale. Should be routine if trust anchors are already managed correctly.

dns pki

items.title: The IRR Landscape and its Implications on Global Internet Traffic
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Daniel Wagner (DE-CIX)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Route-server prefix filters at IXPs are generated from IRR data; when AS-SETs are inconsistent or stale, traffic that should flow through the peering fabric doesn't. This is the data-quality counterpart to the ASPA talk, attacking the same trust gap from the legacy side.
  • What: Latest results from Wagner's RIPE Labs article series on the IRR landscape, including previously unreleased insights on AS-SET heterogeneity, IRR lookup ordering, and the measured traffic impact at a very large IXP, ending in a community call to action. (from abstract only)
  • How: Analysis of IRR database contents and route-server filter-generation behavior, correlated with observed traffic at a large IXP.
  • Where applicable: The measurement is DE-CIX-scale (org-specific), but the mechanism — filters generated from heterogeneous IRR data — applies to every IXP participant and most transit relationships. Direction of findings transfers; absolute numbers do not.

bgp measurement network-security

items.title: The No-Nonsense Approach to Build Infrastructure that Lasts
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Core pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Tony O'Sullivan (RETN)

Video

  • Why: Physical-infrastructure resilience — cable cuts, geopolitical and climate shocks — is core WAN territory for this PM, and this is a hard-won experience report from a network that stayed online through events that took others down.
  • What: An experience talk (the deck is titled "Hardwired for Chaos") on how RETN (AS9002) has scaled a lean, 44-country network and kept it running "under fire, literally," challenging the industry to build infrastructure that is innovative, scalable, and sustainable.
  • How: The abstract gives principles rather than mechanism — expect lessons on physical/route diversity, lean operations, and surviving cable cuts rather than a technical deep dive.
  • Where applicable: RETN-specific scale and geography (pan-Eurasian footprint with distinct geopolitical exposure). The resilience lessons transfer; the specific operating model and cost base do not.

troubleshooting interconnection

items.title: Veeam MCP server
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Wildcard pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Janne Haatainen (Veeam)

VideoPPTX

  • Why: Not about networking at all, but a signal of where ops tooling is heading: local AI agents acting on infrastructure products through MCP — the same wave that will demand identity and authorization models for agents.
  • What: A quick, sponsored lightning talk introducing a Veeam MCP server that lets local AI interact with Veeam products (the materials reference a Claude-based setup).
  • How: An MCP server exposing product operations to a local LLM client — the pattern, not the product, is the takeaway.

ml-for-networking api

items.title: (Why) GPUs are awful (to virtualize)
items.text:
nog.fi meeting 2026.06 digest Program Adjacent pick 16–17 June 2026

Abstract Recording

Johannes Brummer

Video

  • Why: For anyone running networks for AI-era compute, knowing why GPUs are painful to virtualize (device assignment, passthrough, memory mapping) shapes what the fabric must support — SR-IOV/passthrough choices interact directly with RDMA fabrics.
  • What: Hands-on experience virtualizing different GPU types on multiple different hardware platforms, plus approaches to providing them to actually paying customers. (from abstract only)
  • How: Practical experience report; no methodology stated in the abstract.
  • Where applicable: Hosting/service providers offering GPU compute. Useful context for designing networks under GPU clusters, but it is a compute virtualization talk, not a networking one.

gpu-clusters containers

items.title: Achieving Wire-Latency Storage Systems by Exploiting Hardware ACKs (Juneberry)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Qing Wang, Jiwu Shu, Jing Wang, Yuhao Zhang (Tsinghua University). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Touches RDMA datapath internals directly: it questions whether storage requests need a full RPC round trip plus server-CPU involvement to commit, which is relevant to anyone designing lossless-fabric storage paths.
  • What: Juneberry gives storage requests a fast path that commits in a single round trip while bypassing the server CPU, with request execution happening asynchronously on the server afterward.
  • How: An "Ordered Queue" abstraction treats the NIC's hardware ACK as the commit signal while preserving linearizability; durability comes from landing requests in persistent memory. Built on commodity RDMA NICs and integrated into Memcached and PMemKV, with significantly lower latency than RPC under write-intensive workloads.
  • Where applicable: RDMA + persistent-memory storage deployments on commodity RNICs. General mechanism, but the durability story assumes PM availability.

rdma benchmarking

items.title: Efficient Direct-Connect Topologies for Collective Communications
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Liangyu Zhao, Tapan Chugh, Arvind Krishnamurthy (University of Washington); Siddharth Pal, Jason Fantl, Prithwish Basu, Joud Khoury (Raytheon BBN); Weiyang Wang (MIT CSAIL). Adjacent.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Sits at the physical-topology/collective-communication boundary that increasingly drives ML cluster fabric design — relevant context for DC topology and interconnect decisions.
  • What: An algorithmic framework that jointly synthesizes direct-connect topologies and their communication schedules, then picks the topology/schedule best suited to a given workload's latency-vs-bandwidth profile and degree constraints.
  • How: Start from small optimal base topologies and schedules, then iteratively expand them to large sizes; a novel polynomial-time algorithm produces efficient collective schedules for well-known large-scale graph topologies. Validated on multiple testbeds plus large-scale simulation.
  • Where applicable: Degree-constrained direct-connect networks (e.g., optical/cabled interconnects without a central switch). General framework; most valuable where you control the physical topology.

ai-networks data-center-fabric gpu-clusters

items.title: Efficient Multi-WAN Transport for 5G with OTTER
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Mary Hogan (Oberlin College); Gerry Wan (Google); Yiming Qiu (University of Michigan); Sharad Agarwal, Ryan Beckett (Microsoft); Rachee Singh (Cornell); Paramvir Bahl (Microsoft). Adjacent.
VideoPDF

  • Why: WAN interconnect is core to the PM, and multi-WAN coordination for 5G is an operator-grade problem. The paper shows a way to stitch routes across multiple WANs using existing cloud primitives.
  • What: OTTER coordinates transport across multiple WANs to improve performance for 5G traffic, managing route identification and use across providers from one system.
  • How: Uses cloud-native components (VNet peering, VPN gateways, firewalls) configured so that VMs in one region can use a gateway in another and carry transit traffic, with scale-up/scale-out per component to span large geographies without per-component code changes; supports asymmetric paths. Reported >25 Gbps between VMs in their GCP topology.
  • Where applicable: Multi-cloud/multi-WAN operators; the prototype leans on specific cloud networking features, so it's somewhat provider-configuration-specific.

mobile cloud-native

items.title: eTran: Extensible Kernel Transport with eBPF
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zhongjie Chen (Tsinghua); Qingkai Meng (Nanjing University); ChonLam Lao (Harvard); Yifan Liu, Fengyuan Ren (Tsinghua); Minlan Yu (Harvard); Yang Zhou (UC Berkeley and UC Davis). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: New transport designs almost never reach the mainline kernel, and when they do it takes years. eTran is a credible answer to "how do we get customizable transports into production without forking the kernel" — directly relevant to anyone reasoning about datapath internals and congestion control.
  • What: A framework that makes kernel transport extensible: operators implement and customize transports (it ships DCTCP-style TCP and Homa) as eBPF rather than kernel patches, while keeping kernel-level safety and absorbing userspace-transport performance tricks.
  • How: Core transport ops run in the kernel via eBPF; packets reach a thin, untrusted userspace library through AF_XDP sockets, where they are reassembled into TCP flows or Homa RPCs. All packets traverse eBPF hooks, so monitoring, access control, and rate limiting are modular eBPF programs chained via bpf_tail_call. Reported up to ~7.5x lower P99 latency than Linux Homa on RPC workloads. Open source.
  • Where applicable: Datacenter Linux hosts (evaluated on kernel 6.6.0 with AF_XDP). General technique, but tied to a recent kernel and AF_XDP; synchronization support in eBPF is a noted limitation.

ebpf linux-networking

items.title: Everything Matters in Programmable Packet Scheduling (PACKS)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Albert Gran Alcoz (ETH Zürich); Balázs Vass (BME-TMIT); Pooria Namyar (USC); Behnaz Arzani (Microsoft Research); Gábor Rétvári (BME-TMIT); Laurent Vanbever (ETH Zürich). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: PIFO is the ideal programmable scheduler but can't be built at line rate in hardware. Prior approximations (SP-PIFO, AIFO) each capture only one of PIFO's two behaviors. This advances the "one scheduling abstraction on commodity switches" agenda that matters for anyone tuning FCT on Tofino-class hardware.
  • What: PACKS approximates PIFO while capturing both required behaviors — scheduling order and admission control — which prior schemes handled only separately.
  • How: Packets are tagged with ranks; PACKS uses a sliding window of recent ranks plus queue-occupancy to make admission decisions, and maps ranks across a small set of priority queues to minimize rank inversions. Reported: up to 7x and 15x fewer rank inversions than SP-PIFO and AIFO, up to 60% fewer drops vs SP-PIFO, and up to 33%/2.6x lower mean FCT for small flows under pFabric ranks.
  • Where applicable: Existing programmable switches; implemented in P4 and shown to run at line rate on Intel Tofino. General technique within the constraints of fixed-queue hardware.

packet-scheduling programmable-dataplane

items.title: From Address Blocks to Authorized Prefixes: Redesigning RPKI ROV with a Hierarchical Hashing Scheme
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zedong Ni (CNIC, CAS / Southeast University); Yinbo Xu, Hui Zou, Yanbiao Li (CNIC, CAS / UCAS); Guang Cheng (Southeast University / Purple Mountain Labs); Gaogang Xie (CNIC, CAS / UCAS). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: RPKI Route Origin Validation is becoming table stakes for routing security, and its memory/lookup cost on routers is a practical adoption barrier. Directly relevant to the security-and-routing side of the PM's remit.
  • What: A redesign of ROV's validation data structure to make origin validation fast and memory-efficient, reframing the problem from address blocks to authorized prefixes.
  • How: A hierarchical hashing scheme for prefix-to-authorization lookup. (Specific performance numbers were not captured in this digest pass; confirm them from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: Router-side ROV implementations; broadly applicable to any operator deploying RPKI.

bgp pki

items.title: Mitigating Scalability Walls of RDMA-based Container Networks
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

  • Authors / tier: Wei Liu (Tsinghua and Alibaba Cloud); Kun Qian (Alibaba Cloud); Zhenhua Li (Tsinghua); Feng Qian (USC); Tianyin Xu (UIUC); Yunhao Liu (Tsinghua); Yu Guan, Shuhong Zhu, Hongfei Xu, Lanlan Xi, Chao Qin, Ennan Zhai (Alibaba Cloud). Core.
Video

  • Why: RDMA-offloaded container networks deliver big wins (the paper shows ~21 Gbps TCP rising to ~180 Gbps once forwarding and VXLAN move to the RNIC and RDMA carries packets), but performance collapses unexpectedly at the scale of millions of containers. Anyone betting on RNIC offload for container fabric needs to understand this ceiling.
  • What: The "scalability wall" is traced to the RNICs themselves — design/implementation defects that are invisible because RNIC internals are closed. They build ScalaCN, which infers the most likely causes despite that opacity and proactively reschedules NF offload.
  • How: Combinatorial causal testing reconstructs an approximate RNIC architecture and performance model from black-box behavior; ScalaCN then optimizes the network-function offload schedule against that model. On production workloads: ~1.4x end-to-end bandwidth and ~31% lower forwarding latency after resolving 82% of inferred causes. Issues were reported to and confirmed by vendors.
  • Where applicable: Production RDMA container networks at hyperscale; evaluation is on Alibaba's production RCN with NVIDIA ConnectX-6 RNICs, so specifics are vendor- and deployment-tied, but the causal-inference methodology for black-box NICs generalizes.

rdma kubernetes cni

items.title: Mutant: Learning Congestion Control from Existing Protocols via Online Reinforcement Learning
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

  • Authors / tier: Lorenzo Pappone (Saint Louis University); Alessio Sacco (Politecnico di Torino); Flavio Esposito (Saint Louis University). Adjacent.
Video

  • Why: Congestion control is core datapath territory; the "learn to switch among existing CCAs online" framing is a pragmatic middle ground between hand-tuned and clean-slate learned CC, worth watching as a design pattern.
  • What: An online-RL approach that adapts among existing congestion-control protocols rather than learning one from scratch. (Detailed mechanism and results not captured in this digest pass; confirm from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: General transport; treat performance claims as to-be-verified.

congestion-control ml-for-networking

items.title: NDD: A Decision Diagram for Network Verification
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zechun Li, Peng Zhang, Yichi Zhang (Xi'an Jiaotong University); Hongkun Yang (Google). Adjacent. Awarded Outstanding Paper.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Network verification underpins config-change safety and reachability analysis. BDDs have been the standard data structure for a decade; an Outstanding Paper that improves the substrate is worth tracking even if you consume verification rather than build it.
  • What: Network Decision Diagram (NDD), a data structure customized for verification that natively supports equivalence classes and beats BDD on memory and computation.
  • How: NDD wraps BDD in another decision-diagram layer — each NDD node represents a header field, and each edge is labeled with a BDD encoding that field's values. Because field-based matching is local, NDD sharply reduces BDD node counts and makes equivalence-class handling transparent to verifiers. Released as a library; existing verifiers (AP Verifier, APT) were ported to it.
  • Where applicable: General — a drop-in substrate for BDD-based verification tools.

testing orchestration

items.title: ONCache: A Cache-Based Low-Overhead Container Overlay Network
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Shengkai Lin, Shizhen Zhao, Peirui Cao, Xinchi Han (Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Quan Tian, Wenfeng Liu, Qi Wu, Donghai Han (Broadcom); Xinbing Wang (SJTU). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Overlay networks (VXLAN/Geneve CNIs) are the default in Kubernetes but impose a per-packet tax versus bare metal. This is the exact tradeoff a cloud-native networking PM lives with, and the paper quantifies where the kernel datapath actually spends its time.
  • What: The authors profile the overlay datapath segment by segment, observe that most of the extra overhead recomputes the same results across packets of a flow, and cache those invariant results. The result reaches near-bare-metal throughput while keeping overlay flexibility and compatibility.
  • How: Three caches (egress, ingress, filter) hold the invariant per-flow results; implemented as four eBPF programs plus three eBPF maps and a small userspace component, in roughly 524 lines of eBPF C — far less than prior approaches like Slim or Falcon. Reported gains: ~12% TCP throughput and ~36% transaction-rate improvement (20%/34% for UDP), with reduced soft-interrupt CPU.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to overlay CNIs; the prototype is shipped as an Antrea plugin (Broadcom is a co-author), so the cleanest integration path is Antrea/OVS-based fabrics. The technique itself is CNI-agnostic.

kubernetes cni

items.title: PreAcher: Secure and Practical Password Pre-Authentication by Content Delivery Networks
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Shihan Lin, Xiaowei Yang (Duke); Suting Chen, Aleksandar Kuzmanovic (Northwestern); Yunming Xiao (University of Michigan); Yanqi Gu (UC Irvine). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Sits in the identity/authentication lane: it offloads password authentication to CDNs to absorb application-layer DoS against login interfaces, without ever revealing passwords to the CDN. A genuinely novel three-party auth architecture.
  • What: A system that inserts a third-party CDN into the password-auth path to pre-authenticate users and filter ADoS traffic before it reaches the origin, while preserving password secrecy and usability.
  • How: A three-party (client/CDN/server) protocol combining an Oblivious Pseudorandom Function (OPRF) with Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH). The client derives a secret key from the password via OPRF+LSH and interacts with the CDN rather than the server, so the CDN can validate login attempts without learning the password. Demonstrated against a commercial-CDN setup where login-interface ADoS slips past standard WAF/rate-limit protections.
  • Where applicable: Web services fronted by CDNs that want login-layer DoS protection; deployable unilaterally by a server operator. General architecture, though it changes the login flow and assumes CDN cooperation.

authentication ddos cdn

items.title: Pyrrha: Congestion-Root-Based Flow Control to Eliminate Head-of-Line Blocking in Datacenter
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Adjacent pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Kexin Liu, Zhaochen Zhang, Chang Liu, Yizhi Wang (Nanjing University); Vamsi Addanki, Stefan Schmid (TU Berlin); additional co-authors at Nanjing University and Huawei. Adjacent.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Head-of-line blocking in lossless DC fabrics (PFC and friends) is a recurring operational pain. Congestion-root-based flow control is a notable angle for anyone working on RDMA/lossless fabrics.
  • What: A flow-control scheme that targets the root of congestion rather than reacting hop-by-hop, aiming to eliminate HoL blocking. (Detailed mechanism not captured in this digest pass; confirm specifics from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: Lossless datacenter fabrics; involvement of Huawei co-authors suggests hardware-oriented validation. Treat as fabric-class research relevant to RDMA deployments.

congestion-control data-center-fabric rdma

items.title: Quicksand: Harnessing Stranded Datacenter Resources with Granular Computing
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Wildcard pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Zhenyuan Ruan, Kaiyan Fan, Adam Belay (MIT CSAIL); Shihang Li, Malte Schwarzkopf (Brown); Seo Jin Park (USC); Marcos K. Aguilera (VMware Research by Broadcom). Wildcard.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Stranded resources (memory/CPU that exist but can't be allocated) are a real efficiency drain in datacenters. The granular-computing angle is an emerging subfield a DC-infra PM wouldn't necessarily search for but should see.
  • What: A runtime that reclaims stranded datacenter resources by exposing computation at fine (granular) units that can be packed into otherwise-unusable capacity. (Detailed mechanism not captured in this digest pass; confirm from the paper.)
  • Where applicable: Datacenter resource scheduling; research-grade, but points at where utilization-efficiency work is heading.

power orchestration

items.title: Securing Public Cloud Networks with Efficient Role-based Micro-Segmentation (ZTS)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Sathiya Kumaran Mani, Kevin Hsieh (Microsoft); Santiago Segarra (Rice); Ranveer Chandra (Microsoft); Yajie Zhou (University of Maryland); Srikanth Kandula (Microsoft). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Micro-segmentation is the canonical zero-trust control for limiting blast radius, but authoring precise policies at cloud scale is the perennial blocker. This sits squarely in network security and is grounded in real deployment.
  • What: ZTS (Zero Trust Segmentation) ingests large volumes of flow logs, infers endpoint roles, and generates micro-segmentation policies automatically, with continuous communication-graph generation and policy enforcement.
  • How: Role inference combines domain knowledge with communication patterns rather than relying on manual tagging (which breaks as pods migrate or scale). Evaluated against ground truth across 11 first- and third-party deployments; reported up to 21.5x more cost-efficient than Apache Flink for the stream-processing workload, with higher role-inference accuracy than prior algorithms.
  • Where applicable: Large public-cloud networks; built and evaluated inside Microsoft's environment, so the productized form is Azure-flavored, but the role-inference approach is general.

zero-trust cloud-native network-security

items.title: Suppressing BGP Zombies with Route Status Transparency (RoST)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Core pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Yosef Edery Anahory, Yossi Gilad (Hebrew University of Jerusalem); Jie Kong, Nicholas Scaglione, Justin Furuness, Amir Herzberg, Bing Wang (University of Connecticut); Hemi Leibowitz (College of Management Academic Studies). Core.
VideoPDF

  • Why: Withdrawal suppression ("zombie" routes that stay active after withdrawal) has been a known BGP weakness for over a decade, with real reliability and security consequences. This is the first systematic defense, relevant to anyone tracking inter-domain routing security alongside RPKI.
  • What: RoST lets an AS efficiently and securely verify whether a route has actually been withdrawn, defeating both misconfiguration-driven and adversarial withdrawal suppression.
  • How: A verification scheme that is compatible with BGP and composes with existing BGP security enhancements (rather than replacing them). The design targets efficient per-route status checks.
  • Where applicable: Inter-domain routing broadly; an incrementally deployable addition to BGP/RPKI-style security rather than a clean-slate redesign.

bgp network-security

items.title: The Benefits and Limitations of User Interrupts for Preemptive Userspace Scheduling
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Wildcard pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

  • Authors / tier: Linsong Guo, Danial Zuberi, Tal Garfinkel, Amy Ousterhout (UC San Diego). Wildcard.
VideoPDF

  • Why: A clear-eyed measurement study of a newer x86 hardware feature (user interrupts) for preemptive userspace scheduling — the kind of "here's what the new primitive actually buys you, and where it doesn't" result that informs datapath and dataplane-OS design.
  • What: An evaluation of user interrupts as a mechanism for preemptive scheduling in userspace, characterizing both the wins and the limits rather than pitching a single system.
  • Where applicable: Userspace network/dataplane stacks and low-latency runtimes on hardware that supports user interrupts. General, forward-looking.

linux-networking measurement

items.title: Towards Energy Efficient 5G vRAN Servers (RENC)
items.text:
NSDI '25 digest Program Wildcard pick 28–30 April 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

  • Authors / tier: Anuj Kalia (Microsoft); Nikita Lazarev (MIT); Leyang Xue (University of Edinburgh); Xenofon Foukas, Bozidar Radunovic (Microsoft); Francis Y. Yan (Microsoft Research and UIUC). Wildcard.
Video

  • Why: A surprising result at the intersection of real-time systems and power: you can claw back substantial CPU energy from vRAN servers despite hard sub-millisecond deadlines and black-box proprietary software. The eBPF-based slack-measurement trick is a clever pattern beyond RAN.
  • What: RENC saves energy by adjusting CPU frequency in response to sub-second cellular-load variation without missing real-time deadlines.
  • How: It establishes safe low-load intervals by coupling MAC-layer rate limiting to frequency changes; computes safe frequencies by measuring deadline slack in vRAN threads via Linux eBPF hooks (or minor binary rewriting of the closed vRAN binary); and handles control-driven load spikes (e.g., new-user attach). Reported up to 45% CPU power reduction (29% server-wide) on a state-of-the-art vRAN testbed.
  • Where applicable: vRAN/telco edge servers; the technique is specific to real-time-deadline workloads, but the "measure slack with eBPF, then undervolt/underclock safely" idea generalizes to other latency-critical services.

power mobile

items.title: A Composable Emulation Framework for Whitebox Switches
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Adjacent pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Congcong Miao (Tencent), Xianneng Zou (Tencent and Tsinghua Shenzhen), Chuwen Zhang (Tsinghua), et al., with Ang Chen (University of Michigan)

VideoPDF

  • Why: As switches disaggregate into vendor-mixed modules (data plane, control plane, optics), monolithic firmware emulators stop matching reality — and config errors slip through to production. This is the first emulation framework built for that composed world.
  • What: "MirSwitch," a composable whitebox-switch emulation framework deployed in Tencent's production network; operators used it to troubleshoot 97.5% of 203 issues in a recent year, with 2.2x better forwarding-emulation performance.
  • How: An adaptor-centric design that stitches together diverse emulator modules for data plane, control plane, and peripherals (including optical components), reconciling differing interface contracts across modules so mixed-vendor compositions can be emulated faithfully before deployment.
  • Where applicable: Operators building disaggregated/whitebox switches from multiple vendors; the 97.5%-of-issues production statistic is unusually strong validation for an emulation paper.

testing open-source switching

items.title: Bifrost: Alibaba's Next-Generation VPC Network with High-Performance Multipath Reliable Transport
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Zihao Fan (SJTU and Alibaba Cloud), Xing Li (Zhejiang University and Alibaba Cloud), Ye Yang, et al. (Alibaba Cloud), Rong Wen (Fudan and Alibaba Cloud), Shunmin Zhu (Alibaba Cloud), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: This is the logical endpoint of the "TCP in the guest can't survive cloud-network instability" argument: Alibaba moved reliable, multipath transport into the VPC overlay infrastructure itself, tail-latency problem included. An operational-systems paper with 26x-scale production evidence.
  • What: Next-gen VPC networking delivering reliable transport as an infrastructure service: up to 307x tail-latency reduction for Redis and 66x for Nginx, millisecond-level failure recovery, and O(100k) concurrent connections per SmartNIC.
  • How: RTT-aware multipath packet spraying across the underlay (bypasses failures, spreads elephant flows), in-place reordering in the guest for in-order delivery, delayed bitmap ACKs for end-to-end reliability, and reliability-state management engineered for SmartNIC deployment at scale.
  • Where applicable: Alibaba Cloud production (operational systems paper); requires SmartNIC-capable tunnel endpoints, so it presumes a cloud provider's level of control over the hypervisor/SmartNIC layer. The architecture — reliable multipath overlay as a tenant-transparent service — is the transferable idea.

cloud-native load-balancing

items.title: BURST: Seeking High-performance, Interoperability and Scalability in Soft-RDMA
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Huijun Shen (Hunan University), Zelong Yue, Jian Yang, et al. (ByteDance), Xijin Yin, et al. (Hunan University)

Video

  • Why: Heterogeneous pods — commercial RNICs, plain Ethernet NICs, in-house hardware — are now the norm, and non-RNIC↔RNIC traffic keeps falling back to TCP. ByteDance attacks exactly the interoperability wall that limits RDMA estate scaling during LLM-infra buildouts.
  • What: A user-space software RDMA stack that runs unmodified Verbs applications on ordinary Ethernet NICs at 400G: 98.7% line-rate bandwidth, 3.2–6.3x kernel RXE throughput, LLM inference latency at 25.2% of TCP, and 12x faster connection setup than native RDMA CM.
  • How: Runs as an independent user-space process with full Verbs API compatibility; lock-free DPDK data plane for line-rate packet processing; Intel DSA offload to cut CPU cost; kernel-bypass connection manager.
  • Where applicable: Data centers with mixed NIC estates, especially where RNIC hardware can't be everywhere (storage-attached hosts, upgraded clusters). x86-specific today (DPDK + Intel DSA); ByteDance production-workload validation, academic authors.

rdma ai-networks

items.title: CCC: Re-architecting Delay-based Congestion Control in Datacenter Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Wanchun Jiang, et al. (Central South University), Danfeng Shan (Xi'an Jiaotong), Fengyuan Ren (Tsinghua), Jiawei Huang, Jianxin Wang (Central South)

Video

  • Why: TIMELY/SWIFT-style delay CC runs in production, but the paper's key insight — that even perfectly measured delay can yield incorrect congestion-information deduction under certain conditions — explains instability modes practitioners see and haven't had a framework for.
  • What: A re-architecture of delay-based CC that makes rate adjustments depend not just on congestion state but on trustworthiness of the deduction from delay signals. The resulting CCC matches INT-based CCs (HPCC, PowerTCP) using only delay — no INT headers, no special switch support — and beats DCQCN, TIMELY, and SWIFT.
  • How: Demarcates operating regions where delay-derived congestion info is untrustworthy (using congestion criteria plus system inertia), applies probing-style rate adjustment there, and applies analytical adjustment elsewhere to reach the target state while keeping the deduction trustworthy.
  • Where applicable: Standard datacenter fabrics — the whole point is needing nothing beyond RTT signals. Validated with DPDK testbeds and large-scale simulation. General technique, no hardware prerequisites; a serious competitor to deployable delay-based schemes like SWIFT.

congestion-control data-center-fabric

items.title: CrossCheck: Input Validation for WAN Control Systems
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Adjacent pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Alexander Krentsel (UC Berkeley and Google), Rishabh Iyer (UC Berkeley), Isaac Keslassy (Technion and UC Berkeley), Bharath Modhipalli (Google), Sylvia Ratnasamy (UC Berkeley and Google), Anees Shaikh, Rob Shakir (Google)

VideoPDF

  • Why: WAN outages increasingly trace to bad inputs to the SDN controller (telemetry bugs, corrupted state) rather than bad control logic. CrossCheck guards that interface — a class of failure most validation work ignores.
  • What: A shadow validation system for SDN-WAN controller inputs. Four weeks in a production WAN: it caught the single invalid-input incident that occurred with 0% false positives; simulation shows detection of demand perturbations as small as 5% at 100% accuracy, and zero false positives with up to 30% corrupted telemetry.
  • How: Cross-validates controller inputs (demands, topology, telemetry) against consistency constraints before they drive TE decisions, alerting operators pre-outage rather than post-mortem.
  • Where applicable: Google-scale WAN operator deployment; the pre-deployment shadow-mode evaluation pattern is what makes the 0%-FP claim credible. Concept transfers to any SDN-controlled WAN (or even large DCN controller) with telemetry-driven inputs.

sdn testing troubleshooting

items.title: DDoS Detection at the Scale of One Hundred Tbps
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Yunming Xiao (CUHK Shenzhen and Tencent), Xijun Luo, et al. (Tencent), Heng Yu, Jiahao Cao (Tsinghua), Yan Chen (Northwestern), Congcong Miao (Tencent)

Video

  • Why: Existing programmable-device DDoS detectors top out around Tbps per box; cloud incumbents see ~100 Tbps aggregate. This is the production answer to two orders of magnitude more traffic — with the scaling lessons made explicit.
  • What: "Canopy," a DDoS detection system deployed in Tencent production that scales past 100 Tbps via distributed detection across many servers — dynamic load balancing that adapts to mice/elephant mixes, plus traffic compression at the programmable switch to shrink per-server workload.
  • How: Instead of naive flow-level load balancing across detection servers (which skews badly), Canopy dynamically rebalances under fluctuating traffic patterns, and pre-aggregates/compresses traffic in the switch offload stage before it reaches the servers.
  • Where applicable: Tencent-specific production deployment, but the architecture (switch-side compression + adaptive distribution over a detection-server fleet) generalizes to any large scrubbing/detection pipeline. Real-world attack mitigation in production validates it.

ddos anomaly-detection programmable-dataplane

items.title: Defending against Traffic Analysis Attacks with Flexible In-Network Obfuscation
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Adjacent pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Guorui Xie, Qing Li (Pengcheng Laboratory), Zhenning Shi (Tsinghua Shenzhen), Gianni Antichi (Politecnico di Milano), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: Encrypted-traffic side channels (packet sizes, timing) keep working through TLS 1.3 and QUIC; existing defenses trade too much bandwidth or need unrealistic coordination. This makes in-network defense cheap enough to consider.
  • What: "Securitas," an obfuscation framework that cuts traffic-analysis attack accuracy by up to 95.89% while consuming 42.69x less bandwidth than prior defenses; real-Internet tests show ~0.15s added web page load.
  • How: A learning-guided mix of packet fragmentation and insertion, chosen adaptively rather than via fixed padding rules; implemented across four data planes — Tofino switch, FPGA, eBPF, and BMv2 — which is unusual deployability evidence.
  • Where applicable: Any operator that can insert obfuscation on-path (switch, NIC, or eBPF host). The multi-dataplane implementation means the defense isn't tied to one vendor's silicon; evaluation includes real-world Internet paths, not just lab topologies.

privacy encryption

items.title: Express Lane to Efficiency and Reliability: Multi-Dimensional Control in Meta’s Express Backbone Network
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Faisal Iqbal, Vitaly Neganov, et al. (Meta), Aditya Akella (UT Austin), Ying Zhang (Meta)

Video

  • Why: Meta's EBB is one of the largest WANs on earth, and this is the follow-up evolution under AI-era traffic pressure — useful as a reference point for how far you can push a mature multi-plane SDN WAN design before adding new control dimensions.
  • What: An operational account of evolving EBB's control plane along two new dimensions beyond per-plane TE: Unequal Cost Multi-Path (UCMP) for cross-plane load balancing and Fast Re-Route (FRR) for rapid local failure detection/recovery — meeting AI-era efficiency and resiliency demands without fundamental architectural change.
  • How: UCMP extends control across planes so traffic can be split unevenly across parallel planes for utilization; FRR adds per-device, time-slice control for sub-second failure handling. Both are described with design, implementation, and production results.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific production WAN, but the multi-dimensional control framing (global-across-planes + local-per-device + existing per-plane TE) is a clean conceptual model for any large multi-plane backbone. Real deployment experience, not simulation.

sdn load-balancing

items.title: Eywa: Automating Model-Based Testing using LLMs
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Wildcard pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Rajdeep Mondal, Rathin Singha, Todd Millstein, George Varghese (UCLA), Ryan Beckett, Siva Kesava Reddy Kakarla (Microsoft Research)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Model-based testing finds real protocol bugs but has always been gated on humans hand-writing RFC-conformant models — months of expert effort. Eywa removes that gate and immediately found 16 previously-undiscovered bugs in DNS/BGP/SMTP implementations. This is the clearest signal yet of LLMs changing core network-engineering practice (spec → model → tests), with results that survived review.
  • What: A protocol-testing framework that uses LLMs to automatically build models of intended protocol behavior from RFCs, blogs, and natural-language sources; case studies across DNS, BGP, and SMTP found 33 unique bugs, 16 novel despite extensive prior manual testing.
  • How: LLM-synthesized models are combined with mitigation for hallucinations and the inability to monolithically generate complex models (decomposition, validation against spec behavior), then fed into standard model-based test generation to drive high-coverage conformance testing of real implementations.
  • Where applicable: Protocol conformance testing broadly — DNS, BGP, and SMTP demonstrated; the approach is protocol-agnostic in principle where written specs exist. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced). If you own protocol conformance or interop testing, this is the paper to read this cycle.

testing ml-for-networking

items.title: From Bits to Tokens: Knowledge-Driven Generative Communication of Multimodal Data
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Wildcard pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Xingyu Chen (UC San Diego), Zihao Feng (USC), Wuqiong Zhao (UCSD), Jianrong Ding (CUHK), Ke Sun (Michigan), Xinyu Zhang (UCSD)

Video

  • Why: Not your domain — and that's the point. This is the most complete systems argument yet that "the network should transmit task-relevant knowledge, not bits," backed by a working prototype rather than a position paper. It signals where edge/IoT/real-time communication research is going as foundation models meet the network stack.
  • What: Knowledge-Driven Communication (KDC): a framework transmitting semantic tokens rather than raw bitstreams. A full prototype achieves high downstream task accuracy with a fraction of the transmitted data and degrades gracefully under wireless loss, beating state-of-the-art codecs and learned baselines.
  • How: A task-aware transmitter uses multimodal foundation models to abstract source data into tokenized embeddings and prioritize semantically critical content (zero-shot, no task-specific retraining); the receiver reconstructs task-relevant information from pretrained knowledge bases plus incrementally updated context.
  • Where applicable: Wireless, lossy, bandwidth-constrained multimodal settings today (sensors, video analytics at the edge). Long-horizon relevance rather than near-term deployability for DC networking — but the tokens-not-bits framing will increasingly show up in adaptive video and agentic-traffic contexts.

ai-networks ml-for-networking

items.title: HybridMesh: A Hardware-software Hybrid Approach for Accelerating Service Mesh Ingress
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Myoungsung You (University of Seoul), Jaehyun Nam (Dankook University), Minjae Seo (ETRI), Taejune Park (Chonnam National University), Seungwon Shin (KAIST)

VideoPDF

  • Why: The ingress gateway is the spot where service-mesh overhead is worst, and the paper quantifies it: up to 4x throughput loss from CPU-intensive traffic analysis plus a convoluted forwarding path. A clean answer to the "sidecar or no sidecar" debate's ingress half.
  • What: A hybrid ingress gateway that puts traffic analysis and routing on a SmartNIC, augmented by a lightweight CPU-side proxy for features that don't fit the hardware. 4.4x HTTP throughput over existing gateways; 2.3x cost-effectiveness and 2.8x power-efficiency versus software-only or hardware-only designs.
  • How: Split the gateway data path — SmartNIC handles per-packet analysis and forwarding; the CPU proxy retains flexible traffic-management features — so neither the fully-software nor fully-hardware extreme is forced.
  • Where applicable: Any Istio/Envoy-style service mesh with hardware offload available; research prototype (testbed evaluation, not production), so treat numbers as best-case. The hybrid split principle is the transferable part.

service-mesh dpu benchmarking

items.title: In Link We Trust: BFT at the Speed of CFT using Switches
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Lior Zeno, Naama Ben-David, Mark Silberstein (Technion)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Byzantine fault tolerance has always cost a large multiple of CFT performance; this paper erases that penalty using properties of the modern DC network itself. A genuinely novel trust model — trusting the network fabric, not cryptography — that reframes what "trusted network" means in a DC.
  • What: SwitchBFT, a datacenter BFT consensus protocol matching the performance and fault tolerance of the fastest CFT protocols — attaining the speed of NOPaxos (an in-switch CFT) while tolerating Byzantine replicas.
  • How: Exploits packet source authentication to eliminate cryptographic-signature overhead in the fault-free path, and switch programmability to enforce agreement decisions and verify safety, all within tight switch resource budgets. Handles packet loss and switch-crash faults as design cases.
  • Where applicable: Data centers with programmable (Tofino-class) switches and source-authenticated links — the "trusted network" assumption is the constraint. For the identity-minded: this is an alternative to per-message cryptographic attestation, complementing rather than competing with workload-identity approaches like SPIFFE for different threat models.

programmable-dataplane network-security

items.title: Iris: Expressive Traffic Analysis for the Modern Internet
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Adjacent pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Thea Rossman, Diana Qing, Gerry Wan, Zakir Durumeric (Stanford University)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Security/ops teams keep bolting one-off sniffers and Zeek scripts onto high-speed links; Iris asks what a framework for high-performance traffic analysis should look like and delivers one that composes hundreds of tasks on one box.
  • What: A compiler-based framework that turns user-defined filters, stream transformations, and computations written in Rust into an optimized pipeline — executing hundreds of concurrent analysis tasks at 100 Gbps+ on a single commodity server.
  • How: The compiler eliminates redundant logic across concurrent analysis tasks to produce one unified runtime minimizing aggregate work; users get connection- and application-layer semantics exposed as Rust types rather than a constrained DSL.
  • Where applicable: General monitoring/security-analysis infrastructure, not tied to specific hardware. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced), so teams could realistically pilot it against existing Zeek/Graylog-style pipelines.

observability programmable-dataplane

items.title: KRAKENGUARD: Towards Fine-Grained eBPF Isolation
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Jainil Patel (IIT Roorkee), Lucas Graeff Buhl-Nielsen (Quantco), Adrien Ghosn (Microsoft), Marios Kogias (Imperial College London)

VideoPDF

  • Why: eBPF's security model is the dirty secret of the ecosystem — CAP_BPF is all-or-nothing, which is untenable as multi-tenant eBPF/XDP programs from different parties land on the same host. This is a serious attack on exactly that gap.
  • What: A trusted user-space manager enforcing fine-grained, policy-driven constraints on eBPF bytecode at load time: restricting helper usage, memory/map access, and return values. It demonstrably blocks misuse in real-world programs, detects existing CVEs, and enables an XDP-as-a-Service use case where tenants' XDP programs run directly on the host interface without mutual interference.
  • How: Symbolic execution of program paths at load time to check compliance with policy; cross-program interference detection to make co-location on the same hook safe.
  • Where applicable: General Linux/eBPF environments — any platform running third-party or tenant-supplied eBPF. Load-time analysis (not runtime) so the cost is per-load; the trusted-manager design makes assumptions about who controls the host. Highly relevant to Cilium-style deployments where programs multiply across hooks.

ebpf authorization network-security

items.title: Learning to Tune Optical WANs: A Field Deployment of Noise Models in Optical Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Bhaskar Kataria, Howard Hua (Cornell), Andrea D'Amico (NEC Labs), Bill Owens (NYSERNet), Rachee Singh (Cornell)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Rare example of physical-layer optimization (amplifier gain tuning) actually deployed in a live ISP backbone with measured results — the kind of ground-truth that usually stays inside vendor tooling.
  • What: A Gaussian Noise model of a New York state ISP's optical backbone covering amplifiers, fiber spans, ROADM s, and transceivers; hyperparameter search over this model identifies amplifier gain settings that improve end-to-end SNR. In a live field deployment, the tuned settings achieved a 2 dB SNR improvement on a single wavelength.
  • How: Model the full optical chain to predict end-to-end SNR accurately, then treat the model as an opaque box and run ML-style hyperparameter search over amplifier configurations under practical network constraints.
  • Where applicable: Small/mid ISP optical backbones (NYSERNet-scale); the 2 dB single-wavelength result is modest but real. Techniques are broadly reusable for any operator that wants model-driven optical tuning instead of vendor-blessed defaults; not a hyperscale DWDM result.

optics ml-for-networking

items.title: Matryoshka: Realizing Hyperscale Data Center Network Design for the AI Era
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Yan Cai, Jialong Li (Max Planck Institute for Informatics), Kutalmis Akpinar, Tianxiang Li, Hany Morsy, Jason Wilson, Sunil Khaunte (Meta), Yiting Xia (MPI), Ying Zhang (Meta), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: The gap this paper names — between logical DCN designs and the concrete switch configurations that realize them — is exactly the "last mile" problem anyone running multi-generation fabric automation knows. It's also the clearest public account yet of how a hyperscaler's DCN tooling strains under AI-cluster growth.
  • What: Meta's production DCN design system, operational for 6+ years, that compiles high-level design intent (physical connectivity, addressing, routing policy) into working switch configurations. It has guided the design of nearly 900 DCs across 18 distinct types, including Meta's latest 100K-GPU training supercluster.
  • How: Intent-based, model-driven compilation: DCN designs are expressed as machine-readable models and systematically compiled down to per-switch configs, so design, addressing, and routing evolve together and heterogeneous cluster types are treated as first-class variants rather than snowflakes.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific production experience, but the architecture pattern (model-driven intent-to-config compilation for rapidly evolving, heterogeneous AI fabrics) generalizes to any operator building multi-generation DCNs. The 6-year production track record and ~900-DC scale make the claims firmly substantiated.

ai-networks data-center-fabric automation

items.title: Offloading Cloud Network Services at Production Scale with SONiC DASH SmartSwitch
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Shaofeng Wu (CUHK and Microsoft Research Asia), Zhixiong Niu (MSRA), Riff Jiang, et al. (Microsoft), Hong Xu (CUHK) — Community Award Winner

VideoPDF

  • Why: A decade of Azure offload lessons distilled into an open, community-governed architecture — and a concrete datapoint that the DPU pool is collapsing back into the T1 switch itself. Directly relevant to where cloud-network offload roadmaps are heading.
  • What: SONiC DASH SmartSwitch, deployed at Azure production scale for stateful network services: 1.53 Tbps throughput, 19.2M CPS, 256M concurrent connections, ~1.8x power efficiency and ~2.7x space efficiency over the prior generation.
  • How: Three design lessons encoded: an immutable, hardware-friendly DASH pipeline programming model (vs. overly flexible models that block acceleration); a "uni-box" SmartSwitch converging NPU and DPU resources inside a single T1 switch (vs. appliance-style DPU pools); and community-driven P4 behavior specifications (vs. vendor SDKs).
  • Where applicable: Built on the open SONiC/DASH ecosystem rather than a proprietary fork, so this is the rare Microsoft-scale result a non-hyperscaler can actually build on. Requires SmartSwitch-class hardware (integrated NPU+DPU in the T1).

dpu open-source switching

items.title: OpenOptics: Enabling Open Research and Implementation of Optical Data Center Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Yiming Lei, Federico De Marchi (Max Planck Institute for Informatics), Jialong Li (Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology), Raj Joshi (Harvard), Shu-Ting Wang (UC San Diego), Xiaoqi Chen (Purdue), Balakrishnan Chandrasekaran (VU Amsterdam), Yiting Xia (MPI)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Optical DCNs have been stuck as closed, hardware-tied ecosystems — every research prototype is bespoke. This is the first serious open framework, and it lowers the cost of experimenting with circuit-switched fabrics to "Python script" level. If you track OCS-based DC designs, this is the platform to watch.
  • What: An open research/implementation framework that decouples optical DCN software from optical hardware. It implements six optical DCN architectures and seven routing schemes on a real testbed (108 ToRs) and achieves a 2 µs minimum optical circuit duration on commodity devices — a record for circuit-switched DCN granularity.
  • How: Three pieces: a time-flow table abstraction as the common hardware/software interface, a unified workflow + Python API for defining optical DCNs, and a backend that re-architects queue management around time-flow tables so packets are staged for rapidly reconfiguring circuits.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to researchers and builders experimenting with optical/express-loop fabrics; requires programmable (P4-class) switches plus commodity optical hardware. Artifacts were evaluated and reproduced (available/functional/reproduced badges), so it is genuinely usable, not just described.

optics open-source data-center-fabric

items.title: OSCAR: O(1)-Step Convergence and Readily-deployable Congestion Control
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Zhaochen Zhang, Feiyang Xue, Rui Ning (Nanjing University), Keqiang He (SJTU), Gianni Antichi (Politecnico di Milano & QMUL), et al. — Awarded Outstanding Paper

VideoPDF

  • Why: The outstanding-paper pick of the congestion-control cluster. It removes the main barrier to fast-converging CC (precise INT headers that commodity high-speed hardware can't parse) while keeping constant-time convergence.
  • What: The first CC achieving O(1)-step convergence — reaching fair share in constant time regardless of network conditions — without specialized network features. In large-scale simulations with realistic workloads it beats precise-INT-based CCs by 12–48% on average FCT and 40–74% on tail FCT.
  • How: Insight that delay and delay gradient carry precision comparable to INT; then three techniques: accurate low-overhead delay-gradient estimation, eliminating overreaction in MIMD updates, and coordinating independent control loops toward a single target.
  • Where applicable: Commodity datacenter hardware (no INT support needed); testbed evaluation under real-world noise plus large-scale simulation. Pairs naturally with CCC above — the two papers collectively argue delay signals can replace INT for the next generation of deployable DC CC.

congestion-control data-center-fabric

items.title: SPLIDT: Partitioned Decision Trees for Scalable Stateful Inference at Line Rate
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Wildcard pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Recording

Murayyiam Parvez (Purdue), Annus Zulfiqar (Michigan), Roman Beltiukov (UCSB), Shir Landau Feibish (University of Haifa), Walter Willinger (Northwestern), Arpit Gupta (UCSB), Muhammad Shahbaz (Michigan)

Video

  • Why: In-network ML keeps stalling on the same wall — hardware limits force tiny fixed feature sets per flow. SPLIDT's partitioning trick is a real mechanism (not an ML benchmark bump) for getting past that wall, and it generalizes to any stateful line-rate inference problem on switches and SmartNICs.
  • What: A system for deploying decision trees in the data plane that supports up to 5x more stateful features than prior approaches (NetBeacon, Leo) at the same low time-to-detection, scaling to millions of flows with ≤0.05% recirculation overhead.
  • How: Two ideas: group DT subtrees into partitions where each subtree gets its own feature set (instead of computing all features upfront for the whole tree), and use in-band recirculation as a control channel to reuse register/match-key resources across partitions at line rate. A training + design-space-exploration framework jointly optimizes feature allocation, partitioning, and depth.
  • Where applicable: Programmable switches and SmartNICs doing traffic classification, security monitoring, or in-network decisions. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced), so the partitioning approach is reproducible, not vendor-locked.

ml-for-networking programmable-dataplane

items.title: Starfish: A Topology-Routing Co-Design for Small-Scale Data Centers
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Anchengcheng Zhou (Princeton), Vipul Harsh (Conviva), Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi (UC Irvine), Maria Apostolaki (Princeton), Brighten Godfrey (UIUC)

VideoPDF

  • Why: Almost all DC topology research targets hyperscalers, yet most real data centers run hundreds to a few thousand servers on leaf-spine with painful cost/oversubscription tradeoffs. This is a rare, rigorous design for that population — directly useful if your fleet is enterprise/colo-scale rather than 100K-GPU.
  • What: A topology-routing co-design (DRing topology + adaptive routing) that supports 56% more traffic than an equal-cost leaf-spine on real traces with the same equipment. The routing scheme also generalizes to expander topologies, where it yields 52% more traffic than leaf-spine — fixing expander designs' biggest deployment hurdle (no practical routing).
  • How: DRing spreads servers across all switches to raise per-server egress capacity and expose diverse near-shortest paths; routing exploits DRing's structural properties and adapts to traffic using standard hardware and protocols — no exotic switching required.
  • Where applicable: Small-to-mid data centers (hundreds–thousands of servers); uses standard equipment and protocols, making it unusually deployable for a topology paper. Artifact evaluated (available/functional/reproduced).

data-center-fabric routing-protocols

items.title: SyncWise: Error-Aware Time Synchronization for Reconfigurable Data Center Networks
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Yiming Lei (MPI for Informatics), Jialong Li (Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology), Zhengqing Liu (Imperial College London), Raj Joshi (Harvard), Yiting Xia (MPI)

VideoPDF

  • Why: As reconfigurable DCNs (OCS-based) shrink circuit durations to microseconds/sub-microseconds, accurate time sync becomes the correctness backbone of the whole fabric — and this paper shows the problem was previously unformalized. A foundational gap-fill for the reconfigurable-fabric subfield.
  • What: The first time-synchronization protocol designed specifically for reconfigurable DCNs. It formalizes the RDCN sync problem, builds an RDCN-specific error model, and achieves provably optimal sync — sub-10 ns maximum sync error, well beyond what the most accurate traditional-DC protocols achieve.
  • How: Uses the RDCN error model (sources of error specific to dynamic optical circuits) to guide "wise" selection of sync parents — choosing the peers whose sync exchanges will be least corrupted by circuit reconfiguration dynamics.
  • Where applicable: Specific to OCS-based reconfigurable DCNs; prototyped on an Intel Tofino2 + OCS testbed with large-scale simulations backing the testbed numbers. Not relevant to static packet fabrics, but core reading for anyone evaluating express-loop/circuit-switched designs.

time-sync data-center-fabric optics

items.title: ZooRoute: Enhancing Cloud-Scale Network Reliability via Candidate Path Provisioning and Overlay Proactive Rerouting
items.text:
NSDI '26 digest Program Core pick 4–6 May 2026

Abstract Paper Slides Recording

Xiaoqing Sun (Alibaba Cloud), Xing Li (Zhejiang University and Alibaba Cloud), Xionglie Wei, et al. (Alibaba Cloud), Yang Xu (Fudan), Shunmin Zhu (Alibaba Cloud), et al.

VideoPDF

  • Why: Fast, deterministic failure recovery offered by the cloud provider instead of pushing HA plumbing onto tenants — an explicit product decision worth understanding. The mechanism is a clever use of an oft-ignored header field.
  • What: A tenant-transparent, underlay-agnostic failure-recovery service, deployed 26 months in Alibaba Cloud: cumulative outage time reduced 93.19%, and 98.21% of failures masked from tenant awareness.
  • How: Reroutes traffic by varying the outer source port on VXLAN encapsulation — different source ports hash to different underlay paths. Tunnel endpoints proactively probe a set of healthy source-port candidates per destination IP, guaranteeing one-shot deterministic reroute onto a known-good path. Engineering challenges addressed: hypervisor probing overhead, Tofino-gateway memory limits, and stateful middlebox disruption.
  • Where applicable: Planet-scale cloud overlays (Alibaba production, Tofino gateways). The source-port-as-path-selector trick is broadly reusable in any ECMP-overlay network; the full proactive-probing service assumes provider control of both tunnel endpoints.

cloud-native troubleshooting

items.title: AI Networking, UltraEthernet, the road to 1.6T and beyond.
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Core pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Matthew Thurbon (Arista)

Video

  • Why: Sits at the intersection of the PM's core interests: AI/HPC fabrics, lossless Ethernet design, next-generation optics (LPO), and the 800G→1.6T speed roadmap. UltraEthernet Consortium (UEC) is the emerging open-standards answer to InfiniBand for AI clusters — worth tracking for anyone in DC fabric work, since UEC's latency/lossless/reliability semantics will shape merchant Ethernet for AI back-end networks regardless of vendor.
  • What: A survey of the design requirements AI applications impose on networks (bandwidth, scale, latency, energy), how UEC's open-standards approach addresses them, and the optics roadmap — specifically standards-based LPO transceivers and 800GbE/1.6TbE — that enables next-gen AI interconnect. (from abstract only)
  • How: Architectural walkthrough of AI fabric requirements and the UEC transport specification direction, paired with the optical layer: LPO as a power/cost-reduced alternative to full DSP pluggables, and the 800G/1.6T port speeds those enable.
  • Where applicable: Datacenter and AI/HPC fabric design generally. Vendor-presented (Arista), so expect the framing to favor Ethernet/merchant-silicon answers over InfiniBand, but the UEC and LPO content is standards-level and broadly relevant.

items.title: Analyzing network reliability up to 800G - Impact of SNR thresholds on BER for Coherent (16QAM) and Non-Coherent (PAM4) high speed transceivers under environmental variations
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Core pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Thomas Weible (Flexoptix)

Video

  • Why: Directly on the PM's physical-optics beat. As 800G and coherent-lite pluggables move from WAN long-haul into DC interconnect and even intra-fabric links, operators need to know how close to the SNR cliff a link can run and still stay within BER targets — and how temperature and cable length shift that cliff. This is the reliability data that informs margining decisions for 100G/400G/800G deployments.
  • What: A measurement-driven analysis of how much SNR headroom coherent (16QAM) versus non-coherent (PAM4) transceivers need to sustain a tolerable BER, factoring in environmental variation (temperature, cable length) to predict how long a link stays reliable. (from abstract only)
  • How: Data collected via Flexoptix's Flexbox programmable transceiver platform, comparing error behavior of coherent 16QAM and PAM4 optics across the SNR range and environmental conditions, with implications drawn for network performance.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to anyone buying or margining high-speed optics, but note the data comes from the vendor's own Flexbox tooling — the framing favors Flexoptix's ecosystem. The coherent-vs-PAM4 comparison itself transfers to any 400G/800G link budget decision.

items.title: Challenges in simulating LEO satellite networks like Starlink
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Wayne Reiher (UoA)

Video

  • Why: Not the PM's domain, but a genuinely interesting emulation technique: reproducing LEO's time-varying latency, load, and handover dynamics on real physical hardware at ~150 devices — a problem most people solve badly in software simulators. The approach (continuously driving netem and token-bucket parameters from an orbital model) is a reusable pattern for testing any time-varying transport path, and LEO is increasingly a real WAN-transit option to reason about.
  • What: The University of Auckland's work extending an existing hardware-based GEO/MEO satellite simulator to LEO constellations, and the technical challenges of doing so on an extensive physical setup of around 150 devices. (from abstract only)
  • How: Continuous real-time updates to netem delay and token-bucket-filter rate parameters to replicate the changing latencies and data rates a ground station experiences as satellites move, clients hand over, and inter-satellite links switch — as opposed to the static latencies/rates that make GEO and MEO easy to simulate.
  • Where applicable: Test-lab technique; adoption requires a physical emulation rig, so it's academic-lab-scale rather than something to lift directly, but the parameter-driving methodology transfers to any hardware path-emulation setup.

items.title: Chorus is going boost fibre plans for over 700,000 Kiwi homes – find out how we will technically deliver the upgrade and how you can get the best performance out of Chorus' services 😮‍💨
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Brent Marquis (Chorus)

Video

  • Why: A mass-change automation story: re-homing 700k+ live services to new speed tiers without customer impact, across a web of interlocking systems. The decoupling and migration-scripting techniques are what make it worth the PM's time, independent of the access-network specifics.
  • What: How Chorus will apply wholesale plan speed upgrades (50/10→100/20, 300/100→500/100 from June 2025) across its network without impacting live services, including how the network configuration enables the change, the process/scripts used for the service migration, and how RSPs and customers can extract best performance. (from abstract only)
  • How: Decoupling the network change from the surrounding in-flight work and systems interactions, using scripted service migration over a network configuration designed to tolerate live modification.
  • Where applicable: Org-specific in its details (Chorus's GPON wholesale systems), but the pattern — decouple, script, migrate at scale without customer-visible impact — transfers to any operator running mass service modifications.

items.title: Communications Resilience
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Jon Brewer (Telco2)

Video

  • Why: Physical-infrastructure risk modeling is squarely in the "running networks" skillset: knowing that your fiber routes share a road, a transformer, or a liquefaction zone is the difference between claimed and actual redundancy. This is a practical methodology talk for infrastructure dependency mapping.
  • What: An approach to mapping telecom infrastructure to identify vulnerabilities and assess risk: data collection and maintenance strategies, dependency mapping (shared power transformers, single-road access routes), and visualization of natural hazards (fault lines, liquefaction zones, landslide-prone areas). (from abstract only)
  • How: Correlate asset location data with shared-dependency and geohazard datasets, visualize overlap, and use the resulting map to drive risk assessment and hardening priorities.
  • Where applicable: Methodology is broadly applicable to any operator or large enterprise with physical plant; the hazard layers shown are NZ-specific (fault/liquefaction data), but the technique transfers anywhere geohazard data exists.

items.title: DNS Resolvers and Nameservers in New Zealand
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Geoff Huston (APNIC)

Video

  • Why: Rigorous measurement of how resolvers actually pick and re-evaluate authoritative servers, and whether popular domains' NS provisioning matches that behavior — directly useful for anyone reasoning about DNS performance, anycast placement, or NS-set design in production.
  • What: An extension of prior resolver-behavior and RIPE-Atlas studies using APNIC's distributed ad system to observe the authoritative-server selection process from millions of real end-users worldwide, then checking how two name sets — the root-zone TLDs and the .nz domains in the Tranco top 1M — are provisioned against observed resolver behavior. (from abstract only)
  • How: Recruits end-users via APNIC's ad-based measurement network (much larger vantage point base than Atlas probes), instruments their resolvers' selection process for a controlled domain set, and compares the observed selection dynamics against the NS configuration of high-traffic zones.
  • Where applicable: General measurement results, applicable to any operator thinking about authoritative DNS placement; the .nz/Tranco slice gives it a local angle.

items.title: DNSSEC for .nz: post-incident recovery and improvement (or, how to see the train coming down the tunnel next time. For Sure.)
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Core pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Paul Radford (InternetNZ)

Video

  • Why: A concrete, transferable postmortem in network security: the failure wasn't the zone data being internally consistent, it was that nobody validated how the zone behaves against caching recursive resolvers in the real world. The lesson — your correctness checks must model the consumer's cache, not just your own output — generalizes far beyond DNSSEC to any system validated in isolation from its consumers.
  • What: The story of the .nz DNSSEC incident, what observability gaps it exposed, and the "fake root" validation system InternetNZ built afterward: a test harness with caching recursive resolvers in the loop that validates zone outputs against real-world query/validation behavior before publication. (from abstract only)
  • How: Pre-release validation that replays the resolver ecosystem — not just checking zone files for internal consistency but exercising DNSSEC validation through caching recursive servers in scenarios approximating production, catching negative side effects before the zone ships.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any DNS operator (TLD, enterprise authoritative, or hosted zones); the harness approach is adoptable by anyone running authoritative DNS with DNSSEC. Org-specific only in the incident details.

items.title: Implementing Precision Timing / Sync as a Service in a Telecommunications Network
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Core pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Phil Carlisle (Chorus)

Video

  • Why: Timing distribution is physical-network infrastructure: PTP (IEEE1588v2) and SyncE over terrestrial transport is both a hard operational problem (asymmetry, wander, hop budget) and a growing service as GNSS jamming/spoofing makes antenna-per-site architectures risky. Relevant to anyone building or consuming time-sensitive transport — including sync-sensitive DC fabrics — and a good case study in hardening a WAN service against GNSS vulnerability.
  • What: Chorus's investigation and lab/customer trials of delivering precision timing as a network service over its own transport using IEEE1588v2 and SyncE, instead of deploying GNSS receivers at every consumer site, and what rolling that out across the Chorus network implies. (from abstract only)
  • How: Terrestrial time transfer over existing fiber transport (PTP with SyncE frequency assist), replacing per-site GNSS clocks — motivated by both deployment cost (clock + antenna + cabling per site at scale) and GNSS's vulnerability to jamming, spoofing, and space weather.
  • Where applicable: The trial findings are Chorus/topology-specific (NZ access network), but the pattern — PTP-as-a-service over operator transport to eliminate fragile distributed GNSS — transfers to any operator or large campus/DC environment with sync consumers (mobile, power, finance).

items.title: IP Quirks and Features
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Mark Smith

Video

  • Why: For a PM whose interests include protocol internals, this is the "why is IP the way it is" talk — the historical design decisions (ARP's late arrival, IPv4 addressing complexity, why IPv6 grew to 128 bits) that explain today's protocol behavior and deployment friction. Context that makes IPv6 and datapath design decisions more legible.
  • What: A historical tour of IP feature evolution from the 1974 Cerf/Kahn paper through the multi-protocol 1990s (IPX, AppleTalk) to IPv6, framed around design goals and why the protocols became more complicated than their designers intended, with IPv6's design and deployment model as the through-line. (from abstract only)
  • How: Historical analysis rather than new research — the speaker's long IETF IPv6 working-group involvement and multi-protocol-era operating experience used to explain design decisions and their operational consequences.
  • Where applicable: Educational/contextual rather than a technique to adopt; useful background for anyone operating or designing IP networks, especially around IPv6 deployment strategy.

items.title: KINDNS: Promoting DNS Security Best Practices
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Champika Wijayatunga (ICANN)

Video
