  • Why: Security-hygiene framework for DNS operators of all sizes; useful as a checklist and as a signal of what the DNS ecosystem considers baseline defenses. Lightweight on novelty but practical for anyone running authoritative or recursive infrastructure.
  • What: ICANN's KINDNS framework — a curated set of simple, straightforward operational security measures that DNS operators of any size can implement, aimed at closing the patchwork of uneven security levels across the DNS ecosystem that attackers exploit. (from abstract only)
  • How: Norm-setting via a published best-practice framework: identify the highest-impact security measures (the ones smaller operators struggle to track and larger operators selectively skip) and package them for adoption.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any DNS operator; not a technical innovation but a gap-closing checklist.

items.title: Passive Optical Networking
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Daniel Hutchins (Ciena)

Video

  • Why: Marginal for the PM, but PON's evolution beyond 10G (25G/50G time- and wavelength-domain options) is the access-side bookend of the optics roadmap they track — the same traffic-growth forces pushing 800G in the DC push higher split ratios and rates at the edge.
  • What: A recap of PON fundamentals, where standards and deployments stand today, and how PON evolves beyond 10G to support higher speeds and increasing traffic demands. (from abstract only)
  • How: Standards/deployment survey of next-generation PON options and their capacity implications.
  • Where applicable: Access/broadband networks; vendor-presented (Ciena), and pitched as a recap-plus-roadmap, so treat the evolution claims with the usual vendor filter. Skippable if your remit doesn't touch access networks.

items.title: We're not in Kansas anymore: my experiences with IP geolocation
items.text:
NZNOG 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 10–11 April 2025

Recording

Shane Alcock (Alcock Network Intelligence, IODA)

Video

  • Why: Not core, but a candid consumer-side account of geolocation data quality — how the datasets are derived, where they go wrong, and the gotchas in using them — which matters to anyone doing geo-based policy, content access, or outage attribution. The IODA outage-attribution use case makes it concrete.
  • What: The speaker's experiences consuming IP geolocation data inside IODA (Internet Outage Detection and Analysis) to attribute observed Internet outages to geographic regions, plus a documentation of how geolocation datasets are built and the failure modes encountered. (from abstract only)
  • How: Practitioner experience report: working with commercial/derived geolocation feeds against observed outage data, and the mismatches that arise when the data's granularity, freshness, or methodology doesn't match the attribution task.
  • Where applicable: Applicable to anyone using IP geolocation for analytics, geo-blocking, or content delivery decisions; not a technique with infrastructure prerequisites, but a set of caveats.

items.title: AST Space Mobile
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Simon Allard (2degrees)

Video

  • Why: Direct-to-device satellite is a genuine architectural shift in coverage economics — a terrestrial mobile operator integrating an LEO constellation via its own ground station is novel infrastructure work outside the PM's usual beat but worth seeing.
  • What: How AST SpaceMobile's satellite array provides mobile coverage where terrestrial networks can't, and how 2degrees is integrating the service into its network, including a 2degrees-built ground station (from abstract only).
  • How: The technical detail (spectrum sharing with terrestrial LTE, ground-station integration, handover behaviour) is promised in the talk; the abstract stays at the "how it works" overview level.
  • Where applicable: Mobile operators; NZ-specific integration but representative of a global D2D trend.

mobile interconnection

items.title: Automated Network State Checking: Insights from the Field
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Core pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Joe Shaw (REANNZ)

Video

  • Why: This is the best operational postmortem-style talk in the program: a full domestic-backhaul hardware refresh where every service had to be rehomed with evidence of continuity — and the response was to build a generalised, model-driven verification system rather than hand-check services. Deeply transferable to anyone doing migrations.
  • What: REANNZ developed a generalised service model plus Python automation that reasons from live network data: it generated new configuration consistent with the new hardware and produced clear old-vs-new running-state comparisons at implementation time, iterated until it could verify even highly bespoke configurations. The talk demonstrates the system with case studies and the challenges overcome (from abstract only).
  • How: A generalised service model driven off live network state (not hand-catalogued per-service checks), automated config generation, and diff-style continuity evidence produced at cutover — a closed feedback loop between intent, generation, and verification.
  • Where applicable: REANNZ's R&E network context is specific, but the technique is general: any operator facing a hardware refresh, architecture change, or migration where per-service manual verification doesn't scale. Particularly relevant wherever bespoke legacy configurations make off-the-shelf assurance tools insufficient.

testing automation troubleshooting

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Core pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Thomas Weible

Video

  • Why: Planning DWDM channel grids for the 400G → 800G → 1.6T superchannel era is exactly the kind of physical-layer topology tradeoff the PM cares about — this is about how fibre capacity and reconfigurability interact over a 10+ year horizon.
  • What: An argument for moving to 400GHz channel grids: how the shift from narrow grids (200/100/50/25GHz) to wide-grid superchannels changes topology economics, how coherent detection being "blind" to anything but its own wavelength enables filterless designs, and how to keep legacy ≤10G signals coexisting on the same fibre pair while avoiding expensive ROADMs (from abstract only).
  • How: Wider fixed-grid (400GHz) filters plus coherent transceivers' tolerance of unfiltered neighbours: harvest filterless-topology cost benefits while retaining the flexibility to reassign bandwidth and carry legacy wavelengths.
  • Where applicable: Any DWDM operator with long-haul or metro infrastructure planning a decade out. The tradeoff is explicit — reduced flexibility vs. cost — and the "keep 10G and below on the same fibre" constraint matters for networks with legacy OTN payloads. The talk may carry a vendor perspective; the physics and grid economics are general.

optics capacity-planning

items.title: Comfortable Complexity of Network Overlays
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Claudiu Captari

Video

  • Why: Using EVPN as a single consistent service layer across carrier core, DC, and campus — over VXLAN, MPLS, or SRv6 — is a significant architectural trend that collapses the "snowflake per domain" problem, and it directly touches the PM's fabric/overlay territory.
  • What: An argument for network transformation through protocol reduction and consistent operational models, with EVPN as the key to delivering consistent L2 and L3 services across any transport and across core, DC, and campus environments (from abstract only).
  • How: EVPN as a unified control plane abstracted from the underlying transport (VXLAN/MPLS/SRv6), replacing per-domain bespoke protocols and skill sets.
  • Where applicable: Large multi-domain operators get the most from it. The abstract is architectural advocacy rather than a case study with results, and the speaker's affiliation is unstated — treat as a persuasive framing talk and weigh it for vendor-transformation-pitch content on the day.

bgp data-center-fabric

items.title: Datagrid: Unlocking the Potential of New Zealand's South Island
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Pierre Goiffon

Video

  • Why: A 280MW AI datacentre in Invercargill plus the Tasman Ring submarine cable project is a material signal for the NZ DC/WAN interconnect landscape — relevant market intelligence for anyone in DC networking, even if the talk itself is a roadmap.
  • What: Datagrid's vision and roadmap for the Invercargill AI DC, the role of renewable energy and climate advantages, and the international and domestic connectivity plans (Tasman Ring) needed to make the South Island a global AI infrastructure hub (from abstract only).
  • How: As a company roadmap pitch: capacity, site, and connectivity plans rather than engineering detail.
  • Where applicable: This is vision/roadmap content, not an engineering talk — value it as infrastructure and market intelligence on where new DC and submarine capacity will land, not as technique.

ai-networks power interconnection

items.title: Defending Multistakeholder Internet Governance
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Jodi Anderson

Video

  • Why: Not technical, but WSIS+20's outcome shapes the regulatory environment in which every technical decision in this program is made — governance developments increasingly reach into routing, security, and identity requirements.
  • What: Where WSIS+20 ended up and how, what happens next, how it sits in the geopolitical context, and where the technical community has opportunities to defend and promote multistakeholder Internet governance (from abstract only).
  • How: Policy/governance analysis rather than a technique.
  • Where applicable: Global, not NZ-specific; relevant to anyone whose products touch regulated infrastructure or identity.

internet-governance

items.title: Designing a Mikrotik CGNAT Solution that Scales
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Matthew Enger (Leaptel)

Video

  • Why: CGNAT at small/mid-ISP scale is a recurring pain point — statefulness, redundancy, and lawful-enforcement logging requirements all at once — and this is a from-the-field design others can replicate on a budget, distilled from commercial-solution experience.
  • What: A step-by-step redundant, scalable CGNAT solution built from Mikrotik hardware, informed by what the author learned from commercial CGNAT deployments in Leaptel's main POPs, while meeting law-enforcement (logging/accountability) requirements (from abstract only).
  • How: The abstract does not detail the mechanism (stateful NAT distribution, redundancy model, logging pipeline), so the design specifics are in the talk.
  • Where applicable: Small-to-medium ISPs; explicitly scale- and budget-constrained, and Mikrotik-specific — not a technique for large operators, but directly copyable for its target audience.

troubleshooting automation

items.title: Evolving Optical Transport: 400G, Network Design, and Regional Diversity
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Core pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Abouzar Asadi (Chorus)

Video

  • Why: Coherent optics and line-system evolution are core to the PM's physical DC/WAN interconnect interests. A nationwide 400G rollout on NZ's largest open-access fibre network is one of the few talks here with real optical engineering content: line-system readiness, spectrum management, transceiver evolution, and ring diversity/protection.
  • What: The engineering journey to 400 Gbps nationwide on Chorus's network — what had to be true about the optical line system before 400G could ride it, how spectrum is managed, and how regional fibre rings are designed for diversity and protection (from abstract only).
  • How: Advances in coherent modulation and digital signal processing plus open optical architectures; diverse ring design and protection strategies for resiliency and service continuity.
  • Where applicable: Chorus/NZ-specific deployment, but the engineering content (line-system readiness for higher baud, spectrum planning, ring protection) transfers directly to any long-haul or metro optical operator. Watch for whether the "open optical" framing stays vendor-neutral.

optics capacity-planning

items.title: Experiments in Topology Visualization using BGP-LS (RFC-8571)
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Core pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Rick Williamson (Helios Software AU), Rob Simpson (Kordia Networks)

Video

  • Why: BGP-LS is an underused source of live topology and TE data, and this is exactly the kind of experimental, adoptable tooling an operator program should surface. It ties directly to the PM's BGP/datapath-internals interest and offers hands-on access (remote lab network, iOS visualisation client) during the conference.
  • What: An experimental journey using BGP-LS as a practical live source of topology and traffic-engineering data for visualisation — started in a greenfields Public Safety Network, evolved into an approach suitable for organically grown operational networks (from abstract only).
  • How: BGP-LS (RFC 8571) exposes IGP link-state and TE information into BGP; a client consumes that feed to drive visual SPF computation and "what-if" simulations. The demo shows how link-state changes, failures, and metric adjustments propagate through BGP-LS in real time. They also outline a low-risk path for operators to trial BGP-LS in their own environments.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to heterogeneous, organically grown networks running IGP + BGP — which is most of them. The greenfields origin is noted but the authors explicitly generalised it. The offer of lab/client access makes this the most immediately try-it-yourself talk in the program.

bgp observability

items.title: Open Fibre Standards
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Warren Finch

Video

  • Why: Cyclone Gabrielle exposed what happens when nobody has a shared, structured view of physical fibre — shared corridors, thin diversity, no cross-operator picture. An open, machine-readable fibre data schema matters for resilience planning and is conceptually adjacent to how the PM thinks about infrastructure-as-data (and useful for DC site/diversity analysis).
  • What: An introduction to the Open Fibre Data Standard (OFDS): a common, open schema for describing terrestrial fibre infrastructure — routes, nodes, ownership attributes — interoperable and machine-readable, presented from a New Zealand resilience-planning perspective (from abstract only).
  • How: A standardised data model that lets fibre data be shared, analysed, and reused across operators, regulators, researchers, and emergency planners, supporting coordination and post-incident analysis.
  • Where applicable: The schema is general; the value depends on operators actually publishing their data, which is the hard part. Relevant wherever physical-route diversity is a resilience question — NZ context is the motivating case, not a constraint.

cabling measurement

items.title: Optimizing Traffic Flow with Akamai
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Kams Yeung

Video

  • Why: The core insight — that classic BGP traffic engineering (AS-path prepending, MED, more-specifics) is largely ineffective against a large CDN's intelligent routing — is a practical lesson for any operator peering with CDNs, and the remediation list is concrete.
  • What: How Akamai's CDN is structured in NZ and maps traffic, why traditional BGP TE fails against it, and a set of operator best practices: dedicated DNS resolvers, complete and consistent route announcements, avoiding traffic filtering, avoiding CGNAT, and adopting IPv6 (from abstract only).
  • How: CDN-side intelligence (mapping/routing) responds to reachability and resolver signals rather than BGP path metrics — so operators influence delivery through routing hygiene, resolver placement, and IPv6 availability rather than prepending.
  • Where applicable: Any ISP or edge operator interconnecting with major CDNs. Akamai-specific in its mapping details but the pattern generalises to other intelligent-routing CDNs. It is an Akamai-delivered talk, so treat the "adopt IPv6 / avoid CGNAT" recommendations with the usual vendor-adjacent scepticism — though these align with broad community practice.

cdn peering capacity-planning

items.title: Options for Data Centre Interconnect
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Core pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Matthew Hayes

Video

  • Why: DCI is a named core interest, and NZ/ANZ is seeing genuine DC-to-DC demand growth from hyperscaler and AI service buildout. A structured comparison of DCI approaches is directly useful for interconnect planning.
  • What: A survey of common DCI approaches, from physical-layer solutions (fibre/DWDM) to higher-layer technologies, with how each works and the pros and cons of each, framed by ANZ market dynamics (from abstract only).
  • How: Comparative walkthrough of interconnect models rather than a single solution — the abstract does not name the specific technologies, so the depth depends on the talk.
  • Where applicable: DC operators and interconnect providers generally; not org-specific. Likely most valuable as a decision framework for choosing between dark-fibre/own-optics versus higher-layer managed options at different distance/capacity points.

interconnection data-center-fabric

items.title: Radius Futures
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Core pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Alan DeKok

Video

  • Why: RADIUS is still the default AAA protocol for network access (802.1X, Wi-Fi, VPN) and sits squarely in the PM's identity/authentication territory. Its 1993 design shows its age — known operational and security pain points — and "next-generation" standards work determines how network AAA coexists with modern identity stacks (OIDC, passkeys, workload identity).
  • What: A survey of real-world problems affecting RADIUS deployments, and how emerging next-generation RADIUS standards can reduce them (from abstract only).
  • How: Protocol-level standards evolution rather than a product; the abstract does not enumerate the specific extensions, so expect the detail to be in the talk itself.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — any operator or enterprise running AAA today. Protocol work, not vendor-specific. The main caveat is that the abstract stays high level; the value depends on which concrete drafts/problems get named.

authentication standardization

items.title: Rethinking NetOps with Open-Source LLMs & RAG
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Basem Al-Sabri

Video

  • Why: LLM copilots for network operations are an emerging subfield, and the data-sovereignty framing (no sensitive configs/logs leaving the organisation) is the specific angle that makes this credible for network operators rather than hype.
  • What: A practical architecture combining open-source LLMs with retrieval-augmented generation, grounding model reasoning in the organisation's own knowledge base, configurations, and logs to reduce hallucinations and produce context-aware responses (from abstract only).
  • How: Fully open-source components across data ingestion, vector retrieval, inference, and orchestration — giving operators control over data sovereignty and compliance while avoiding vendor lock-in and usage-based fees.
  • Where applicable: Any operator, in principle. Early-stage — the abstract describes the architecture and its promises rather than measured results, so the proof will be in any demonstrated accuracy/evaluation shown live.

ml-for-networking privacy automation

items.title: Routeviews Update
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Philip Smith

Video

  • Why: RouteViews is the community's reference external view of BGP announcements, and this update covers a governance change (now run by NSRC) plus concrete new tooling — an API and a new BMP processor — that operators can directly use.
  • What: An introduction to the new team behind RouteViews, its operation on behalf of the global Internet community by NSRC, and new developments: the API, a new BMP processor, how operators use the system, and future plans (from abstract only).
  • How: Distributed route collectors giving operators an external perspective on their announcements; the new API and BMP processing extend how that data can be consumed programmatically.
  • Where applicable: Broadly useful — any operator wanting third-party verification of their routing visibility, and researchers tracking global infrastructure. Community project, not vendor.

bgp measurement open-source

items.title: The Evolution of Network Configuration Management
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Tim Raphael

Video

  • Why: Config management is where the PM's declarative/intent-driven world (Kubernetes-style APIs) meets traditional networking — a well-structured survey of the evolution from hand-crafted configs to intent-driven operations is useful context for anyone building network tooling.
  • What: A journey through the evolution of configuration technologies and lessons learned: scripting, imperative operations, workflows, playbooks, APIs, RPCs, declarative models, and intent-driven operations — and how networks should be configured going forward (from abstract only).
  • How: Conceptual/survey talk tracing the maturity curve rather than a single tool or case study.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable; most valuable as a shared-vocabulary framing for where an organisation sits on the imperative-to-declarative spectrum.

configuration-management automation

items.title: The Evolution of TCP Transport Protocols
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Geoff Huston

Video

  • Why: Congestion-control fundamentals cut across everything the PM touches — from lossless/DC fabrics to internet transport — and the shift from loss-based control to BBR (with ECN being reconsidered) changes how buffers should be sized and how traffic behaves on your network.
  • What: A look at the fundamental feedback-loop problem in packet networking: various TCP flow control protocols, their relationship with network buffers, the reconsideration of explicit congestion notification, and the growth of BBR (from abstract only).
  • How: Analysis of the design space of sender/receiver feedback loops — loss-based, delay/ECN-based, and model-based (BBR) — and how each interacts with buffer sizing in the network.
  • Where applicable: Universal — every operator's queue/buffer behaviour is affected. Especially relevant as BBR-driven senders (large content/CDN players) increasingly set the tone for how paths are used.

congestion-control linux-networking

items.title: Tuatahi First Fibre: Network Update
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Murray Pearson

Video

  • Why: A live production vendor transition (legacy Huawei GPON → Adtran architecture) at regional scale, plus a 100G handover product on the new platform — and it includes an actual failure story (multicast replication during the Whanganui cutover), which is exactly what an operator program should surface.
  • What: A Project Manawanui progress update: aggregation migration complete, staged regional access cutovers underway (Whanganui done, New Plymouth next), OLT replacement, large-scale service migration, TCFL aggregation modernisation with new handover points (Napier, Hastings, Rotorua), and 100G NNI migrations — with lessons learned including the multicast replication issue (from abstract only).
  • How: Staged regional cutover sequencing, OLT replacement with service continuity across a live network, and integration into updated operational systems.
  • Where applicable: NZ fibre-operator-specific in its topology and regulatory context, but the migration-sequencing and multicast-replication lessons transfer to any GPON/XGS-PON operator doing vendor transition or scaling aggregation to 100G.

troubleshooting multicast

items.title: Using Open Rack V3 to Enhance your Data Centre Infrastructure
items.text:
NZNOG 2026 digest Program Core pick 26–27 March 2026

Recording

Conrad Bullock

Video

  • Why: Rack-level power, thermal, and mechanical standards are what make high-density AI/HPC fabrics physically possible — ORv3 (and OCP generally) is core physical-DC infrastructure territory, not adjacent to it. The NZ case study gives local grounding.
  • What: How the OCP Open Rack V3 standard improves efficiency, thermal management, and rack density, translating to lower opex, better cooling for high-density computing, and simplified maintenance — plus a New Zealand customer deployment case study with "real benefits" (from abstract only).
  • How: ORv3's modularity and standardised rack infrastructure supporting AI/HPC workloads and future scalability; the abstract does not detail the specific mechanisms (busbars, power levels, blind-mate designs), so the depth is in the talk.
  • Where applicable: DC operators building or refreshing high-density halls. The abstract's tone is promotional and the speaker's affiliation is not given, so assess on the day for vendor-pitch content — the case study is the part worth weighing.

power data-center-fabric open-source

items.title: Accurate Cable Length Measurement for Optimized Data Center Networking
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Jasmeet Bagga (Facebook), Mehak Mahajan (Broadcom)

Video

  • Why: Cabling is a named core interest, and this pairs a Meta production deployment (operational benefits, real use cases) with a Broadcom technical deep dive including the SAI attributes that make it deployable — an unusually complete story for a plumbing topic.
  • What: Inferring physical cable length via silicon-driven link delay measurement, with Meta presenting real-world deployment experience and observed operational benefits, and Broadcom detailing the delay-measurement methodology and the SAI attributes/APIs that support it. (from abstract only)
  • How: High-precision link delay measurement from switch silicon, exposed through SAI, used both for accurate cable-length inventory and for performance monitoring.
  • Where applicable: Broadcom silicon with the SAI delay-measurement attributes (silicon-dependent), deployed at Meta — the use cases (cable inventory accuracy, layout validation, latency anomaly detection) apply to any large DC.

cabling data-center-fabric

items.title: Agile AI Architectures: The Fungible Data Center for the AI Era
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract

Speakers: Partha Ranganathan (Google)

  • Why: The counterpoint keynote to every fixed-architecture session above: the argument that infrastructure — networks included — must become modular, fungible, and reconfigurable because AI's growth and volatility outpaces any single design. Worth an hour as a framing check on all the fabric decisions elsewhere in the program.
  • What: The case for fungible datacenter architectures: modular, interoperable, standards-based designs across the systems stack to deliver improvements in compute efficiency, reliability, and sustainability as AI demand grows and shifts. (from abstract only)
  • How: Architecture-research framing (Ranganathan leads systems research at Google) — modular cross-stack design plus industry-wide standardization as the mechanism; a keynote, so expect thesis and direction, not mechanisms.
  • Where applicable: Cross-industry framing rather than a deployable design; useful as strategic context for topology and platform bets with multi-year horizons.

ai-networks data-center-fabric orchestration

items.title: Capacity Aware Adaptive Routing
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Session recording Materials

Speakers: Yikai Lin (Meta), Midhun Somasundaran (Meta)

  • Why: This is exactly the failure-mode analysis a fabric designer needs: what breaks in local-load-aware adaptive routing at Meta's topology scale, and the fix. Real production architecture, open-source linkage (FBOSS).
  • What: Meta's next-generation backend routing design. Their existing adaptive routing scheme (ARS), which relies on local load awareness, degrades on larger topologies — parallel links plus shallow-buffer switches plus silent capacity loss from remote link failures. The new approach combines remote capacity information with local-congestion-aware spray. (from abstract only)
  • How: Dynamically adjusts load balancing based on end-to-end link capacity so partial failures reduce performance gracefully; adds algorithms for merging ARS groups and uses non-load-aware ECMP spray groups to address scaling limits.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific topology and switch-buffer assumptions (shallow-buffer Ethernet, parallel-link spines), but the technique — capacity-aware rather than purely queue-aware spray — is a general idea for any large Clos fabric. FBOSS reference code is linked from the session materials.

ai-networks load-balancing data-center-fabric

items.title: Cryptography in Caliptra
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Session recording Materials

Speakers: Christopher Swenson (Microsoft), Jeff Andersen (Google)

  • Why: Caliptra is the open-source silicon RoT shipping in real hardware, and this talk covers how hardware identity is actually derived and wielded (DICE, DPE, attestation) plus the post-quantum migration plan — the grounding for the PM's identity interests at the hardware layer, and a preview of what every accelerator will be expected to do.
  • What: How Caliptra derives and uses hardware identity via DICE and DPE, provides attestation and secure boot, exposes generic crypto services through mailbox commands powering ownership and device encryption, and how it adapts to post-quantum requirements with the Adams Bridge hardware. (from abstract only)
  • How: Open-source hardware RoT design (caliptra.io materials linked) with a mailbox interface to the parent SoC security subsystem; DICE-style identity derivation layered into DPE for delegation.
  • Where applicable: OCP-server and accelerator ecosystems broadly — Caliptra is a shared open design adopted across vendors, not a single-company design.

attestation identity encryption

items.title: CSIG: Congestion Signaling in the AI Era
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Abhiram Ravi (Google), Jai Kumar (Broadcom)

Video

  • Why: Millisecond-duration AI bursts expose the limits of ECN-only congestion signals; this is the mechanism-level answer, and it's deployed, standardized, and multi-vendor — the trifecta for judging whether something is real.
  • What: Congestion Signaling (CSIG) — line-rate, always-on telemetry in application context, plus fine-grained per-packet congestion feedback that captures both the state and the location of the bottleneck on a path. Includes Google production results showing improvements to congestion control and load balancing. (from abstract only)
  • How: Sub-millisecond-granularity switch traffic measurements embedded in signaling, feeding both congestion control responsiveness and load-balancing quality; being standardized under UEC with multiple switch vendors supporting it.
  • Where applicable: Deployed at Google production scale — Google-specific results, but the mechanism is being standardized at UEC and supported by multiple switch vendors, so it is broadly relevant to anyone designing AI fabric feedback loops.

congestion-control ai-networks telemetry

items.title: Development Challenges and Next-Generation Opportunities for Linear Drive Pluggable Optics (LPO) and Linear Receive Optics (LRO)
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Nan Ge (Meta Platforms), Amin Yekani (Meta)

Video

  • Why: LPO/LRO is the pragmatic alternative to CPO for cutting optics power — no DSP on the link — and this is a development-experience talk with lessons learned and feasibility studies, not a vendor roadmap deck.
  • What: Meta's optical interconnect architecture around 200G/L transceivers for front-end and back-end AI networks, a comparison of photonics technologies at 200G/L, desired diagnostic features for large-scale training, and development experience with LPO and LRO including feasibility studies. (from abstract only)
  • How: Removing (LPO) or halving (LRO) the DSP to reduce power and cost, then working through the consequences: technical challenges, system compatibility with switch ASICs, and diagnostics — which are notoriously weaker without a DSP to measure the link.
  • Where applicable: Meta's 200G/L architecture, but LPO/LRO tradeoffs (power vs. diagnosability vs. reach) are general to any 800G/1.6T network. The "desired diagnostic features" list is useful input for anyone specifying optics requirements.

optics power ethernet

items.title: Disaggregated Leaf-Spine Architecture for Next-gen Azure T2 Network
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Kamini Santhanagopalan (Broadcom), Rita Hui (Microsoft)

Video

  • Why: SONiC Disaggregated Chassis is the most consequential open-networking architecture idea of the last few years — replacing chassis boxes with pizza-box fabrics — and this is a concrete Microsoft/Broadcom spine-layer deployment with named silicon.
  • What: A fully disaggregated spine-layer solution built from pizza boxes on xgs and dnx chipsets: TH5-512 silicon in the lower-disagg-T2 and Q3D (Jericho-based) in the upper-disagg-T2, replacing monolithic chassis for the Azure T2 spine. (from abstract only)
  • How: SONiC Disaggregated Chassis separates hardware and software components with clean hardware abstractions so the spine scales past a single chassis's physical limits; the talk covers the design and the advantages of the model.
  • Where applicable: Azure-specific and explicitly Broadcom-silicon-specific (TH5-512 and Q3D) — the architecture pattern (pizza-box disagg spine under SONiC) is general, but the implementation details are tied to this chipset pairing.

open-source switching data-center-fabric

items.title: Driving Innovation in Network Infrastructure: Key Advances from the Sonic Routing Workgroup
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Patrice Brissette (Cisco Systems Inc.), Eddie Ruan (Alibaba)

Video

  • Why: This is the "where is the open routing stack actually heading" session — BGP/datapath internals on the PM's list — covering real SONiC community work with named contributors from Cisco and Alibaba rather than a single vendor's roadmap.
  • What: A year-in-review of the SONiC Routing workgroup: SRv6 development and the Phoenixwing initiative, VxLAN Multi-Homing progress, upgrading Free Range Routing (FRR) to 10.x, RIB/FIB separation architecture, and the effect of the new mid-week workgroup meetings. (from abstract only)
  • How: Contributor-led engineering status and next steps for each initiative; the abstract names the projects but not their technical detail, so value is in the status/roadmap clarity.
  • Where applicable: General to SONiC deployments; RIB/FIB separation and FRR 10.x are directly relevant to anyone running or building on SONiC control planes.

open-source bgp standardization

items.title: eCore: Architecture and Whitebox Evolution of Alibaba's Service-oriented DCI network
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Dennis Cai (Alibaba), Manish Mukherjee (Cisco)

Video

  • Why: DC/WAN interconnect is core to the PM's remit, and Alibaba's eCore is one of the few publicly detailed whitebox DCI architectures — modular, service-aware, and with claimed measurable impact.
  • What: Alibaba's Data Center Interconnect network built on a modular whitebox-based architecture with service-aware traffic forwarding powered by SRv6, co-presented with Cisco on design philosophy, deployment challenges, measurable impact, and the roadmap. (from abstract only)
  • How: Service-aware SRv6 forwarding over a whitebox chassis/architecture rather than traditional DCI routers; details of the custom whitebox solutions are promised in the talk.
  • Where applicable: Alibaba-specific production DCI, but the pattern (whitebox + SRv6 service awareness for DC-to-DC) is the direction hyperscalers are generally taking. Watch for the "measurable impact" claims being quantified in the room rather than the abstract.

interconnection switching open-source

items.title: Enabling Technologies for Next Generation Large Scale AI Backend Networking
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Guohan Lu (Microsoft), Mehak Mahajan (Broadcom)

Video

  • Why: Complements the SRv6 talk with the rest of Microsoft's next-gen backend feature set — high-frequency streaming telemetry and "trimming" — plus an honest read on whether SAI/SONiC can actually support hyperscale AI backends yet.
  • What: Microsoft's next-generation backend AI network architecture as clusters grew from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of GPUs: SRv6, High-Frequency Streaming Telemetry (HFST), and trimming, with the driving factors and implementation details, and an assessment of SAI/SONiC readiness. (from abstract only)
  • How: Backend networks get distinct requirements from traditional DCs — low latency, high throughput, proactive fault detection — which push traffic engineering and telemetry to first-class features; the talk covers how each is implemented.
  • Where applicable: Microsoft-scale AI backend, co-presented with Broadcom — some content will track specific silicon capabilities via SAI. The SAI/SONiC readiness discussion is directly relevant to anyone on the open-networking stack.

ai-networks telemetry open-source

items.title: Evaluation of CPO Performance and Pluggable Optics Health for Reliable AI Infrastructure
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Siamak Amiralizadeh (Meta), VIRAL LOWALEKAR (Meta)

Video

  • Why: CPO is the biggest pending change in DC physical-layer architecture, and the honest questions are reliability, availability, and serviceability — exactly what Meta claims to test here, with multi-month methodologies rather than lab anecdotes.
  • What: Meta's comprehensive evaluation of co-packaged optics against current pluggable transceivers, plus their multi-month reliability testing methodology for both current and next-generation optical technologies (including CPO) to enable robust link-failure detection and long-term optical reliability. (from abstract only)
  • How: Power/cost optimization assessment of CPO (optics integrated on-ASIC) against improving pluggables, combined with systematic multi-month reliability testing across Meta's diverse transceiver fleet supporting AI/ML connectivity.
  • Where applicable: Meta datacenter fleet and AI/ML connectivity — the results should be interpretable industry-wide since CPO tradeoffs are physical, but the failure-detection tooling is Meta's own.

optics ai-networks measurement

items.title: Evolution of Ethernet based switch platforms and fabrics to meet Meta's AI training clusters' scale-out AI fabric demands
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Session recording Materials

Speakers: Parvez Shaikh (Meta), Lingjun Wu (Meta)

  • Why: The sequel to Meta's OCP 2024 fabric talk — the ground truth on how one of the largest Ethernet AI fabrics is actually evolving from 4K-GPU cells to much larger non-blocking clusters, including the SAI/FBOSS changes required.
  • What: Meta's journey moving from disaggregated deep-buffered switch platforms (OCP 2024, up to 4K-GPU cells) to disaggregated shallow-buffer Ethernet platforms for significantly larger non-blocking fabrics and GPU clusters, with the unique scaling problems they hit along the way. (from abstract only)
  • How: Evolution of switching and routing platform features to build larger non-blocking fabrics, plus the SAI and FBOSS enhancements that adapted the software stack to the new features.
  • Where applicable: Meta-specific production architecture, but the SAI/FBOSS work is in the open OCP repos (linked materials) and the buffer-depth tradeoffs are a general design decision for anyone building AI scale-out fabrics.

ai-networks data-center-fabric ethernet

items.title: Firefly: Scalable, Ultra-Accurate Clock Synchronization for Datacenters
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Yuliang Li (Google)

Video

  • Why: Sub-10ns device-to-device sync is two orders of magnitude past what PTP practice delivers, and the technique — consensus on a random overlay rather than a spanning tree — is a genuinely different way to solve time in a fabric. Cloud financial exchanges are the driver, but precise time increasingly matters for telemetry correlation and distributed debugging.
  • What: A software-driven datacenter clock sync system achieving sub-10ns device-to-device and ≤1µs device-to-UTC accuracy in a 248-machine Clos network, resilient to time server failure and unstable clocks. (from abstract only)
  • How: A distributed consensus algorithm over a random overlay graph converges devices to a common time with gradual hardware-clock adjustments; "layered synchronization" decouples internal (device-to-device) from external (UTC) sync so external jitter doesn't disturb internal consistency.
  • Where applicable: Software-only, demonstrated on a 248-machine Clos network — no special hardware claimed. Google research system; results are from that testbed, so hyperscale behavior is inferred rather than shown.

time-sync data-center-fabric measurement

items.title: INSPECT: Data analysis tool for Proactive Link Failure Detection on Meta's AI Infrastructure
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Session recording Materials

Speakers: Granthana Rangaswamy (Meta), Arushi Sharma (Meta)

  • Why: At 100K-GPU scale, interconnect health is the availability problem, and this is a deployed ML-based early-warning system over SerDes telemetry with a concrete standardization angle — collecting SerDes parameters uniformly across vendors.
  • What: INSPECT, a software daemon that collects and analyzes SerDes parameters to predict link failures before they cause unplanned downtime and job restarts, used for new-system provisioning, training-job deployment, and continuous monitoring across Meta's AI systems. (from abstract only)
  • How: ML-based anomaly detection with pass/fail criteria over SerDes telemetry; standardizes collection and analysis across SerDes vendors by mapping common SerDes building blocks to a predefined schema, enabling a single trained model across heterogeneous AI systems.
  • Where applicable: Meta AI infrastructure (100K-class clusters); the vendor-neutral SerDes schema idea is the generalizable piece for any operator running multi-vendor optics/SerDes fleets. Linked materials point to related NSDI work.

ml-for-networking ai-networks anomaly-detection

items.title: Methodology and Observation of Congestion Control Impact on MoE Training Job Completion Time
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Alex Bortok (Keysight)

Video

  • Why: A methodology talk rather than a vendor pitch: how to emulate an AI fabric and measure the effect of congestion-control and load-balancing schemes on MoE training JCT — useful for anyone building test harnesses before spending production GPUs on it.
  • What: An emulation technique and methodology to quantify AI network fabric performance for Mixture-of-Experts training, comparing the impact of different congestion control and load-balancing schemes. (from abstract only)
  • How: Lab emulation of GPU-cluster fabrics running MoE workloads, with JCT as the outcome metric across congestion control / load balancing configurations.
  • Where applicable: Test-lab methodology (Keysight tooling implied) — vendor-presented, so expect the tool to feature, but the emulation-vs-production calibration questions are worth taking into the room.

benchmarking ai-networks

items.title: New Strategic Initiative: Open Cluster Designs for AI
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Lowell Lamb (Broadcom), Loren Staley (Celestica)

Video

  • Why: Not deep tech, but a formation announcement for OCP standardizing pod and cluster topologies — directly relevant to anyone whose physical DC designs must interoperate, and a place to influence reference designs early.
  • What: A new OCP Strategic Initiative for standardized designs of Open Pod Groups and Open Clusters: scale-up and scale-out networks in scope, physical and logical topology in scope, modularity as a fundamental objective, and management built on OCP management specifications. (from abstract only)
  • How: Reusing existing OCP platform and component contributions wherever possible to build best-practice reference cluster designs rather than new spec work from scratch.
  • Where applicable: Industry-wide reference-design effort, not operator-specific; value now is scope and participation, concrete designs come later.

ai-networks data-center-fabric open-source

items.title: OCP Optical Circuit Switching Subproject Update
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Brian O'Connor (Google), Richard Yu (Google)

Video

  • Why: Google's OCS deployment reshaped the fabric-topology conversation (static Clos vs. reconfigurable); this new OCP subproject is about standardizing and open-sourcing the OCS control stack — a direction signal for physical DC topology design.
  • What: Status of the OCS subproject (formed June) within the OCP Networking project: developing open software standards and a fully open software stack for optical circuit switching, targeting high bandwidth, low latency, and energy efficiency for AI/ML and HPC. (from abstract only)
  • How: Standardization plus an open-source software stack so that OCS from multiple manufacturers can interoperate and be orchestrated — the abstract is a project-status announcement, so expect scope and roadmap rather than deep technical results.
  • Where applicable: Aimed at general data center and AI/ML networking, not Google-specific; this is early-stage standards work, useful mainly as a where-is-this-heading read.

optics open-source data-center-fabric

items.title: Performance Evaluation of Interconnect Technologies for AI Scale-Up Computing: UAL vs UALoE/SUE vs RoCE
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Srihari Vegesna (Upscale AI), Srinivas Gangam (Upscale AI)

Video

  • Why: Scale-up interconnect choice (proprietary memory-semantic links vs. Ethernet-based alternatives) is the biggest architectural fork in AI cluster design right now, and head-to-head evaluations with real transfer-size sweeps are rare.
  • What: A comparative evaluation of Ultra Accelerator Link (UAL), Ethernet-based UALoE/SUE, and RoCE for AI-optimized, memory-semantic XPU-to-XPU transfer. Reported result: UAL wins on small transfers via deterministic latency and transaction-based load balancing; Ethernet protocols suffer variable latency and inefficient small-packet handling. (from abstract only)
  • How: Transaction-level load balancing, DMA thread efficiency, and bandwidth utilization measured across small- and large-transfer scenarios for memory-semantic workloads.
  • Where applicable: Applicable to scale-up (in-pod) AI systems rather than scale-out fabrics; findings favor link-level memory semantics, which constrains how far Ethernet-based scale-up can currently go. Note the authors' UAL bias is visible in the framing — read the methodology carefully.

gpu-clusters rdma ethernet

items.title: SPDM Update
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Materials

Speakers: Jeff Hilland (Hewlett Packard Enterprise), Brett Henning (Broadcom Inc.)

  • Why: SPDM is the emerging standard for hardware device identity and attestation — the physical-layer cousin of the PM's workload-identity interests — and this session covers the year's spec additions including post-quantum crypto.
  • What: DMTF SPDM working-group update: PQC support, new bindings, an Authorization specification, and updates to the SPDM spec suite, plus expectations for the coming year. (from abstract only)
  • How: Standards-body status update — the mechanics will be in the spec drafts (DMTF materials linked), not the abstract.
  • Where applicable: Any hardware procurement or RoT program; the PQC timeline discussion is the part with planning consequences.

attestation identity

items.title: SRv6 for AI Backend
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Session recording Materials

Speakers: Changrong Wu (Microsoft), Abhishek Dosi (Microsoft)

  • Why: Using WAN traffic-engineering machinery (SRv6) inside an AI backend fabric is a significant architectural bet — it directly addresses the failure of BGP+ECMP to meet AI training's path-control requirements, and it's Microsoft in production, not a proposal.
  • What: Microsoft's use of Segment Routing over IPv6 in Ethernet-based AI backend networks for fine-grained network path control, maximizing fabric utilization and delivering resiliency — including how SRv6 enables continental-scale GPU clusters. (from abstract only)
  • How: SRv6 segment lists provide explicit per-flow path steering and traffic engineering in the backend, replacing the coarse hashing of BGP+ECMP; a video and the speakers' segment-routing.net materials are linked.
  • Where applicable: Microsoft Azure AI backend production. The SRv6-in-the-DC idea is broadly applicable to any routed Ethernet fabric needing engineered paths, but note the scale assumptions (continental GPU clusters) behind the requirements.

segment-routing ai-networks data-center-fabric

items.title: Technical Aspects of Ultra Ethernet 1.0
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Session recording Materials

Speakers: J Metz (AMD)

  • Why: UEC 1.0 is the industry's coordinated attempt to retune the entire Ethernet stack for AI/HPC — the lossless-fabric problem the PM works on daily. This is the architecture overview talk by a UEC board member, not a product pitch.
  • What: An explanation of the newly published UEC 1.0 specification: what it changes versus classic Ethernet, and the roadmap beyond 1.0. (from abstract only)
  • How: Covers the stack from physical layer up through software APIs — the abstract does not detail specific mechanisms (e.g., telemetry, congestion control, transport profiles), so expect those in the talk itself.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — UEC is a multi-vendor standardization effort, not a single-vendor design. Relevant to anyone building or buying AI backend fabrics over the next few years.

ai-networks rdma ethernet standardization

items.title: The Path to Zero Flap: Reinventing Optical Reliability for Scalable AI Clusters presented by Credo
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Stephen Manley (Oracle), Bill Brennan (Credo)

Video

  • Why: The headline number — commodity pluggable optics at up to 30,000 FITs — is the reliability crisis in AI fabrics in one figure, and a single flapping link can kill a training run. This also launches a new OCP optical-reliability workstream, so it's a standards signal, not just a vendor demo.
  • What: A joint Oracle/Credo "Zero Flap" optical solution aiming to eliminate unplanned link flaps in million-GPU backend networks, combining host- and line-side telemetry, in-band messaging, event logging, and predictive analytics. Architecture is being contributed to OCP to seed a new workstream; initial results are promised. (from abstract only)
  • How: Correlate host-side and line-side telemetry with in-band messaging between link endpoints, log events, and predict failures before they become flaps — moving reliability from reactive BER monitoring to prediction.
  • Where applicable: Jointly developed for Oracle's AI infrastructure with Credo silicon — partly vendor-specific — but the contribution to OCP is intended to make the framework open and general. The FIT figure for commodity pluggables is an industry-wide baseline.

optics ai-networks troubleshooting

items.title: Unifying P4 with eBPF and DPDK via XDP2
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Core pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Tom Herbert (XDPnet)

Video

  • Why: The PM's eBPF/datapath interest makes this directly relevant: XDP2 attacks the fragmentation between P4 (switch ASICs), eBPF/XDP (hosts), and DPDK (userspace fast paths) — a real pain point for anyone building programmable network functions across targets.
  • What: XDP2, a unified programming model that takes the best of P4, XDP/eBPF, and DPDK so users can program in their language of choice and run the same code unmodified across a variety of targets. (from abstract only)
  • How: A target-agnostic model that lets datapath code be written once and compiled to switch ASICs, kernel eBPF, and userspace/DPDK execution — the abstract does not describe the compiler/IR mechanism, so expect that in the talk.
  • Where applicable: General-purpose infrastructure programming; Tom Herbert's track record (XDP, XDPnet) lends credibility. Early-stage effort — the abstract is a vision plus workshop pointer rather than results, so judge maturity from the live demo.

ebpf p4 programmable-dataplane

items.title: XASM: A Foundation to Program the X2 With P4
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick 13–16 October 2025

Abstract Recording

Speakers: Fabian Ruffy (XSight Labs), Vladimir Gurevich (XSight Labs)

Video

  • Why: The P4 ecosystem has been pipeline-model-bound since Tofino; if a new switch architecture (X2) breaks that model, it forces the P4 language itself to evolve. Watching a language's assumptions get stress-tested by new silicon is valuable even if the PM never programs an X2.
  • What: The X2 architecture contrasted with the traditional P4 pipeline model (Tofino-style), how XASM maps P4 constructs onto X2, where current P4 cannot express X2's capabilities, and candidate paths for evolving the P4 language. (from abstract only)
  • How: XASM serves as a programming foundation/abstraction layer between P4 and the X2 hardware, with concrete mapping examples and a candid limitations discussion.
  • Where applicable: XSight Labs X2 silicon-specific, but the language-evolution conclusions (what P4 must gain) affect the whole programmable-datapath community.

p4 silicon programmable-dataplane

items.title: 6–12x Route Programming Acceleration in SONiC: A Collaborative Profiling and Optimization Journey
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Session recording Materials

Deepak Singhal (Microsoft), Amol Rawal (Nokia)

  • Why: Contributor-led SONiC internals with hard numbers (2K–4K routes/sec baseline → 6–12x), a reproducible benchmarking methodology, and upstreamed code — the archetype of a talk that reveals where an open-source project is actually heading.
  • What: A joint Microsoft–Nokia effort that built a Snappi-based benchmarking framework, profiled existing optimization proposals and their combinations across multiple hardware platforms, then contributed fresh optimizations: replacing Redis-based IPC with direct ZMQ communication, offloading synchronous recording from the hot path, and integrating tcmalloc into FRR daemons (from abstract only).
  • How: Measurement-first — the framework identifies which optimizations actually matter and how they interact, rather than merging proposals blindly; results were driven through SONiC Routing Working Group consensus with published HLDs across multiple sonic-net repositories.
  • Where applicable: SONiC on any supported platform (multi-platform profiling included); most relevant to fabrics pushing 1M+ route scale, e.g. large AI clusters with heavy ECMP.

open-source benchmarking

items.title: Achieving AI Cluster Reliability at Scale: Lessons in Reducing Workload Interruptions
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Bob Wang (Meta), Ramachandra Reddy Kallam (Meta)

Video

  • Why: Not a networking talk per se, but network events are one of the correlated signals — and the root-cause methodology (attributing every interruption across host, firmware, network, and workload telemetry) is reusable by anyone operating large fabrics.
  • What: A framework for diagnosing AI workload interruptions at 32K→100K+ GPU scale, built on root-cause classification via Perfetto time trees correlating host telemetry, firmware logs, network events, and workload signals; key contributors include NVLink failures, HBM fragmentation, thermal failures, silent data corruption (SDC), and firmware bugs (from abstract only).
  • How: Data-driven root-cause analysis feeds back into next-gen hardware requirements, including vendor decisions on error reporting, fault isolation, and resilience; the diagnostic framework is being offered to the broader OCP community.
  • Where applicable: Meta GBx00 clusters — org-specific failure data, but the methodology (correlated time-tree attribution) and the hardware-requirements feedback loop generalize well.

ai-networks sre observability

items.title: An Introduction to Attesting Hitlessly Updatable Systems
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Matt King (NVIDIA)

Video

  • Why: A sharp conceptual contribution to the PM's identity/attestation interest: hitless firmware updates break the standard attestation model, because the platform can change between evidence production and relying-party use.
  • What: An analysis of what attestation must become for platforms that update firmware while tenant workloads run: conventional measurements of the TCB that has run are insufficient; the relying party must also assess whether future updates could compromise the properties it depends on (from abstract only).
  • How: Combine three evidence classes — current TCB measurements, the history of prior updates, and the policy governing future updates — so a relying party can make an informed decision about a system that changes while it runs.
  • Where applicable: General technique for any attested platform doing hitless updates (switches, NICs, BMCs, accelerators); an introductory/conceptual talk, but it defines the problem shape the DMTF/OCP attestation work will have to address. Pairs with the SPDM provisioning talk below.

attestation standardization

items.title: Beyond Traditional BGP: Decoupling Route Distribution for Large-Scale AI Clusters at Alibaba
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Eddie Ruan (Alibaba), Dennis Cai (Alibaba)

Video

  • Why: Directly in the PM's BGP/datapath-internals interest: a concrete alternative to Microsoft's Fairwater host-SRv6 approach for AI-cluster routing scale, from a provider that can't mandate host-side changes — a real architectural debate with numbers attached.
  • What: An architectural decoupling of service route distribution from infrastructure route distribution: regular BGP continues to carry infrastructure routes within spine/leaf, while service routes are redistributed among leaf switches by multiple route reflectors, recursively resolved over the loopback of the anchoring leaf switch (from abstract only).
  • How: A "Group RR" concept coordinates multiple RRs to provide Graceful Restart capability and high availability for critical service prefixes, so service routes survive RR cluster outages; positioned explicitly against Fairwater's <1,000-route / 256-way-ECMP host-SRv6 model from OCP 2025.
  • Where applicable: Alibaba-specific architecture for multi-tenant clouds that cannot impose host changes — broadly applicable to any provider facing the same constraint; BGP-only, no host or silicon requirements.

bgp ai-networks data-center-fabric

items.title: Clock-Aligned Telemetry for AI Clusters: From BMC to GPU to Fleet
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Ahmad Byagowi (TBD), Lukas Landgraf (turbalance)

Video

  • Why: The observability gap this addresses — many dashboards, no common evidence model — sits exactly at the junction of the PM's telemetry and Kubernetes/eBPF interests, and clock alignment as the basis for cross-machine trust is an idea worth stealing.
  • What: A lab-built reference architecture for clock-aligned AI telemetry: a source-bundle contract, live agents, a conservative benchmark ladder, a Redfish/BMC lane, and a lakehouse path that preserves provenance and never synthesizes unsupported metrics; links DCGM/NVML, host counters, Prometheus, Kubernetes, Redfish, eBPF/OTel evidence, and PTP/NTP clock state (from abstract only).
  • How: Per-datacenter ingestion without global shared state feeds one Iceberg layer over cold and fresh stores; a six-level benchmark ladder (metric to global baseline), auto-discovery, credential-gated agents, 1s freshness, and capability labels — PTP/NTP state as a first-class signal changes what cross-machine comparison can be trusted.
  • Where applicable: Prototyped on a heterogeneous lab fleet (not hyperscale production yet), with an open-source repo and a proposed OCP collaboration path — early-stage, which is exactly why it's a wildcard rather than core.

telemetry ai-networks time-sync

items.title: Clustermapper: Deterministic path diagnosis for AI backend networks using SRv6
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Paper Session recording Materials

Ryder Lewis (OpenAI), Guohan Lu (OpenAI)

  • Why: Turns path diagnosis from statistical inference into ground truth — a genuinely clever use of SRv6 source routing, and the operational companion to the MRC spec from the same OpenAI team.
  • What: A path-diagnosis system for MRC/SRv6 AI backend networks: a lightweight agent on every node sends SRv6 source-routed self-probes through T0/T1 switch paths, producing a deterministic link-health map used to localize faults (NIC-T0 links, T0-T1 links, switch forwarding) and turn urgent link-failure incidents into scheduled maintenance (from abstract only; the linked arXiv paper — titled "Resilient AI Supercomputer Networking using MRC and SRv6", 18 pages, 22 figures — was not retrievable beyond its landing page).
  • How: SRv6 deterministic source routing pins each probe to an exact path, eliminating ECMP ambiguity and routing-convergence noise so failures localize to specific links even between training jobs; output feeds path-avoidance policy for MRC.
  • Where applicable: Requires SRv6 (and works best with MRC) in the backend network — OpenAI production, but the technique is general to any SRv6 fabric and notably valuable for small network teams operating huge clusters.

segment-routing ai-networks observability

items.title: Co-Designing AI Fabrics: Inside Google's Virgo Network and the Campus-as-a-Computer
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Sunil Ahluwalia (Google), JK Lee (Google)

Video

  • Why: One of the few public looks inside Google's AI fabric — the architectural shift from "data center as a set of servers" to campus-scale supercomputer is the defining physical-networking problem of this cycle, and Google is unusually specific here about the transport and telemetry mechanisms.
  • What: Virgo, a megascale multi-plane AI datacenter fabric running open-source SONiC, built for synchronized-burst ML traffic with a stated value proposition of predictable low latency and maximized "goodput" (from abstract only).
  • How: Open-source RDMA transport (Falcon), Congestion Signaling (CSIG), and High-Speed Telemetry (HST), on a multi-plane architecture over open standards and merchant hardware ecosystems.
  • Where applicable: Google-specific production design, but the constituent technologies (CSIG, HST, Falcon) are being pushed into SONiC/open ecosystems — see the Google SONiC CSIG/HST talk below, which is the deployable version of this story.

ai-networks data-center-fabric silicon

items.title: Enabling AI Networking @ Scale with Multi-path Reliable Connections (MRC)
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Session recording Materials

Guohan Lu (OpenAI), Eric Spada (Broadcom Inc.)

  • Why: MRC is now a ratified OCP specification co-authored by OpenAI and Broadcom — a concrete, open alternative for AI-fabric transport that a PM in this space will need to track against MetaRoCE and Falcon.
  • What: MRC combines multipath transport, adaptive load balancing, reliable delivery, and path-aware congestion management to keep utilization high and tail latency low in fabrics of hundreds of thousands of XPUs (from abstract only).
  • How: Multipath reliable connections at the transport layer with awareness of per-path congestion state; the OCP MRC 1.0 document is the spec itself, which the session walks through.
  • Where applicable: Designed for open Ethernet-based AI infrastructure broadly, not one operator's fabric; requires switch/NIC support for the MRC semantics (Broadcom involvement signals merchant-silicon intent).

ai-networks load-balancing open-source

items.title: ESUN: Open Ethernet for the AI Scale-Up Era
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Session recording Materials

Pratik Marolia (Microsoft), Manoj Wadekar (Meta)

  • Why: Scale-up (in-rack/in-pod XPU interconnect) was the last proprietary holdout — NVLink territory. ESUN 1.0, ratified by OCP in March 2026 with 170+ contributors from 20+ organizations including NVIDIA itself, is the strongest signal yet that open Ethernet is expanding from scale-out into scale-up.
  • What: An operator-requirements specification for Ethernet-based scale-up networks: minimizing header/framing overhead designed for general internet traffic, and breaking single-vendor interconnect lock-in (from abstract only).
  • How: Cross-industry coalition (Meta, Microsoft, AMD, Arista, Broadcom, Cisco, Marvell, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Oracle) producing an OCP spec in months; the talk covers the what and the roadmap for future versions.
  • Where applicable: Industry-wide; it is a requirements/spec document, so its impact depends on silicon (Tomahawk-class and similar) implementing it — pair with the SUE-T and Tahan talks for the transport and hardware instantiations.

ethernet gpu-clusters open-source

items.title: From Fleet to Firmware: Bringing AI-Native Security to Open Hardware with Project Equilibrium presented by Google
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Andres Lagar-Cavilla (Google)

Video

  • Why: AI turned on the systems that run AI — a genuinely novel direction: autonomous, continuous security for open-source firmware that outpaces what periodic audits and static scanning can do as frontier models accelerate vulnerability discovery.
  • What: Google's Project Equilibrium, an AI-native security architecture pairing live, repo-colocated threat models with autonomous pre-submit scanning and automated patching — catching deep bugs and cutting false positives before merge — plus a path to extend the workflow from fleets to bare-metal firmware via open security cookbooks (from abstract only).
  • How: Threat models live next to the code they describe; autonomous pre-submit analysis and patching run against the millions of lines of low-level code in OpenBMC, Caliptra, CXL, and NVMe.
  • Where applicable: Open-hardware ecosystem broadly (cookbooks are explicitly meant as a shared baseline); currently a Google internal capability being externalized, so treat maturity accordingly — but for anyone whose supply chain includes open firmware, this is where the field is heading.

attestation ml-for-networking network-security

items.title: Integrated Optics at Scale for AI Infrastructure: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta's 102.4T Integrated Optics Switch
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Granthana Rangaswamy (Meta), Siamak Amiralizadeh (Meta), Xu Wang (Meta Platforms, Inc.)

Video

  • Why: The strongest quantified case at this conference for integrated optics over pluggables — real power and reach numbers from a platform moving from 51.2T validation into a 102.4T product, at the exact 200G/lane inflection point where pluggables struggle.
  • What: A 1.5OU, 100% liquid-cooled, fanless blade with 64 optical ports via 16 four-port MMC interfaces and 16 ELSFP external-laser modules, delivering ~60% optics power reduction, ~30% system power reduction, and 500m reach versus pluggables (from abstract only).
  • How: Optical engines placed on (CPO) or near (NPO) the ASIC substrate, eliminating pluggables; decoupling the laser lifecycle from the ASIC via ELSFP external lasers; fanless liquid cooling to reduce fiber contamination risk.
  • Where applicable: Meta platform, but the power/reach trade-offs and the laser-decoupling architecture are broadly applicable to any operator weighing CPO/NPO at 102.4T; built on prior-generation 51.2T validation, so the numbers have production lineage.

optics switching power

items.title: Large-Scale Deployment of 800Gb/s Active Electrical Cables (AEC) in Meta Data Centers for AI Applications
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Jingyu Yu (Meta), Abhijit Chakravarty (Meta)

Video

  • Why: Cabling is a first-order cost/power lever in AI clusters and rarely gets a full methodology talk; this covers multi-vendor qualification to volume production, which is the hard part.
  • What: Meta's qualification, validation, and deployment methodology for 800 Gb/s AECs (112 Gb/s/lane) in large-scale GPU clusters, spanning component characterization, environmental reliability, multi-vendor interoperability, system-level traffic validation, and manufacturing readiness across multiple suppliers and production sites (from abstract only).
  • How: Lab plus in-cluster validation of link stability, packet integrity, latency, and firmware compatibility; the program resolved signal-integrity, manufacturing-consistency, and firmware-interoperability issues to reach multi-sourced volume adoption.
  • Where applicable: Meta AI clusters but the qualification framework is general; AECs apply to short-reach in-cluster interconnect (rack-to-rack distances), as a power- and cost-efficient alternative to optics and passive DAC at 800G.

cabling ai-networks power

items.title: Lessons learned from GW-scale AI deployments
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Mark Filer (Oracle)

Video

  • Why: An end-user case study with production statistics on one of the world's largest 800G 2xDR4 LPO deployments — exactly the real-numbers, real-failure-mode content this PM values over vendor demos.
  • What: Hard-won operational learnings from OCI's deployments supporting top AI customers at 10,000+ GPU scale, where single link flaps stall multi-million-dollar training jobs; includes production statistics on the LPO deployment and how the experience translates to 1.6T (from abstract only).
  • How: Operational discipline at "laws of large numbers" scale — treating per-link instability as the primary availability adversary, with forward-looking paths to uptime/resilience in massive distributed systems.
  • Where applicable: OCI-specific production data, but the failure-mode taxonomy and the 800G→1.6T extrapolation are relevant to any operator of GPU backbones; pairs naturally with the LPO talk above as the customer-side view.

ai-networks troubleshooting power

items.title: Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch
items.text:
OCP Global Summit 2026 digest Program Core pick 12–15 October 2026

Abstract Recording

Rongchun Zhou (Meta), Reza Niazmand (Meta)

  • Why: The switch platform that much of Meta's next-gen AI fabric story runs on — a concrete OCP hardware contribution on the newest merchant silicon, directly in the PM's physical switching interest.
  • What: IceCube, a 102.4T non-blocking Ethernet switch on the Broadcom TH6C ASIC running FBOSS: 2OU form factor, 64× OSFP-RHS user ports, liquid-cooled; IecPack is an ORv3-HPRv1 rack integrating eight IceCube blades plus servicing equipment for versatile switch roles (from abstract only).
