items.title: How we are scaling Crusoe cloud using OVN interconnect approach
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Numan Siddique, Crusoe; Ketan Supanekar, Crusoe

  • Why: Crusoe is an AI-cloud operator re-architecting its OVN control plane — and it's led by Numan Siddique, OVN's longtime maintainer. A production AI-cloud at the point where the central Southbound DB becomes the bottleneck is a rare, candid data point.

Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Patryk Diak, Red Hat, LLC.; Dumitru Ceara, Red Hat, LLC.

  • Why: The canonical modern debugging story — a scaling problem that turned out to be distributed across every layer of the stack. items.title: One API to Rule Them All: Reworking the OVS Hardware Offload Layers
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Eelco Chaudron, Red Hat, LLC.

  • Why: Offload in OVS was historically duplicated per provider (kernel TC flower vs. DPDK rte_flow via netdev-offload), making vendor integration invasive. The new dpif-offload API layer that has landed upstream unifies this — foundational plumbing for every DPU/SmartNIC story elsewhere in the program.

(from abstract only)
  • How: A single offload API above provider-specific implementations (kernel TC flower and DPDK rte_flow behind it), so new offload features land in one place instead of N.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building or consuming OVS hardware offload (TC flower, DPDK rte_flow, DOCA-style providers); landed upstream, so this is the new baseline architecture rather than a fork.

items.title: One Shared Gateway, a Thousand Routers: Scaling ARP/NDP in OVN-Kubernetes
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Jaime Caamano, Red Hat, LLC.; Matteo Dallaglio, Red Hat, LLC.; Tim Rozet, NVIDIA

  • Why: A beautiful datapath pathology: with hundreds/thousands of UDNs sharing one uplink/IP/MAC, ARP replies can't be mapped back to their originating router (conntrack can't track them), so OVN-Kubernetes fans them out to every patch port — duplicating neighbor state, ballooning the OpenFlow footprint, and eventually exceeding OVS recirculation limits. This is exactly the "K8s networking meets datapath internals" intersection.
  • What: The full arc of an ARP storm at UDN scale: how fan-out surfaced, the constraints any fix must preserve, a short-term flow fix constraining fan-out on the shared gateway bridge, a mid-term prototype steering discovery through the default gateway router, and the resulting upstream OVN feature — Shared MAC-binding scopes, letting related logical router ports share one set of learned neighbor bindings instead of per-router duplication. (from abstract only)
  • How: Learn through a single gateway router and steer ARP/NDP to it, propagating learned bindings to the UDNs, rather than fanning discovery traffic to every gateway router.
  • Where applicable: OVN-Kubernetes shared-gateway deployments at high UDN count; the Shared MAC-binding scope is a general OVN feature usable beyond ovn-k. Red Hat/NVIDIA collaboration shaping the fix at the right layer.

kubernetes cni linux-networking

items.title: One Tunnel Too Many: No-Overlay Mode in OVN-Kubernetes
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Riccardo Ravaioli, NVIDIA

  • Why: Directly hits the PM's BGP + datapath interests. When the fabric already provides an overlay, stacking Geneve on top wastes MTU and adds encapsulation cost — this is OVN-Kubernetes learning to be fabric-aware.
  • What: A new no-overlay mode letting the cluster default network and primary L3 ClusterUserDefinedNetworks route inter-node traffic via BGP-learned routes with no Geneve encapsulation, while OVN still handles local networking, policy, and Services. Per-network choice, so Geneve and no-overlay networks coexist in one cluster. (from abstract only)
  • How: BGP-learned routes replace the tunnel for inter-node forwarding (administrator-configured BGP or a managed full-mesh option); the talk follows a packet across nodes and covers the config choices that matter — outbound SNAT, MTU, tenant isolation. NVIDIA's DPU-based VM networking is one concrete example.
  • Where applicable: Clusters sitting on a fabric that already provides the overlay/underlay (typical DPU- or ToR-terminated environments). Joint Red Hat/NVIDIA effort; constraints around primary L3 networks and SNAT shape deployment.

items.title: Route scope delimitation as a control plane scalability mechanism for OVN Interconnect using route tags
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Lucas Vargas Dias, Magalu Cloud; Julio Cesar Vanti, Magalu Cloud

  • Why: One of the few talks with a hard quantified result: topological isolation (per-peering transit switch) costs 2.56x the Southbound logical flows of tag-based route scoping for identical connectivity. That's a real, transferable design trade-off for anyone building multi-AZ VPC peering on OVN-IC.
  • What: A comparison of two ways to bound route exchange between peered VPCs in OVN Interconnect: a transit switch per peering (data-plane isolation, expensive) vs. one shared transit switch with declarative scoping via ic-route-tag / ic-route-learn-tag-rules / ic-route-filter-tag (control-plane isolation, substantially cheaper in memory, in northd full-recompute latency, in flow installation after reconnect, and in every unrelated NB write). The trade-off is stated plainly: tag scoping constrains route learning only; a manual static route can still cross the shared L2 domain, so per-pair topology remains necessary where data-plane isolation must hold. (from abstract only)
  • How: Measurement-driven comparison of lflow-node recomputes, flow counts, and operation latency between the two topologies on identical connectivity.
  • Where applicable: Any OVN-IC VPC-peering deployment; the technique is upstream OVN configuration (general), the numbers come from Magalu Cloud's production-derived testing. Isolation requirements (control-plane-only vs. data-plane) decide which option is valid.

cloud sdn benchmarking
path: Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference

items.title: Stateless Load Balancing in OVN
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Adjacent pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Alexandra Rukomoinikova, K2 Cloud

  • Why: Horizontal gateway scaling is blocked by conntrack pinning every connection to one gateway chassis. Rather than sync conntrack (the usual answer), this moves the NAT to the backend's hypervisor — a different architectural point in the design space, in production at a cloud provider.
  • What: The story of the new "deferred-nat" load balancer option: backend selected statelessly per packet on the router, packet delivered by MAC, DNAT and conntrack state created on the backend's own hypervisor; established sessions survive backend changes via incremental select-group updates instead of rebuilds. Includes why conntrack synchronization, extending use_stateless_nat, and cross-AZ backends were rejected. (from abstract only)
  • How: NAT deferred to the backend hypervisor, eliminating per-gateway conntrack state as the horizontal-scaling bottleneck.
  • Where applicable: OVN deployments needing horizontally scalable load-balancer gateways (public/private cloud). K2 Cloud runs it in production; work remains (per the speakers). Requires OVN support for the deferred-nat option.

items.title: Targeted Megaflow Revalidation in Open vSwitch
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Gaetan Rivet, NVIDIA

  • Why: A diagnosed failure mode that "has limited the scale of our Open vSwitch deployments at NVIDIA": after any configuration change, OVS revalidates all megaflows, which can cascade into flow eviction, revalidator destabilization, and megaflow population collapse — a rebuild under overload. A concrete fix with a dependency-tracking design, implemented and running in production fork form.
  • What: Targeted megaflow revalidation, implemented in the OVS-DOCA fork: record the reason for each revalidation and extend xcache to track each megaflow's dependencies, so only affected megaflows are retranslated after a change. Also gives controller authors a way to structure OpenFlow pipelines so configuration changes have bounded impact; upstreaming is intended. (from abstract only)
  • How: Dependency tracking including indirect and negative dependencies (watched ports, missing groups), with AI-assisted testing used to cover the dependency matrix; part of a wider revalidation-stabilization effort that continues with a better flow-capacity control law.
  • Where applicable: Any large OVS deployment, but the current implementation lives in NVIDIA's OVS-DOCA fork (DOCA/BlueField context) — upstream availability is the thing to watch. The dependency-completeness caveat is the main risk.

items.text:

Keshav Kabra, NVIDIA; Surya Seetharaman, Red Hat, LLC.

items.title: Two OVN-Kubernetes, One DPU
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Alin Serdean, NVIDIA; Igal Tsoiref, Red Hat, LLC.

  • Why: DPU-mode ovn-kubernetes today serves only the host cluster — pods scheduled on the DPU's own node get nothing. Running two full ovn-k instances on one card, sharing only what must be shared, is a concrete step toward DPUs as first-class compute, which matters for accelerator-adjacent infrastructure.
  • What: A proposal and working prototype for a second, full-mode ovn-kubernetes instance on the same DPU, each instance keeping its own OVN databases and Kubernetes API, with the genuinely shared resources carefully partitioned. Built on co-hosted ovn-controller (experimental since 23.03, untagged in 26.09.0). (from abstract only)
  • How: The enumerated hard parts: system-id as the one key that can't be chassis-specific, conntrack zones staying clear of shared gateway zones, 15-character management-port name limits, two instances can't share a gateway bridge (ovnk owns its whole flow table), and ownership assignment for bridges, nftables tables, metrics ports and socket paths. Prototype demo; PRs referenced.
  • Where applicable: DPU-accelerated Kubernetes (NVIDIA BlueField-class cards, Red Hat + NVIDIA joint work). The resource-partitioning lessons generalize to any two network stacks sharing one host.

items.title: Upgrading network control plane and ovs-vswitchd with kernel datapath without impacting users
items.text:
Open vSwitch and OVN 2026 Fall Conference digest Program Core pick 2–4 November 2026

Abstract

Aleksandr Ankudinov, Nebius

  • Why: Live-upgrading the network data plane of a large public cloud without user-visible impact is one of the hardest ops problems in the field. Nebius shares the actual tricks — including running two ovs-vswitchd in parallel, "doing the forbidden" — which is gold for anyone operating OVS-based infrastructure in Kubernetes.
  • What: Techniques for restarting/replacing the three components (vpc-agent, ovs-vswitchd, OVS kernel module) while existing flows keep traffic flowing: flow cookies as version tags for cleanup, OpenFlow note actions as cross-restart storage, disciplined group-ID allocation, and the parallel-vswitchd upgrade dance with flow-restore-wait — including how to make two daemons fight and how to make them stop. Plus the Kubernetes-specific oddities, and a theoretical scheme for loading two OVS kernel modules at once. (from abstract only)
  • How: Desired-state reconciliation over versioned flows, plus dual-daemon handover during upgrade; kernel module itself is not hot-upgraded today.
  • Where applicable: Nebius public-cloud specifics (kernel datapath, agent-based control), but the versioning/reconciliation patterns apply to any OVS/OpenFlow deployment. The parallel-daemon scheme carries real risk — treat as inspiration, not recipe.

items.title: 30 Years of Interconnection: Experience from an Italian IXP
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Maurizio Goretti, NAMEX

PDF

  • Why: A three-decade operator's view of how regional interconnection actually evolves — good strategic context for anyone whose products ride IXP/edge infrastructure, though light on transferable technique.

items.title: Agentic DDoS OPS/AI-Powered Operations Layer for GenieATM
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Siarhei Matashuk, Genie Networks

PDF

  • Why: Not optics, not BGP — it's an early, concrete look at how LLM agents get wired into live NOC operations, and the design patterns (git-versioned markdown skills, a hard privacy boundary, an earned-autonomy trust model) generalize far beyond DDoS tooling, including into the identity and authorization questions agentic systems raise for the PM's own portfolio.
  • What: An agent layer ("DjiNN") on top of GenieATM implementing nine virtual NOC/SOC roles as "skills" — Baseline Analyst (continuous detection-threshold tuning with auto-rollback, replacing set-and-forget thresholds), Traffic Analyst (natural-language queries over a 1M-flow in-memory snapshot, e.g., breakdown of a new uplink by origin ASN/protocol with no query syntax), Peering Coordinator (cross-referencing per-AS traffic against PeeringDB to surface peering ROI, e.g., "40% of traffic to AS 13335 rides transit but they're at AMS-IX where you already peer, est. €2,400/month savings"), plus Incident Responder, Platform SRE, and others clearly staged as MVP vs Phase ⅔. Notably honest limitations: LLM latency handled by rule-based fallback for time-critical detection (the LLM does enrichment, not first-trigger); trust via a maturity model from L0 alert-only to L3 autonomous-with-audit-trail, with all destructive actions human-approved; data privacy via an MCP anonymization layer (IP→prefix_UUID, Router→router_XXX) so only tokenized data crosses to the LLM provider, with a local-model option for zero exposure.
  • How: Skills are plain ~30-line .md job descriptions in git — a NOC engineer can read and modify one in five minutes, no SDK; an orchestrator routes tasks → skills → tools → data sources; southbound to GenieATM's Snapshot API/NetFlow plus PeeringDB, RIPE RIS, RouteViews, and threat intel.
  • Where applicable: The data source is GenieATM-specific and the closing slide recruits for an early-access program (vendor session — discount accordingly), but the skill-file architecture, trust maturity model, and anonymization boundary are platform-agnostic patterns worth borrowing.

ml-for-networking ddos automation

items.title: Demystifying Coherent Optics for Network Professionals
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Core pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Marcin Bala, Salumanus

PDF

  • Why: Coherent pluggables (100ZR, 400G ZR/ZR+/ZR++, 800G ZR/ZR+) are collapsing the router-to-DWDM boundary and changing DC/WAN interconnect economics — squarely the PM's physical-optics territory. This is a working engineer's guide, not a marketing deck.
  • What: A market/standards map (OIF 400ZR/800ZR, OpenZR+, CMIS) and a four-step deployment method: link requirements (length, dark fiber vs DWDM, grid, OSNR, throughput) → transceiver selection → matching application to link budget → configuration. Worked examples: a 200 km DWDM link on a 50 GHz grid at 19 dB OSNR served by either QSFP28 100ZR or QSFP-DD OpenZR+ ZR100-OFEC-QPSK; a 21 dB/100 GHz path running ZR300-OFEC-8QAM with 3x100GbE host-side, or ZR++ to keep 400GbE host-side; an 18 dB flex-grid path forcing ZR200-OFEC-QPSK or an 800G module in ZR400-OFEC-QPSK (150 GHz passband). Also covers the 400G-to-100G interconnect case via muxponder (75 GHz spectrum instead of 200 GHz, future-ready for direct 400G optics), and SFF modules emulating QSFP28 LR4/LR1/DWDM2 for CMIS-less legacy gear.
  • How: Concrete CLI on four platforms — Juniper (optics-options application mediaid/hostid, tx-power, wavelength), Nokia (optics-profile 400ZR, dwdm coherent target-power, frequency), Cisco (zrp-optics fec oFEC muxponder …), OcNOS (qsfp-dd application, laser grid/fine-tune). Parameter guidance: OSNR ~24 dB for 400G 16QAM vs ~16 dB for 200G QPSK; Q-factor >8 dB good, 6.5–8 monitor, <6.5 failure risk. Common failure modes: mismatched host/media applications between ends, mismatched channel number, ignored optical budget.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — open OIF/OpenZR+ standards, multi-vendor config. Speaker is an optics vendor CTO, but the content is standards- and config-centric, with deployment mistakes/checklists rather than product claims.

optics interconnection

items.title: EVPN - One control plane to rule them all
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Core pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Patrick Prangl, Arista Networks

PDF

  • Why: Consolidating all L2/L3 VPN service delivery onto one BGP control plane across DC and WAN is exactly the PM's DC/WAN interconnect space, and this maps the RFC landscape, the SR-MPLS→SRv6 migration tiers, and the gateway designs that make it real.
  • What: The case for EVPN as the single service control plane: EVPN-VPWS (RFC 8214) for E-LINE, EVPN-L2VPN (RFC 7432) for E-LAN, EVPN-L3VPN Type-5 (RFC 9136), and EVPN multicast (RFC 9625 OISM) — replacing LDP/BGP-VPLS, MC-LAG, Draft-Rosen/NG-MVPN, and per-service signaling protocols. Transport strategy: SR-MPLS reusing existing MPLS hardware and BGP control plane (TI-LFA for 50 ms FRR, FlexAlgo for controller-less macro-TE, controller-based micro-TE), with three SRv6 maturity tiers — SR-MPLSv4 (no hardware change), SR-MPLSv6 (IPv6 forwarding plane, possible HW upgrade), SRv6 uSID (likely HW upgrade, new control plane). EVPN gateway design per BESS RFCs/drafts (8365, 9014, draft-ietf-bess-evpn-ipvpn-interworking): VXLAN↔MPLS interworking where Type-⅖ routes are re-advertised across domains with re-encapsulation while Type-⅓/4 stay local; gateway next-hop chaining so leaves only learn local next-hops; D-PATH attribute for inter-domain loop prevention. Forward-looking pieces: Unknown MAC Route (MAC=0 + gateway ESI) to bound MAC scale in multi-domain fabrics, and the multicast gateway family (MEG, PEG, EEG).
  • How: One BGP AFI/SAFI across all service types; gateways translate encapsulation and own inter-domain next-hop re-advertisement, containing control-plane state per domain; D-PATH domain-ID tagging prevents route loops across gateway meshes.
  • Where applicable: Explicitly covers greenfield build-outs and brownfield MPLS/SR coexistence with interop gateways; transport per use case (VXLAN in DC/campus, MPLS-SR/SRv6 in WAN, VXLAN-over-IPSec for SD-WAN). Arista vendor session, but anchored in IETF standards — the architecture applies to multi-vendor EVPN deployments.

bgp data-center-fabric

items.title: Get the benefits of a non-profit local/sub-regional IX

PDF

items.title: Peering market at a glance
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Flavio Luciani (with John Souter), NAMEX

PDF

  • Why: An evidence-based counter to the "peering is dying" narrative, useful for interconnect strategy and for anticipating where IXP/edge investment flows next.
  • What: A synthesis of a multi-region paper (published on RIPE Labs, APNIC, LACNIC, ARIN blogs): peering is structurally transforming, not declining. The misread comes from mature-hub stabilization, lost visibility as traffic moves to PNIs/in-network caching/edge, and hyperscaler selective interconnection (CAIDA port-capacity trends for Meta/Microsoft/Apple/AWS shown). Growth is strongest in emerging markets (Kenya, Nigeria, Philippines, Indonesia, Japan, Mexico, Colombia, Peru). IXP success factors: telecom liberalization, local content and eyeballs, population scale, carrier-neutral DC ecosystems. Forward look: IXPs as strategic infrastructure for resilience and sovereignty, micro-IXPs, and edge/low-latency architectures.
  • How: CAIDA snapshots, PeeringDB, and IXPDB data compared across regions.
  • Where applicable: Strategy level — relevant to interconnection planning generally; country specifics vary and the slides are a condensed version of a longer paper worth reading for depth.

peering capacity-planning

items.title: Securing IXP Fabric
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Core pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Alessandro Bulletti, Nokia

PDF

  • Why: An IXP fabric is a giant shared L2 exchange LAN, and the hardening techniques here — proxy ARP/ND, BUM policing, duplicate MAC-IP detection — transfer to any shared L2 fabric including DC interconnect. The talk also carries current, concrete DDoS threat numbers.
  • What: Two parts. First, inherent fabric protection with EVPN Proxy-ARP/ND in three "gated lines of defense": (1) static MAC per customer logical interface + ACL filters blocking unknown multicast/broadcast so only assigned MAC/IPv4/v6 can source traffic into the fabric; (2) ingress policers for BUM and ARP per customer interface, with hardware rate-limiters keeping CPU load controlled; (3) Proxy-ARP/ND with static ARP entries, dynamic proxy ARP with MAC lists, and EVPN MAC-duplication detection — eliminating ARP/ND flooding and enforcing that customers only use assigned addresses. Second, DDoS mitigation at the IXP itself: detection keyed on the peering partner's destination MAC (SPM or IPFIX IE315) on L2 interfaces, with auto-mitigation via IP filters in the fabric rather than rerouting to a scrubbing center. Includes Nokia 2025 threat-intelligence data: attacks over 10/20/40 Tbps recorded within a single month (Sep–Oct 2025); 78% of attacks complete within five minutes (up from 44% in 2024), 37% within two minutes; 52% carpet-bomb multiple hosts; AI-orchestrated vector switching and botnet proxy wars.
  • How: EVPN proxy-ARP/ND converts flood-and-learn L2 into controlled control-plane learning, with distributed CPU protection so punted ARP is handled in hardware; references DE-CIX's EVPN peering-LAN work and IX.br's SRv6 fabric as real-world precedents.
  • Where applicable: The fabric-hardening mechanics apply to any EVPN fabric (all major vendors implement proxy-ARP/ND variants); the DDoS-as-a-service portion is Nokia Deepfield-specific and partly a pitch. Take the techniques and the threat statistics, treat the product framing accordingly.

data-center-fabric network-security peering

items.title: Technical Workshop: A focus on ROAs and ASPAs, and how to handle them with Krill
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Core pick 23–25 March 2026

Massimiliano Stucchi

  • Why: RPKI is mainstream; ASPA is the next routing-security primitive and directly addresses the class of route leaks that ROV cannot catch (path leaks) — the same gap the AS-SETs talk in this program quantifies. Hands-on delegated RPKI with Krill is adoptable tooling, not theory.
  • What: A refresher on RPKI and ROAs, an introduction to ASPAs (what they assert, how to create them, their role in global routing), and the bulk of the session is practical Krill setup for delegated RPKI, including preparing different publication setups. (from abstract only)
  • How: Workshop format: software setup and publication-architecture walkthroughs. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: Any operator running or considering delegated RPKI; vendor-neutral open-source tooling. The ASPA portion's practical payoff depends on how far ASPA verification has spread among your transits. No slides or paper were in the source material, so depth beyond the abstract is unknown.

bgp pki network-security

items.title: The Scourge of Excessive AS-SETs
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Core pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Jac Kloots, Kentik

PDF

  • Why: IRR AS-SETs remain the operational backbone of BGP filtering, and this talk quantifies — with real case data — how uncontrolled nesting has made many of them useless as allowlists, then points at the actual fix (ASPA, RFC 9234). Directly relevant to network security and BGP-internals work.
  • What: An analysis anchored on the March 11, 2024 MTS (AS8359) / HKIX route leak. The leaker's AS-MTU expands to 43,823 ASNs; bgpq4 -J produces a ~1.29M-line Junos config (271k lines even with -A aggregation) covering 1.8 billion of the ~3 billion routable IPv4 addresses — so any transit filtering on AS-MTU is effectively filtering nothing. The largest AS-SETs (e.g., AS39533:AS-PEERS) expand past 100k ASNs, exceeding the ~90k ASNs in the global table, because nested sets pull in unrouted ASNs; 2,192 AS-SETs expand beyond 1,000 ASNs. A traced nesting chain from AS-XUA-UA runs Ukraine → NL-IX → Balkan-IX → TTK → CN2 → South Africa → CTGNet → Rostelecom before landing on an unrouted Russian air-traffic-corporation ASN. Root cause: AS-SETs mix semantically undefined member types (customers, peers, IXP members) with no limits on membership or recursion depth.
  • How: Recursive IRR expansion mechanics; tools (bgpq4, irrtree, bgp.tools) as measurement instruments; a key operational gotcha — AS-SET contents differ by source IRR (NTT mirror is bgpq4's default), so authoritative source must be declared, e.g., in PeeringDB. Proposed long-term fix: RFC 9234 BGP role signaling in-band, RPKI ASPA verification, and Signed Prefix Lists, rather than ever-larger self-asserted allowlists.
  • Where applicable: Every transit operator filtering with IRR data. Speaker is from an observability vendor, but this is data analysis with named collaborators (bgp.tools, Comcast, Cogent, Google, Telia), not a product pitch.

bgp measurement network-security

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings
items.text:
Peering Days 2026 digest Program Core pick 23–25 March 2026

Slides

Gerhard Stein (with Thomas Weible), Flexoptix

PDF

  • Why: Optics power draw is a real DC cost line at 400G/800G scale, and this is one of the few talks with actual measurements of where transceiver watts go — a topic the PM works on physically and strategically.
  • What: A measurement study across 100G QSFP28, 400G QSFP-DD coherent ZR, and 800G QSFP-DD transceivers on Cisco Nexus 93600CD-GX, Catalyst C9500, and Juniper QFX5120. Findings: laser and TEC draw is negligible at any transceiver temperature (laser at its ~50 °C target is most efficient, but it barely matters); the real consumers are the MCU/DSP, flagged as the next research step; shutting a port forces low-power mode and cuts transceiver consumption 7–20x; "doubling the speed does not double the Watts." VDM (CMIS calculated metrics) vs DDM support varies sharply by platform — only the Nexus 93600CD-GX with a 400G coherent module reported a real laser temperature (49.98 °C); the QFX5120 and C9500 expose DDM only.
  • How: VDM reads calculated values from module bytes (e.g., P_laser = V_fwd × I_laser, P_TEC = V_Trc × I_TEC) where DDM gives raw currents; power budget and fan/heat-exchange modeling (Nusselt/Prandtl/Reynolds); measurements taken via a Flexbox-based research tool, including a frozen-transceiver experiment showing laser behavior across a ~20 °C differential.
  • Where applicable: The port-shutdown power lever and platform-dependent VDM support are broadly useful to any switch operator. Flexoptix is a vendor, but the work is measurement-based and spans three switch vendors' hardware.

optics power

items.title: A Risk Assessment Framework for Digital Identification Systems
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Authors: Allison Woodruff (Google), Dirk Balfanz (Google), Will Drewry (Google), Mariana Raykova (Google)

For anyone building passkeys, federation, or national/enterprise digital ID, this is a meta-level artifact worth reading even if you skip the rest of the proceedings.

identity standardization

items.title: CensorLess: Cost-Efficient Censorship Circumvention Through Serverless Cloud Functions
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Dayeon Kang (University of Massachusetts Amherst), Jade Sheffey (University of Massachusetts Amherst), Mingshi Wu (GFW Report), Pubali Datta (University of Massachusetts Amherst), Amir Houmansadr (University of Massachusetts Amherst)

Video

  • Why: Houmansadr's group treating circumvention as a cost problem: serverless functions give you disposable, auto-scaling egress from cloud provider ranges that censors are reluctant to block wholesale. It's a systems/economics answer rather than a protocol trick, and the GFW Report co-author again signals real-adversary grounding.
  • What: Apparently a circumvention design that uses serverless cloud functions as ephemeral proxies, driving per-use cost down and re-provisioning speed up so address-blocking is ineffective (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Inference: clients reach FaaS endpoints (function URLs, API gateways) that relay traffic; blocked functions are replaced cheaply, exploiting the shared, economically-entangled cloud IP space.
  • Where applicable: Client tools that can reach major cloud providers; constrained by provider acceptable-use enforcement and function runtime/networking limits. Adversary economics are specific to censors that tolerate cloud IP ranges.

censorship cloud-native

items.title: CODoH: Privacy-Preserving Caching for Oblivious DNS over HTTPS
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Pankaj Niroula (William & Mary), Lily Gloudemans (William & Mary), Aashutosh Poudel (William & Mary), Collin MacDonald (William & Mary), Stephen Herwig (William & Mary)

Video

  • Why: ODoH's fatal flaw for deployment is that relaying through an oblivious proxy destroys resolver-side caching, inflating latency and cost. Solving cache while preserving obliviousness is a real distributed-systems problem at the heart of privacy-preserving network infrastructure — the same tension as anonymous credentials vs. CDN economics.
  • What: Apparently a mechanism that restores caching benefits for ODoH without letting the resolver or proxy link queries to clients (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Not described in the program; plausible routes are oblivious caching (private information retrieval over cache contents) or cache-shared constructions where hit/miss patterns don't leak identity. Herwig's group works in network measurement and systems security, so expect implementation and latency evaluation.
  • Where applicable: DNS resolution infrastructure — DoH/ODoH deployments, corporate resolvers, privacy-relay services. Broadly applicable to any CDN/caching service that wants unlinkability, not DNS-specific in concept.

dns privacy

items.title: Cryptographically-Secured Domain Validation
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Henry Birge-Lee (Princeton University), Grace H. Cimaszewski (Princeton University), Cyrill Krähenbühl (Princeton University), Liang Wang (Princeton University), Aaron Gable (Let's Encrypt), Prateek Mittal (Princeton University)

Video

  • Why: Domain control validation is the weakest link in web PKI, and it fails at exactly your intersection — routing (BGP/IP hijack of ACME challenges) meets certificate identity. The Princeton group has previously published real attacks on certificate issuance via network-level manipulation, and the Let's Encrypt co-author signals this is aimed at deployable CA-side change, not a paper-only fix.
  • What: Apparently a scheme to make the domain validation step of certificate issuance cryptographically verifiable rather than trusting the network path (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Not described in the program; given the team's prior work, expect mechanisms that bind validation evidence to authenticated infrastructure or challenge exchanges so a network adversary can't satisfy a challenge they don't control.
  • Where applicable: The ACME/web PKI ecosystem broadly — any CA, and by extension every TLS-terminated service. The Let's Encrypt involvement makes the deployment path unusually credible for a PETS paper.

pki bgp

items.title: Di5Guise: 5G Privacy with vSIM
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Shirin Ebadi (University of Colorado Boulder), Zach Moolman (University of Colorado Boulder), Tamara Lehman (University of Colorado Boulder), Eric Keller (University of Colorado Boulder)

Video

  • Why: This hits both halves of your identity/networking background at once: 5G subscriber identity (SUPI/SUCI, IMSI-catcher history) and network function virtualization — Eric Keller's presence signals an SDN/NFV systems approach rather than pure crypto theory.
  • What: Apparently the use of virtualized SIMs (vSIM) — decoupling subscriber credentials from a physical SIM/eSIM — to improve subscriber privacy in 5G, presumably by making identity easier to rotate or compartmentalize per device/service (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Not described in the program; plausibly per-context virtual identities provisioned on demand so that long-term subscriber identifiers are never exposed on the radio or core interfaces.
  • Where applicable: 5G core and RAN ecosystems, MVNOs, and eSIM/iSIM device fleets. Realistically operator-dependent: requires core-network support for virtualized credentials, so nearer-term for private 5G or MVNO deployments than for consumer carriers.

privacy mobile identity

items.title: Ephemeral Network-Layer Fingerprinting Defenses
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Tobias Pulls (Karlstad University), Topi Korhonen (Independent), Ethan Witwer (Linköping University), Niklas Carlsson (Linköping University)

Video

  • Why: Passive network-layer fingerprinting (TCP/IP stack and header-level characteristics, p0f-style) is how censors and adversaries identify proxies, bridges, and tunnel traffic without decrypting anything. Pulls is a long-time traffic-analysis researcher, and this sits squarely in network security operations: it's the same fingerprinting your anti-abuse or DLP stack might do — from the other side.
  • What: Apparently defenses that make a host's network-layer fingerprint ephemeral — changing over time so long-lived passive classifiers can't match or block on stack characteristics (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Presumably systematic mutation of network-layer identifiers (header options, timing, fragmentation behavior) on a rotating basis, with evaluation against real classifiers.
  • Where applicable: Circumvention/proxy infrastructure (Tor bridges, VPN endpoints) and any deployment that must survive passive, low-cost classification by a network observer. General technique at the OS/network-stack level.

privacy censorship

items.title: Evaluating connection migration based QUIC censorship circumvention
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Seungju Lee (Princeton University), Mona Wang (Princeton University), Watson Jia (Princeton University), Qiang Wu (GFW Report), Henry Birge-Lee (Princeton University), Liang Wang (Princeton University), Prateek Mittal (Princeton University)

Video

  • Why: This is QUIC protocol internals (connection IDs, migration, path validation) weaponized for censorship resistance — and the GFW Report co-authors signal measurement against a live national censor, not a lab adversary. For anyone who reasons about QUIC/HTTP3 deployment, seeing the protocol's mobility feature double as an evasion primitive is valuable.
  • What: Apparently an evaluation of using QUIC connection migration — moving an established connection across paths/addresses without re-handshaking — as a censorship circumvention strategy, including how a censor responds (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Inference: leverage migration to relocate a connection away from blocked paths (e.g., blocked server IPs or links), evaluating blocking asymmetries the GFW exploits and whether CID rotation defeats correlation.
  • Where applicable: Circumvention tools on QUIC-capable endpoints and, in the mirror direction, any middlebox/policy enforcement design that assumes connection↔address binding. Adversary-specific results (GFW) but the technique is general QUIC.

censorship http

items.title: More Space, Less Privacy? Measuring the Effectiveness of IP-based Website Fingerprinting in IPv6
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Sumeer Ahmad (Stony Brook University), Michalis Polychronakis (Stony Brook University), Theophilus A. Benson (Carnegie Mellon University), Nguyen Phong Hoang (University of British Columbia)

Video

  • Why: IPv6's address-space semantics — per-flow addresses, rotating /64s, SLAAC privacy extensions — are usually framed as a privacy win. This paper asks whether the expanded space (or its addressing habits) actually enables IP-based website linking/fingerprinting instead. That's a networking-semantics question with direct privacy consequences, from a strong measurement group (Polychronakis, Benson).
  • What: Apparently a measurement of how effectively websites or on-path observers can fingerprint/link clients by IP address in the IPv6 world — testing the assumption that IPv6 rotation defeats tracking (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Not described in the program; expect large-scale measurement of IPv6 address stability, prefix behavior, and address-to-identity linkability across visits.
  • Where applicable: Web tracking, CDN/anti-abuse design, and any privacy engineering that relies on IPv6 address rotation; broadly applicable, not org-specific.

privacy ipv6 measurement

items.title: OAuthHub: Mitigating OAuth Data Overaccess through a Local Data Hub
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Authors: Qiyu Li (University of California, San Diego), Yuhe Tian (University of California, San Diego), Haojian Jin (University of California, San Diego)

  • Why: OAuth over-granting is a chronic production problem — relying parties request broad scopes, users press Allow, and tokens hoover up data forever. A mitigation paper from Jin's group (which works on usable system security at UCSD) addresses the day-to-day OAuth design question every platform PM faces.
  • What: Apparently a client-side "local data hub" that sits between OAuth flows and relying parties, mediating and limiting the data actually released so that granted scope doesn't equal unlimited access (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Inference from the title: an on-device broker that intercepts token/data handoffs, enforces least-privilege per request, and possibly surfaces granular revocation to the user.
  • Where applicable: Consumer OAuth/OIDC ecosystems on personal devices (browser or mobile). Browser- or OS-integration dependent; not a server-side-only fix.

authorization identity

items.title: Obscura: Enabling Ephemeral Proxies for Traffic Encapsulation in WebRTC Media Streams Against Cost-Effective Censors
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Authors: Afonso Vilalonga (NOVA LINCS, NOVA School of Science, Technology), Kevin Gallagher (NOVA LINCS, NOVA School of Science, Technology), João S. Resende (Universidade do Porto), Henrique Domingos (NOVA LINCS, NOVA School of Science, Technology)

  • Why: Post-domain-fronting, the circumvention field has moved to embedding traffic in legitimate-looking media protocols. Tunneling inside WebRTC media streams (DTLS/SRTP) is an engineering-heavy approach that treats the browser's real-time stack as cover traffic — relevant both to circumvention and to understanding what DPI can and can't classify cheaply.
  • What: Apparently a proxy design that encapsulates arbitrary traffic inside WebRTC media streams, with proxies that are ephemeral — cheap to spin up and discard, so blocking by address is economically futile against "cost-effective" censors (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Inference: proxied connections are tunneled through WebRTC's media path so the observable traffic is indistinguishable from a video/audio session, plus orchestration for short-lived proxy instances.
  • Where applicable: Browser-based circumvention; constraints are WebRTC's congestion control interacting with tunneled traffic (throughput/latency cost). The "cost-effective censor" threat model is explicitly budget-limited — results may not hold against well-resourced adversaries.

censorship encryption

items.title: Personalizing Agent Privacy Decisions via Logical Entailment
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: James Flemings (University of Southern California), Ren Yi (Google), Octavian Suciu (Google), Kassem Fawaz (University of Wisconsin--Madison), Murali Annavaram (University of Southern California), Marco Gruteser (Google)

Video

  • Why: This is the agentic-identity paper of the program. As AI agents act on users' behalf, the question shifts from authentication ("is this agent who it says it is") to authorization policy ("what may it disclose, to whom, in this context"). A Google co-authorship suggests the problem is real at production scale.
  • What: Apparently a formal-logic approach to encoding user privacy preferences and checking whether a proposed agent action follows from them — turning agent decisions into a personalized policy-entailment problem (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Inference: user preferences expressed as logical rules; an agent's intended action (or data disclosure) is evaluated by entailment against those rules, with personalization meaning the rule set is learned/derived per user.
  • Where applicable: Assistant/agent platforms and any system where delegated AI acts for a user — the natural companion to SPIFFE-style workload identity: proving who the agent is only matters once you can also decide what it may do.

identity privacy ml-for-networking

items.title: Pirouette: Query Efficient Single-Server PIR
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 20–25 July 2026

Authors: Jiayi Kang (COSIC, KU Leuven), Leonard Schild (COSIC, KU Leuven)

  • Why: The single biggest obstacle to practical PIR has always been the cost of the client's query (uploading a padded database-sized vector). Query-efficient single-server PIR is the enabler behind private password-breach checking, private contact discovery, and private key-value lookups — identity-adjacent infrastructure use cases you'd otherwise have to trust a third party for.
  • What: Apparently a single-server PIR scheme whose contribution is driving client query size down while keeping server computation tolerable (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Not described in the program; COSIC's recent line of work has pushed homomorphic-encryption-based PIR with preprocessing and compact queries, so expect that machinery with a new efficiency point on the upload/compute curve.
  • Where applicable: Any "server holds a list, client learns only its own entry" service — credential-breach alerting, presence lookup, blocklist checks. General technique, no trusted third party required.

privacy encryption

items.title: Privacy Pass is Anamorphic: Practical Consequences and Attacks in the Black-box Model
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Mirosław Kutyłowski (NASK National Research Institute), Oliwer Sobolewski (NASK National Research Institute)

Video

  • Why: Privacy Pass is deployed, IETF-standardized anonymous-access token infrastructure (Cloudflare, Apple) — essentially blind-signature rate-limiting credentials sitting in your identity perimeter. A paper showing it admits "anamorphic" properties (hidden information flowing inside otherwise sound protocol runs) is a property-type analysis of a protocol you may actually run.
  • What: Apparently a demonstration that Privacy Pass exchanges can carry concealed channels in the black-box model, with practical consequences for deployments that assumed the tokens reveal nothing beyond validity (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Anamorphic cryptography lens: a party with secret knowledge (e.g., a malicious or colluding issuer/verifier) can encode hidden bits into seemingly random protocol fields such that normal participants detect nothing.
  • Where applicable: Any Privacy Pass / private-access-token deployment (privacy passes, PATs, anti-bot integrations); the black-box model makes the results deployment-relevant rather than purely theoretical.

privacy identity

items.title: Redefining Website Fingerprinting Attacks with Multi-Agent LLMs
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 20–25 July 2026

Authors: Chuxu Song (Rutgers University), Dheekshith Dev Manohar Mekala (Rutgers University), Hao Wang (Rutgers University), Richard P. Martin (Rutgers University)

  • Why: Two fields you track — network traffic analysis and LLM agents — collide here. If multi-agent LLM pipelines can replace hand-crafted website-fingerprinting feature engineering, the barrier to sophisticated traffic analysis drops dramatically, and the same shift threatens every hand-tuned classifier in your security stack.
  • What: Apparently a re-formulation of website fingerprinting (inferring visited sites from encrypted traffic traces) where multi-agent LLM systems perform the analysis instead of fixed ML models (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Inference: traffic traces are serialized into representations that LLM agents reason over, possibly with role-specialized agents (feature extraction, pattern matching, decision) orchestrated together.
  • Where applicable: Traffic-analysis research and, adversarially, any encrypted-traffic classification problem — VPN/anonymity users today, but the methodology generalizes to flow-based monitoring generally. Compute cost likely limits real-time use for now.

privacy ml-for-networking measurement

items.title: SoK: Can Fully Homomorphic Encryption Support General AI Computation? A Functional and Cost Analysis
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 20–25 July 2026

Authors: Jiaqi Xue (University of Central Florida), Xin Xin (University of Central Florida), Wei Zhang (University of Central Florida), Mengxin Zheng (University of Central Florida), Qianqian Song (University of Florida), Minxuan Zhou (Illinois Institute of Technology), Yushun Dong (Florida State University), Dongjie Wang (The University of Kansas), Xun Chen (Samsung Research America), Jiafeng Xie (Villanova University), Liqiang Wang (University of Central Florida), David Mohaisen (University of Central Florida), Hongyi Wu (University of Arizona), Qian Lou (University of Central Florida)

  • Why: You wouldn't search for an FHE SoK, but the question it answers is one your roadmap will eventually force: is encrypted computation of AI workloads anywhere near economic? This is the field's cost-accounting checkpoint, with a Samsung Research co-author signaling industry attention — and it frames the budget conversation for every "privacy-preserving inference" pitch you'll be pitched next year.
  • What: A systematization of running general AI computation under FHE, centered on a functional-completeness and cost analysis — what class of computation is even expressible, and what it costs in time and money (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Expect a taxonomy of FHE schemes and compiler/frameworks for neural inference, benchmarked across operators and models, with the cost analysis giving concrete latency/overhead figures per workload class.
  • Where applicable: Private inference services, confidential ML in regulated environments; the SoK's value is telling you where the boundary of practicality currently sits — treat its conclusions as the reality check for vendor FHE claims.

privacy encryption ml-for-networking

items.title: SoK: Offline Finding Protocols for Lightweight Location Tracking
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Akshaya Kumar (Georgia Institute of Technology), Carolina Ortega Pérez (Cornell University), Joseph Jaeger (Georgia Institute of Technology), Thomas Ristenpart (Univeristy of Toronto), Michael Specter (Georgia Institute of Technology)

Video

  • Why: The Find My-style crowdsourced location ecosystem (Apple, Google, Samsung, third-party tags) is a large, deployed, cryptographically interesting protocol family with live standardization pressure (unwanted-tracking mitigation). A SoK from the GT/Cornell/Toronto systems-security corridor is the map of that ecosystem.
  • What: A systematization of offline-finding protocols — how lightweight devices with no connectivity broadcast cryptographically protected beacons that nearby crowd devices relay to the owner (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Expect a taxonomy of beacon privacy mechanisms (rotating public keys, address rotation), relay and discovery architectures, and attacker models including stalking/unwanted tracking.
  • Where applicable: Device-finding networks and BLE-based crowd location infrastructure; increasingly relevant as anti-stalking features become a cross-vendor interoperability problem.

privacy iot

items.title: Understanding Privacy and Quality Tradeoffs in Synthetic Network Data
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Andrew Chu (University of Chicago), Kyle MacMillan (University of Chicago), Paul Schmitt (Cal Poly), Nick Feamster (University of Chicago)

Video

  • Why: The closest thing to your home turf in the whole program: network measurement data (topologies, flow records, telemetry) is notoriously hard to share across orgs — vendors, operators, researchers — because it's simultaneously sensitive and operationally precious. Feamster's group doing a privacy/utility tradeoff study means real network datasets and network-quality metrics, not generic tabular-DP benchmarks.
  • What: Apparently an empirical study of how privacy mechanisms applied when generating synthetic network data degrade the properties that make the data useful — quantifying the privacy/quality frontier (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Presumably generative models over network data (topology and/or traffic) with differential privacy or sanitization on the training side, evaluated on downstream network-analysis tasks.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any org that shares network telemetry externally (benchmarks, incident collaboration, regulatory reporting, research datasets); not tied to a single operator's setup, though dataset specifics will matter.

privacy measurement

items.title: What-App? App usage detection using encrypted LTE/5G traffic
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: Jinjin WANG (University of Birmingham), Zishuai Cheng (Beijing University of Posts, Telecommunications), Mihai Ordean (University of Birmingham), Baojiang Cui (Beijing University of Posts, Telecommunications)

Video

  • Why: Even with full payload encryption, the radio-access layer leaks enough (bearer patterns, QoS flows, timing) for a passive observer to classify which app is in use. For a PM with RAN and security background, this is the canonical "encryption is not traffic confidentiality" result, measured on modern 4G/5G.
  • What: Apparently a traffic-analysis attack that identifies applications from encrypted LTE/5G captures, demonstrating app-level fingerprinting despite payload and much metadata protection (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Presumably supervised classification over radio-layer and flow features (bearer/QCI characteristics, timing, volume) rather than packet contents.
  • Where applicable: Threat model is the mobile network operator or an on-path observer with RAN visibility — relevant to zero-rating, lawful-intercept debates, and privacy claims of 5G (SUCI protects identity, not behavior).

privacy mobile

items.title: zkRevoke: Configurable Untraceability for Verifiable Credentials using ZKPs
items.text:
PETS 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–25 July 2026

Recording

Authors: praveensankar manimaran (University of Oslo, Norway), Mayank Raikwar (University of Oslo, Norway), Thiago Garrett (University of Oslo, Norway), Arlindo F. da Conceição (Federal University of São Paulo, Brazil), Leander Jehl (University of Stavanger, Norway), Roman Vitenberg (University of Oslo, Norway)

Video

  • Why: Revocation and unlinkability are in direct tension in the W3C Verifiable Credentials / digital wallet world: naive revocation checks let the issuer or verifier correlate presentations. This is a live standards debate (Status List 2021 vs. accumulators vs. ZK approaches) that any identity PM building on VCs has to reason about.
  • What: Apparently a scheme letting credential holders prove validity (including non-revocation) via zero-knowledge proofs with a configurable knob for how much untraceability they get (title/author line only — no abstract in program).
  • How: Presumably ZK proofs over credential attributes and revocation state (accumulator- or commitment-based), with the "configurable" part trading proof size/verification cost against correlation resistance.
  • Where applicable: VC/DID wallet ecosystems, enterprise credentials, and any selective-disclosure identity scheme; general technique, not tied to one issuer.

identity privacy

items.title: IETF 122 (Bangkok)
items.text:
Program source is the datatracker documents API, filtered to a curated set of 26 working groups touching cloud-native networking, network security, and identity. As with any standards meeting, the unit of work is the Internet-Draft, not the session — sessions are thin, drafts carry the substance. All write-ups below are grounded in draft abstracts only; no PDF/page links were available in the program text to enrich from, so treat "What/How" as abstract-level, not full-text analysis. draft-ietf-* means a working group has adopted the work (it carries real weight); a bare draft-<author>-* is an individual submission that may or may not go anywhere — noted per item where it matters. Datatracker links are added per draft (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/<name>/) since the program text itself carried no reference links.

The headline this cycle: workload identity (WIMSE) has gone from architecture sketch to a nearly-complete, implementable protocol stack, and it's flanked by matching moves in OAuth (cross-domain identity propagation), attestation (RATS), and supply-chain transparency (SCITT) — all converging on the same underlying problem of proving what is talking to what, and on whose behalf.

Selection is from the program; every write-up below is grounded in the draft abstract only (no paper links were available to enrich from), and is flagged as such.

A note on maturity, since it's the whole game in a standards venue: draft-ietf-* means a working group has adopted the work (it carries weight); draft-<author>-* is an individual submission (early, may go nowhere). Where both exist for the same title, the WG copy is the one to track.

items.title: Beyond Collectives: Building Fused Compute-Communication Kernels with PyTorch Symmetric Memory
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Ke Wen (NVIDIA), Natalia Gimelshein (Meta), Kapil Sharma (Meta, PyTorch Distributed)

  • Why: One-sided RMA issued from inside GPU kernels is the biggest change in how accelerators use the fabric since collectives; this is the guided tour of the programming model, and it pairs directly with the new torch.distributed window APIs.
  • What: PyTorch Symmetric Memory gives every rank a direct window into its peers' GPU memory, erasing the compute/communication boundary. A practical tour across five themes: compute–communication fusion (pushing partial results to a peer from inside a kernel), one-sided puts/gets plus torch.distributed.TokenSwitch supporting expert-parallel MoE with autograd, binding NCCL device primitives into a CUDA DSL (cute-DSL), device-side profiling plus CUDA Graph capture, and community adoption. (from abstract only)
  • How: Communication becomes something a kernel does inline, hidden behind compute, instead of a black-box collective the compute waits on.
  • Where applicable: NVIDIA-backed (NVSHMEM) today, with the AMD rocSHMEM counterpart covered separately; relevant to anyone reasoning about when fused communication beats a collective — and about what next-gen RDMA APIs need to expose.

rdma ai-networks

items.title: Compute, Latency, and Safety: Architecting Stateful Guardrails for Multi-Agent Workflows
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Purva Chiniya — Amazon Ads

  • Why: Securing inter-agent handoffs is the agentic analogue of service-to-service authentication and authorization — your workload/agentic-identity interest. The threat model here (untrusted data corrupting downstream agent privileges) is a delegation/privilege-escalation problem, not just an ML one.
  • What: MLOps infrastructure for securing multi-agent systems at enterprise scale: continuous, stateful red-teaming pipelines built on the open-source SecRepoBench evaluation framework, and specialized low-latency SLMs deployed as deterministic orchestration guardrails — cross-agent payloads routed through high-speed checks that catch prompt injection ("indirect orchestration exploits") and operational drift without frontier-model cost or throughput collapse. (from abstract only)
  • How: Small, fast validators placed in-line on the agent-to-agent data path, evaluating state changes continuously — architecturally the same shape as a sidecar policy check in a service mesh.
  • Where applicable: Enterprise multi-agent deployments; abstract-level with no scale numbers given, so treat the effectiveness claims with caution. The enforcement pattern is the transferable part.

network-security offensive-security authorization

items.title: Crossing the Divide: Co-Evolving Kubernetes and Ray for the AI Era
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Jago Macleod (Google, Kubernetes & GKE), Ion Stoica (Anyscale / UC Berkeley)

  • Why: Kubernetes is where your cloud-native world has to absorb AI workloads; this session is the strategic map of how K8s and Ray are converging rather than fragmenting — directly relevant to K8s networking, scheduling, and resource-management roadmaps.
  • What: A discussion of the co-evolution of Kubernetes and Ray into a unified open-source AI stack, spanning the PyTorch Foundation side (PyTorch, vLLM, Ray) and the CNCF side (Kubernetes, Envoy, OpenTelemetry, llm-d, containerd), with Google and Anyscale actively collaborating to prevent ecosystem fragmentation. (from abstract only)
  • How: A jointly built, open, vertically integrated stack rather than parallel universes users must bridge themselves.
  • Where applicable: Vision/direction session by engineering leadership — expect roadmap-level framing, not implementation detail. Useful for planning where AI workload requirements will pull K8s networking and scheduling next.

kubernetes cloud-native orchestration

items.title: Demo Theater: OpenCLIC: Open Communication for Distributed Inference
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Jesse Treger

  • Why: This is the Ultra Ethernet / connectionless-RDMA story arriving at the framework layer — squarely in physical-fabric territory. Its core argument is that MoE inference traffic (dynamic, many-destination all-to-all) is a structural mismatch for the connection-oriented RDMA transports most AI clusters run today.
  • What: OpenCLIC, an open communication framework for connectionless networks, being integrated with vLLM. First use case is expert-parallel dispatch/combine; planned support for one-sided operations — KV-cache transfer, cache reuse/offload, and model-state movement. It separates framework interfaces, GPU kernels, and transport implementations so inference code isn't tied to one accelerator or network stack. (from abstract only)
  • How: Built on Ultra Ethernet Transport, modeled on HPE Slingshot: no per-peer connections, improving multipathing, loss recovery, and scalability. The initial Slingshot implementation uses kernel-initiated OpenSHMEM so GPU code drives the network directly and the CPU stays out of the critical path.
  • Where applicable: Initial implementation is HPE Slingshot-specific (HPC heritage), with the architecture positioned to extend across accelerators and fabrics. Demo-theater short format, and the program attaches a sponsored-content notice — expect a direction statement and early integration, not a full evaluation.

rdma ai-networks ethernet

items.title: EP-Overlap: Hiding Expert-Parallel Communication in MoE Training
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Sanket Jayant Purandare (PyTorch Distributed and Compilers), Syed Ahmed (NVIDIA, PyTorch Core)

  • Why: MoE expert-parallel all-to-all is the dominant new traffic pattern on AI fabrics; knowing how much of it can be hidden by framework-level scheduling tells you how much fabric headroom a MoE fleet actually needs.
  • What: Graph passes that hide EP communication by splitting each MoE layer into independent slices and overlapping token exchange with any available compute (experts, recompute, weight-gradient math), forward-with-forward and backward-with-backward. The same machinery also hides "page stashing," compacting worst-case activation memory from O(worst_case × L) to O(worst_case + actual). On DeepSeek-V3: 76–86% of EP comm hidden, ~1.3x throughput, +4% absolute MFU — and the authors call that a lower bound. (from abstract only)
  • How: Implemented as graph passes in TorchTitan's GraphTrainer, working under FSDP and PP with any schedule (not just DualPipe), no model changes, bitwise-matching eager numerics — overlap rather than wire-byte reduction.
  • Where applicable: DeepSeek-V3-scale MoE training; a framework-level (TorchTitan) technique that generalizes across schedules and parallelism strategies.

ai-networks rdma

items.title: Five Bottlenecks, Five Fixes: Systematic Performance Diagnosis for PyTorch Distributed Training
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Paulo Aragao, Aravind Neelakantan — AWS

  • Why: A repeatable diagnostic methodology for the question you get paged about — "is it the network?" Case 3 in particular (0.4% network utilization with MoE expert parallelism turning out to be a pipeline bubble, not a network problem) is exactly the misattribution pattern that wastes fabric-engineering time.
  • What: Five real case studies mapped onto a decision framework (compute-, memory-, communication-, or I/O-bound), each with specific torch.profiler signatures, NCCL debug patterns, and targeted fixes. Headline results: 83x data-loading gain (1.2% → usable GPU utilization), 28% throughput recovered from pipeline stages, and 6.8x end-to-end improvement on a production autonomous-driving model. (from abstract only)
  • How: Structured profiling → classify the bottleneck → apply the matched fix; delivered as a repeatable checklist for any distributed training workload.
  • Where applicable: Workload-agnostic methodology from AWS architects; the case studies are customer-specific but the framework and profiler signatures transfer cleanly.

troubleshooting benchmarking ai-networks

items.title: Future of Distributed Communication in PyTorch: New APIs for Fault Tolerance, RDMA and Extensibility
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Tristan Rice, Kapil Sharma — Meta (PyTorch Distributed)

  • Why: torch.distributed is the layer where every training collective maps onto your RDMA/Ethernet fabric. These API changes define how large jobs interact with the network — fault recovery, one-sided RDMA, and observability — and they are landing upstream for everyone.
  • What: Five new capabilities being upstreamed from TorchComms into torch.distributed: torch.distributed.reconfigure() for live process-group reconfiguration after rank failures (no job restart); window APIs for one-sided RDMA put/get (zero-copy, aimed at RL workloads); composable hooks for tracing, logging, and NaN detection on all collectives across all backends; backends shipped as pip-installable wheels via entry_points; and cleaned-up backend interfaces for vendors. (from abstract only)
  • How: Reconfiguration treats rank failure as a recoverable event rather than a job abort; window APIs expose peer memory directly; hooks make collective traffic observable in transit — the collective-layer analogue of flow telemetry.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — hardware-agnostic by design, with backend registration as the extension point. Zero claimed migration cost for existing users.

rdma ai-networks observability

items.title: Guardrails at the Infrastructure Layer: Sandboxing and governing Agentic AI in production
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Sai Charan Teja Gopaluni, Aaresh Sharma — AWS

  • Why: Agent governance is moving down from application-layer filters to infrastructure controls — K8s network policies, seccomp, runtime isolation — which is exactly the cloud-native security surface you work on. This is the zero-trust/microsegmentation conversation applied to agents.
  • What: A BoF on infrastructure-level governance of agentic AI: container sandboxing for agent tool execution (network policies, seccomp profiles, runtime isolation on Kubernetes); GPU-level resource boundaries so one agent's runaway inference can't starve safety-critical workloads; and observability as governance — audit trails, token-level logging, kill switches for agentic chains. (from abstract only)
  • How: Discussion format with a three-part agenda; no finished system or results — this is a community working session.
  • Where applicable: Kubernetes-centric and generalizable across environments; a good venue to contribute a networking/identity practitioner's lens to an emerging practice.

kubernetes network-security zero-trust

items.title: Introducing NCCL Extensions: Communication Patterns for Modern AI
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Sreeram Potluri, Artem Polyakov — NVIDIA

  • Why: NCCL is the dominant collective library on GPU fabrics; these domain extensions change what traffic patterns the library can express — MoE dispatch/combine and cross-mesh resharding — which is precisely the traffic your inference and RL-rollout fabrics will carry.
  • What: Two NCCL domain extensions built on NCCL's Device APIs. NCCL-EP brings MoE dispatch and combine natively into NCCL — one automatically tuned API spanning latency-optimized decode and throughput-optimized training, with GPU-initiated RDMA and NVLink out of the box. NCCL-M2N does zero-copy resharding between disjoint device meshes, moving weight snapshots from trainers to inference replicas with no CPU staging. Performance results promised in the talk. (from abstract only)
  • How: Specialized libraries inheriting NCCL's topology awareness and transport stack, but designed for customization, kernel fusion, and rapid prototyping of emerging patterns rather than classic collectives.
  • Where applicable: NVIDIA-centric (NCCL ecosystem), and a vendor talk by NVIDIA architects — but it defines the de-facto API surface that open alternatives (OpenCLIC, TorchComms backends) will be measured against.

rdma ai-networks gpu-clusters

items.title: MCCL: Fault-Tolerant Collective Communication for Large-Scale GPU Training
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Ben Carver — Meta

  • Why: Dynamic communicator membership — shrinking and growing as ranks fail or recover — is the collective layer learning what routing protocols learned decades ago about membership churn. Pairs directly with torch.distributed.reconfigure() and the TorchPass work.
  • What: MCCL, Meta's open-source fault-tolerant C++ collective library: hardware failure treated as a first-class design principle, with dynamic communicator reconfiguration that doesn't interrupt the training job. Production-grade AllReduce and Send/Recv via TorchComms integration, with claimed performance parity with NCCL. (from abstract only)
  • How: Redefines the communication lifecycle around failure and recovery instead of static membership and full-job restarts.
  • Where applicable: Aimed at tens-of-thousands-of-GPU fleets where failure is routine; open source, so broadly inspectable — but the parity claim is from the abstract, with numbers presumably in the talk.

ai-networks gpu-clusters sre

items.title: Monarch - Single-Machine DevX at Distributed Scale
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Thomas Wang, Zach DeVito — Meta

  • Why: An RDMA fabric used as a general-purpose actor IPC substrate to make a cluster feel like a laptop — a use of RDMA well beyond collectives, and a credible answer to the ergonomics gap that pushes developers away from clusters.
  • What: Monarch, a library for programming an entire cluster as if it were a single machine: imperative APIs launch processes across the cluster communicating via fast actor-based IPC, with data transfer over RDMA. Services built on the fabric include broadcasting the local filesystem to the whole cluster and surfacing remote logs locally; iteration takes seconds rather than minutes, and distributed processes exit like local ones. (from abstract only)
  • How: The RDMA-backed actor fabric supports local-feeling services; the talk demos the experience and how to build post-training frameworks on the primitives.
  • Where applicable: A Meta project aimed at post-training development loops (including for coding agents); assumes a cluster with RDMA and capacity for interactive use.

rdma ai-networks

items.title: Native Tiered KV Cache Offloading in vLLM: From Storage Offloading to Disaggregated Serving
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Or Ozeri — IBM

  • Why: Long-lived agentic sessions turn KV-cache preservation into a storage/I-O tiering problem with idle sessions holding state for hours or days — the memory-side complement to the KV-transfer talk, and a new consumer of fabric bandwidth.
  • What: vLLM's native tiered KV-cache offloading framework, newly integrated upstream with no external dependencies. The key design choice: all transfers route through CPU memory as a universal transport hub. (from abstract only)
  • How: Routing through host memory yields minimal GPU overhead (a simple copy), consolidated I/O from a single CPU buffer, hardware-agnostic operation with no specialized transfer APIs, and independence from KV cache memory layout (which varies across hardware, attention backends, parallelism schemes, and model architectures).
  • Where applicable: vLLM deployments generally — the design is deliberately layout- and hardware-agnostic; deployment and extension guidance promised.

ai-networks load-balancing

items.title: Precompile for Training
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Bob Ren; Aaron Orenstein (Meta)

  • Why: A genuinely surprising distributed-systems failure mode: in nominally identical SPMD programs, per-rank compilers and autotuners can diverge — choosing different kernels on different ranks, causing NCCL hangs, numerical inconsistencies, and hard-to-debug job failures. Anyone who has chased a "one rank hung" incident will recognize the shape of this problem.
  • What: Precompile for Training, an abstraction that compiles a distributed SPMD program once and reuses the resulting graph artifact across all ranks — guaranteeing identical execution and kernel selection cluster-wide, moving compilation ahead of GPU allocation, and eliminating redundant compile work across thousands of GPUs. (from abstract only)
  • How: All ranks share one compiled graph artifact; compilation is decoupled from GPU provisioning so idle-GPU-during-compile waste disappears.
  • Where applicable: Large SPMD training fleets, vendor-agnostic in principle; short talk with abstract-level detail — the rank-divergence problem statement is the durable takeaway.

ai-networks testing

items.title: rocSHMEM Symmetric Memory in PyTorch for AMD GPUs
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Prachi Gupta — AMD

  • Why: Ports of GPU-initiated one-sided RMA to a second vendor are evidence this is becoming a cross-vendor fabric primitive rather than an NVIDIA trick — worth tracking for multi-vendor estate planning.
  • What: rocSHMEM backend for PyTorch symmetric memory, now upstream: the device-side OpenSHMEM API (one-sided put/get, non-blocking get, put-with-signal, wait-until) exposed as Triton-callable primitives so a kernel initiates its own communication. MoE all-to-all dispatch and combine are constructed within the kernel and overlapped with expert compute; comparison against RCCL host-driven all-to-all on representative MoE workloads promised. (from abstract only)
  • How: AMD-specific engineering — per-architecture device-bitcode linking and post-compile HIP-module initialization — organized behind a backend-agnostic layer shared with NVSHMEM so a single Triton kernel runs on both AMD and NVIDIA.
  • Where applicable: AMD GPUs (ROCm); the transferable design is the backend-agnostic layering that keeps one kernel portable across vendors.

rdma gpu-clusters ai-networks

items.title: Scaling Foundation Models: From Broken to Near-Linear Multi-Node Training
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Sheng Huang — Pinterest

  • Why: A measured production case of "the network is the bottleneck" — GPUs busy waiting on cross-node traffic — with a diagnosis-first playbook that any operator of multi-node training can copy. The numbers are unusually honest (they show the broken starting point).
  • What: Pinterest's TorchRec foundation-model training went from 5x slower at 2 nodes and 1.21x scaling at 4 nodes to 3.9x at 4 nodes (97.5% of ideal) and 7.5x at 8 nodes (93.75%) — by attacking cross-node All-to-All from distributed embedding lookups, identified via PyTorch Profiler and NCCL traces. (from abstract only)
  • How: Reduce bytes on the wire (FP8 communication with FBGEMM), balanced TorchRec embedding sharding and reshaping, Distributed Checkpoint for load-time resharding, and a 2D parallel topology that keeps expensive All-to-All local and syncs replicas with AllReduce — i.e., topology designed around the slowest link.
  • Where applicable: Pinterest production on AWS (EFA networking) — org- and cloud-specific in its specifics, but the playbook (measure, cut wire bytes, checkpoint portably, design around the slowest link) is broadly transferable.

ai-networks rdma benchmarking

items.title: Self-Healing PyTorch Training Through Live GPU Migration
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Pavneet Ahluwalia, Gavin Cohen — Microsoft Azure (product) and Clockwork Systems

  • Why: Link flaps and node failures are the physical-fabric failure modes you live with; this talk is about the job layer's counter-move — live migration instead of checkpoint-restart. The structural diagnosis (every step ends in a collective needing all ranks; a communicator can't be rebuilt around a missing peer) is the clearest statement of why training jobs are so brittle to fabric events.
  • What: TorchPass, a training-failover system presented jointly by Together AI and Clockwork Systems: on link degradation it reroutes traffic; on GPU/memory/component failure it live-migrates the affected rank's device and communicator state to a spare and resumes from the same step. Their claim: a single checkpoint-restart failure burns 45–90 minutes of wall-clock across every GPU in the job. Live demo with injected link flaps and GPU failures; a decision framework for when live migration beats checkpoint-restart, plus a TCO framing for recovered goodput. (from abstract only)
  • How: End-to-end system — monitoring, health checks, failover, rank-state migration — keeping a multi-node job in continuous forward progress.
  • Where applicable: Vendor joint presentation with a product and TCO calculator attached; the companion demo talk reports a published TorchPass benchmark at Llama 4 Scout scale on 64 H200 GPUs, independently validated by SemiAnalysis. The mechanism assumes spare capacity and their product; the accountability/verification framing (does a failure resume from the same step, does throughput ever hit zero, can the claim be verified?) transfers to any fabric.

ai-networks sre troubleshooting

items.title: State-of-the-Art KV Transfer for Disaggregated LLM Serving in vLLM
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Core pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Nicolò Lucchesi (Mistral AI, vLLM maintainer), Sunita Nadampalli (Amazon), Zhanqiu Hu (Red Hat)

  • Why: P/D disaggregation turns KV-cache transfer into a first-class network workload — bidirectional, latency-sensitive, stateful — that inference fabrics must now be designed for. This is the talk defining that transfer layer's requirements.
  • What: Developments in vLLM's disaggregated serving stack: hybrid-model transfer with heterogeneous TP (Nemotron, Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-V4 with interleaved attention, KV compression, sliding windows), bidirectional KV transfer for agentic multi-turn sessions, a KV Push connector that reduces TTFT, and KV cache leases for reliability under failures and traffic spikes. On Nemotron, disaggregated P/D Pareto-dominates co-located serving across concurrency levels. (from abstract only)
  • How: A flexible transfer interface generalizing across diverse cache layouts/sharding semantics and heterogeneous hardware (NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium), composing with prefix caching and CPU offloading.
  • Where applicable: vLLM-specific implementation but explicitly hardware-agnostic; the cross-vendor maintainer group suggests this becomes the reference interface. The hard constraint is cache-layout diversity across hybrid model architectures.

ai-networks load-balancing gpu-clusters

items.title: Who Owns Production When the Agent Does the Fixing? Governance in AI-Assisted SRE
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Aditi Mewada — Apple

  • Why: Not a networking topic, but a direct signal of where operations are heading: agents shipping fixes autonomously into production — the same production your change-management, automation guardrails, and identity controls govern. The accountability question ("an agent misconfigures a service at 3am — who is answerable?") will land on security and identity teams first.
