  • What: Governance frameworks, guardrails, and human-in-the-loop patterns for AI-assisted SRE: where autonomy genuinely delivers (faster MTTR, less toil, smarter alerting), where unchecked agent authority creates new failure classes, and a practical mental model for what agents should fix vs. flag vs. never touch. (from abstract only)
  • How: A patterns-and-mental-model talk rather than a system; no empirical evaluation claimed.
  • Where applicable: Any operations organization adopting autonomous remediation; conceptual, so weigh it as a framing device rather than validated practice.

sre automation

items.title: XCCL: Scaling PyTorch Collectives to Exascale on Intel GPUs with TorchComms
items.text:
PyTorch Conference 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 20–21 October 2026

Abstract

Panagiotis Kourdis, Tanima Dey — Intel

  • Why: A rare, detailed account of building and validating a new accelerator's collective backend at exascale — including the CI and testing strategy — useful as the reference playbook for any multi-vendor comm-stack work.
  • What: XCCL, an in-tree Intel-GPU backend for TorchComms built on oneCCL, validated on Aurora (Argonne's exascale supercomputer): over 90% scaling efficiency across thousands of nodes running TorchTitan and other AI workloads. Covers bridging PyTorch collective semantics to oneCCL, a stream-ordered asynchronous execution model that overlaps compute and communication, CI combining mock-based validation with real Intel hardware, and comparisons against NCCL and RCCL. (from abstract only)
  • How: Backend integration plus semantic bridging between PyTorch's collective API and oneCCL's execution model.
  • Where applicable: Intel GPUs on Aurora — a specific supercomputer deployment; the transferable content is the backend-building and validation methodology, not the silicon.

ai-networks gpu-clusters testing

items.title: A Farewell to ARPs - IPv6 resolved gateways
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (Keynote) Recording

Remco van Mook

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: IPv6-only fabrics with native IPv4 reachability is a live design problem for DC/WAN interconnect. This proposes a clean mechanism to give IPv4-capable hosts on an IPv6-only network a working IPv4 default gateway without ARP, tunnels, or translation — complementary to RFC 8950 (IPv4 NLRI with IPv6 next-hop).
  • What: A draft I-D requesting 192.0.0.11/32 from the IANA IPv4 special-purpose registry. The address is a signal: hosts configured with it as their IPv4 default gateway resolve the gateway's link-layer address from the IPv6 default gateway learned via RA/ND — reusing the IPv6 neighbor cache instead of running ARP. IPv4 packets remain native and unaltered; no IPv4 subnets, no tunneling, no NAT.
  • How: The host treats the gateway IP as a pure identifier for "use the IPv6 gateway's L2"; working code exists in Linux user space (kernel 5.2+) using rtnetlink to track the IPv6 gateway. A transitional deployment — DHCP-assigned /32 address plus a host route for 192.0.0.11 with the address answered on router interfaces — is essentially what some hosting providers (Hetzner-style) already do.
  • Where applicable: General technique for IPv6-only datacenters and hosts; cleanly it needs OS network-stack support (currently user-space/known-config), but the transitional method is deployable today. Aligns with ongoing IETF v4-via-v6 work; the presenter was soliciting review of the draft and code.

ipv6 data-center-fabric standardization

items.title: An empirical evaluation of longitudinal anycast catchment stability
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Adjacent pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Remi Hendriks, University of Twente (with Bernhard Degen, Bas Palinckx, Raffaele Sommese, Roland van Rijswijk-Deij)

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Anyone running an anycast service (DNS, CDN edges, global ingress) needs to know how often to remap catchments — too rarely and traffic engineering is stale, too often and you burn effort. This replaces guesswork with six months of daily measurements.
  • What: Daily Verfploeter catchment mappings on an industry-grade 32-PoP anycast testbed (20 countries, 6 continents) across IPv4 and IPv6 for six months (~3.5M responsive /24s, ~0.5M IPv6 /48s probed). Result: catchments are very stable short-term — 95% of prefixes route to the same PoP at one-week granularity, >99% day-to-day — and an IPv4 mapping stays valid roughly two months at a 10% error rate. But sudden routing events can shift catchments dramatically: in July, the Tokyo PoP lost most of its traffic to a Sydney PoP that expanded five-fold; north-eastern China switched to Frankfurt; Vietnamese addresses moved to Seoul.
  • How: Active probing with one target per smallest propagated BGP prefix, using the USC/ISI and TUM IPv6 hitlists; stability measured across timescales from days to months.
  • Where applicable: The recommendations (how frequently to run catchment analysis) apply to anycast operators generally, but absolute stability numbers come from a Vultr-hosted testbed — your mileage will vary with topology, peering, and remote-peering prevalence. The event-driven instability finding (plan for sudden shifts, not gradual drift) is the transferable lesson.

load-balancing measurement

items.title: Are NTP Clients Always Right?
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Adjacent pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Shreyas Konjerla, TU Delft

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Time infrastructure trust underpins everything else — TLS, Kerberos, log forensics — but client-side NTP hardening is rarely examined. This stress-tests the default time clients of major operating systems and finds the weakest of them are trivially manipulable.
  • What: Eight (S)NTP clients across three OSes were baselined for 60 hours and then attacked. All SNTP clients — the defaults of major OSes — are vulnerable to time-shift attacks (macOS accepted injected offsets from 900 s up to two years); none of the full NTP clients were. Five bugs and one vulnerability were disclosed, including: NTPD-RS flooded with queries under certain Kiss-of-Death packets, OpenNTPd unable to handle the NTP timestamp rollover, and TimesyncD using a single server (a single point of failure). Also forecast: Ubuntu's planned default move to NTS/chrony will multiply query volume ~11x and traffic ~25x per host.
  • How: Controlled testbed of three local NTP servers with a threat model of malicious-server redirection (via NTP pool or DNS hijack); clients measured for query behavior, server rotation, and spec compliance.
  • Where applicable: Directly actionable for fleet configuration choices (which client, how many servers, panic thresholds); thesis-scale work but with real vendor disclosures. The Ubuntu/NTS traffic forecast matters to anyone operating NTP infrastructure at enterprise or ISP scale.

time-sync measurement

items.title: Assessing the feasibility of routing security compliance tests
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Moritz Müller, Lisa Bruder — SIDN Labs, University of Twente

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Routing-security hygiene (MANRS and its elevated "MANRS+" tier) has been self-attested; this work asks whether it can be measured — and builds an open-source, containerlab-based harness to do it. Two interests in one: routing security plus a transferable use of Containerlab as an automated audit testbed.
  • What: A prototype that audits an AS's routing-security controls (route origin validation, customer prefix filtering, bogon filtering) by standing up the audited AS between two local ASes in a containerlab topology: one exports prefixes to it, the other imports what it re-advertises. Analyzing the imported prefixes reveals the filters actually configured. In the testbed it reliably audits correct filter implementation — for example, by mutating a route object to disallow a prefix and observing whether the audited AS stops exporting it.
  • How: Fully containerized local testbed (code open source on GitHub as SIDN/manrs-prototype); import filters compiled with bgpq4 against IRR; test prefixes withdrawn immediately to avoid unintended propagation.
  • Where applicable: The prototype works locally; auditing production ASes is future work with identified pitfalls (RPKI/IRR propagation delays, multi-control-plane ASes, risk of test announcements leaking). The community was being asked for feedback on what a production deployment (led by GCA) should handle. The containerlab-as-auditor pattern is adoptable by anyone wanting to verify routing hygiene of partners or their own network.

bgp network-security testing

items.title: Collecting and analyzing routing information with Rotonda
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Luuk Hendriks, Jasper den Hertog — NLnet Labs

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Route monitoring at scale is hard: vendor platforms give limited insight, especially into RPKI's effect on routes. Rotonda is adoptable, open-source tooling that lets an operator ask their own questions of their BGP/BMP data — the kind of tooling the triage guidance says to up-rank.
  • What: A single self-contained Rust binary that ingests routing data via BMP (pre/post-policy Adj-RIB-in/out and Loc-RIB), live BGP, and MRT files, combines it with RPKI data via RTR, and exposes HTTP API, MQTT, and file outputs. Its distinguishing feature is Roto, a strongly-typed scripting language for filtering routes and monitoring events — compiled to native machine code (via Cranelift, to x86_64 or ARM64), so customization costs negligible overhead even in the hottest ingestion paths.
  • How: Operators write small typed filters (reject iBGP, drop specific peers, log prefixes matching prefix lists) that run inside the collection pipeline rather than as post-processing. Designed to scale from 50 routes to 50 million with the same single binary.
  • Where applicable: General-purpose and self-hostable by networks of any size — explicitly built for small operators who find heavyweight monitoring disproportionate. Still young; the presenters were actively soliciting feedback and use cases.

bgp open-source telemetry

items.title: Cyberattack Observation Using IoT Honeypots at Yokohama National University
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Wildcard pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Takayuki Sasaki (with Katsunari Yoshioka), Yokohama National University

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Not IoT per se — the signal is the operational pattern: a hybrid rule-engine-plus-LLM triage pipeline that turns a honeypot into a near-real-time exploit classifier. That AI-assisted-triage design is where security operations tooling is heading, demonstrated on real long-running data with a public dataset release.
  • What: X-POT, an adaptive HTTP honeypot that emulates a wide range of IoT devices using real WebUI HTML collected by scanning IP ranges around observed attackers — so the honeypot presents genuinely realistic device interfaces. The analysis pipeline: identify attacks (payloads fetching malware via wget/curl), tag against rules, classify novel exploits by request-path/parameter patterns, alert the operator immediately on new exploits, and auto-generate analysis reports with GPT-5 plus web search — sent to Slack, manually verified, then turned into new tagging rules. Long-term operation captured entire exploit lifecycles from emergence to decline, including zero-days and campaigns against industrial targets like solar power monitors.
  • How: Two components — attack observation (emulation + malware collection) and HTTP response collection (scanning attacker neighborhoods to harvest device WebUIs); the LLM proposes, the human verifies before rules ship.
  • Where applicable: University research deployment, but the rule+LLM hybrid with human-in-the-loop verification is a pattern any SOC or honeypot operator can adopt today; the public dataset makes the data reusable for collaborative research.

ml-for-networking anomaly-detection

items.title: Exploring the Blind Spot of IXP Route Server
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Stefano Servillo, Sapienza University of Rome

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Most peering-edge routing security attention goes to RPKI, but IRR-based route-server filtering — still the primary mechanism at most IXPs — has a structural hole that enables prefix hijacking. If you peer via route servers, this is a direct exposure assessment.
  • What: The blind spot: IRR validation expands a member's AS-SET into a prefix list but never binds a prefix to its real owner. So an attacker whose route object for a prefix lists an AS that appears in some member's AS-SET gets their (hijacked or misconfigured) announcement accepted by the route server. The authors found most analyzed IXPs in the EURO-IX community affected, and validated the practical impact against real route-server RIBs of two major European IXPs. Feasibility is real: roughly a third of prefixes are RPKI NotFound (no ROA coverage), leaving IRR as the only filter — and AS-SETs are badly maintained (they accumulate inactive ASes against ~77k active of ~130k allocated, plus duplication in non-authoritative IRRs).
  • How: Walks through how IXPs compile IRR data (bgpq4 expansion into prefix lists linked to peer sessions), derives the attack preconditions (no covering ROA, prefix in a route object for an AS that's in a member's AS-SET), and proposes fixes for both IXP operators (filtering changes) and members (ROA coverage, AS-SET hygiene).
  • Where applicable: Applies to any IXP using IRR-based RS filtering and any member relying on RS filtering instead of bilateral sessions. The validation data is from two large European IXPs, but the mechanism is protocol-level and general.

peering bgp network-security

items.title: Free and open-source network labs with Containerlab: an intro, an update, a workshop
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Adjacent pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Gordon Gidofalvy, Nokia

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Lab-as-code is the closest thing network engineering has to CI for topology and config change — useful for prototyping fabrics, regression-testing config, and reproducing vendor claims before they touch production. This is the tool's 5-year status review plus a hands-on workshop.
  • What: Containerlab at ~300K installations, 140+ contributors, 35+ supported network OSes (13 added in the last 12 months). Node types span containerized NOSes (SR Linux, SR OS, cEOS, XRd, cRPD, and more), VM-based NOSes wrapped in containers via vrnetlab (Juniper vMX/vJunosRouter, Arista vEOS, Cisco XRv9k/NX-OS, Fortinet, Palo Alto, OcNOS), and arbitrary regular containers — FRR, traffic generators, telemetry stacks, IPAM/DCIM, flow collectors. Declarative YAML topologies make labs versionable, shareable artifacts.
  • How: Docker-based; a topology file defines nodes and links; the workshop walks from a first FRR lab through expanding topologies to collaboratively building a working "Internet". Requires a Linux host on kernel 5.4+ (physical or VM).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable anywhere Docker runs; the intro half is 101 material, but the ecosystem update (including non-labbing use cases like the SIDN routing-security audit prototype) is where the value is for someone already past the basics.

testing open-source automation

items.title: Getting 1+ Tbps from an x86 server
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Branimir Rajtar, 5x9 Networks

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A concrete, quantified datapath-tuning story: a virtualized BNG went from 160 Gbps to 1.2 Tbps on a single commodity x86 server with no specialized hardware. The optimization methodology (profiling-driven, cache-focused) transfers to any high-packet-rate software datapath — exactly the kind of datapath-internals work that is core here.
  • What: A CUPS (control/user-plane separation) vBNG — dashboard, controller, and DPDK-based forwarder — was pushed through successive optimization waves: ~30% from newer hardware plus application tuning, ~30% from deep DPDK/CPU/PCIe/BIOS/NIC configuration, and ~20% from Intel vTune-guided code rewrites. The final revelation: the dominant residual cost was CPU cache misses — data structures not fitting 64-byte cache lines, plus 4K memory pages, causing constant main-memory round trips. A major cache-alignment rewrite and a shift from many small 4-vCPU VMs to one large instance closed the gap to 1.2 Tbps.
  • How: SR-IOV and Intel DPDK bypass the kernel entirely (with the known tradeoff of CPU running at 100% in poll mode); vTune identifies hot spots; code is restructured to separate read/write data sections, reorder instructions for multiple execution units, use full cache lines, and force compiler optimizations. Each change was performance-tested in isolation.
  • Where applicable: Results are specific to their PPPoE/IPoE BNG workload on Intel Xeon Gold with DPDK-supported NICs — treat the numbers as one datapoint, not a guarantee. The method (profile, fix cache behavior, consolidate instances) is generally applicable to anyone writing or buying software datapaths.

linux-networking benchmarking

items.title: gNMI and you: The death of SNMP was greatly exagerated
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Tom Strickx, Cloudflare

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Network observability is a core ops responsibility, and gNMI/OpenConfig is the leading SNMP replacement — but real production experience, including failures, is rarely shared. Cloudflare's honest accounting of what works and what still hurts is exactly the decision-support material needed before betting a monitoring stack on it.
  • What: An introduction and comparison: gNMI (gRPC-based, OpenConfig YANG models, ProtoBuf, TLS required by default, pub/sub) versus SNMP (OID sprawl, ASN.1, plaintext by default, pull-plus-traps). Then the unvarnished problems: uneven vendor adoption ("your fridge probably ships with SNMP"), vendor inconsistency, and thin documentation. Production pain points include distributed counting (correctly counting events across a fleet is genuinely hard) and per-linecard counters on Juniper requiring monotonicity handling (Prometheus-style counter-reset adjustment).
  • How: Cloudflare runs gNMIc (Nokia-developed, now OpenConfig-owned, actively maintained) with internal processors and an aggregation layer; the talk surveys the wider toolchain (gNMI-gateway, ExaRing's exporter, Telegraf with gNMI plugins) and notes which are unmaintained-but-working.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable — the gNMI/SNMP comparison and tooling recommendations are vendor-neutral. The scale and some quirks are Cloudflare/Juniper-specific; vendor consistency caveats should be validated against your own fleet before migration.

telemetry observability

items.title: Internet Resiliency Club update
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Wildcard pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Valerie Aurora, Bow Shock Systems Consulting

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Not a fit for any of the core areas — and exactly why it's a wildcard: a grassroots operator collective building a LoRa/Meshtastic mesh for text communication during power and Internet outages. It's a failure-mode frame (total infrastructure loss) that DC/WAN people rarely practice, assembled by exactly the kind of people who could pull it off.
  • What: The Amsterdam Internet Resiliency Club (started January 2025) now has ~20 members, monthly in-person meetups, a working private Meshtastic channel, a partnership with Waag Futurelab, €10K received in grants (of €50K applied for), and contact with the city of Amsterdam and the Dutch defense ministry. Key operational lesson: Meshtastic worked great at the WHY hacker camp (high node density) but is unreliable across Amsterdam — the constraint is node density, and the fix is more nodes, i.e., money for hardware.
  • How: Low-power LoRa radios running Meshtastic in a decentralized mesh; the human layer is Doodle-scheduled meetups, a mailing list, and personal invitations. Hardware recommendations given (solar-powered WisMesh Repeater Mini enclosures, card-shaped trackers, T-Beam home stations; avoid the T-Deck keyboard).
  • Where applicable: Explicitly replicable — the recipe quoted is 1–2 hours/week, ~€200 of floatable cash, and a large personal network. Amsterdam-density findings will differ by city; the model is aimed at the gap before government disaster-recovery programs arrive (~2028 by their estimate).

iot open-source

items.title: Network Measurement in the Dark
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Wildcard pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Geoff Huston, APNIC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The premise underneath every observability investment — that the network can see what traverses it — is being dismantled by protocol design. This is the big-picture frame for why measurement and monitoring assumptions need rethinking, delivered by the person who has been documenting that shift for a decade.
  • What: A synthesis of ~15 years of change: operators were once the trusted observers of who-talks-to-whom; that trust eroded through ad-tech profiling and state surveillance (the Snowden papers as watershed), and the IETF responded with RFC 7258 declaring pervasive monitoring an attack. The consequences, with adoption data: HTTPS became near-universal; DNS queries moved behind DoH/DoT/DoQ; and the next step — MASQUE with two-layer encryption and relays — hides the endpoints entirely, so no single network observation point ever sees both ends of a transaction plus the content. The implicit question: what is left for network measurement, and what should operators do about it?
  • How: Narrative argument anchored in public adoption statistics (Cloudflare radar for HTTPS, APNIC's encrypted-DNS measurements).
  • Where applicable: Universal — it's a framing talk, not a solution talk. Directly relevant to anyone planning traffic measurement, network forensics, capacity planning, or policy enforcement that presumes visibility into flows.

measurement encryption

items.title: PON in the Datacenter: Hyperscale for Management and Console
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PDF) Recording

Mike Joseph, Meta

VideoPDF 1PDF 2

Watch the recording

  • Why: A genuinely novel direction in physical datacenter networking: Meta is running Passive Optical Networking — residential access technology — as the management, console, and out-of-band fabric in production hyperscale DCs. For anyone whose job includes DC cabling plant and topology, this is a production data point on killing copper at scale.
  • What: Meta's Infrastructure Network Engineering team replaced per-row fixed Ethernet switches and terminal servers with a PON-based handoff: each rack gets up to 20 Ethernet + 20 console connections (or 32 + 8 tradeoff), configurable per rack without row-level coordination. Two centralized OLT routers serve 12 rows; a row can carry up to 1,280 Ethernet and 800 console connections. Copper cable trays and copper distribution are eliminated entirely from the data halls.
  • How: Passive splitters plus per-rack ONUs and purpose-built console cards; OLT configuration is generated from Meta's network modeling service and asset databases. ONUs are barcode-scanned as racks are deployed, updating asset management in real time; because ONUs are stateless, hardware replacement is just scanning a new one. OMCI-based management gives uniform control over multi-vendor ONUs and console devices.
  • Where applicable: The scale and automation stack are Meta-specific, and the technique targets low-speed (≤1GE + RS-232) connectivity, not production fabric. But the concept — PON as a cheap, flexible, copper-free fan-out for management/OOB — is broadly adoptable by any DC operator; it requires buying into the PON ecosystem and OMCI tooling rather than any Meta-internal dependency.

optics data-center-fabric cabling

items.title: PQC for the RPKI
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Dirk Doesburg, Radboud University / SIDN Labs

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The RPKI is RSA-only, and a quantum-capable attacker is worse than no RPKI at all: forged ROAs can make legitimate announcements ROV-Invalid while malicious ones validate. Migration will take years, so the groundwork — which signatures, how to migrate — matters now. This is routing security with a long planning horizon.
  • What: An MSc thesis laying out the full migration path. (1) Attack analysis: forged ROAs/revocations (including entire CAs), AS0-roa DoS, and ASPA forgery. (2) Signature evaluation across post-quantum schemes: Falcon-512 wins (NIST level 1, 897 B public key, 666 B signature; RPKI grows from 838 MB to ~1.4 GB, download from ~14.5 s to ~24 s, versus catastrophes like SLH-DSA at ~14 GB). (3) The "null scheme": replaces the one-time EE key and signature in each signed object with a SHA256 digest, cutting the median hybrid (Falcon-512 + RSA-2048) ROA from 4,354 to 2,295 bytes and ~35% of verification CPU — largely paying for the PQC switch; documented as an Internet-Draft with working prototypes in Krill and Routinator. (4) A mixed-tree migration procedure simpler than RFC 6916: no globally coordinated milestone days, no top-down switch, ordinary RFC 6489-style key rollovers per CA, with relying-party software and trust anchors updated first.
  • How: Measured real costs (RPKI download ~14.5 s, ~13 CPU-seconds of verification as baseline) across candidate algorithms; hybrid signatures recommended for safety during transition.
  • Where applicable: RPKI-wide — every RIR, CA, and relying party, not org-specific. Prototypes exist for two of the main open-source tools; actual migration requires SIDRops standards work and multi-year lead time, which is precisely the argument for engaging now.

quantum-safe pki bgp

items.title: Querying the DFZ
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Ties de Kock, RIPE NCC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: MRT parsing has always been the barrier to doing your own BGP analysis — most teams default to whatever prebuilt tools offer. RIPE RIS publishing its data as indexed Parquet makes DFZ-scale analysis a SQL problem, which changes what a network team can realistically do for itself.
  • What: RIPE RIS BGP RIBs and updates are now published as Parquet files: a daily RIB of ~350M rows (~2.4 GB) and hourly update files (~50M rows, 350–400 MB), with columns for timestamp, prefix, origin AS, peer, AS path, and communities. Query with DuckDB, SQL, or dataframe tools instead of MRT parsers; analyses that previously took 10+ minutes run in seconds. RIPE NCC has already used it operationally — assessing BGP impact of the Baltic Sea cable damage and the Iberian power outage in minutes instead of hours.
  • How: Parquet plus DuckDB replaces both custom MRT parsing scripts and expensive database indexing; the schema is designed to be ergonomic for queries and correct for analysis (AS sets are supported rather than flattened away).
  • Where applicable: Free and broadly usable by any operator or researcher. Caveat: the short-term archive covers 14 days of RIBs/updates (an 18-month experiment with a go/no-go decision), so deep historical work still goes through MRT files.

bgp measurement

items.title: Rewriting BGP Origin
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Core pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

James Bensley, Inter.link

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A rare public airing of a quiet interdomain game: carriers rewrite the BGP ORIGIN attribute to IGP because IGP beats INCOMPLETE in best-path selection, thereby attracting traffic. Anyone buying or selling transit — or wondering why traffic prefers a peer's path — needs to know this is happening.
  • What: Based on looking-glass captures of all Tier-1s, 6 of 16 were rewriting ORIGIN to IGP at the time of the talk (AS1299, 2914, 3356, 3491, 6453, 6939; note the speaker's post-talk correction that AS3320 was incorrectly listed and does not do this). The DFZ is already >90% IGP-origin. Inter.link (AS5405) resisted, but lost customers over the resulting traffic asymmetry and will now rewrite to IGP on all eBGP advertisements — with a per-customer opt-out — arguing that universal adoption implicitly deprecates the attribute. Bonus intel: some T1s use addresses in 2/8 as BGP router IDs to win router-ID tie-breaks.
  • How: Exploits the ORIGIN tie-break in best-path selection; RFC 4271 says ORIGIN "SHOULD NOT" be changed, and rewriting carriers lean on RFC 2119's wiggle room to justify "normalization".
  • Where applicable: Relevant to any network announcing prefixes or selecting transit providers. The who-does-it list is a point-in-time snapshot (October 2025) and the game is zero-sum — expect more networks to follow once competitors start.

bgp measurement

items.title: The BGP Clock and the BGP Observatory: Hunting Stuck Routes
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Adjacent pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Antonis Chariton, Cisco

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Stuck BGP routes (withdrawals lost to router bugs) silently keep traffic flowing toward dead paths — and after a route goes stale, nobody notices. This provides both a permanent public measurement beacon and a free detection tool anyone can point at their own network.
  • What: Follow-up to the RIPE 89 study (which found prefixes still stuck in RIBs months after withdrawal, despite being RPKI Invalid). The BGP Clock announces time-encoded prefixes on a fixed schedule: IPv6 2a0d:3dc1:NNNN::/48 indexed by 10-minute period since New Year (recycled yearly), and IPv4 147.189.(216+N).0/24 by hour-of-day modulo 8, announced at XX:00 and withdrawn at XX:10. The BGP Observatory is a free, no-login service that detects and surfaces stuck routes, searchable by AS. RFC 9687 attempts to reduce the impact but needs vendor support.
  • How: Beacon prefixes are originated from a dedicated AS (AS4601, moving to AS210312); operators can sanity-check their own RIBs directly (show route for the beacon prefixes) or use the Observatory's automated analysis.
  • Where applicable: Any operator or researcher; the phenomenon's prevalence depends on the vendor/bug mix in the forwarding path, so absolute numbers will shift over time — the value is the standing instrument, not a single result.

bgp measurement troubleshooting

items.title: What happens when you overshare? A Look into the BGP Maximum-Prefix Feature
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Adjacent pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Orlando Eduardo Martínez-Durive — NetAI & IMDEA Networks (work done as a research intern at Cisco ThousandEyes); Antonis Chariton — Cisco

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Everyone configures max-prefix limits, almost nobody knows what actually happens when they're exceeded. This quantifies it over 6.5 months, which turns a superstition into data for setting limits.
  • What: Using RIPE RIS RIBs (Jan 1 – mid-July 2025) plus historical PeeringDB data: of 88,223 identified ASes, only 16,351 (18.5%) had PeeringDB entries updated within two years and were analyzable. Findings: only a relatively small number of ASes exceed their advertised limit; on average only a small fraction of peers drop the session when it happens — but there are extreme cases where a network loses >80% of its peers, with obvious connectivity impact. Notably, the authors could not confirm that observed drops were actually caused by the limit being exceeded.
  • How: Correlating announced prefix counts against PeeringDB-listed maximum-prefix values over time, plus tracking peer-count changes after exceedance.
  • Where applicable: General BGP session-management practice. Big caveat: PeeringDB-listed limits are a proxy for actual peer-side configuration, and the analyzable population is skewed toward networks that maintain their PeeringDB entries. Practical takeaway offered: set peer limits "just slightly higher" than expected, and the open question of per-session limit signaling (à la OPEN extension) is worth community thought.

bgp measurement troubleshooting

items.title: What's new at the IETF?
items.text:
RIPE 91 (Bucharest) digest Program Adjacent pick Bucharest · 20–24 October 2025

Abstract Slides Recording

Suresh Krishnan, Cisco (IAB)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A standards radar sweep — and for this reader, the standout is one line item rather than the survey itself: Web Bot Auth, a group in chartering around cryptographic identity for bots/agents as UA- and IP-based signals fail. That is an early standards-body signal on agentic identity, the only one in this entire program.
  • What: Operator-relevant IETF developments: newly started AI work — aipref (expressing preferences about AI collection/use of content) and Web Bot Auth (likely a WG before the November IETF); AI agents and networking research-group proposals, agent-to-agent lists, AI agent discovery via DNS; DNS work — DELEG (authoritative servers signaling capabilities via SVCB-like records), Domain Connect (DCONN), DNSOP rechartered around split operations and DNSSEC crypto refresh; the green WG on energy-efficiency metrics; and space networking topics.
  • How: Structured as an area/working-group survey (Routing, Internet, Transport, Ops, Security) with a filter for operator impact.
  • Where applicable: General context for anyone tracking standards adoption; the Web Bot Auth item is pre-charter/early-charter and worth watching rather than acting on yet.

standardization identity bgp

items.title: BitSquatting... ...or the infinite monkeys theorem...
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Wildcard pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Warren Kumari, Google LLC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A weird, memorable, and real attack class: hardware bit-flips during DNS resolution silently redirect traffic to attacker domains one binary bit away — with live capture data showing what actually leaks.
  • What: An update on 2011-era bitsquatting research: register domains one bit-flip away from popular names (microsont.com, googneapis.com, cxase.com...) and collect the traffic that hardware errors (cosmic rays, contaminated ceramics — the talk traces this back to 1970s DRAM and cites Qantas Flight 72) accidentally send you.
  • How: A ~1-month capture across registered variants gathered ~54,000 requests, including expanded hostnames (msdn.microsont.com), SNI of legitimate domains, cookies, OAuth-style login URLs, executables, and JavaScript — each request proving a memory error happened somewhere and leaking what the affected host was doing.
  • Where applicable: Mostly relevant as threat-model awareness for security teams and a reminder that DNS is a hardware-reliability observation channel; the "register typos-at-the-bit-level" strategy is trivially cheap for attackers and nearly impossible to fully defend.

dns vulnerability-management

items.title: Channelmania! – future proof your DWDM network topology while keeping it flexible for 1.6T
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Thomas Weible, FLEXOPTIX

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: As IPoDWDM collapses the IP/transport split, IP network people now need coherent-DWDM literacy — grid planning, superchannels, and what 400GHz COTS filters mean for upgrade paths to 1.6T.
  • What: A technical primer-plus-argument: higher-order coherent modulation (16-constellation, dual-polarization, ~425Gbps at 53.125GBd) replaces OOK; 800G/1.6T superchannels need ~400GHz grids rather than shrinking 50/25GHz grids; and coherent detection being "blind" to other wavelengths enables filterless/colorless topologies at the cost of flexibility. The practical pitch: 12×400GHz COTS channels in the C-band future-proof the plant while staying backward-compatible with legacy 50GHz services.
  • How: Walks through coherent receiver architecture (phase- and polarization-diversity, homodyne/heterodyne/intradyne), and even a DIY superchannel approach using cheap PLC 1x4 splitters to combine TX/split RX and run subbands through regular 50GHz muxes (with a nod to Blake Willis finding 100GHz spacing optimal in practice). Closing advice: plan in THz/GHz, not nm or channel numbers; 800G coherent ZR+ in DD/OSFP is here, and ~12.8T liquid-cooled XPO is approaching.
  • Where applicable: Anyone planning or buying DWDM capacity. Vendor-authored (FLEXOPTIX sells optics tooling), so the COTS-400GHz-filter framing is partly self-serving, but the physics and frequency-planning methodology are sound and generally applicable.

optics capacity-planning

items.title: Detecting and Characterizing DDoS Scrubbing from Global BGP Routing: Insights from Five Leading Scrubbers
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Shyam Krishna Khadka, University of Twente

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Helps solve a practical monitoring problem: BGP path changes caused by DDoS scrubbing look like hijacks or leaks in your alerting, and 48% of scrubber-originated prefixes aren't properly covered by ROAs.
  • What: A PAM 2026 paper detecting scrubbing activations/deactivations purely from public RIS BGP data (30 days, five scrubbers: Cloudflare, Akamai Prolexic, Vercara, Imperva, Radware). Always-on protection dominates (11k prefixes vs 5.6k on-demand); on-demand scrubbing splits into upstream-change (dominant) and origin-change modes.
  • How: Inference requires at least two route-collector peers observing the AS-path change; characterization covers protection modes, session durations (median ~10h45m; 25% under 1h45m), and RPKI/IRR practice — finding 12.5% Invalid and 35.5% NotFound among temporarily-originated prefixes.
  • Where applicable: BGP monitoring/anomaly-detection toolbuilders, and scrubbing customers who should fix their ROA coverage before an attack makes their scrubber originate their prefixes.

ddos bgp measurement

items.title: DNS, Transitive Trust and How Many is Many
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ondřej Surý, ISC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A genuinely surprising measurement: resolving teams.microsoft.com on a cold cache triggers 247 outgoing queries from a single recursive resolver — with real implications for latency, load, and the transitive trust surface CDNs are building.
  • What: A cold-cache tour through delegation types: in-domain delegations are cheap (glue mandatory, no extra cost), in-bailiwick adds 0–N×2 queries, and out-of-bailiwick delegations force the resolver to resolve each NS name from scratch — 3 + 3×N queries per name. CNAME chains make this multiplicative, not additive: each target zone may be out-of-bailiwick and each NS-set spans TLDs.
  • How: All numbers from BIND 9, adding one complexity source at a time; notably, resolver software matters enormously — the same name cost 168 queries on BIND 9.11 but only 16 on 9.21. DNSSEC and the often-forgotten PTR case add more.
  • Where applicable: Resolver operators, CDN/zone architects thinking about delegation hygiene, and anyone debugging cold-cache latency spikes.

dns measurement

items.title: Evolution of Meta's Edge and Backbone Networks
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Fredrik Korsbäck, Meta Platforms, Inc

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The most direct window at this conference into hyperscaler physical backbone and DC fabric design — scaling strategy, ZR optics economics, and how AI traffic is reshaping both DC metro fabric and edge compute placement.
  • What: How Meta grew the backbone >10X via two levers: scaling up (8-slot/288-port to 12-slot/432-port chassis; 288×400G to 288×800G interfaces) and scaling out (4→8 planes, multiple devices per plane). One site more than doubled platform capacity every year for 7 years (~192x cumulative). The Edge side is shifting toward an "Elastic Edge" with a global GPU footprint closer to users for uncacheable AI-generated content, plus a move away from route-server peering toward an automated bilateral peering portal.
  • How: Two distinct backbones: EBB (DC-to-DC, IPv6-only, multi-plane, with Meta's own TE/routing software, deployed in DCs and midpoints) and CBB (DC-to-PoP, traditional IP/MPLS, single-plane). DC-metro architecture keeps paired DCs within 10km connected with 100,000s of 400G on single fiber pairs via frontend/backend switches; >10km AI backbone links run 10,000s of 800G ZR (ILA-free to 120–150km, 500km+ with ILAs) with optical protection switches. ZR pluggables (10–15W/plug) replace ~2kW transponders: a 1Pb midpoint scenario shrinks from 58 racks to 21 (400G-ZR) or 14 (800G-ZR).
  • Where applicable: The scale numbers are Meta-specific, but the ZR rack/power math, DC-metro fiber strategy, and plane-scaling approach transfer to anyone building DC interconnect or long-haul fabric.

ai-networks optics capacity-planning

items.title: How much of BIRD is vibecoded
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Wildcard pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Maria Matejka, BIRD | CZ.NIC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Not a talk the PM would search for, but one of the more honest datasets available on what LLMs can and cannot do in core network software — from the maintainers of a production routing daemon.
  • What: The answer to "how much of BIRD is vibecoded" is essentially: none of the hard parts. LLM-generated lockless multithreaded C was "pathetic." Attempts to use AI for bug fixing failed ("most of our bugs need complex thinking"), as did texts about BIRD, release notes, slide generation, and RFC review.
  • How: Beyond the failures, it catalogs the social pressures arriving via LLM: survivor bias (nobody posts their failures), confirmation bias ("the code should do what the commit declares"), "it works, just merge it" pressure, and the emerging phenomenon of LLM-fortified forks of real projects. The uncomfortable conclusion: BIRD's problem isn't AI — it's that their documentation "sucks or is outright wrong," their future intents aren't written anywhere, and background is scattered; that's bad for humans and LLMs alike.
  • Where applicable: Anyone maintaining open-source network infrastructure, or thinking about where AI-assisted development can safely enter their toolchain. Read alongside "Brace for Upgrades" (same conference) for the flip side — LLM-equipped security researchers flooding projects with CVE reports (~5–8% validity rates).

bgp ml-for-networking open-source

items.title: IP Address space for Outer Space
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Wildcard pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (Keynote) Recording

Tony Li

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A genuinely novel addressing-policy question: there is no RIR for outer space, and the current ad-hoc practice (space agencies getting resources from their local, geography-based RIR) precludes aggregation on extremely bandwidth-constrained links.
  • What: The IETF TIPTOP working group's proposal (draft-li-tiptop-address-space) for one RIR and one address block covering all of outer space, with one prefix each for the Moon, each planet, Lagrange points, and possibly the asteroid belt.
  • How: The argument is aggregation economics: space links are modem-class and mission-critical, so per-planet prefixes minimize precious routing overhead; space agencies are generally cooperative (ISS precedent) and expected to interconnect in space. Notably IPv4-first pragmatism — IPv6 header overhead is a serious concern on these links, and a reclaimed /16 might suffice alongside the IPv6 block.
  • Where applicable: Niche today, but it's a real IETF work item with ARIN in discussion for the custodian role, and an early signal of how Internet architecture extends into non-terrestrial networks.

address-policy ipv6

items.title: Manipulating RPKI (and more) with marquees in TLS certificates (and more)
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Sasha Romijn, Reliably Coded (IRRD, IRRexplorer, internet.nl)

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A year-long, systematic XSS campaign against the tooling layer around routing infrastructure — culminating in a chain that modifies RPKI ROAs from a single clicked link. Directly relevant to network security and to anyone building tools that render protocol-derived strings.
  • What: The author injected marquee/XSS payloads into every protocol field he controls — TLS certificate SANs, DNS version.bind/NSID/TXT, RIPE Database objects, HTTP Server headers, DHCP hostnames, wifi SSIDs, LoRa node names — and catalogued where downstream tools execute them. Findings span two RIRs, hosting providers (WHMCS on the main domain → one click adds an admin to a customer account), router firmware, and wirelessly rootable OpenWRT boxes. Most seriously: multiple paths through the RIPE NCC single sign-on session mean one click on a real ripe.net link can silently change your ROAs and take over your Database objects — you'd only notice when packets start dropping.
  • How: The recurring pattern: tools treat protocol fields as safe data, and some of those tools share a trust boundary with critical systems. The punchline: "RPKI has HSMs and key ceremonies, but the thing that actually changes your ROAs is a web app authenticated by a cookie."
  • Where applicable: Universal for anyone operating RPKI/IRR portals or writing tooling that displays untrusted fields; concrete guidance on what to watch for in your own tools.

bgp pki vulnerability-management

items.title: Measuring The Impact of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Complex Applications: A Case Study on Federated Identity Management
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ginevra Fabrizio, University of Twente

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: One of the few PQC-migration studies grounded in a real, complex identity stack (SAML + OIDC hub-and-spoke federation) rather than isolated TLS benchmarks — directly relevant to the identity side of the PM's portfolio.
  • What: Benchmarks of the five NIST-finalized PQC algorithms against real-world load from SURF's SURFconext federation (25 days of data: authentication counts, HAProxy logs, TLS connection info, SAML request/response volumes), quantifying the computational and hardware-capacity toll of switching a production federated identity hub to PQC.
  • How: The Hub'n'Spoke model is the worst case: the central hub (SURF.Engine) performs most cryptographic operations — each SAML flow involves validating the home IdP's response signature and signing a new response for the SP, and equivalents exist in the OIDC flow. Real authentication flows run from one second to several minutes, so added per-operation cost compounds visibly.
  • Where applicable: Identity federation operators and anyone planning PQC migration of OAuth/OIDC/SAML infrastructure. Findings: the transition is fragmented, with many ecosystem components still unaccounted for. Specific to hub-and-spoke scale but the methodology transfers.

quantum-safe identity measurement

items.title: OpenPenny: Identifying Legitimate Traﬃc to Reduce Monitoring Noise
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Petros Gigis, UCL

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Fills a real gap in ISP observability: packet counters and control-plane data can't tell you whether observed traffic is genuine or spoofed — which makes routing-change alerts noisy and stealthy hijacks hard to confirm.
  • What: An open-source data-plane primitive that validates whether traffic aggregates are non-spoofed, enabling trustworthy ingress maps, fewer false routing alerts, and detection of data-plane path anomalies invisible to BGP monitoring alone (including ROV-bypassing "stealthy hijacks" where the only visible signal is an unexpected ingress point).
  • How: Exploits a structural difference between real and spoofed TCP: legitimate connections are closed-loop (loss triggers retransmission), spoofed traffic is open-loop and cannot react. Active mode carefully drops a few packets and watches for retransmission; passive mode collects signals (e.g., per-packet load-balancing behavior) without touching traffic. Runs on commodity x86 using XDP/AF_XDP and DPDK; demonstrated on a real UCL testbed.
  • Where applicable: ISPs and large network operators with sFlow/NetFlow telemetry; the active mode injects small, deliberate loss, so it suits telemetry/monitoring paths rather than every production link. Solidly in the eBPF/XDP space the PM tracks.

measurement anomaly-detection

items.title: Overdoing NSEC3 Hurts
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Petr Špaček, Internet Systems Consortium

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A crisp security nugget: NSEC3 iteration counts that operators set for "extra security" are actually a DoS amplifier and enable a poorly documented downgrade attack.
  • What: Measured cost of extra iterations under random-subdomain attacks: ~⅓ performance loss at 5 iterations, ~⅔ at 25, across NSD, Unbound, and BIND. Worse, when iterations exceed a resolver's limit, the answer may be treated as insecure — and an attacker who controls any over-limit NSEC3 zone can craft a fake delegation that makes a delegation validate as insecure.
  • How: Walks through the iteration-limit collapse over time (2500 in RFC 5155 → 150 in implementations → 0 per RFC 9276 → 50 in BIND 9.19.18 → ~20 next), then the downgrade mechanics using real records.
  • Where applicable: Every DNSSEC-signed zone operator. Advice: use NSEC if you can, otherwise follow RFC 9276 exactly (0 iterations, no salt, no opt-out).

dns network-security

items.title: Persistent unknown unicast - A peering-LAN case study
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

James Rice, Jump Networks Ltd

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A textbook-quality L2 postmortem: a single MAC change can flood member traffic (including HTTPS SNI and emergency-call signalling) to hundreds of ports indefinitely, via a kernel-level neighbor-discovery quirk. This is the kind of hard-won operational lesson that transfers to any shared L2.
  • What: Shows that unknown unicast on peering LANs is not always transient. RFC 4861 §7.3.1 "forward-progress confirmation" lets a stale ND entry stay REACHABLE indefinitely: when member B changes MAC, A keeps sending to the old MAC; the exchange floods those frames to all member ports; some members' devices (skipping the L2 my-station check) forward the packet onward to B; B's reply via that third-party path counts as forward progress, so no Neighbor Solicitation is ever sent. A unicast NS to the stale MAC gets flooded too, and the NA arriving from the new MAC without a TLLA option confirms reachability without updating the cached MAC (RFC 4861 §7.2.5) — the entry stays stale and REACHABLE.
  • How: Kernel-level trace through neigh_confirm()/neigh_timer_handler() and ndisc_recv_na()/neigh_update(); a reproducible demo (published Nov 2024) using ip neigh replace with a dead MAC produces duplicate ping replies — each duplicate being a different member's device routing a packet it had no business handling. Includes a five-year timeline of reports and partial remediations at one IXP, plus a frank operator self-examination about disclosure.
  • Where applicable: The five-year timeline is one-IXP-specific, but the mechanism is general to any Linux/BSD host on a shared L2 segment — DC fabrics, exchange LANs, any environment where MAC changes meet ND caches. Valuable for L2 design and failure-mode reasoning.

troubleshooting ethernet

items.title: Redefining Netflix BGP architecture
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Elise Vennegues, Netflix; Frederic Cuiller, Cisco

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Real BGP architecture evolution at serious scale (20,000+ eBGP sessions, 2800+ peer ASNs, 400+ PoPs, ~175 countries) — the RR design questions and migration choreography are transferable even if the chosen platform is not.
  • What: Netflix's replacement of a full iBGP mesh across edge switches, aggregation routers, and PEs with a route-reflector architecture, including the option analysis (traditional router vs VNF appliance vs integrated UCS M7 appliance), production scale figures (e.g., NA region: 38M IPv4 / 9M IPv6 paths, 300+ clients), a phased migration (staging → pilot prefixes → per-device deprefer/raise → remove the mesh), and OpenConfig YANG-based BGP telemetry with BMP activation planned.
  • How: Validation via an early-field-trial process with Cisco; lessons include: cross-functional projects take longer than planned, and the lab is necessary but production churn/scale is unique.
  • Where applicable: Any large edge network with full-mesh iBGP pain. Caveat: this is an openly joint Netflix–Cisco presentation and the IOS XRv9000 UCS M7 appliance gets prominent placement — treat the product comparison table as vendor-tinged and extract the architecture methodology.

bgp troubleshooting

items.title: Route Filtering at Scale
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Fedor Vompe, Deutsche Telekom; Sebastian Becker, Deutsche Telekom

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Concrete, adoptable tooling for one of the hardest operational BGP problems — generating correct filters for thousands of sessions when the underlying IRR data is rotten. Up-ranks well on the "tooling others can adopt" criterion.
  • What: A tier-1's (AS3320) account of why AS-Set documentation in RIR databases remains foundational and systematically overlooked: missing documentation, explosive AS-Set expansion, and cyclic dependencies all break filter generation, and RPKI ROV alone does not replace this layer — bogon filters, community policy, Peerlock, IRR filters, ROV, ASPA, and OTC all work together.
  • How: Presents their toolchain, including the Route Query Specification (RQSpec) language and RIPEDiff, which compensate for poor AS-Set quality. Key framing: AS-Sets are fail-closed, so their contents and changes should be monitored — adding/removing a member set silently changes every parent set. Includes a worked route-leak prevention example (AS3320 requiring a customer's AS-DOWNSTREAM set before accepting prefixes).
  • Where applicable: Large operators generating customer/peer filters from IRR; the AS-Set hygiene findings apply to anyone consuming IRR data at any scale. Deutsche Telekom's toolchain specifics are theirs, but RQSpec is worth a look.

bgp automation

items.title: RPKI: Do we need Garbage Collection now?
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Antonis Chariton, AS4601 | Cisco

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Quantifies a genuine routing-security hygiene problem: newly assigned ASNs arriving with pre-existing ROAs that make their holders' hijacks look RPKI-valid.
  • What: Methodology-driven measurement: cross-referenced all RIPE ASN assignment dates against RPKI archives (RPKIviews) for ROAs pointing at each ASN the day before assignment — any such ROA is definitionally unintentional. Result: ~21% of new assignments in 2025 (18% in 2026) came with pre-existing ROAs, including double-digit-percentage chances of IPv4-covering ROAs; examples found in every RIR except AFRINIC. The RIPE NCC's re-assignment cleanup covers IRR but not RPKI.
  • How: A personal anecdote (a fresh ASN with ROAs authorizing other people's IPv4) turned into a systematic study; the follow-up Address Policy WG session ("Discussion on AS Reallocation") explores fixes: longer quarantine periods, alerting on RPKI objects pointing at unassigned ASes, expanding cleanup policy.
  • Where applicable: Anyone relying on RPKI ROV for security decisions; the data is RIPE-region-centric but the problem class exists in all RIRs.

bgp pki measurement

items.title: The €30 attack box: inside the Android TV botnet ecosystem
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Jérôme Meyer, Nokia

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Documents a step-change in the DDoS and abuse landscape — botnets no longer scan for exposed IoT; they recruit via residential proxy SDKs pre-installed on consumer hardware, behind CGNAT, invisible to conventional scanning.
  • What: Nokia Deepfield's analysis of the Oct 2025 33 Tbps attack and the ecosystem behind it: budget Android TV boxes ship with proxy software that routes requests to 0.0.0.0 — which resolves to the device's own loopback, where an unauthenticated ADB shell listens. No scanning, no CVE; the proxy SDK delivers the victim. Kimwolf alone runs ~3M active bots with ENS-based C2; the exploitable surface is estimated at 100–200M endpoints.
  • How: Linking six botnet families via shared code, a common cryptographic fingerprint (RC4+LCG, fixed seed), and co-located infrastructure; notable capabilities include Katana compiling its rootkit on-device via a bundled C compiler and CECbot abusing HDMI-CEC to survive factory resets. Operator-facing impact: outbound attack traffic from your own subscribers causes CGNAT failures and peering congestion; C2 signals to monitor are provided.
  • Where applicable: Any access network operator (CGNAT/peering impact), and security teams tracking proxy/botnet infrastructure. Nokia-authored but built on original lab analysis and reverse engineering.

malware-analysis ddos threat-intelligence

items.title: The year of IPv6-only desktop
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ondřej Caletka, RIPE NCC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Marks the moment IPv6-only operation crosses from mobile networks to desktops — macOS already opts out of IPv4 on IPv6-mostly networks, Windows 11 has it in preview, and NetworkManager on Linux supports it.
  • What: The "IPv6-mostly" model: the network signals NAT64 support via DHCPv4 option 108, and devices with CLAT (or enforced IPv6 compatibility) autonomously opt out of IPv4. Framed by the RIPE meeting network's own decade-long journey (failed experiment in 2013 → working IPv6-mostly main network today), and the argument that dual stack failed as a transition mechanism: double the work, with IPv6 problems masked by the IPv4 safety net.
  • How: NAT64 won because it's the one-box solution the industry actually chose; CLAT handles IPv4-only applications on the client. Practical pitfalls called out: IPv4-only VPNs with IPv6 killswitch features, and devices opting out even when they shouldn't.
  • Where applicable: Enterprise/access network design; the WinCLAT arrival makes IPv6-only enterprise LANs genuinely deployable, which will change DC and edge design assumptions.

ipv6

items.title: Understanding and optimising transceiver efficiency using internal metrics for improved power savings
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Gerhard Stein, Flexoptix GmbH

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Transceiver power is becoming a first-order DC design constraint; this is one of the few talks showing how to actually measure and optimize it from data already readable off modern optics.
  • What: How to use Versatile Diagnostics Monitoring (VDM, available on >100G optics) — especially Thermoelectric Cooler (TEC) current — alongside temperature and cable length to find the efficient operating point per transceiver, in Watts, on real hardware.
  • How: TEC power is computed as V_trc × I_TEC from VDM (vs DDM which only exposes laser current); tested across 100G QSFP28, 400G coherent ZR, and 800G QSFP-DD transceivers on Cisco Nexus 93600CD-GX, Catalyst 9500, and Juniper QFX5120. Support is patchy: QFX5120 and IOS XE expose DDM only; NX-OS reads CMIS VDM but assumes a 50°C laser target. Includes power-trend data (400G FR4: 12W→9W; 800G OSFP: 16.5→15.5W; 1.6T: 30→26W as DSP nodes shrink) and an entertaining frozen-transceiver experiment showing the laser re-warms within seconds.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to optics power budgeting; requires CMIS/VDM-capable transceivers and switch support, so check your NOS before counting on it. Vendor talk, but methodology is transferable.

optics power

items.title: VXLAN and EVPN on Linux (with BIRD)
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Core pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Maria Matejka, BIRD | CZ.NIC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: DC fabric fundamentals — VXLAN and EVPN — taught from raw Linux primitives upward, using the open-source daemon the speaker's team actually implements EVPN in, rather than a commercial stack.
  • What: A hands-on tutorial building VXLAN tunnels manually (ip link add ... type vxlan, VNI, UDP 4789), VLAN-filtering bridges, and hypervisor L2 domains, then layering EVPN control-plane on top with BIRD, so attendees understand what actually happens under the hood before the abstractions arrive.
  • How: Labs run in EduHawk (CZ.NIC's container-based network simulator, user namespaces, no root needed), starting with veths and bridges, moving to manual VXLAN links for VM mobility and traffic isolation, and progressively adding scalability layers. The setup is keepable for future fiddling.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building or operating DC overlay fabrics on Linux/commodity hardware, or anyone who wants to debug EVPN/VXLAN rather than just configure it. Tutorial format — worth the recording if you missed it live.

bgp data-center-fabric open-source

items.title: Why is ASPA still a draft
items.text:
RIPE 92 (Edinburgh) digest Program Adjacent pick Edinburgh · 18–22 May 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Maria Matejka, BIRD | CZ.NIC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: An implementer's-eye view of why ASPA (AS Provider Authorization) keeps stalling — useful both for BGP protocol understanding and as a case study in how draft specs mislead even careful implementers.
  • What: Clarifies what ASPA is and isn't ("ROA for the rest of the AS path": each AS signs its provider list — not whole-path authorization, not neighbor-pair authorization, not a BGPsec replacement), then walks through BIRD's implementation history: their first validation algorithm was wrong (assuming neighbor-pair authorization), and the wrongness survived review because the draft text suggested that reading on first pass.
  • How: Details the RTR ASPA PDU design confusion (a redundant AS Count field questioned after the document had passed last call) and a 2024 clarification exchange that exposed deeper ambiguity in the validation algorithm.
  • Where applicable: Anyone implementing or planning to deploy ASPA; also a good cautionary tale for anyone writing specs that will be implemented by third parties.

bgp standardization

items.title: ASPA: the new protocol for improving BGP routing security
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Ondřej Caletka, RIPE NCC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization) is the 2026 RPKI deployment milestone — the first broadly deployed step beyond origin validation toward path verification — and this tutorial is the operator's manual for both signing and validating sides.
  • What: A deep dive covering ASPA principles, creating ASPA objects for your ASNs, configuring validation in routers, and troubleshooting validation failures. An ASPA object lists the set of provider ASNs for a customer AS, signed via the RPKI chain of trust; validating operators can drop routes arriving via unauthorized providers. It complements ROV (which stops misorigination but not path spoofing or route-leak types 1–4), supports partial deployment, and is address-family agnostic.
  • How: Signing works through the standard RPKI models (hosted, delegated, hybrid) and the RIPE NCC portal; the tutorial includes practical guidance on what belongs in the object — transit providers, backup providers, DDoS-scrubbing providers, non-transparent IXP route servers — and what does not (customers, lateral peers, unless they can act as providers under some circumstances).
  • Where applicable: Every ASN holder and every operator doing inbound filtering; value grows with adoption, so early signers shape the ecosystem.

bgp network-security

items.title: Beyond NIS2: Software Supply Chains and the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Barry O'Donovan, INEX

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: NIS2 governs how you run your network; the CRA governs the software you run it with — including the open-source stacks most operators depend on. With mandatory vulnerability reporting live since September 2026, this is now procurement-reality, not policy theory.
  • What: A bridge from NIS2 operator obligations to CRA software requirements: the critical distinction between Commercial OSS Manufacturers (full product liability, CE marking, fines) and Open-Source Software Stewards (non-profit foundations under a light-touch regime, duties from 11 December 2027), with ecosystem examples — INEX and NLnet Labs as stewards vs. enterprise Linux vendors as manufacturers. Also covers what operators can legally expect from upstream maintainers on SBOMs, vulnerability disclosure and patch timelines, and reporting duties (24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification).
  • How: Walkthrough of the Commission's scope examples and the "intended for commercial activities" test, plus a roadmap for auditing open-source dependencies and consuming standardized security feeds.
  • Where applicable: EU-market entities, but the checklist is useful for any operator publishing community tools or procuring network software.

internet-governance vulnerability-management

items.title: BIRD on an Open Linux Switch: Mainline Linux, switchdev and Hardware L3 Offload
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Bruno Banelli, Novarq d.o.o.

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: This is a real engineering report on the question every open-networking skeptic asks: can a fully Linux-native stack — no SAI, no FPM, no vendor NOS — route at line rate on commodity switching silicon?
  • What: BIRD 3.1.7 running on the Novarq Tactical 1000 (LAN969x/Sparx5 silicon, Debian arm64), establishing dual-stack eBGP sessions and installing routes through the standard kernel path. Results: four eBGP sessions up, IPv4 hardware offload at 9.41 Gbit/s of TCP and IPv6 at 9.28 Gbit/s with the switch CPU never seeing transit packets; route changes propagate from peer withdrawal to the Linux FIB in 0.40–0.45 s; a 256-route add/withdraw batch works cleanly (a functional test, not a capacity test).
  • How: BIRD exports routes via its kernel protocol over rtnetlink; FIB notifiers drive the LAN969x driver, which programs the ASIC; switchdev carries bridge, VLAN, FDB and multicast state, with neighbour entries supplying next-hop MACs. Explicit BIRD filters keep the kernel table clean; a per-layer observability checklist (birdc, ip -d route, ip -s neigh, captures at receiver and switch CPU) verifies offload.
  • Where applicable: Hardware-specific today — the L3 routing driver lives in the Novarq kernel tree, not mainline Sparx5, and two setup steps need care. The architecture and the collaboration gaps (BIRD devs, kernel/switchdev maintainers, open hardware vendors) generalize to the whole open-Linux-switching effort.

open-source linux-networking switching

items.title: Debugging Stupid Things: If it only was DNS for once...
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Tobias Fiebig, TU Wien

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The program's purest "hard-won lessons" talk: weird corner-case bugs, the debugging process used to find them, and the belief systems that got in the way — exactly the kind of content that transfers across environments.
  • What: A tour of production corner cases, including a PMTUD failure where downloads for users on one transit path crawled because ICMP "need to frag (mtu 1420)" messages were being lost or ignored while other paths were fine; Microsoft treating ED25519 DKIM signatures as a syntax error while RSA validated; FRR treating 'extended-nexthop' as 'unnumbered' and emitting rogue Router Advertisements onto the AMS-IX exchange LAN; and solar-panel power monitoring causing random shutdowns whose reconnect pattern triggered a null-pointer crash in OpenBGPD. No DNS packets were the root cause in any case.
  • How: Reproduce, then PCAP ("PCAP or didn't happen"), then work outward from what the packets actually say — with each case paired by a lesson about questioning the assumptions ("why one has not yet understood what one told said system").
  • Where applicable: Universal; the methodology and the humility travel to any network or systems team.

troubleshooting dns

items.title: Detecting and Characterizing Exposed BGP Routers​
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Shyam Krishna Khadka, University of Twente

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: RFC 7454 told operators to restrict TCP 179 to configured peers twenty years ago; this measurement shows 20,432 routers across 4,194 ASes still accept unsolicited BGP OPENs — a concrete, checkable exposure for any network.
  • What: An Internet-wide IPv4 scan (February 2026): 6.25M IPs respond on TCP/179, 277k speak BGP, and 141k (51%) complete an OPEN exchange. Using the BGP Identifier (unique per router per ASN per RFC 6286) plus OPEN ASN and interface ASN mapping, these resolve to 20,432 unique routers — 16,124 internal, 1,127 border, 3,181 unclassified — across 4,194 ASes. Around 75% of border routers face one AS; ~90% have fewer than 10 IPs, while 10% of internal routers expose up to 1,208 IPs. A partial vendor view via Shodan's SNMPv3 data identifies 8,871 routers (43.4%), dominated by Juniper (5,448) and Teldat (2,956).
  • How: ZMap TCP/179 scan → custom BGP speaker sends OPEN → OPEN-response analysis → router/AS association and border-vs-internal classification by ASN visibility.
  • Where applicable: The finding is Internet-wide and vendor-agnostic; the operator action is trivial to execute — audit your edge ACLs with nmap/zmap from outside — and the talk explicitly invites operators to explain why these ports are open.

bgp measurement network-security

items.title: Digital Coherent Optics Tutorial
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Michel Lanners, LU-CIX

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Coherent pluggables (400ZR/800ZR-class) are becoming the default way to light DC-to-DC and metro dark fiber, and spec sheets for them are notoriously hard to read. This is a rare vendor-neutral, operator-led on-ramp to the technology.
  • What: A full tutorial (grown out of a Euro-IX workshop, co-presented with Flexoptix and Arista) covering fundamentals, choosing optics from standards and datasheets, host compatibility, power and cooling, link/network design, commissioning, monitoring, troubleshooting, and deployment case studies.
  • How: The material goes deep enough to be useful: NRZ→PAM4 trade-offs (half the spectrum, ~9.5 dB less SNR margin per eye, KP4 FEC RS(544,514)), coherent modulation tables (DP-QPSK for long-haul 100G/200G ZR+, DP-16QAM for 400ZR/800ZR/1600ZR), dual-polarization MIMO equalization tracking PMD and polarization transients, and the line-rate math (a 59.84 GBd 400ZR fits a 75 GHz DWDM slot; 800ZR at 118.2 GBd needs 150 GHz).
  • Where applicable: Anyone buying or deploying coherent optics for router-to-router or DCI links, on any vendor's platform — the physics and the standards are the same. The form-factor/host-compatibility sections matter for mixed-estate DCs.

optics interconnection

items.title: Early Attestation is Very Harmful. Why is it Required?
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Muhammad Usama Sardar, GA4GH

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Attested TLS — binding remote attestation into the TLS handshake — is being standardized and deployed for confidential computing and workload identity; this talk shows the early-attestation variant carries critical-severity CVEs, directly relevant to workload/TEE identity design.
  • What: Formal verification (ProVerif) surfaced a family of critical and high CVEs in early (intra-handshake) attestation: relay attacks from missing connection binding (CVE-2026-33697, CVSS 7.5), diversion attacks from missing hardware/machine-ID binding, and the EarlyAttestationBleed/EAT series at CVSS 9.1–9.6 — in deployments handling the health data of more than 40 million Germans. Still-vulnerable implementations include Cocos AI ≤ v0.8.2, Privasys rustls/Go, and code following the withdrawn early-attestation draft.
  • How: Symbolic security analysis of the attested-TLS handshake, root-caused into two failures — no binding to the connection and no binding to the hardware — plus an architectural argument: early attestation leaks hardware-level information, can only express boot-time claims, adds handshake latency and failure modes, and every use case works with standard post-handshake attestation instead.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building or procuring attested TLS, TEE-based workload verification, or confidential-computing pipelines; the talk feeds directly into IETF standardization (SEAT-adjacent) and explicitly invites operator feedback.

tls attestation standardization

items.title: Embracing NETCONF
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Maria Matejka, BIRD | CZ.NIC

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Twenty years after RFC 4741, NETCONF/YANG/RESTCONF are the default network-automation interfaces — and this is a practitioner's fine-print audit of whether the zoo of protocols, formats and schemas can actually be relied on.
  • What: A critical tour of the ecosystem: NETCONF's datastore and locking semantics, RESTCONF's HTTP mapping and its quirks (it cannot manipulate NETCONF locks, and auto-commits the candidate datastore after every successful edit — silently committing other sources' staged edits), YANG modeling with XML and JSON encodings (RFC 7951), and where canonical vs. alternate representations diverge.
  • How: Quote-the-spec analysis: each claim is anchored to the exact RFC text, contrasting what the documents promise with what implementations deliver — the "have you read the fine print?" framing from the abstract.
  • Where applicable: Anyone consuming NETCONF/RESTCONF/YANG in automation or tooling; the practical constraint is vendor support variance, which is precisely what the talk surfaces.

automation standardization api

items.title: Expanding Routing Visibility at IXPs with BMP
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Thomas Holterbach, bgproutes.io

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Route-server looking glasses only show what survived policy; BMP exposes the whole routing pipeline at an IXP — pre-policy, filtered, and non-best routes plus peer/session state — which changes what both IXP operators and participants can detect (hijacks, leaks, misbehaving peers).
  • What: A proposal and practical demonstration (the bgproutes.io IXP Explorer) for BMP-based monitoring at IXPs, plus an honest treatment of the open problems: processing and storing large BMP volumes at big IXPs, efficient data serving, and consistent access across collection platforms and storage architectures, ending with a roadmap for community adoption.
  • How: Both BIRD and FRRouting can export BMP when deployed as route servers; BMP is positioned as complementary to existing approaches (direct route-server queries à la Alice-LG, and dedicated add-path collection sessions). The talk frames IXP monitoring as serving two audiences: IXP operators securing the fabric, and participants making peering and troubleshooting decisions.
  • Where applicable: Any IXP operator; of the 1,226 IXPs listed on PeeringDB most are small/medium and can adopt this sooner — the scaling challenges are specific to the largest exchanges.

bgp telemetry peering

items.title: InterLAN IX Lighthouse - Yet Another Network Automation Tool
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Andrei Dinu, InterLAN IX

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A production self-service portal with checked, reversible, recorded changes over a multi-vendor estate (Nokia SR OS + Arista EOS) — a transferable template for anyone automating a physical fabric, including how to keep humans in the loop.
  • What: Lighthouse (network automation) alongside BirdNest (Rust-based BIRD route servers with IRR/RPKI/looking-glass) and NoSignal (live TV) behind one member portal. Lighthouse automates Nokia L2/L3/EVPN services, ports/LAGs/multihoming, routing and traffic policy, plus Arista access ports/trunks/VLANs/ACLs. One member request fans out to several routers as an atomic multi-device transaction with per-device preview, a rollback timer, a reachability check, and confirm-one-router-at-a-time; when safe recovery can't be proven, a human takes over.
  • How: gNMI for Nokia config/state/streaming telemetry, eAPI+SNMP for Arista; the database owns intended state so hand-made device changes surface as deviations and are never silently adopted; a digital twin built from production snapshots (same topology, same NETCONF/gNMI writes) rehearses changes; an AI assistant with strictly read-only tools writes reports and migration plans; IPFIX/sFlow lands in ClickHouse for who-exchanges-with-whom analytics and trial attack detection.
