  • Where applicable: Built for an IXP (Nokia core, Arista access), but the pattern — intended-state database, preview/rollback transactions, deviation surfacing, rehearsal twin — generalizes to any multi-vendor DC or campus estate.

automation orchestration

items.title: Let's talk about some topics of interest at the IETF
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Suresh Krishnan, Internet Architecture Board

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: This IAB/IESG BoF is the most direct hit on the agentic-identity agenda at the whole meeting: workload identity standards (WIMSE) being applied to AI agents, OAuth working-group work on AI-agent authorization, and two new AI-focused WGs.
  • What: An interactive session on IETF topics relevant to operators: AI (AGENTPROTO for AI-agent application interoperability; DAWN for AI resource discovery over mDNS), identity/authentication/authorization/audit (WIMSE guidelines for AI-agent authN/authZ and gap analysis — workload identity methods designed to apply to AI agents; OAuth WG work on AI-agent authorization; a new "audit" BoF on auditing distributed, time-evolving systems), post-quantum cryptography (PQUIP operational guidance, RFC 9958, hybrid work across tls/jose/cose/lamps, Merkle-tree certificates in PLANTS), plus IPv6, DNS, routing and space topics.
  • How: Presentation-light, feedback-heavy: the explicit goal is to collect operator positions and feed them back into the IETF process.
  • Where applicable: Anyone whose roadmap depends on workload identity, OAuth/OIDC extension points, or PQC migration timelines for BGP/DNS security.

identity standardization ml-for-networking

items.title: Maybe it is time to consider layer 3 internet exchanges
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

James Rice, Jump Networks Ltd

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A structured challenge to thirty years of IXP orthodoxy — should exchanges offer routed, point-to-point L3 ports instead of a shared L2 peering LAN with route servers? The whole industry replaced large L2 domains with routed ones everywhere else.
  • What: The case for L3 exchanges built on three qualities of connectivity: correct forwarding (L2 fabrics have silent forwarding failure modes with confidentiality and availability consequences), shorter physical paths (an L2 participant picks next-hops without knowing which is closer; an L3 fabric does closest-exit routing like a transit provider), and capacity headroom (with a real 9/11 case study where LINX port headroom let the BBC keep broadcasting). Historical reasons for L2 (1990s: expensive CPU routers vs cheap switches) no longer hold since switches and routers both forward L2/L3 in hardware. Followed by a panel including Inter.link, LINX, Cloudflare, Google and Zayo.
  • How: Argument plus worked example of where a shared peering LAN falls short; the rest was structured audience/panel discussion on whether networks would prefer L3 ports and which IXs would offer them.
  • Where applicable: IXP operators and anyone buying exchange ports — a design conversation, not a deployment; the remote-peering latency caveat (attracting traffic via distant PoPs) applies to participants more than the fabric model.

peering interconnection

items.title: Measuring Propagation Time of RPKI Validity Changes on the Dataplane
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Alexander Männel, TU Dresden

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: When you change a ROA — including an emergency change during a hijack — how long until actual dataplane reachability changes? This is the first Internet-wide answer, and the numbers should inform every operator's incident playbook.
  • What: RPKI propagation is at least an order of magnitude slower than plain BGP: invalid-to-valid transitions take 9–12 minutes and valid-to-invalid transitions 30–42 minutes to take effect at 50% of vantage points. The public measurement platform ReRPKI lets operators observe how RIPE Atlas probes connected through their AS experience reachability during ROA changes.
  • How: The method uses the CDN origin of the RIPE RRDP repository plus an optimized validator to detect ROA changes earlier than the ecosystem (at least 57 seconds faster, median 5:07 minutes before the fastest public validator, n=24,886), then triggers traceroutes from 300+ CAIDA Ark vantage points every three minutes for an hour, covering all RIPE prefixes in the RPKI hosted model.
  • Where applicable: Internet-wide and vendor-neutral; the latencies reflect current relying-party fetch intervals and validator configurations, so they bound what any ROV deployment can expect today.

bgp pki measurement

items.title: Multi-Layer Routing Domain Protection at Hyperscale: From Route Leak to Automated Enforcement
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Daria Shantalova, Express Backbone Team, Meta

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A concrete, high-quality postmortem plus the system built in response — exactly the failure-driven content that transfers, because the preconditions (multiple routing domains, BGP between them, community-based policy) describe most large networks.
  • What: An internal domain advertised a large volume of prefixes toward Meta's Express Backbone (the DC-to-DC backbone), each carrying a community the ingress route-map legitimately matched. The routes propagated through the iBGP mesh to every site, DC aggregation routers exhausted memory and restarted, and service disruption followed. The core insight: community-based filtering answers "is this tag allowed at this boundary?" but not "is this prefix allowed to carry this tag?" — that gap is where leaks live.
  • How: Three independent layers at every domain boundary: (1) ID Communities — a registered tagging scheme where each prefix carries exactly one identity community defining origination and propagation scope, with missing/wrong/multiple tags as violations; (2) a Route Registry — an internal IRR-equivalent permit list per boundary, auto-generated into inbound prefix filters with a freshness SLA; (3) control-plane health monitoring that continuously validates the RIB against intent. Deployment exposed pervasive violations that were remediated within months, and automated enforcement now prevents recurrence.
  • Where applicable: Built at Meta scale (dozens of data centers), but the three-layer pattern is deliberately presented as applicable without their stack — any operator running multi-domain BGP with community-scoped policy can copy the architecture.

bgp automation network-security

items.title: Networks as Sensors: Passive Measurement as a Lens on Society, A case study on two European elections
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Wildcard pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Orlando Eduardo Martínez-Durive, IMDEA Networks Institute & Net AI

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Not a networking-ops talk, but a genuinely surprising result about what the passive measurements operators already run for engineering can reveal: per-antenna app demand from a major French mobile operator (market share ~31%, ~22M subscribers) predicts political alignment — and the study is an open invitation to operators to build this instrumentation together.
  • What: Using aggregated, GDPR-compliant mobile metadata (per-antenna demand for 22–27 apps, residential evening window) across the 2019 and 2024 European Parliament elections, digital consumption carries an independent signal about vote share that for several parties matches or exceeds traditional socioeconomic indicators; combining both increases explanatory power by up to 28.23%, consistently across both elections. The illustrative case: two demographically near-identical towns 10 km apart with far-right vote shares of 31% vs 20% differ mainly in app-consumption profiles (Facebook +5% vs −26%; online news −21% vs +43%).
  • How: Revealed Comparative Advantage normalization to make per-app volumes comparable across antennas, alignment of antenna-level demand with commune-level socioeconomic and vote data, and regression modeling of vote shares.
  • Where applicable: Research collaboration with MNO/ISP/IXP vantage points; the broader argument is that operator passive measurement could become a platform-independent instrument for observing society — with all the privacy and governance questions that implies.

measurement mobile privacy

items.title: Nothing left to take away
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (Keynote) Recording

Remco van Mook

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: draft-ietf-intarea-ipv6-resolved-gateway removes ARP from access and hosting segments while keeping dual-stack hosts unmodified — a structural simplification aimed squarely at datacenter fabrics, containers, Kubernetes and GPU clusters running out of RFC1918.
  • What: A mechanism that lets IPv4 service endpoint identifiers survive on an IPv6-only segment: hosts get a sentinel IPv4 gateway (DHCPv4 Option 3, placeholder 192.0.2.11) and resolve its MAC from the IPv6 neighbour cache instead of ARPing; unmodified hosts still ARP for the sentinel and the router answers — both host generations coexist on the same segment, with no DHCPv4 client/server/relay changes.
  • How: Updated hosts use the RFC 4861 default-router list and RFC 4191 preferences (no ARP at all); gains include active/active gateways without FHRP, inbound ECMP to the last hop, no ARP spoofing, no broadcasts, per-host /32s anywhere in the footprint, and — via RFC 8950 — IPv4 service addresses delivered straight to pods without SNAT/DNAT/conntrack. Running code exists on the host side (v4gwd.py for ifupdown/NetworkManager, a systemd-networkd patch, FreeBSD 13.1+).
  • Where applicable: Target use cases are explicitly DC fabrics, campuses, DOCSIS MAC domains, FTTH/PON aggregation, containers/Kubernetes, and AI/GPU clusters. Draft stage (-01 will add ND health prerequisites and a MAY-level ARP fallback), so it needs host-side adoption; the design is general.

ipv6 data-center-fabric standardization

items.title: Post-Quantum DNSSEC at Cloudflare
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Joe Abley, Cloudflare

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: The first production deployment of a post-quantum DNSSEC algorithm in a large public resolver — a working answer to "how do we even start?" for PQ migration of Internet infrastructure.
  • What: Cloudflare implemented ML-DSA-44 (algorithm 18, via draft-westerbaan-dnssec-mldsa) in the 1.1.1.1 resolver, fully live for all clients since 10 September 2026, handling 2,420-byte signatures; a public checker (dnstest.dev) tells users what their local resolver does. The wider landscape remains at zero: no PQ algorithms specified for DNSSEC, no registries accepting PQ DS records, root still on RSA/SHA-256 — and the response-size/TCP-fallback problem is the gating issue.
  • How: Implementation and measurement experience, plus a new problem class: DNSSEC has no downgrade protection, and a failing PQ signature alongside a valid legacy signature is indistinguishable from a quantum attack — motivating draft-jabley-dnsop-local-signing-algorithm-policy for local validation policy. Framed against NIST IR 8547's ~2030 deprecation and 2035 disallowance clock.
  • Where applicable: DNS operators and anyone planning PQC timelines for signing infrastructure; the multi-signature downgrade problem generalizes to other PQ migrations.

dns quantum-safe pki

items.title: PSA: Removing AS-SET Ambiguity
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

James Bensley, Inter.link

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: AS-SET names are not globally unique, and the same name can resolve differently per database (AS-APPLE in RIPE: 2 ASNs, 0 prefixes; in RADB: 2 ASNs, 244 prefixes) — producing silently empty or silently wrong prefix filters. The ecosystem has just changed a lot at once, and this rounds it up.
  • What: A public service announcement consolidating independent fixes: RIR enforcement of hierarchical AS-SET names (RIPE, APNIC and LACNIC done; AFRINIC and ARIN coming); PeeringDB requiring registry-scoped AS-SETs (with auto-suggested scope) and limiting networks to a single AS-SET (of 37,130 networks, 19,942 declare an AS-SET and 304 declared more than one); MANRS considering making both mandatory; and IETF drafts for registry-scoped members (src-members: RIPE::AS-BAR) and member exclusion (excl-members:, motivated by an AS-SET expanding to 76,337 ASNs and 1.32M prefixes).
  • How: Concrete database/policy changes already shipped or in flight, each with links to the enforcing organization and draft.
  • Where applicable: Anyone generating IRR-derived filters today — the action items (rename to hierarchical, scope your AS-SETs in PeeringDB) are immediate.

bgp peering network-security

items.title: RS-API - Accept announcments as legit as possible
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Evann Dreumont and Alarig Le Lay, Breizh-IX

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Route-server filter generation is a solved-looking problem that isn't: PeeringDB max-pref values are self-reported and unreliable, and an AS-SET can quietly pull in hundreds of thousands of prefixes (one shown bgpq4 expansion: 202,416). This is adoptable open-source tooling that confronts registry data with observed reality.
  • What: RS-API, a caching proxy around bgpq4, bgp.tools and bgproutes.io that generates route-server configuration: RPKI (ROA + ASPA), OTC checks (RFC 9234), bogon and specificity filters, IRR prefix-lists, and a recomputed max-pref derived from the peer's actual AS cone rather than their PeeringDB claim, with AMS-IX-style scaling applied.
  • How: JSON API with a 24-hour TTL cache (config generation across 2 route servers × 4 cities would otherwise hammer the upstream APIs); AS-cone sizing via the bgp.tools API with a bgproutes.io looking-glass fallback; deployed in production at Breizh-IX (Rennes, Nantes, Lille, Strasbourg); open source.
  • Where applicable: Any IXP route server, especially small and medium ones; it depends on third-party APIs (bgp.tools, bgproutes.io) being available and accurate — the talk explicitly asks larger IXPs how they solve the same problem.

peering bgp network-security

items.title: The End of Prefix Filtering
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

James Bensley, Inter.link

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A deliberately provocative operator thesis with data behind it: IRR-derived prefix filtering may now cost more to generate, deploy and maintain than the security it adds, and ROA coverage has grown enough to switch edge filtering to RPKI alone.
  • What: A three-way comparison of DFZ, IRR and ROA datasets (single-day snapshots) showing DFZ data tracking ROA data more closely than IRR, IRR containing substantial redundancy, and redundant ROA data beginning to accumulate; decision-flow analysis of what each filtering combination actually rejects; and the observation that tier-1 transit feeds are already accepted as full tables without prefix or AS-path filters.
  • How: Snapshot-based dataset comparison plus stepwise filter decision trees (origin in AS path → ROA valid/unknown → IRR presence → reject/accept), ending with the "are we there yet?" assessment.
  • Where applicable: Explicitly scoped to the standard edge case (excludes RTBH, private ASNs, Flowspec). Read it against When Routing Evidence Conflicts in the same program — that talk quantifies exactly the IRR/RPKI disagreements that make a wholesale cutover non-trivial. Operator judgment required; the debate itself is the value.

bgp network-security

items.title: The Internet's Path MTUs: How Big Can You Go?
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Tobias Fiebig, TU Wien, and Vaishnavi Raghavajosyula, Max Planck Institute for Informatics

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: PMTUD is unreliable, so protocols fall back to conservative sizes; knowing where the real MTU bottlenecks are — and that they're at the edges, not the core — is directly useful for interconnect and MSS-clamp decisions.
  • What: A measurement of 76,700 paths (access, core, and web-serving) using a PMTUD-independent traceroute-based method: 97 distinct PMTUs, but three dominate — 1500 B (80.5%), 1492 B (11.7%), 1480 B (1.5%). 99% of IPv4 paths support at least 1420 B; IPv6 paths commonly operate at 1280 B. Sub-1500 breaks concentrate near network edges (1492 B maps cleanly to PPPoE overhead in fiber/DSL ASes) while core paths are rarely constrained. PMTU is asymmetric: reverse-direction PMTUs are larger in >92% of sub-1500 pairs (~64% of those are 1500 B). 18.5% of paths show PMTU-vs-MSS-inferred mismatches.
  • How: RIPE Atlas anchors and probes, traceroute-based PMTU discovery independent of PMTUD (iterative search over a coarse size list), cross-checked against ICMP PTB hints and TCP-MSS, with heuristic attribution of break locations using AS, TTL and external network documentation.
  • Where applicable: WAN/DC-interconnect MTU planning and any jumbo-vs-1500 end-to-end decision; the edge-vs-core finding means the core can safely run large MTUs while edge paths need clamping.

measurement ethernet troubleshooting

items.title: The State of ECN Adoption in the Internet
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Adjacent pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Danesh Zeynali, Max Planck Institute for Informatics

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: L4S and low-latency transport depend on ECN surviving end-to-end; this re-measures adoption a decade after the classic studies and finds a specific, named blocker.
  • What: A revisiting and extension of the Bauer and Trammell ECN characterization studies: the majority of Internet service infrastructure is now ECN-aware, but a nontrivial fraction of hosts, routers and middleboxes bleach ECN bits — and many hyper-giants bleach along the path, with substantial implications for L4S. IPv6 endpoints and paths show stronger ECN support than IPv4.
  • How: Active measurements covering endpoint support (handshake negotiation), network support (marking and bleaching on path), and a longitudinal view.
  • Where applicable: Anyone counting on ECN or L4S — including teams whose lossless/low-latency DC designs assume ECN works beyond the fabric; the hyper-giant bleaching is the deployment blocker to watch.

congestion-control measurement

items.title: TTL Jumps: Unexpected TTL Rewrites Impacting Inferences from Traceroutes
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Wildcard pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Tobias Fiebig, TU Wien, and Johannes Zirngibl, Max Planck Institute for Informatics

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A systematic blind spot in the field's most-used measurement tool: some devices rewrite TTL (often to 255), hiding the rest of the path and corrupting topology inference — and the affected paths include a large fraction of one major Tier-1's IPv6 network.
  • What: At least 47 ASes contain path-impairing devices that rewrite TTL. The flagship example: more than 90% of outgoing IPv6 paths from CAIDA Ark nodes have been affected at AT&T since 2023. Measurement towards a single node found 365 probes (138 IPv4, 236 IPv6) seeing rewrites, with 63 ASes implicated on-path; extending to all IPv4 RIPE Atlas traces, 1.8M traces end in ICMP errors, 86.3k contain a TTL > 1, and 23.1k are genuine rewrites (others are liveness probes using TTL 255 after five unresponsive hops).
  • How: Controlled experiments plus public RIPE Atlas and CAIDA Ark data; the authors distinguish true rewrites from liveness-check artifacts and trace where along the path the rewriting happens.
  • Where applicable: Anyone building topology inference, AS-link datasets, or traceroute-based triage tooling — the spurious-router/AS-link failure mode directly affects measurement products the PM may depend on.

measurement troubleshooting routing-protocols

items.title: Using IPv6 and DNS to implement a new addressing architecture for the Internet
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Wildcard pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides Recording

Saleem Bhatti, University of St Andrews, UK

VideoPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: A follow-up born from RIPE 92 attendee demand: the identifier/locator split is a decades-old idea whose time may be coming back, and this is a working IPv6-native implementation rather than a position paper.
  • What: ILNP (Identifier Locator Network Protocol) — the "Why/What/How" of splitting the IP address's semantic overload into an Identifier (node identity, DNS-published) and a Locator (network location), reducing global routing state, enabling multihoming, multipath and mobility without extra machinery, and improving privacy. Unlike LISP, HIP and SHIM6, it does not overload the IP address semantics. It runs across today's IPv6 infrastructure and is backwards-compatible with IPv6 applications.
  • How: Locators and identifiers as new addressing data types bound dynamically to protocol-stack objects, with DNS supplying the mapping; a FreeBSD implementation is ongoing (with ICANN Grant Program support) and the talk covers what works across today's Internet — protocol, routing, API and naming compatibility.
  • Where applicable: Research and standards exploration, not deployment — but relevant to anyone designing the next iteration of DC addressing, mobility, or identity-adjacent network architecture.

ipv6 dns standardization

items.title: When Routing Evidence Conflicts: Measuring IRR and RPKI for BGP Filtering
items.text:
RIPE 93 digest Program Core pick 26–30 October 2026

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Antonis Chariton and Usama Ejaz, Cisco ThousandEyes

VideoPPTXPDF

Watch the recording

  • Why: Operators treat IRR route objects and RPKI ROAs as corroborating evidence for the same announcement; this measurement shows they disagree in specific, quantified ways that directly affect filter correctness.
  • What: A time-aligned comparison of BGP, IRR and RPKI for 8–14 August 2026 (57 RIS/RouteViews collectors, 19 IRR sources, 18 relying-party views). Findings: 64.6–65.1% of daily public BGP prefix-origin pairs had an exact IRR match, and 79.9% of those matches existed in only one IRR source; 786 exact IRR matches stayed RPKI Invalid all week (371 maxLength, 415 wrong-origin), concentrated in a handful of origins — five ASNs account for 43.4% of maxLength and 50.4% of wrong-origin cases, and 99.5% of the persistent conflicts were registered in a single IRR source; 22.2% of exact-match pairs remained RPKI NotFound. A PeeringDB AS-SET replay retained 99.27% of exact matches.
  • How: Daily snapshots at a fixed time, recursive AS-SET expansion through declared IRR sources, consensus classification across relying-party views, and a separate replay of PeeringDB-declared AS-SETs.
  • Where applicable: Any edge-filtering pipeline using IRR and/or RPKI. The operational guidance is the point: an exact IRR match does not imply RPKI Valid, and incomplete AS-SET evidence is not grounds to exclude an origin ASN from a filter.

bgp measurement pki

items.title: Achieving High-Speed and Robust Encrypted Traffic Anomaly Detection with Programmable Switches (Mazu)
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Han Zhang et al. (Tsinghua, Peking U., Sangfor, China Telecom)

Video

Why: Inline line-rate NIDS for encrypted traffic is a core network-security capability, and this one is production-proven across two ISPs over two years.

What: An inline switch-based IDS detecting malicious traffic at ~90% accuracy within minutes, having caught 10+ critical attack events protecting 10M+ servers.

How: A dual-plane feature-extraction model at near line speed plus a one-class classifier trained only on benign traffic, with an online update mechanism for drift.

Where applicable: ISP/data-center-edge deployment on programmable switches; benign-only training is a sensible general answer to label scarcity.

anomaly-detection encryption programmable-dataplane

items.title: Alibaba Stellar: A New Generation RDMA Network for Cloud AI
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Jie Lu et al. (Alibaba Cloud)

Video

Why: RDMA virtualization (SR-IOV) pain — slow container spin-up, resource limits, traffic steering — is exactly the multi-tenant cloud-AI networking the PM works on.

What: A production RDMA virtualization stack that spins up virtual devices in seconds, cuts container init time 73%, and improves LLM training speed up to 14%.

How: Para-Virtualized DMA (PVDMA) for on-demand memory pinning, an extended Memory Translation Table (eMTT) for GPUDirect RDMA performance, and RDMA Packet Spray for multipath.

Where applicable: Alibaba-specific production setup; the PVDMA/eMTT ideas generalize but the numbers are from their cluster.

rdma ai-networks cloud-native

items.title: ByteDance Jakiro: Enabling RDMA and TCP over Virtual Private Cloud
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Yirui Liu et al. (ByteDance)

Video

Why: Carrying RDMA and TCP over one VPC overlay with real VPC semantics (security groups, QoS) is a concrete cloud-native multi-tenancy problem.

What: A vNIC design supporting both RDMA and TCP inside a VPC with QoS and security-group enforcement, near-physical RDMA performance, deployed a year in production.

How: A unified vNIC framework that applies VPC features to both stream types while staying compatible with intra-host RDMA optimizations and guaranteeing weighted-fair QoS between RDMA and TCP.

Where applicable: ByteDance-specific production VPC; the dual-stack-over-one-overlay pattern transfers, the deployment specifics don't.

cloud-native rdma

items.title: Censys: A Map of Internet Hosts and Services
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Zakir Durumeric et al. (Censys Inc.)

Video

Why: Attack-surface and security-measurement context the PM tracks adjacent to network security.

What: A retrospective on Censys's re-architecture for continuous Internet-wide scan data, with a visibility evaluation and lessons learned.

How: Operational account of redesigning collection/packaging and serving research/industry/government users; discusses unsolved problems.

Where applicable: Internet-measurement infrastructure; general reference.

measurement network-security

items.title: Centralium: A Hybrid Route-Planning Framework for Large-Scale DC Network Migrations
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Paper Recording

Yikai Lin et al. (Meta, UMass)

Video

Why: BGP datapath/migration pain is a real operational problem; native BGP can't express the staged, topology-aware conditions migrations need.

What: A Route Planning Abstraction augmenting BGP for centralized planning with distributed enforcement, with 10+ production migration use cases and a substantial reduction in migration time/risk.

How: RPA encodes both sequential and spatial migration conditions BGP can't, driven by a centralized controller deployed alongside existing BGP.

Where applicable: Meta-specific deployment but the abstraction generalizes to any large BGP-routed DC facing migrations.

items.title: Confucius: Intent-Driven Network Management with Multi-Agent LLMs
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Paper Recording

Zhaodong Wang et al. (Meta, JHU, Harvard, Stony Brook)

Video

Why: First credible hyperscale report on multi-agent LLMs for network ops — useful signal on agentic operations adjacent to the PM's agentic-identity interest.

What: A production multi-agent framework, operational two years with 60+ apps, modeling management workflows as DAGs.

How: LLMs integrated with existing tools, RAG for long-term memory, human/model interaction primitives, and tight coupling to existing validation to prevent regressions.

Where applicable: Meta-scale ops; the architecture is a reference point for agentic network management generally.

ml-for-networking orchestration

items.title: Designing Transport-Level Encryption for Datacenter Networks (SDP)
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Tianyi Gao et al. (University of Edinburgh)

Video

Why: Encryption for next-gen DC transports (NDP, Homa) is where DC transport security is heading; touches both fabric and security.

What: A protocol design integrating data encryption into emerging datacenter transports with TLS-style NIC offload.

How: Supports NIC offloading modeled on TLS-over-TCP, a native protocol number alongside TCP/UDP, and a message-based abstraction for low-latency parallel RPCs. (Short paper — abstract is thin; treat as a direction-setter, not a finished design.)

Where applicable: General DC-transport proposal; early-stage.

encryption data-center-fabric

items.title: Direct-to-Cell Satellite Network without Satellite Navigation (SN²)
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Wei Liu et al. (Tsinghua)

Video

Why: The failure mode is fundamentally an authn/authz-and-location problem in disguise — GNSS as an implicit trust dependency for access control is a framing the identity-minded PM will appreciate.

What: Shows direct-to-cell satellite networks' over-reliance on GNSS for geolocation/timing causes mis-billing, unauthorized service, and denials, and proposes self-navigation from the satellites themselves.

How: A "fate-sharing" approach reusing the direct-to-cell satellites for built-in navigation, trading navigation accuracy for availability; validated with commodity satellite phones on 3GPP NTN stacks.

Where applicable: Direct-to-cell / NTN satellite systems; the trust-dependency lesson generalizes beyond space.

mobile routing-protocols

items.title: Falcon: A Reliable, Low Latency Hardware Transport
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Arjun Singhvi, Nandita Dukkipati et al. (Google, with Meta/Nvidia/Microsoft)

Video

Why: RoCE's PFC/special-fabric dependence limits where hardware transport can go; a multi-vendor general-purpose alternative is strategically significant for DC NIC direction.

What: The first hardware transport supporting multiple Upper Layer Protocols and heterogeneous workloads on lossy, general-purpose Ethernet without special switch support.

How: Delay-based congestion control with multipath load balancing, a layered request-response transaction interface for multi-ULP support, hardware retransmission/error handling, and a programmable engine; first implementation hits 200 Gbps / 120 Mops/sec with op-completion up to 8x lower than CX-7 RoCE under congestion.

Where applicable: Broad ambition (general Ethernet DC), but it's hardware transport — realization depends on NIC silicon adoption; the cross-vendor authorship is itself the signal.

ai-networks rdma silicon

items.title: Firefly: Scalable, Ultra-Accurate Clock Synchronization for Datacenters
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Pooria Namyar et al. (Google, USC, NVIDIA)

Video

Why: Precise time quietly underpins distributed consistency, certificate/token validity windows, and ordering — sub-10ns in software is a striking result with security and distributed-systems reach.

What: A software-driven clock-sync system hitting sub-10ns device-to-device and ≤1µs device-to-UTC in a 248-machine Clos, resilient to time-server failure and unstable clocks.

How: Distributed consensus on a random overlay graph with gradual hardware-clock adjustment, plus "layered synchronization" decoupling internal (device-to-device) from external (to-UTC) sync.

Where applicable: Datacenter timing (e.g., cloud financial exchanges); software-only, broadly applicable where hardware PTP is impractical.

time-sync data-center-fabric

items.title: Formalizing Dependence of Web Infrastructure
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Rumaisa Habib, Kimberly Ruth, Gautam Akiwate, Zakir Durumeric (Stanford)

Video

Why: Relevant to identity/PKI via the CA-dependence lens and to resilience reasoning generally.

What: A rigorous statistical metric for Internet centralization that disentangles centralization from regionalization across hosting, DNS, and CAs in 150 countries.

How: A suite of statistical tools applied across three web-infrastructure layers.

Where applicable: General measurement/policy toolkit. (Note: the program text for "Hummingbird: Fast, Flexible, and Fair Inter-Domain Bandwidth Reservations" is an identical copy of this centralization abstract — Hummingbird's title is about bandwidth reservations, so its abstract appears mis-pasted in the program; flagging rather than guessing its content.)

measurement dns

items.title: Fornax: A Hardware-Centric Session Management in Large Public Cloud Network
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Heng Yu et al. (Zhongguancun Lab, Tencent, Peking U.)

Video

Why: SmartNIC-accelerated cloud network functions live or die on their management mechanism; flow-as-unit, one-way command models don't scale to huge tables.

What: A shift from software-centric to hardware-centric management using session (not flow) as the unit, managing up to 16M sessions while cutting software storage 80% and CPU 77%.

How: A session-empowered hardware engine plus two-way hardware-driven management protocols and a lightweight software manager for scalability.

Where applicable: Tencent-specific SmartNIC production setup; the session-as-unit + two-way-protocol idea is a transferable design principle.

cloud-native silicon

items.title: From ATOP to ZCube: Automated Topology Optimization Pipeline and a Cost-Effective Topology for Large Model Training
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Paper Recording

Zihan Yan, Dan Li et al. (Tsinghua, Zhongguancun Lab, ByteDance)

Video

Why: DC topology design for training clusters is core physical-networking work, and an automated search plus a concrete new topology is more useful than another hand-tuned fabric.

What: A pipeline that treats topology as hyperparameters to search at tens-of-thousands-of-GPU scale, yielding ZCube, which claims 3–7% faster training and 26–46% lower hardware cost vs ROFT/Rail-only/HPN.

How: Models topology as an optimization problem over training traffic, collective performance, fault tolerance, and cost; evaluated in build/optimize/expand scenarios and validated on a real testbed (25% cost cut vs rail-optimized).

Where applicable: General topology-design methodology for GPU clusters; results are simulation-heavy with a testbed check.

ai-networks data-center-fabric

items.title: Hermes: Enhancing Layer-7 Cloud Load Balancers with Userspace-Directed I/O Event Notification
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Tian Pan et al. (Alibaba Cloud)

Video

Why: eBPF on the datapath solving a real L7 LB connection-distribution problem (epoll-exclusive LIFO skew, reuseport blindness to worker health) is squarely cloud-native networking.

What: A framework making userspace worker status drive kernel connection dispatch, deployed on O(100K) cores across 33 Alibaba regions, cutting daily worker hangs 99.8% and L7 LB unit cost 18.9%.

How: Lock-free worker-status management plus eBPF overriding reuseport socket selection in a closed loop from userspace to kernel.

Where applicable: General Linux/eBPF technique usable in any Envoy/proxy-style fleet; the scale numbers are Alibaba-specific.

load-balancing linux-networking cloud-native

items.title: InfiniteHBD: Datacenter-Scale High-Bandwidth Domain for LLM with Optical Circuit Switching Transceivers
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Paper Recording

Chenchen Shou et al. (Peking U. / StepFun / Lightelligence)

Video

Why: HBD architecture (NVL-72 vs TPU-style) is a live topology/cost/fault-domain debate; this proposes a genuinely different point in that space.

What: A transceiver-centric HBD that embeds optical circuit switching into each transceiver, giving reconfigurable point-to-multipoint links and variable-size ring topologies at ~31% of NVL-72 cost with node-level fault isolation.

How: A silicon-photonic OCS transceiver (OCSTrx), a reconfigurable k-hop ring topology, and an HBD-DCN orchestration algorithm; evaluation claims near-zero GPU waste and 3.37x MFU vs DGX.

Where applicable: Aimed at LLM-training fabrics; depends on custom silicon-photonic transceivers, so it's a direction/architecture signal rather than commodity-deployable today.

optics ai-networks data-center-fabric

items.title: Inter-domain Routing with Extensible Criteria (IREC)
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Seyedali Tabaeiaghdaei et al. (Anapaya, ETH Zurich, others)

Video

Why: BGP/datapath internals and path-aware networking are in scope; extensible inter-domain criteria is a forward-looking control-plane idea.

What: An inter-domain routing architecture for SCION enabling path optimization on extensible, end-domain-specified criteria.

How: Parallel execution and real-time addition of independent route computations over SCION's stateless forwarding, with negligible global cost vs static routing in large-scale simulation.

Where applicable: SCION/path-aware networks specifically; not deployable on vanilla BGP.

routing-protocols network-security

items.title: Mosaic: Breaking the Optics versus Copper Trade-off with a Wide-and-Slow Architecture and MicroLEDs
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Kaoutar Benyahya et al. (Microsoft Research / Microsoft Azure)

Video

Why: Link reach/power/reliability is the binding constraint on future DC fabric scaling; this directly targets the copper-vs-optics wall the PM cares about.

What: A new link technology that abandons the few-high-speed-channels model for hundreds of parallel low-speed channels, claiming copper-beating reach at up to 69% lower power and better reliability than current optics.

How: "Wide-and-slow" spatial multiplexing using directly-modulated microLEDs (not lasers) over massively multi-core imaging fibers, eliminating laser drivers and complex electronics; prototype shows 100 channels × 2Gbps scaling toward 800Gbps+ at up to 50m.

Where applicable: Protocol-agnostic and designed to drop in without server/switch changes — broadly applicable in principle, but still a research prototype, not a shipping transceiver.

optics data-center-fabric cabling

items.text:

Paper Recording

Yifei Yuan et al. (Alibaba Cloud)

Video

Why: A multi-year production verification story with hard before/after numbers (misconfig incidents 56% → 5%) is the kind of operational evidence worth seeing.

What: A distributed evolution of Hoyan scaling to O(10^4) routers, millions of prefixes, billions of flows, plus a route-change-intent specification language (RCL).

How: Centralized-to-distributed simulation (5x faster), RCL for expressing/verifying route-change intents, and an enhanced accuracy-diagnosis framework.

Where applicable: Alibaba-specific WAN, but the RCL idea and the distributed-simulation approach transfer.

items.title: Orderlock: A New Type of Deadlock and its Implications on HPN Protocol Design
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Wildcard pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Paper Recording

Weihao Jiang et al. (SJTU, Nanjing U.)

Video

Why: A genuine impossibility result is the kind of conceptual lever that outlasts any benchmark and reshapes how to reason about transport feature combinations.

What: Proves that in-order delivery + lossless transmission + out-of-order capability are jointly impossible without risking a new deadlock class ("Orderlock"), and explores Orderlock-free designs.

How: Formal necessary-and-sufficient-condition proof, plus a case study tuning AI-workload performance under Orderlock-free protocols.

Where applicable: General theory for HPN protocol/hardware co-design — a reasoning tool, not a system.

rdma ai-networks

items.title: PreTE: Traffic Engineering with Predictive Failures
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Congcong Miao et al. (Tencent, MIT, UCSB, Meta, Tsinghua)

Video

Why: Fiber cuts are rare-but-disruptive WAN events; folding measured optical-layer degradation into TE is a fresh, physically grounded angle on availability.

What: A TE system that factors dynamic fiber-cut probabilities into tunnel planning, supporting up to 2x more demand at equal availability.

How: Per-second optical-layer measurements show failure probability jumps orders of magnitude in an ephemeral degradation state; PreTE predicts from that and proactively updates tunnels then re-optimizes allocation.

Where applicable: WAN operators with optical-layer telemetry; assumes access to per-second optical data.

sdn ml-for-networking

items.title: RevDNS: Reliable and Decentralized Certificate Revocation via DNS
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Paper Recording

Protick Bhowmick, Dave Levin, Taejoong Chung (Virginia Tech, U. Maryland)

Video

Why: Web-PKI revocation is broken and OCSP-over-CDN recentralizes trust (Akamai serves ~62% of revocation responses) — directly relevant to the PM's PKI/identity interest.

What: A DNS-based revocation scheme where resolvers answer ~99.8% of checks locally without contacting a CA, with no added latency and no extra user disclosure.

How: Revoked serials live in DNSSEC-signed TXT records; NSEC proofs enable aggressive negative caching; a large CA like Let's Encrypt can publish 612M certificates in a 345MB zone.

Where applicable: General web-PKI proposal; a concrete alternative to OCSP and short-lived certs that keeps revocation authority with CAs.

pki dns

items.title: Revisiting RDMA Reliability for Lossy Fabrics (DCP)
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Wenxue Li et al. (HKUST, Huawei)

Video

Why: Getting RDMA off PFC/lossless is one of the cycle's central transport problems and directly relevant to lossless-fabric work.

What: A switch+RNIC co-designed transport that is PFC-independent, RTO-free, packet-spray-compatible, and offload-friendly, claiming 1.6x/2.1x gains over SOTA lossless/lossy RDMA.

How: DCP-Switch adds a simple lossless control plane that DCP-RNIC uses for header-only-based retransmission and bitmap-free packet tracking; prototyped on Tofino2 + FPGA.

Where applicable: General DC RDMA technique, but requires coordinated switch and RNIC changes (prototype silicon), so deployment implies a fabric+NIC co-upgrade.

rdma congestion-control

items.title: S2: A Distributed Configuration Verifier for Hyper-Scale Networks
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Dan Wang et al. (Xi'an Jiaotong, Northwest U., ByteDance)

Video

Why: Config verification is operationally adjacent; single-box verifiers stall past ~10K switches / 1000M routes that large providers actually run.

What: A scale-out verifier reaching 10K routers and 1000M routes within 2 hours by distributing across servers.

How: Partitions the network model and distributes control-plane simulation + data-plane verification across machines, with prefix sharding to cut per-server memory; built on Batfish.

Where applicable: Large service-provider/DC networks that outgrew single-server Batfish; general approach.

testing automation

items.title: Software-based Live Migration for RDMA (MigrRDMA)
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Xiaoyu Li et al. (Tsinghua / Microsoft Research)

Video

Why: RDMA live migration has been "needs NIC support, never ships"; doing it in software on commodity RNICs unblocks host maintenance without hardware changes.

What: A software RDMA live-migration layer with little downtime and only 3–9% datapath overhead, adding ~3s to migrated Hadoop job completion.

How: A software indirection layer that keeps RDMA state identical across source and destination from the application's view, enabling transparent switchover; prototyped on Mellanox RNICs.

Where applicable: General technique on commodity RNICs (validated on Mellanox) — broadly relevant to anyone running RDMA workloads in VMs/containers.

rdma orchestration

items.title: SpliDT: Partitioned Decision Trees for Scalable Stateful Inference at Line Rate
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Murayyiam Parvez et al. (Purdue, Michigan, UCSB, Open U. Israel, NIKSUN)

Video

Why: In-network ML for security monitoring usually assumes all features upfront; this confronts the data-plane stateful-feature constraint honestly.

What: A framework supporting up to 5x more stateful features and scaling to millions of flows by partitioning decision-tree inference over a sliding packet window.

How: Sequential subtrees each using their own top-k features, with an in-band control channel via packet recirculation managing transitions and reusing match keys/registers; a joint training/DSE workflow optimizes feature allocation, depth, and partitioning.

Where applicable: RMT programmable switches/SmartNICs; a general data-plane-ML technique constrained by switch resources.

ml-for-networking programmable-dataplane

items.title: Threading the Ocean: Mapping Digital Routes Across Submarine Cables using Calypso
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Caleb Wang et al. (Northwestern, U. Oregon)

Video

Why: Submarine cables are the physical WAN backbone with real security/economic exposure; mapping traffic to cables is genuine DC/WAN-interconnect infrastructure work.

What: A framework mapping traceroutes to the submarine cables they traverse, plus "Route Stress," a metric estimating cable criticality.

How: Infers traceroute-to-cable mappings despite industry opacity and validates with case studies on SCN vulnerability.

Where applicable: Global connectivity/resilience analysis; research framework.

optics measurement interconnection

items.title: Understanding and Profiling CXL.mem Using PathFinder
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Adjacent pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Abstract Paper Recording

Xiao Li et al. (UW-Madison/Beihang, Intel)

Video

Why: CXL memory pooling is becoming widely deployed and can stall co-located apps; the community lacks end-to-end profiling, which matters for DC resource disaggregation.

What: A utility that captures CXL.mem execution end-to-end between CPU and remote DIMM for profiling, bottleneck analysis, and anomaly diagnosis.

How: Models the CXL.mem data path as an execution graph from architectural performance counters and applies graph analysis to associate CXL with competing memory flows.

Where applicable: Servers with CXL.mem; a general diagnostic tool, increasingly relevant as memory disaggregation lands.

cxl benchmarking

items.title: Unlocking Superior Performance in Reconfigurable DCNs with Credit-Based Transport (Flare)
items.text:
SIGCOMM 2025 digest Program Core pick Coimbra · 8–11 September 2025

Paper Recording

Federico De Marchi et al. (MPI-INF, Meta, NVIDIA)

Video

Why: Reconfigurable (microsecond-switched) DCNs are a credible post-Moore alternative to Clos, but transport has been the gap; this closes part of it.

What: A credit-based transport that lets RDCNs beat Clos on throughput (up to 1.15x even under adversarial traffic) and substantially cut flow completion times vs NDP/ExpressPass/TDTCP/Bolt.

How: Reliable credit-based delivery that opportunistically routes over the RDCN's rapidly reconfiguring short-path circuits; testbed on programmable switches + DPDK.

Where applicable: Applies to reconfigurable-DCN designs specifically — relevant if/when RDCNs are on the table; mostly simulation plus a feasibility testbed.

congestion-control optics

items.title: ZENITH: Towards a Formally Verified Highly-Available Control Plane
items.text:

Abstract Paper Recording

Pooria Namyar et al. (USC, Google)

Video

Why: The "correct-by-construction vs. periodic reconcile" argument maps directly onto Kubernetes-style controller design the PM will recognize.

What: A microservice SDN controller that avoids state inconsistency by design, machine-verified, resolving inconsistencies 5x faster than reconciliation-based designs.

How: A formally verified specification with code auto-generated from it, plus abstractions letting developers independently verify SDN apps.

items.title: AIOps: Prove It! An Open Letter to Vendors Selling AI for SREs
items.text:
SREcon25 Americas digest Program Wildcard pick 25–27 March 2025

Charity Majors and Fred Hebert, Honeycomb.io (Closing Plenary) — Wildcard

ml-for-networking sre observability

automation capacity-planning

items.title: Lies Programmers Believe About Memory

Chris Down, Meta (Linux kernel memory management maintainer) — Adjacent

Video

  • Why: A from-the-source explanation of Linux kernel memory internals (TLBs, page tables, cgroup memory classes) from an actual kernel memory-management maintainer — low-level systems knowledge that underlies performance/reliability work on any Linux-hosted infrastructure, DC or cloud.
  • What: A tour of kernel memory management internals — CPU memory hardware abstractions (TLBs, page tables) and Linux's own internal memory classes and their often-misunderstood properties — aimed at helping SREs reason correctly about application memory behavior. (from abstract only)
  • How: Explains the actual mechanics of virtual memory, page tables, and cgroup-based memory accounting rather than treating them as opaque abstractions. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for anyone debugging memory-related performance or reliability issues on Linux, DC or cloud; particularly relevant to cgroups-based container/Kubernetes memory limits.

linux-networking

items.text:
SREcon25 Americas digest Program Core pick 25–27 March 2025

Recording

Steve Dodd, Slack — Core

Video

  • Why: An argument that classical network-engineering techniques (graph theory, the discrete math underlying traditional routing/traffic-engineering work) are directly applicable to modern cloud service-oriented architecture — and a concrete method for per-service traffic attribution without paying for vendor flow-logging products.
  • What: A framework for building per-service network traffic attribution in cloud infrastructure using network-graph analysis techniques borrowed from traditional network engineering (the kind of work "manual OSPF metric tuning" represents), without relying on expensive vendor logging solutions. (from abstract only)
  • How: Applies graph-theoretic analysis of network topology/flow to optimize data flow, routing, and resilience visibility at the service level — essentially traffic engineering applied to service-mesh-era cloud infrastructure. (from abstract only)

items.text:

Video

items.title: 25 Years of SwissIX – A Quarter Century of Peering in Switzerland
items.text:
SwiNOG #41 digest Program Adjacent pick 28 April 2026

Slides Recording

Arist Volger - SwissIX

VideoPDF

  • Why: Beyond the retrospective, this doubles as the SwissIX operational update, and the IXP industry trends it names (big flows moving to PNIs, cross-connects as a hot topic, rising expectations of free ports, IX bandwidth growth slowing) are directly relevant to DC interconnect and peering strategy anywhere.
  • What: SwissIX crossed the 1 Tbps peak mark (Terabit Club member #77), serving >240 peers across 8 PoPs. Recent and planned changes: backbone upgraded to 400 Gbps (enabling retirement of the end-of-life "Groove" platform), 400G ports now available at ColoZueri, Digital Realty ZUR1, and Equinix ZH4 (second maintenance window in June), a new PoP at CERN Geneva (initially an aggregation switch, to be upgraded to a Nokia 7750-2s like the other PoPs), and secured expansion space at Equinix ZH4. Organizationally: a lean model of 5 volunteer board members, 1 FTE peering development manager, and outsourced 24x7 operations. Pricing: 100G port prices cut from HY2 2026, free upgrades for the rest of 2026, no OTCs for new ports >1G for new peers.
  • How: N/A — an operational and organizational update, not a technique.
  • Where applicable: Swiss-market-specific details, but the structural trends (PNI offload of large flows, free-port expectations, outsourced IXP ops) generalize to similar national IXPs (their comparison set: BCIX, BIX.hu, LU-CIX, NAMEX, VIX.at).
