items.title: Federated Network Troubleshooting: Deploying HAWAT and Looking Glass Across the R&E Community
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Karl Newell, Matt Mullins (Internet2)

PPTX

  • Why: Federated troubleshooting is a collective-goods problem no single operator can solve alone, and this is one of the first working examples — plus an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) cross-organization diagnostic PoC that previews where AIOps goes next. (from abstract only; slides were not extractable)
  • What: HAWAT has moved from experimental to production on Internet2's network, with open-source containers available. The breakthrough is federation: a Looking Glass service lets each organization independently deploy and control which commands it exposes, and HAWAT queries multiple instances to diagnose cross-network issues — isolating packet loss between universities or tracing BGP behavior across peers. An A2A interoperability PoC with SURF demonstrated AI agents from independent NRENs collaborating on network diagnostics across organizational boundaries.
  • How: Each org runs its own Looking Glass instance under its own policy; HAWAT aggregates queries across instances; demonstrations ran in a multi-network virtual environment, with a participation path for other networks.
  • Where applicable: R&E community context and requires peer organizations to actually deploy instances (the perfSONAR-style network-effect problem). The A2A piece is proof-of-concept stage, not production.

ai troubleshooting observability

items.title: From Public Cloud AI to National Infrastructure: Lessons from Sunet Scribe
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Adjacent pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Erik Lundberg (Sunet)

PDF

  • Why: A rare, fully-costed-in-public view of running a national AI inference service on a small GPU fleet — the operational reality behind "sovereign AI services."
  • What: Sunet Scribe, a self-hosted, Whisper-based speech-to-text service inside the Swedish NREN, born because institutions didn't trust commercial providers with sensitive recordings and commercial STT wasn't optimized for Nordic languages (the fine-tuned Swedish model comes from the Royal Library). Timeline: community request mid-February 2026 → prototype and first GPU machines in May → institutional pilot October 1 → national launch December 1. Traction: 30 universities, ~3,000 users, ~650,000 minutes transcribed in 2026 (3–4× the 2025 baseline) — handled by three GPU servers.
  • How: Deliberate architecture choices: self-hosted with federated login, zero-access model, automatic retention; integrated with Kaltura (and NextCloud in 2026) with a published API; open-source, modular, with swappable models and components — consolidating what had been parallel commercial/secure/internal STT pipelines into one operational platform.
  • Where applicable: Nordic-language and trust context is specific, but the pattern — small GPU fleet, open models, platform integration, one year from request to national service — is a transferable template for institutions weighing public-cloud AI vs. self-hosted.

ai cloud open-source

items.title: Honeypots and beyond – LLMs in cyberdefence
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Wildcard pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PDF)

Maciej Miłostan, Michał Ślusarczyk (PCSS)

PDF 1PDF 2

  • Why: An unusual, operationally grounded intersection of LLMs and security: LLMs inside the honeypot, engaging attackers — and the new attack surface that creates.
  • What: Threat-intel collection from the GN5-2 honeynet (T-Pot based, with Kibana visualizations and sandboxing pipelines), plus the synergy of pairing honeypots with LLMs. Crucially, they instrument the failure modes: LangFuse monitoring tracks session abandonments caused by LLM failures (e.g. unrealistic interaction), and they compare robust, secure system prompts against poorly crafted ones that leak system details or allow instruction hijacking — showing prompt quality directly influences both detection accuracy and resistance to prompt injection.
  • How: LLM-driven interactive decoys produce richer attacker behavioral data than static honeypots, at the cost of becoming a prompt-injection surface themselves; the evaluation methodology (tracking abandonment, comparing prompt classes) is the transferable part.
  • Where applicable: Self-hosted LLM stacks in defensive security operations; findings are from a live NREN honeynet rather than a lab.

ai threat-intelligence

items.title: Instant Data Structures via Shared Memory
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Wildcard pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Roman Janota (CESNET)

PPTX

  • Why: A small systems idea with an outsized, verified result — and it generalizes well beyond network tooling.
  • What: The boot-up bottleneck of network management systems: every tool re-parses hundreds of device configuration files to build its structural map of the network, serially, on every start. CESNET's answer: parse once, share the result. The first program to start builds the data structure, publishes a handle ("link") to it in a shared-memory region; every subsequent program checks for an existing link and skips parsing entirely. Changes (e.g. a new node) are published by generating a new link to the changed structure and atomically replacing the old one, with consumers checking for a newer link on access — a copy-on-write publication pattern.
  • How: Plain shared memory plus handle indirection; no exotic infrastructure. Benchmarks show boot-up times up to 400×+ faster than re-parsing, with the gap so large the improved bars are barely visible on the charts.
  • Where applicable: General technique for any tool family that re-derives the same large, mostly-static data structure from source files at startup — network inventory, config linting, query engines. Linux-centric; the pattern is cheap to adopt.

automation configuration-management benchmarking

items.title: Machine Learning for Anomaly Detection in RNP Network Operations
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Guilherme Branco Ladvocat (RNP)

PPTX

  • Why: A realistic template for ML adoption in network operations by a team with no data scientists — increasingly the default situation, and a useful counterweight to the ESnet approach.
  • What: RNP (Brazilian NREN, ~1800 connected sites, MPLS-TE full-mesh between PoPs) applied ML anomaly detection to interface metrics, ping loss/latency, netflow, and syslog categorization (standard vs. rare message groups). The deliberately pragmatic choice: Elastic's ELSER v2, an out-of-domain model requiring no fine-tuning, running inside the Elastic observability stack they already stood up in 2024 — avoiding "reinventing the wheel" and the need for ML expertise.
  • How: Baseline learning on telemetry time series flags deviations where static thresholds fail (interface delay, utilization, netflow anomalies, latency); dashboards group anomalies so the algorithm does the first pass of analysis and engineers interpret. The observability journey started in 2018 with push-model, high-resolution telemetry.
  • Where applicable: RNP-specific stack (Elastic), but the incremental, no-data-scientist adoption path is broadly replicable. The stated limitations are honest and important: the model doesn't reason about values, root-cause analysis isn't achieved by a single anomaly-detection job, and engineers still have to interpret the output.

ml-for-networking anomaly-detection observability

items.title: Network Flow Monitoring: An Evaluation of Modern Collector Software
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX)

Yannick Huber (BelWü / University of Stuttgart), with Benjamin Steinert, Lukas Pietzschmann, Gabriel Paradzik, Michael Menth (Tübingen, Ulm)

PPTXPDF

  • Why: Firmly substantiated, quantitative tool evaluation — exactly the kind most teams never have time to do. Benchmarks six actively maintained, self-hostable open-source flow collectors (Akvorado, GoFlow2, IPFIXcol2, nfdump, pmacct, SiLK) for sFlow and IPFIX.
  • What: Combines a feature/usability matrix (protocol support, enrichment, anonymization, Kafka/file outputs, telemetry endpoints) with sustainable-throughput benchmarks in a controlled testbed (synthetic generator, 20 flows per packet, 4 CPU cores / 12 GB RAM). Headline numbers: to Kafka, pmacct sustains ~186–209k flows/s, IPFIXcol2 ~375–446k, GoFlow2 ~13–15k (JSON) vs. ~77–86k (protobuf), Akvorado ~510–548k (raw forwarding); to file, nfdump reaches up to ~842k flows/s (IPFIX) and IPFIXcol2 ~680k. Main findings: input format matters (IPFIXcol2 and nfdump do best on IPFIX; SiLK and pmacct lag on sFlow), output serialization is crucial (GoFlow2's JSON path is an order of magnitude slower than protobuf), and message brokers enable horizontal scaling and redundant deployments.
  • How: Found the sustainable processing rate by ramping packet rate while verifying flows in equals flows out; also documents production drop-detection tactics (canary flows, indirect CPU/memory/interface monitoring) since most collectors lack adequate telemetry endpoints.
  • Where applicable: Results are dimensioned to a specific testbed (4 cores, 20 flows/packet — decapsulation overhead rises with fewer flows per packet) and the authors flag open questions (custom IPFIX fields, resource scaling). The load-testing tool is open-sourced (go-nflow-stresstest on Codeberg), so the benchmark is reproducible. No single winner — the value is the selection/dimensioning guidance.

observability benchmarking open-source

items.title: Procurement of dark fiber and optical spectrum for the new research network in Norway. Strategies and learnings
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Olaf Schjeldrup (Sikt)

PPTX

  • Why: Physical WAN infrastructure strategy with real numbers and two years of negotiation scar tissue — squarely relevant to anyone whose job includes DC/WAN interconnect economics. Norway's NREN renewal covers ~13,000 km of renewed optical long-haul topology across punishing geography (3,000 km north–south, 103,000 km of coastline), with geopolitical tension explicitly cited as a driver for higher validated redundancy.
  • What: Requirements: national coverage, terabit capacities with a preference order of dark fiber > optical spectrum (1–1.2 THz, flexigrid, license-free) > waves; 20-year IRU matching Open Line System lifetime; fiber sensing and bidirectional time-and-frequency transfer capability; extra fiber pairs reserved for research (quantum, sensing). Process: RFI spring 2023, RFQ end-2023, award criteria 60% quality / 40% TCO, 10 tenderers (3 hybrid fiber+spectrum, 7 fiber-only), negotiated procedure running over two years with six offer/negotiation phases, BAFO May 2025, award January 2026 to 8 sub-providers, main contracts May 2026, rollout 2026–28 — with "huge cost savings, increased optical footprint and redundancy."
  • How: The evaluation complexity (choosing one path alters preferences for many others) was made manageable by dividing the country into 5 regions, evaluating inter-regional legs with add/drops at essential locations, backed by purpose-built evaluation models. Tactical tips: dark-fiber monopolies are consolidating and prices are rising on datacenter-industry demand; asking for both fiber and spectrum widens real competition; spectrum providers with greenfield DWDM plans will install L-band sensing and bidirectional T&F channels for you; multi-subprovider strategies cost more effort but save money and add diversity.
  • Where applicable: Norwegian market and geography, but the procurement playbook (competition structure, evaluation decomposition, IRU terms, research fiber pairs) transfers to any large fiber buyer. Explicitly org-specific in outcomes; the strategy is the export.

optics cabling interconnection

items.title: Saz: Engineering Safe Agentic Workflows for Real-World Operations
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Fariman Torkashvand (GÉANT)

PPTX

  • Why: Agentic AI that plans actions, calls tools, and triggers real network automation is arriving in operations; this is a concrete architecture for doing it without losing control. The risk framing — hallucinated decisions, escalating costs, unclear accountability — matches what any operator planning agent deployment should be worrying about.
  • What: Saz, a self-hosted agentic workflow engine designed to embed AI in operational environments through structured workflows, human-authored instructions, and strict policy enforcement. Its distinguishing feature is a dual-agent safety model: a verifier agent evaluates the planner agent's output before execution. (from abstract only; slides not extractable)
  • How: Constraints over autonomy — workflows are structured and authored by humans, policy is enforced engine-side, and the verifier/planner split provides an internal check step. The output is patterns for AI-driven workflows that remain controlled, auditable, and human-governed.
  • Where applicable: General pattern, GÉANT-flavored implementation. Self-hosted, which matters for the sovereign-AI theme of the session. Early-stage work rather than a long-production retrospective.

ai automation orchestration

items.title: Streamlining Multi-Vendor Automation: Auto-generated RESTCONF Clients from YANG Models
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Matteo Colantonio (GARR)

PPTX

  • Why: Attacks a tax every multi-vendor automation team pays: hand-written RESTCONF/NETCONF clients per device family. (from abstract only; lightning talk, slides not extractable)
  • What: A GARR-built tool that converts YANG models into developer-friendly, type-safe Python RESTCONF clients (Pydantic-based), giving runtime validation of network configurations before they hit devices.
  • How: Code generation from the device's own YANG schemas rather than hand-maintained bindings — the schema is the contract, and validation falls out of the generated types.
  • Where applicable: General technique for any YANG-speaking fleet; five-minute lightning format, so expect depth to be limited, but the idea is directly stealable.

automation api configuration-management

items.title: The CERN experiments' network journey to IPv6-only
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Adjacent pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Tim Chown (Jisc)

PPTX

  • Why: The best-documented large-scale argument that dual-stack is a waypoint, not a destination — with measured traffic shares to back it.
  • What: The WLCG (170 sites, 40 countries; LHCOPN private optical Tier-0/Tier-1 links, LHCONE L3VPN/VRF, NREN catch-all) IPv6 program: Phase 2 dual-stack is complete at data servers and 75% complete at worker nodes (ticket campaign running since December 2023); Phase 3 — removing IPv4 from WAN links — is underway, starting with CERN–Tier-1 LHCOPN links. Measured shares: >99.5% IPv6 on the KIT OPN link, >93% in FTS logs (including non-WLCG transfers), >99.9% of SciTags flows into RAL.
  • How: HEPiX IPv6 WG methodology — readiness/gap analysis (2011), dual-stack enable-and-prefer (2018–), then active IPv4 decommissioning on WANs, motivated by simpler operation, simpler security, no NAT.
  • Where applicable: Research-grid context, but the phased playbook and the "plan where and when you can turn off IPv4" message apply to any distributed infrastructure that has finished dual-stack and is wondering what's next.

ipv6 interconnection

items.title: The Journey: From Cloud Complexity to Platformisation
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Adjacent pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Joao Pedro Milhome, Alberto Viana (RNP)

PPTX

  • Why: A candid platform-engineering story: adopting containers and cloud tooling made RNP's service delivery more complex, not less — a failure mode most cloud platform teams will recognize.
  • What: RNP's response is an Internal Developer Platform organized around four pillars (Speed, Safety, Efficiency, Scalability), treating the platform as a product with golden paths that reduce cognitive load while leaving flexibility for service teams. The slides narrate the diagnosis: fragmented tools, inconsistent environments, split responsibilities, and days spent configuring plumbing instead of writing code.
  • How: Paved roads as product strategy — the safe, observable path is made the easiest path; declarative intent replaces manual fulfillment (their database-provisioning example); observability and security are built into the road rather than being separate ticket queues.
  • Where applicable: NREN service-organization context (small expert teams, public-interest services, governance requirements), but the platform-as-product approach is the standard enterprise pattern applied honestly — useful as validation rather than novelty.

cloud cloud-native

items.title: This is the end of the network as we know it, and we feel fine
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Aleksandr Kurbatov, Karel van Klink (GÉANT)

PPTX

  • Why: GÉANT has finished migrating its backbone packet layer to a new equipment vendor — and the interesting part is that the orchestration stack (the GÉANT Service Orchestrator, grown out of the Workflow Orchestrator programme) is what made a vendor swap of a pan-European backbone tractable. For anyone building network automation, the hard-won modeling decisions here transfer directly.
  • What: A migration retrospective plus the orchestration model it enabled. The core of the presentation (per the slides) is how GÉANT models commercial peers: each peer is a single entity (ASN, prefix limit) that can hold multiple connections to different placement port types — IX port, private peering port, or transit port — explicitly avoiding a data-duplication anti-pattern. The same operator workflow produces different router configurations (communities, policies, BGP groups, prefix-limit handling) depending only on which port type the connection targets.
  • How: A layered model in the orchestrator where connection Type is derived automatically from the target placement port; Ansible extracts the type, pulls the correct variables, and translates the orchestrator abstraction (one Peering Connection grouping IPv4+IPv6) into two independent BGP neighbor statements on the router. Per-connection Session States (Provisioning → Active → Disabled) act as predefined configuration shortcuts — e.g. Provisioning establishes BGP without route exchange, Disabled keeps all config in place but shuts down the neighbors. "One update, one workflow" propagates a peer change (e.g. prefix limit) across all of that peer's connections while leaving co-located peers untouched.
  • Where applicable: GÉANT-specific backbone and orchestrator, but the patterns — model per organization not per port, port-type-derived config, session-state shortcuts, safe scoped deletion in multi-peer environments — are broadly applicable to any operator automating multi-site peering across IX, private, and transit contexts.

automation bgp orchestration

items.title: Time Travels in the L-Band: Deploying a National White Rabbit Infrastructure over Active DWDM Networks
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Core pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Michal Hazlinsky (CESNET)

PDF

  • Why: A blueprint for running nanosecond-grade time distribution on an active, revenue-carrying DWDM network instead of dedicated dark fiber — plus one of the best examples of real NetDevOps automation at the optical layer (L0).
  • What: CESNET distributes time traceable to UTC(TP) with better than 1 ns stability to 22 locations, with White Rabbit running in the L-band (1570/1571/1572 nm) coexisting with 8 C-band data channels on the same fiber of its 5,700 km multivendor network (Cisco, Ribbon/ECI, CzechLight). Spectrum-sharing was designed in from procurement: custom channel filters per line (8 C + 4 L channels, <1 dB insertion loss), bidirectional single-fiber transmission to defeat WR's path-asymmetry problem, and CzechLight SDN bidirectional EDFAs for long-haul.
  • How: Open-source SDN-controlled BiDi amplifiers (NETCONF/RESTCONF, YANG model, IETF YANG-Push streaming telemetry with sub-second latencies) managed via Ansible with a NetBox inventory — actual DevOps playbooks at the photonic layer. Calibration is treated as a first-class engineering problem: measuring Tx/Rx filter delay asymmetry, chromatic-dispersion asymmetry per line, and a field procedure using the Safran Z16's port-mode survey plus switched Tx/Rx wavelengths so a second WR switch and external counter aren't needed on site. Lessons: transceiver Tx-power variance means power budgets must be recalculated on replacement (keep fixed attenuators in reachable locations), and logical topology reconfiguration can require WRS reboots.
  • Where applicable: Requires a spectrum-sharing design (reserved L-band channels and filters) — cheapest on greenfield builds — and CESNET's own CzechLight hardware, but the hardware designs and software are open. The calibration methods and the L-band coexistence technique are broadly reusable; "standard APIs are MUST HAVE" is the summary lesson.

time-sync optics automation

items.title: Toward Scalable Quantum Networks: Lessons from InterQnet
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Wildcard pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Rajkumar Kettimuthu (Argonne National Laboratory)

PPTX

  • Why: Not the PM's daily bread, but a two-year progress report on the US DOE's full-stack quantum networking program that frames quantum networks as an operations problem — and argues NRENs already own the prerequisites (deployed fiber, automation, synchronization, optical-channel engineering).
  • What: InterQnet runs two tightly coupled goals. InterQnet-Achieve: a three-node heterogeneous quantum network (Yb atom arrays, Er³⁺ ions, superconducting qubits) over deployed campus fiber with dark-fiber paths toward Fermilab, UChicago, and StarLight, using frequency conversion and microwave-to-optical transduction, under centralized SDN-style orchestration with automated calibration. InterQnet-Scale: architecture studies via SeQUeNCe, Argonne's ~7-year-old quantum network simulator, with device-faithful simulations checked against real measurements. Hardware progress cited: 0.95 spin–photon fidelity with parallelized entanglement demonstrated on a 5-atom Yb array at 1389 nm; 1000× linewidth narrowing and telecom-band emission for Er; improved resonator yield for transducers.
  • How: The co-design loop is the point — devices inform simulation, simulation guides architecture, architecture feeds back into hardware requirements — explicitly because the field's gap is between lab experiments and scalable architecture (no interoperable abstractions, no standard way to request entanglement, no common scalability metrics).
  • Where applicable: Research program, not deployable today — but the framing that quantum networking resembles early classical networking (manual setup, static config, platform-specific interfaces) and that scale requires architecture, abstraction, and operations is exactly the signal to watch.

quantum-networking

items.title: Traffic at 3am: Armed with a Toothpick against AI Scrapers
items.text:
TNC26 (GÉANT research networking conference) digest Program Adjacent pick 8–12 June 2026

Abstract Slides

Cheryl Andrea Fernando (SURF)

PPTX

  • Why: AI training scrapers are now an operational cost and risk problem for anyone serving public content — and the defensive landscape is fragmenting fast. Lightning-talk depth, but a useful map.
  • What: A survey of mitigation strategies: robots.txt (voluntary, widely ignored), Cloudflare's AI Labyrinth (trapping non-compliant crawlers), monetization via Cloudflare Pay-per-Crawl and Akamai's Tolbit/Skyfire, open-source countermeasures like Anubis (proof-of-work gating that makes bot traffic expensive) and tarpits (Nepenthes, Quixotic, Iocane — feeding Markov babble to poison training data, with real caveats: SEO damage and self-inflicted resource costs). The genuinely hard problem: residential proxies, which defeat datacenter-IP blocklists because the IPs are real home connections, often resold without their owners' knowledge.
  • How: The promising detection thread is TLS fingerprinting (JA4+ from FoxIO, already adopted by Cloudflare and DataDome): deprecated cipher suites and odd extension combinations flag scraper clients, complementing approaches like the Amadeus research on TCP-vs-TLS round-trip-time differences for detecting residential proxy use. The recommended posture is modular — combine robots.txt, experimental setups, and fingerprinting to fit your risk tolerance.
  • Where applicable: General web-serving context, NREN-specific only in the tension between openness (discoverability) and protection (research data).

ai network-security tls

items.title: 5G and Cellular Network Security
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Multiple papers/teams — see below — Adjacent

  • Why: A dense cluster of 5G/cellular protocol-security papers this cycle — worth a combined mention as a vertical, even though cellular/RAN isn't explicitly named in the PM's core interests, because the architectural patterns (control/data-plane separation, standardized network functions) echo cloud-native networking design.
  • What: AKMA+ (Singapore Management University et al.) finds and fixes vulnerabilities in 5G's Authentication and Key Management for Applications protocol while preserving standards compatibility. SNI5GECT (SUTD) sniffs and injects into pre-authentication 5G NR messages without a rogue base station, achieving 70–90% attack success within 20m. CoreCrisis (Penn State) is a stateful fuzzer that found 13 crashing and 7 spec-deviation vulnerabilities across three open-source and one commercial 5G core implementation. GLaDoS (ETH Zurich / Oxford) is a full-scale deployed system for geofenced cellular denial-of-service in sensitive areas, neutralizing 99.3% of connections across 100+ commercial cells. (from abstract only)
  • How: Varies by paper — protocol formal analysis (AKMA+), pre-auth sniff-and-inject (SNI5GECT), stateful black-box fuzzing with FSM learning (CoreCrisis), and combined overshadowing + localization (GLaDoS). (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: 5G core/RAN operators and equipment vendors specifically; GLaDoS is also relevant to physical-security/sensitive-facility contexts wanting legal, geofenced cellular control.

mobile network-security

items.title: A Framework for Abusability Analysis: The Case of Passkeys in Interpersonal Threat Models
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Alaa Daffalla et al., Cornell University / Cornell Tech; University of Wisconsin–Madison; New York University — Adjacent

  • Why: The first analysis of how passkeys — the largest current push toward passwordless authentication — interact with interpersonal threat models (intimate partner violence, elder abuse), a threat class that's easy to overlook when passkey security is evaluated only against remote attackers.
  • What: An abusability-analysis framework applied to 19 passkey-supporting services, finding abuse vectors including flawed implementations that let an abuser maintain ongoing illicit access with no recovery path for the victim, and vectors that let attackers lock victims out or gaslight them. (from abstract only)
  • How: A general framework for identifying how new authentication features can be exploited by an adversary with routine physical device access and partial credential knowledge — applied specifically to passkey account-recovery and device-management flows. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General framework applicable beyond passkeys; the passkey-specific findings are directly relevant to anyone implementing or evaluating passkey account-recovery UX.

authentication identity privacy

items.title: An Industry Interview Study of Software Signing for Supply Chain Security
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Kelechi G. Kalu et al., Purdue University — Adjacent

Video

  • Why: Software signing is widely recommended by supply-chain security frameworks but adoption remains low — this is the first in-depth practitioner account of why, complementing the technical PKI/cert-validation picks above with the human/organizational side.
  • What: Interviews with 18 experienced security practitioners across 13 organizations on software-signing adoption, surfacing technical, organizational, and human barriers; finds experts disagree on signing's importance and documents how internal/external events (breaches, new regulation) drive adoption. (from abstract only)
  • How: Qualitative interview study producing a refined software-supply-chain factory model highlighting where and why signing practices break down. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for organizations evaluating or mandating software signing as part of supply-chain security policy.

vulnerability-management attestation

items.title: Ares: Comprehensive Path Hijacking Detection via Routing Tree
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Yinxiang Tao et al., Tsinghua University / Zhongguancun Laboratory / Quan Cheng Laboratory; Congcong Miao, Tencent — Core

Video

  • Why: Path hijacking (manipulating AS-path attributes rather than just the origin) is the stealthier successor to origin hijacking specifically designed to evade existing detection — this is a system that closes that gap with real-event validation, not just simulation.
  • What: Ares, a system detecting path hijacking by tracking changes to an AS's "observed prefix routing tree" (OPRT), validated against 12 real-world hijacking events (detected within 5 minutes each) and large-scale simulation (97.2%–99.3% detection rate, 1.06% false-positive rate). (from abstract only)
  • How: Uses weighted edit distance between routing trees to quantify anomalous change, combined with clustering to accelerate detection and heuristics to reduce false positives; generates ~2.31 alerts/hour across the entire Internet. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General BGP route-hijacking detection for network operators and Tier-1/content ASes; a deployable detection system rather than a protocol change.

bgp network-security anomaly-detection

items.title: Assessing the Aftermath: The Effects of a Global Takedown Against DDoS-for-hire Services
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Anh V. Vu et al., University of Cambridge; University of Edinburgh; University of Strathclyde; University of Illinois Chicago — Adjacent

Video

  • Why: A rare quantitative, multi-year measurement of whether law-enforcement disruption actually works against the DDoS-for-hire ecosystem — useful context for anyone evaluating DDoS threat trends rather than just technical mitigation.
  • What: An assessment of the largest booter takedown effort to date (since December 2022), finding over half of seized sites returned within a day, traffic to re-emerged domains dropped 80–90%, and the first takedown wave cut global DDoS volume 20–40% (with a significant effect specifically on UDP-based attacks) — but the overall market proved resilient, with effects lasting at most ~6 weeks. (from abstract only)
  • How: Combines web traffic data, ground-truth visits to seized sites, millions of DDoS attack records, and underground-forum/Telegram chat analysis. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General threat-intelligence context for DDoS trend forecasting; policy-relevant more than technically actionable for network defenders directly.

ddos measurement threat-intelligence

items.title: BGP Vortex: Update Message Floods Can Create Internet Instabilities
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Felix Stöger, ETH Zurich; Henry Birge-Lee, Princeton University; Giacomo Giuliari, Mysten Labs; Jordi Subira-Nieto and Adrian Perrig, ETH Zurich — Core

Video

  • Why: A new BGP instability attack that neither BGPSEC nor RPKI can prevent, because every message involved is a legitimate, standards-compliant BGP UPDATE — a reminder that route-origin validation alone doesn't close the routing-security gap.
  • What: Discovery of the "BGP Vortex," a configuration where just three legitimate BGP UPDATE messages trigger persistent instability, weaponizable to cause router overload and forwarding loops across the Internet. All major router implementations tested were susceptible. (from abstract only)
  • How: Exploits standards-compliant BGP Communities extensions (used for traffic engineering) that allow route-preference modification; the paper proposes a framework for classifying which BGP extensions are similarly dangerous versus safe to deploy. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any BGP-speaking network; the mitigation framework is for router vendors and operators using BGP Communities-based traffic engineering.

bgp network-security

items.title: Catch-22: Uncovering Compromised Hosts Using SSH Public Keys
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Cristian Munteanu et al., Max Planck Institute for Informatics; Delft University of Technology (Distinguished Paper Award Winner) — Wildcard

Video

  • Why: A clever, minimally-invasive Internet-scale detection technique — using SSH's own public-key-authentication challenge behavior to fingerprint compromise without ever needing valid credentials or touching the compromised system — that found state-actor-associated keys inside sensitive ASes.
  • What: A method identifying 21,700+ compromised SSH servers across 1,649 ASes and 144 countries by checking for the presence of known-malicious attacker public keys, without needing to log in or test passwords; surfaced new context on botnets (fritzfrog), threat actors (teamtnt), and state-actor-linked keys in sensitive networks. (from abstract only)
  • How: Exploits the fact that SSH only sends a public-key-authentication challenge if the corresponding key is actually present on the server — letting a scanner test for known malicious keys' presence with zero access and zero risk of triggering an actual login. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General Internet-scale compromise detection; the technique's elegance (a side effect of protocol behavior, not a vulnerability) is the interesting part, applicable anywhere an authentication protocol leaks presence information.

authentication anomaly-detection measurement

items.title: Deanonymizing Ethereum Validators: The P2P Network Has a Privacy Issue
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Lioba Heimbach et al., ETH Zurich; University of Bern; IMDEA Networks — Wildcard

  • Why: Not a blockchain-economics paper — a peer-to-peer network privacy/deanonymization finding (any node can link validator identities to peer IP addresses) that's really a P2P protocol design lesson wearing blockchain clothing, relevant to anyone reasoning about identity-unlinkability guarantees in P2P systems generally.
  • What: Demonstrates the Ethereum P2P network fails to provide its intended validator anonymity — any participating node can link a validator's identifier to a peer's IP address. Using data from just four nodes over three days, the authors located 15%+ of all Ethereum validators, including geographic location and hosting organization. Awarded a bug bounty by the Ethereum Foundation. (from abstract only)
  • How: A methodology for any P2P node to correlate validator identifiers with connected peers' network-level metadata, empirically validated at scale rather than theorized. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: Directly Ethereum-specific in its finding, but the underlying lesson — that P2P protocols claiming participant anonymity need explicit defenses against peer-correlation attacks, not just identifier obfuscation — generalizes to any P2P system with an unlinkability goal.

privacy measurement

items.title: Detecting Compromise of Passkey Storage on the Cloud (CASPER)
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Mazharul Islam et al., University of Wisconsin–Madison; Visa Research — Core

  • Why: Directly addresses a real gap in FIDO2 passkey deployments: cloud-synced passkeys solve the account-recovery problem but reintroduce a breach surface (the passkey management service's cloud storage) that today's defenses can't close without breaking recovery or login UX.
  • What: CASPER, the first framework letting web service providers detect abuse of passkeys leaked from a passkey management service (PMS), even against attackers who strategically adapt to evade detection. (from abstract only)
  • How: Integrates into existing passkey backup/sync/authentication flows with minimal UX impact, negligible performance overhead, and low deployment complexity for participating services. (from abstract only — detection mechanism specifics not given)
  • Where applicable: General for any relying party accepting FIDO2 synced passkeys; directly actionable for services already on the passkey adoption path.

authentication identity vulnerability-management

items.title: Exposing and Circumventing SNI-based QUIC Censorship of the Great Firewall of China
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Ali Zohaib et al., University of Massachusetts Amherst / GFW Report / University of Colorado Boulder / Stanford University — Core

  • Why: A rigorous measurement of a nation-state QUIC-blocking system reveals a real architectural weakness (decryption overhead collapses effectiveness under load) and a real weaponization risk (it can be triggered to block arbitrary UDP traffic between third parties) — directly relevant to anyone reasoning about QUIC/UDP behavior at the network edge.
  • What: The GFW decrypts QUIC Initial packets at scale to apply SNI-based blocking, using a blocklist distinct from its other censorship mechanisms; the paper finds this decryption is computationally expensive enough to fail under moderate traffic and can be weaponized to block unrelated UDP traffic. Circumvention strategies were integrated into Firefox, quic-go, and major circumvention tools. (from abstract only)
  • How: Active measurement characterizes what triggers GFW QUIC blocking; the weaponization angle exploits the same decryption-at-scale mechanism against arbitrary third-party UDP flows. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for QUIC/UDP traffic traversing state-level middleboxes; the weaponization finding is a general lesson about any inline-decryption censorship/inspection architecture, not GFW-specific.

censorship http measurement

items.title: Haunted by Legacy: Discovering and Exploiting Vulnerable Tunnelling Hosts
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Angelos Beitis and Mathy Vanhoef, DistriNet, KU Leuven — Core

  • Why: The same tunneling encapsulation families underlying datacenter and WAN overlay networking — GRE, IPIP, and IPv4/IPv6 translation tunnels — turn out to have over 4 million open, unauthenticated hosts on the public Internet, directly relevant to anyone running or securing tunnel endpoints.
  • What: An Internet-wide scan finding 4M+ hosts that accept unauthenticated IPIP, GRE, 4in6, or 6in4 tunneling traffic, exploitable as one-way proxies, for source-address spoofing, or for access into private networks — plus two new amplification-based DoS attacks (16x and 75x amplification) and an Economic DoS attack that drains a host's outgoing bandwidth. (from abstract only)
  • How: Seven distinct IPv4/IPv6 scan methods identify hosts accepting unauthenticated tunneling traffic; the amplification attacks work by concentrating traffic in time or looping packets between vulnerable hosts. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any network exposing GRE/IPIP/4in6/6in4 tunnel endpoints to the Internet without authentication — directly applicable to DC/WAN overlay and legacy IPv6-transition tunnel deployments specifically, not just an academic curiosity.

vulnerability-management network-security

items.title: Lemon: Network-Wide DDoS Detection with Routing-Oblivious Per-Flow Measurement
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Wenhao Wu et al., Institute of Computing Technology / Chinese Academy of Sciences — Core

  • Why: A DDoS-detection system implemented and evaluated on real programmable switch hardware (Tofino), directly relevant to datapath/programmable-networking work, that solves a genuine correctness problem (over-counting from unpredictable routing) rather than just adding another ML classifier.
  • What: Lemon, a network-wide DDoS detection system that stays accurate even when traffic routing is unpredictable and invalidates the operator's assumed network topology — a failure mode that breaks existing sketch-based measurement systems. (from abstract only)
  • How: A novel "Lemon sketch" data structure in the data plane avoids over-counting and mis-allocation across measurement points; a control plane aggregates sketches for network-wide, per-flow DDoS detection and victim identification. Implemented in both software (Bmv2) and programmable hardware (Tofino) switches. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General DDoS-detection deployments on programmable data-plane hardware (P4/Tofino-class switches); the routing-obliviousness is specifically valuable for networks with dynamic or asymmetric routing.

ddos programmable-dataplane p4

items.title: LEO-Range: Physical Layer Design for Secure Ranging with Low Earth Orbiting Satellites
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Daniele Coppola et al., ETH Zurich; CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security — Wildcard

  • Why: Not a fit for the PM's terrestrial DC/WAN focus directly, but LEO satellite constellations are an increasingly real backhaul/connectivity layer, and this is provably-secure physical-layer ranging design for exactly that emerging infrastructure — the kind of "where the physical network is heading" signal worth having on the radar.
  • What: A physical-layer design for secure distance ranging between LEO satellites and ground devices, compatible with OFDM (used by high-bandwidth satellite links), with a formal security proof bounding an attacker's probability of a distance-reduction attack. Tested with a hardware satellite-channel emulator, limiting spoofing to under a 2⁻²⁰ success probability for a 117m distance-reduction attempt in realistic channel conditions. (from abstract only)
  • How: A novel frequency-domain verification scheme provides provable security against arbitrary physical-layer attack strategies, rather than relying on a specific attacker model. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: LEO satellite communication systems specifically; general technique for physical-layer secure ranging that could generalize to other wireless ranging contexts.

mobile encryption

items.title: Post-Quantum Secure Messaging: Signal, MLS, and iMessage PQ3
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Multiple papers/teams — see below — Adjacent

  • Why: A cluster of formal-methods papers rigorously analyzing post-quantum secure-messaging protocols already in production (Signal's PQXDH, Apple's iMessage PQ3, IETF-standardized MLS) — the identity/crypto-agility theme from the Netflix Enigma talk playing out at the protocol-design layer.
  • What: Bundled Authenticated Key Exchange (AIST/PQShield) formally shows Signal's X3DH and PQXDH don't achieve "optimal" security under a new unified model, and introduces RingXKEM, a fully post-quantum handshake that does. A companion paper does the same for deniability guarantees specifically, building an efficient deniable ring-signature scheme from NIST-standardized Falcon. A third paper machine-verifies Apple's iMessage PQ3 protocol in the TAMARIN prover, including previously-thought-infeasible unbounded-loop ratchet analysis. A fourth explores more efficient post-quantum authentication modes for IETF-standardized MLS group messaging, trading some security for up to 75x lower post-quantum communication overhead. (from abstract only)
  • How: Formal/symbolic verification (TAMARIN) and unified concrete-security models applied to already-deployed or standardized PQ messaging handshakes, rather than proposing yet another new protocol from scratch. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for anyone implementing or evaluating post-quantum secure messaging; directly relevant given Signal, Apple, and IETF (MLS) are all production deployments, not research prototypes.

quantum-safe encryption

items.title: Red Bleed: A Pragmatic Near-Infrared Presentation Attack on Facial Biometric Authentication Systems
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Wildcard pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Bowen Hu, Kuo Wang, and Chip Hong Chang, Nanyang Technological University — Wildcard

Video

  • Why: A practical, sub-$400 hardware attack defeating a widely-deployed commercial biometric authentication system (Windows Hello, confirmed by Microsoft's own security response center) — a concrete demonstration that "commercial-off-the-shelf NIR biometric = secure" is no longer a safe assumption.
  • What: Red Bleed, a presentation attack against near-infrared (NIR) facial biometric authentication (e.g., Windows Hello, Apple Face ID) using a custom-built consumer LCD display costing under $400, converting ordinary visible-light face images/video into convincing NIR spoofs. Confirmed against a commercial Windows Hello module with a CVE scheduled for disclosure. (from abstract only)
  • How: A generative framework (VAE-based) converts RGB/visible-spectrum face images or video into the NIR domain, combined with face-swapping, so attackers can use easily-obtainable RGB material (social media photos, video calls) rather than needing rare NIR footage of the target. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: NIR-based facial biometric authentication specifically (a widely deployed modality); a hardware/software technique that generalizes to any NIR liveness-detection system relying on the assumption that commodity displays can't emit convincing NIR.

authentication vulnerability-management offensive-security

items.title: Robustifying ML-powered Network Classifiers with PANTS
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Minhao Jin and Maria Apostolaki, Princeton University — Core

  • Why: ML-based traffic classification is increasingly load-bearing for resource allocation and intrusion detection in cloud-native networking, and this is a practical, white-box framework for finding and fixing adversarial blind spots in exactly that class of system.
  • What: PANTS, a white-box framework combining adversarial ML with SMT solvers to generate realizable adversarial inputs against ML-based network traffic classifiers (MNCs), plus an iterative adversarial-training process that hardens MNCs against them. Outperforms prior baselines (Amoeba, BAP) by 70%–2x in finding adversarial inputs and improves target-model robustness by 52.7% without sacrificing accuracy. (from abstract only)
  • How: Integrates SMT solving to handle MNC-specific challenges — non-differentiable components like traffic engineering, and semantic/reliability constraints on realizable inputs — that block direct use of standard gradient-based adversarial ML methods. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for network operators deploying ML-based traffic classification (intrusion detection, resource allocation); a practical robustness-testing and hardening tool, not just an attack demonstration.

ml-for-networking anomaly-detection testing

items.title: S/MINE: Collecting and Analyzing S/MIME Certificates at Scale
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Gurur Öndarö et al., Münster University of Applied Sciences; Fraunhofer SIT / ATHENE — Adjacent

  • Why: The first broad empirical look at S/MIME's real-world PKI health (41M+ certificates), complementing the Verdict/X.509DoS/Trust-Agility picks above with a specific-but-large PKI ecosystem case study.
  • What: Analysis of 41M+ real-world S/MIME certificates collected from public LDAP address books, finding the trust-chain and cryptographic health of the S/MIME PKI is generally improving (weak keys expiring, weak algorithms phasing out) but many certificates are issued by non-publicly-trusted CAs, and RFCs/clients should be more stringent about what counts as a valid S/MIME cert. (from abstract only)
  • How: Large-scale collection and trust-chain construction from public LDAP directories, cross-referenced against CA/Browser Forum S/MIME Baseline Requirements. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General email security / S/MIME PKI ecosystem health; most directly useful to CAs and email client implementers.

pki email-security measurement

items.title: STEK Sharing is Not Caring: Bypassing TLS Authentication in Web Servers Using Session Tickets
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Sven Hebrok et al., Paderborn University — Core

  • Why: A concrete, large-scale-confirmed TLS authentication bypass in virtual hosting — exactly the multi-tenant TLS-termination pattern common in cloud/CDN infrastructure — affecting Apache, nginx, (Open)LiteSpeed, and Caddy, plus real providers including Fastly.
  • What: Session ticket confusion vulnerabilities in TLS session resumption under virtual hosting, where a shared Session Ticket Encryption Key (STEK) across virtual hosts on one physical server breaks isolation, enabling bypass of client and server authentication. All four tested server implementations were vulnerable to client-auth bypass; a large-scale scan found six clusters of providers vulnerable to server-auth bypass. (from abstract only)
  • How: Exploits inconsistent STEK handling across virtual hosts sharing one physical server during TLS session resumption to confuse which host a resumed session actually authenticates. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any TLS termination point serving multiple virtual hosts/tenants from shared infrastructure with session-ticket resumption enabled — a direct operational risk for multi-tenant edge/CDN/load-balancer deployments.

tls vulnerability-management

items.title: Towards Internet-Based State Learning of TLS State Machines
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Adjacent pick 13–15 August 2025

Marcel Maehren et al., Ruhr University Bochum; Paderborn University — Adjacent

  • Why: Extends TLS state-machine learning (previously only usable in controlled local environments) to work across the real, noisy Internet at scale — a methodology advance more than a single vulnerability finding, though it did surface a real Citrix NetScaler integrity bug and new CBC padding oracles.
  • What: The first large-scale (7,337 domains, 1,304 extracted models) study of TLS implementation state machines learned directly over the Internet, handling jitter, load balancers, and non-determinism that previously confined this technique to lab settings. Found a handshake transcript integrity vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler and new CBC padding oracle vulnerabilities. (from abstract only)
  • How: Extends Mealy-machine state-learning techniques with new handling for large protocol alphabets and automated analysis of the resulting automata, plus support for session resumption, renegotiation, and CBC padding-oracle-relevant features previously excluded. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General TLS implementation testing methodology; directly useful to anyone auditing TLS stacks at scale rather than one implementation at a time.

tls testing measurement

items.title: Towards Practical, End-to-End Formally Verified X.509 Certificate Validators (Verdict)
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Zhengyao Lin et al., Carnegie Mellon University; Northeastern University — Core

  • Why: X.509 validation bugs have a long history of real security vulnerabilities precisely because the standards are ambiguous and every validator deviates idiosyncratically — this is the first end-to-end formally verified validator, proven to match Chrome/Firefox/OpenSSL's actual (not just documented) behavior at scale.
  • What: Verdict, a formally verified X.509 certificate validator (parsing, path building, path validation) with customizable, formally-specified validation policies compiled to efficient Rust code; validated against Chrome, Firefox, and OpenSSL policies on over ten million real Certificate Transparency certificates. (from abstract only)
  • How: Validation policy is specified in first-order logic; a proof-producing compiler generates Rust code proven to conform to a subset of RFC requirements, and Verdict is shown to match each baseline's actual behavior and performance. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General; directly relevant to anyone building or auditing a TLS/PKI stack who wants provable conformance rather than "matches OpenSSL's quirks by accident."

pki testing

items.title: Trust Agility in an Era of Transient Ties: Rethinking TLS Trust in a Rapidly Evolving Ecosystem
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Hoss Shafagh, Netflix (Enigma track) — Core

Video

  • Why: A practitioner-level look at the most consequential near-term shift in the Web PKI — root programs shortening server certificate lifetimes to a maximum of 47 days by 2029 — from someone who runs PKI and workload-identity infrastructure at Netflix scale, not a standards document.
  • What: An argument for "trust agility" — the ability to rapidly and securely update trust relationships as certificate authorities, cryptographic standards, and threat models evolve — as the operational response to shortening cert lifetimes, slower-upgrading consumer devices, and growing non-browser (machine-to-machine, workload identity) use cases that fall outside traditional browser trust models. (from abstract only)
  • How: Draws on real-world PKI operations at Netflix to describe automation and lifecycle-aware certificate management strategies across diverse endpoints, including preparing for post-quantum cryptographic transitions. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: Anyone operating PKI/TLS infrastructure at scale, workload-identity systems, or IoT/embedded fleets with slow upgrade cycles; general but grounded in a large-scale production environment.

pki tls

items.title: Universal Cross-app Attacks: Exploiting and Securing OAuth 2.0 in Integration Platforms
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Kaixuan Luo et al., The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Samsung Research America — Core

Video

  • Why: A platform-wide OAuth account-linking design flaw affecting Microsoft, Google, and Amazon integration platforms — a concrete, high-severity (CVSS 9.6) example of exactly the kind of OAuth/identity-integration failure that matters at the architecture level, not the implementation level.
  • What: Two new attacks — Cross-app OAuth Account Takeover (COAT) and Request Forgery (CORF) — exploiting the lack of app differentiation in multi-app OAuth account-linking on integration platforms (Workflow Automation, Virtual Assistants, Smart Homes). 11 of 18 tested platforms were vulnerable to COAT and 5 to CORF. (from abstract only)
  • How: Built COVScan, a semi-automated black-box tool that profiles OAuth designs across platforms to find cross-app vulnerabilities; a victim risks account takeover simply by linking any single malicious app, or even clicking a crafted link. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any platform supporting third-party app marketplaces with OAuth-based account linking; the architectural lesson (differentiate apps, not just users, in the OAuth trust model) generalizes beyond the specific platforms tested.

authorization identity vulnerability-management

items.title: X.509DoS: Exploiting and Detecting Denial-of-Service Vulnerabilities in Cryptographic Libraries Using Crafted X.509 Certificates
items.text:
USENIX Security '25 (34th USENIX Security Symposium) digest Program Core pick 13–15 August 2025

Recording

Bing Shi et al., Alibaba Group; Luyi Xing, Indiana University Bloomington — Core

Video

  • Why: A systematic study of an underexplored class of cryptographic-library vulnerability — availability, not confidentiality/integrity — finding 18 new and 12 previously known CVEs across seven mainstream crypto libraries, all reachable via crafted certificates rather than exotic inputs.
  • What: X.509DoS, a class of denial-of-service attacks against cryptographic library implementations, launched via specially crafted X.509 certificates; a tool for rapidly generating such certificates and detecting the underlying DoS vulnerabilities. (from abstract only)
  • How: Systematically probes implementations handling X.509 certificates for availability-impacting bugs, showing that spec/standard compliance alone does not guarantee resistance to resource-exhaustion attacks. (from abstract only)
  • Where applicable: General for any service parsing/validating X.509 certificates from untrusted input (TLS servers, mTLS endpoints); the finding that standards-compliance ≠ DoS-safety generalizes beyond the seven libraries tested.

pki ddos vulnerability-management

items.title: A Guide to Open PON Environment
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract

Radosław Ziemba, Piotr Golubski

  • Why: Access-network PON is outside the PM's DC/cloud core, but this is a genuinely interesting anti-lock-in technique: an ONT that adapts itself to whichever OLT it faces. Interoperability-vs-vendor-control fights are universal across networking domains, and the access network is currently the most live one.
  • What: How operators escape OLT-vendor lock-in using multi-vendor HALNy Networks terminals with an "Adaptive OMCI Stack" — plug-and-play ONTs that automatically discover and adapt to a range of OLTs (Huawei, ZTE, Nokia) without firmware changes — plus cloud management via OpenOLT.com and Smart WiFi dashboards, with claimed benefits of fewer truck rolls and lower OPEX (from abstract only).
  • How: The ONT detects the OLT's management dialect and adapts its OMCI behaviour — inverting the usual model where the OLT vendor whitelists terminals — with remote troubleshooting and optimisation via cloud dashboards.
  • Where applicable: GPON/XGS-PON access operators. Caveat: the Adaptive OMCI Stack is a specific vendor's (HALNy) feature and the session is effectively vendor-flavoured, so apply pitch-grade skepticism to the interoperability claims; the open-interoperable-access-hardware direction is the signal worth taking away.

optics open-source

items.title: ASPA
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Core pick 21–23 April 2026

Massimiliano Stucchi

  • Why: ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization) is the newest piece of the RPKI puzzle and targets exactly the gap left by ROAs and BGPsec: route leaks (invalid AS paths) rather than misorigination. If the PM's organisation runs BGP with upstreams, this is the next deployment decision after ROV.
  • What: No abstract is provided in the program or on the session page — content cannot be confirmed. Judging from title, speaker, and the adjacent routing-security session, expect an introduction to ASPA: what the objects are, what attacks they address, and the current state of implementation and adoption. Treat this write-up's mechanism description as background, not as confirmed talk content.
  • How: (Mechanism background.) An ASPA is an RPKI-signed object in which a customer AS lists its authorized transit providers. Relying parties use these provider sets to verify AS-path plausibility — a route announced to an unauthorized upstream is flagged as a leak — without requiring the full cryptographic path signing of BGPsec, so it is deployable incrementally.
  • Where applicable: Any AS with upstream providers; verification value grows with ecosystem adoption (RPKI relying parties, IXP route servers). Caveat: with no abstract, the talk's actual depth and specifics are unknown — check the recording if it matters.

bgp network-security

items.title: Certificate Transparency: Running Static CT Logs
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Core pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract

Pim van Pelt - IPng Networks

  • Why: CT is the audit layer that makes misissued TLS certificates detectable — core trust/identity infrastructure, and this is a rare operational talk about running it. The PM gets both an architecture update (the new Static-CT log design) and a production postmortem-style account from a small operator doing ecosystem-critical work.
  • What: The hands-on experience of IPng Networks operating four production CT logs (Rennet, Lipase, Gouda, Halloumi) using Sunlight and TesseraCT — two open-source implementations of the Static CT protocol — covering technical setup, operational lessons learned, and the role of community-run logs in Internet security (from abstract only).
  • How: Static-CT logs replace the classic RFC 6962 continuously-updating Merkle log with a pre-populated, shardable, statically-servable structure; the talk walks deploying the two open-source implementations and the ongoing operational burden of keeping production logs healthy.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to anyone operating or auditing certificate-trust infrastructure; both implementations are open source, and the story proves a small community operator can run production-grade trust infrastructure — not a hyperscaler-only or org-specific result.

pki tls

items.title: DNS Resolution from Operators in South Africa
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Wildcard pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract Recording

Yazid Akanho

Video

  • Why: Included as a flagged gamble. The only content signal is the track title — "Thirty Years, A Few DNS Queries and Way Too Many Metrics" — which suggests a metrics-heavy, operator-perspective retrospective on DNS resolution. Measurement practice from a regional operator community is the kind of thing worth a skim even when it isn't on the core beat.
  • What: Unknown — no abstract is provided in the program or on the session page. Based on title and track alone, expect an operator-perspective, data/metrics-driven look at DNS resolution in South Africa rather than a technique talk.
  • How: Unknown; nothing in the program or session page describes the approach.
  • Where applicable: South African operator context. Given the missing abstract, this pick stands or falls on the delivered content — check the recording before investing time.

dns measurement

items.title: From Light to Leverage
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract Recording

Byren Meinjes, Brett van Rooyen - NEC XON | Pre-Sales Consultant

Video

  • Why: For a PM in optical/WAN networking, this is less about new physics and more about packaging: how a provider turns WDM from a bespoke engineering discipline into a productised 100G/400G enterprise service. The product-model framing is directly relevant to product strategy even if the optics is familiar.
  • What: The Managed Optical Fibre Network (MOFN) model — a WDM-based service framework that lets operators productise optical networking, extend fibre asset life, and deliver high-capacity connectivity to enterprise customers who lack in-house optical expertise, illustrated with real-world use cases and deployment models (from abstract only).
  • How: WDM layered as a managed-service framework over fibre already in the ground: the provider absorbs the optical transmission engineering, and enterprises consume native 100G/400G connectivity for cloud and AI platforms without bespoke design per circuit.
  • Where applicable: Aimed at service providers selling high-capacity connectivity to enterprises — the demand signal (enterprises moving past 1G/10G, AI/cloud workloads) is real and broadly applicable, but MOFN itself is a vendor's service model (NEC XON pre-sales presenting), so treat the framework partly as a services pitch.

optics capacity-planning

items.title: gNMIc — On Your Marks, GET / SET / Subscribe / Collect
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract

Nardus le Roux - Nokia | IP Consulting Systems Engineer

  • Why: The SNMP-polling-to-streaming-telemetry shift is the network-ops equivalent of a transition the cloud-native world already made; this session covers a concrete, open-source tool an operator can deploy this quarter.
  • What: An introduction to gNMIc — a scalable gNMI collector with full protocol support (GET / SET / Subscribe / Collect) — and how it delivers continuous visibility into network state, moving beyond SNMP-based monitoring toward a data-rich operational model (from abstract only).
  • How: Devices expose state via gNMI Subscribe RPCs; gNMIc collects, aggregates, and feeds the stream into downstream operational systems, replacing periodic polling with event-driven telemetry.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any environment with gNMI-capable devices (most modern router/switch OSes) — multi-vendor and not org-specific. The speaker is Nokia consulting staff, but gNMIc is a community open-source project, so this reads as tool adoption rather than a product pitch.

telemetry open-source automation

items.title: IPv6 - Measuring Uptake
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Adjacent pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract

Jaco Kroon

  • Why: The PM already runs IPv6; the value here is measurement methodology and an honest data read on where South Africa and the continent actually stand — useful input for regional capacity/feature planning, and part of this program's most persistent theme (an entire track is named "Please Just Deploy IPv6").
  • What: Why continued IPv6 migration matters, the methodologies available for tracking adoption across networks and regions, and what the data reveals about IPv6 uptake in South Africa and the broader African continent (from abstract only).
  • How: Survey of adoption-measurement approaches — content-side user statistics, routing-table/BGP visibility, per-network enablement metrics — plus a regional read-out; the abstract does not specify which methods are used.
  • Where applicable: Regional focus (South Africa/Africa), but the methodology generalises to any operator or product with a regional footprint; worth skimming for the measurement framework more than the conclusion.

ipv6 measurement

items.title: Securing Internet Routing - The Puzzle Pieces
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Core pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract

Tashi Phuntsho

  • Why: Route leaks and hijacks are the systemic risk of the interdomain routing system, and this is the program's main survey of the defense stack — squarely in the intersection of network security and BGP internals. Worth the PM's time as a structured view of how the pieces (origin validation, path validation, filtering) do and don't compose.
  • What: A review of the full routing-security toolkit — RPKI, Route Origin Authorisations (ROAs), BGPsec, IRR-based filtering, and emerging proposals — examining how the pieces fit together, where each excels, and the practical and organisational challenges blocking universal adoption (from abstract only).
  • How: Mechanism-by-mechanism comparison: cryptographic origin validation via RPKI/ROAs against misorigination, IRR route objects for prefix filtering at AS boundaries, BGPsec for AS-path integrity, and newer proposals for leak detection — against a frank accounting of why adoption remains partial despite mature tooling.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any network announcing or accepting BGP routes; vendor-neutral and global in scope despite the regional venue. A 30-minute slot, so expect survey depth rather than new results. Pairs naturally with the ASPA session immediately before it.

items.title: Submarine Overland Cable Technology
items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Core pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract

Nic Breytenbach - Seacom (Senior Transmission Architect), Afrim Beka - Nokia | Director of Subsea Networks Solutions

  • Why: Long-haul optical transport is squarely in the PM's physical-networking core (WAN interconnect, optics). The premise — carrying subsea cable engineering onto terrestrial routes — speaks to two live problems: extending resilient capacity into remote and climate-challenged regions, and meeting AI/ML-driven traffic growth.
  • What: How subsea transmission techniques — spanning thousands of kilometres without regeneration and long distances without amplification — can be applied as powerful solutions for extending resilient, high-performance connectivity into terrestrial networks (from abstract only).
  • How: Mechanism detail is thin in the abstract; expect coherent long-reach optics and cable-system design that minimises regeneration/amplification sites, presented as a new approach for terrestrial builds serving both basic connectivity and AI/ML demand.
  • Where applicable: Long-haul subsea and terrestrial transport builds; most relevant where routes are long and terrain/climate makes frequent regeneration sites costly — an Africa-flavoured problem, but the engineering transfers to any long-haul WAN build. Vendor-anchored session (Nokia subsea solutions), jointly presented with Seacom's transmission architect — expect some product positioning around the technique.

items.text:
ZANOG@iWeek 2026 digest Program Core pick 21–23 April 2026

Abstract

Andy Chadwick - Shadowserver Foundation | Director for Africa

  • Why: Free, immediately adoptable threat intelligence — the highest "tooling others can adopt" value in the security track, with a regional Southern Africa lens the PM won't get from global feeds.
  • What: An introduction to what the Shadowserver Foundation does and why its cyber threat intelligence benefits network operators and all network owners, at no cost (from abstract only). Expect an overview session rather than deep technique — the digest value is knowing the resource and the regional picture, not new methods.
  • How: (Mechanism background.) Shadowserver aggregates internet-wide scanning and sinkhole/honeypot telemetry into free per-network reports — exposed vulnerable services, malware callbacks, etc. — that any network owner can request and act on.
  • Where applicable: Any network, any size, no product purchase (non-profit). The service is global even though this talk's framing is Southern Africa.
